

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Affordable housing
======================================================================

{{short description|Housing affordable to those with a median household income}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=November 2020}}
{{Globalise|article|the United States|date=September 2025}}
{{Living spaces}}
'''Affordable housing''' is housing which is deemed affordable to those with a [[household income]] at or below the [[median household income|median]], as rated by the [[Government|national government]] or a local government by a recognized [[housing affordability index]].<ref name="Bhatta, Basudeb 2010 23">{{cite book |author=Bhatta, Basudeb |title=Analysis of Urban Growth and Sprawl from Remote Sensing Data |publisher=Springer |year=2010 |isbn=978-3-642-05298-9 |series=Advances in Geographic Information Science |page=23}}</ref> Most of the literature on affordable housing refers to [[mortgage loan|mortgages]] and a number of forms that exist along a continuum – from emergency [[homeless shelter]]s, to [[transitional housing]], to non-market [[Rental housing|rental]] (also known as [[Social housing|social]] or [[subsidized housing]]), to formal and informal rental, indigenous housing, and ending with affordable home ownership.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.calgary.ca/CSPS/CNS/Documents/homelessness/ff-01_definition_affordable_housing.pdf | title=Definition Affordable Housing | access-date=12 December 2011 | archive-date=25 January 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200125124353/http://www.calgary.ca/CSPS/CNS/Documents/homelessness/ff-01_definition_affordable_housing.pdf }}</ref><ref>[http://www.cnhed.org/shared/layouts/singleblock.jsp?_event=view&_id=120130_U127242__194346 CNHED] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120204163809/http://www.cnhed.org/shared/layouts/singleblock.jsp?_event=view&_id=120130_U127242__194346 |date=4 February 2012 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.qahc.asn.au/images2/website/affordabilitychart.pdf | title=Queensland Affordable Housing Consortium &#91;QAHC&#93;, Australia | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426044456/http://www.qahc.asn.au/images2/website/affordabilitychart.pdf | archive-date=26 April 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite conference
 |url         = http://www.actu.org.au/Images/Dynamic/attachments/5552/ACTU-Housing-Options-jul07.pdf
 |title       = Affordable Housing: Issues, Principles and Policy Options.
 |publisher   = Australian Council of Trade Unions
 |conference  = Affordable Housing Summit
 |location    = Canberra, Australia
 |date        = July 2007
 |access-date  = 8 December 2011
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20120526195606/http://www.actu.org.au/Images/Dynamic/attachments/5552/ACTU-Housing-Options-jul07.pdf
 |archive-date = 26 May 2012}}
</ref> Demand for affordable housing is generally associated with a decrease in housing affordability, such as rent increases, in addition to increased homelessness.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-08-22 |title=How Housing Costs Drive Levels of Homelessness |url=https://www.pewtrusts.org/en/research-and-analysis/articles/2023/08/22/how-housing-costs-drive-levels-of-homelessness |access-date=2024-10-04 |website=pew.org |language=en}}</ref>

Housing choice is a response to a complex set of economic, social, and psychological impulses.<ref name="Hulchanski, J. David 1995">{{cite journal|author = Hulchanski, J. David|url = http://www.urbancenter.utoronto.ca/pdfs/researchassociates/Hulchanski_Concept-H-Affd_H.pdf|title = The Concept of Housing Affordability: Six Contemporary Uses of the Expenditure to Income Ratio|journal = Housing Studies|date = October 1995|volume = 10|issue = 4|access-date = 8 December 2011|doi = 10.1080/02673039508720833|archive-date = 27 April 2012|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20120427113725/http://www.urbancenter.utoronto.ca/pdfs/researchassociates/Hulchanski_Concept-H-Affd_H.pdf}}</ref> For example, some households may choose to spend more on housing because they feel they can afford to, while others may not have a choice.<ref>{{cite journal
|url=http://www.statcan.gc.ca/pub/75-001-x/11106/9519-eng.htm
|title=Measuring housing affordability
|author=Luffman, Jacqueline
|journal=Perspectives on Labour and Income
|date=November 2006
|volume=7
|issue=11
|pages=16–25
|publisher=Statistics Canada
}}</ref>

Increases in any housing supply (whether affordable housing or market-rate housing) leads to increased housing affordability across all segments of the housing markets.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mast |first=Evan |date=2023 |title=JUE Insight: The effect of new market-rate housing construction on the low-income housing market |journal=Journal of Urban Economics |volume=133 |article-number=103383 |doi=10.1016/j.jue.2021.103383 |issn=0094-1190}}</ref><ref name=":05">{{Cite journal |last=Mense |first=Andreas |date=2025 |title=The Impact of New Housing Supply on the Distribution of Rents |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/733977 |journal=Journal of Political Economy Macroeconomics |volume=3 |issue=1 |pages=1–42 |doi=10.1086/733977 |issn=2832-9341|hdl=10419/224569 |hdl-access=free |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Definition and measurement==
There are several means of defining and measuring affordable housing. The definition and measurement may change in different nations, cities, or for specific policy goals.<ref>{{Cite web|title=WHO {{!}} Practical measurement of affordability: an application to medicines|url=https://www.who.int/bulletin/volumes/90/3/10-084087/en/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150129050637/http://www.who.int/bulletin/volumes/90/3/10-084087/en/|archive-date=29 January 2015|access-date=2021-03-28|website=WHO}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Housing conditions – OECD|url=http://www.oecd.org/housing/data/affordable-housing-database/housing-conditions.htm|access-date=2021-03-28|website=www.oecd.org|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Is There a Better Way to Measure Housing Affordability? {{!}} Joint Center for Housing Studies|url=https://www.jchs.harvard.edu/blog/is-there-a-better-way-to-measure-housing-affordability|access-date=2021-03-28|website=www.jchs.harvard.edu|date=26 September 2018 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Defining Housing Affordability {{!}} HUD USER|url=https://www.huduser.gov/portal/pdredge/pdr-edge-featd-article-081417.html|access-date=2021-03-28|website=www.huduser.gov|archive-date=29 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210329193942/https://www.huduser.gov/portal/pdredge/pdr-edge-featd-article-081417.html}}</ref>

=== Definitions ===
The definition of affordable housing may change depending on the country and context. For example, in Australia, the National Affordable Housing Summit Group developed their definition of affordable housing as housing that is "...reasonably adequate in standard and location for lower or middle income households and does not cost so much that a household is unlikely to be able to meet other basic needs on a sustainable basis."<ref name="qahc.asn.au">[http://www.qahc.asn.au/modules/tinyd0/index.php?id=8 "Definition: Affordable Housing"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426044505/http://www.qahc.asn.au/modules/tinyd0/index.php?id=8|date=26 April 2012}}, ''Queensland Affordable Housing Consortium'', Australia</ref> [[Affordable housing in the United Kingdom]] includes "social rented and intermediate housing, provided to specified eligible households whose needs are not met by the market."<ref>{{cite web |date=29 November 2009 |title=Good practice and guidance, Reports and summaries |url=http://www.communities.gov.uk/housing/housingresearch/housingstatistics/definitiongeneral/ |access-date=8 December 2011 |number=6HC04260}} 
</ref> 

In some US contexts, affordable housing may only mean subsidized or public housing whereas in other cases it may include naturally occurring affordable housing or "affordable" by different incomes levels from no income households to moderate income but cost-burdened households.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Preserving the largest and most at-risk supply of affordable housing {{!}} McKinsey |url=https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/public-and-social-sector/our-insights/preserving-the-largest-and-most-at-risk-supply-of-affordable-housing |access-date=2022-03-26 |website=www.mckinsey.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Town of Chapel Hill |date=October 2017 |title=Affordable Housing Glossary of Terms |url=https://www.townofchapelhill.org/Home/ShowDocument?id=38267 |website=Town of Chapel Hill}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=State of Oregon |date=May 1, 2021 |title=Oregon Transit and Housing Study Glossary of Terms |url=https://www.oregon.gov/odot/Planning/Documents/ODOT%20THS%20Glossary%20Final-May21.pdf |website=State of Oregon }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

===Median house price to income ratio===
{{main|Median multiple}}
The median multiple indicator, recommended by the [[World Bank]] and the United Nations, rates affordability of housing by dividing the median house price by gross (before tax) annual median household income).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Zheng |first=Dawei |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-Nc_CQAAQBAJ&dq=The+%22median+multiple%22+indicator%2C+recommended+by+the+World+Bank+and+the+United+Nations%2C+rates+affordability+of+housing+by+dividing+the+median+house+price+by+gross+%28before+tax%29+annual+median+household+income%29.&pg=PA377 |title=Information Engineering and Education Science: Proceedings of the International Conference on Information Engineering and Education Science (ICIEES 2014), Tianjin, China, 12-13 June, 2014 |date=2015-04-30 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-315-75227-3 |language=en}}</ref>

<blockquote>A common measure of community-wide affordability is the number of homes that a household with a certain percentage of [[median household income|median income]] can afford. For example, in a perfectly balanced housing market, the median household (the wealthier half of households) could officially afford the median housing option, while those poorer than the median income could not afford the median home. 50% affordability for the median home indicates a balanced market.<ref name="Bhatta, Basudeb 2010 23"/></blockquote>

Some countries look at those living in [[relative poverty]], which is usually defined as making less than 60% of the [[median household income]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is poverty? |url=https://trustforlondon.org.uk/news/what-is-poverty/ |access-date=2024-07-29 |website=Trust for London |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-03-21 |title=Relative income poverty {{!}} GOV.WALES |url=https://www.gov.wales/relative-income-poverty |access-date=2024-07-29 |website=www.gov.wales |language=en}}</ref> In their policy reports, they consider the presence or absence of housing for people making 60% of the median income.

===Housing costs as percentage of gross income===
Determining housing affordability is complex and the commonly used housing-expenditure-to-income-ratio tool has been challenged. In the United States<ref>{{cite web
 |title       = Affordable Housing and Homelessness
 |author1= Washington State Labor Council (AFL-CIO)
 |year        = 2009
 |url         = http://www.wslc.org/legis/afford.htm
 |access-date  = 8 December 2011
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20120208113159/http://www.wslc.org/legis/afford.htm
 |archive-date = 8 February 2012
}}</ref> and Canada,<ref name="Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation">{{cite web
 |url=http://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/en/corp/faq/faq_002.cfm 
 |format=.cfm 
 |title=Affordable Housing: What is the common definition of affordability? 
 |author1=Canada Mortgage 
 |author2=Housing Corporation 
 |date=28 September 2011 
 |publisher=Government of Canada 
 |access-date=8 December 2011 
 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070507183022/http://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/en/corp/faq/faq_002.cfm 
 |archive-date=7 May 2007
}}</ref> a commonly accepted guideline for housing affordability is a housing cost, including utilities, that does not exceed 30% of a household's [[gross income]].<ref>{{cite book |author1=Christine C. Cook |author2=Marilyn J. Bruin |author3=Becky L. Yust |editor1-last=Carswell |editor1-first=Andrew T. |editor2-last=Anacker |editor2-first=Katrin B. |editor3-last=Tremblay |editor3-first=Kenneth R. |editor4-last=Kirby |editor4-first=Sarah D. |title=Introduction to Housing |date=2018 |publisher=University of Georgia Press |location=Athens, Georgia |isbn=978-0-8203-4968-8 |page=171 |edition=2nd |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=AnhUDwAAQBAJ&dq=housing+percent+of+gross+income+utilities+inpublisher:university+inpublisher:press&pg=PA171 |access-date=August 26, 2021 |chapter=Chapter 10. Housing Affordability}}</ref> Some definitions include maintenance costs as part of housing costs.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wheeler |first1=Stephen M. |last2=Rosan |first2=Christina D. |title=Reimagining Sustainable Cities: Strategies for Designing Greener, Healthier, More Equitable Communities |date=2021 |publisher=University of California Press |location=Oakland, California |isbn=978-0-520-38121-6 |page=83 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7bY-EAAAQBAJ&dq=housing+percent+of+gross+income+utilities+inpublisher%3Auniversity+inpublisher%3Apress&pg=PA83 |access-date=August 26, 2021}}</ref> Canada, for example, switched to a 25% rule from a 20% rule in the 1950s. In the 1980s this was replaced by a 30% rule.<ref name="Hulchanski, J. David 1995" /> India uses a 40% rule. Some ways to achieve these ratios are to live with [[roommate]]s and split rent or to have a cheap [[lease-by-room]] agreement.

===Housing affordability index approaches ===
{{Main|Housing affordability index|l1 = Housing Affordability Index}}

There are several types of housing affordability indexes that take a number of factors, not just income, into account when measuring housing affordability.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Econsult Corporation and Penn Institute for Urban Research|date=February 2012|title=REVIEW OF THE CENTER FOR NEIGHBORHOOD TECHNOLOGY'S HOUSING AND TRANSPORTATION AFFORDABILITY INDEX|url=https://www.hud.gov/sites/documents/HTA-INDEX.PDF|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190408083420/https://www.hud.gov/sites/documents/HTA-INDEX.PDF|archive-date=8 April 2019|website=HUD.GOV}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Urban Institute.|title=Housing Affordability Local and National Perspectives|url=https://www.urban.org/sites/default/files/publication/97496/housing_affordability_local_and_national_perspectives_1.pdf|website=Urban Institute}}</ref>

The American [[National Association of Realtors]] and other groups measure market housing through a housing affordability index which measures whether or not a typical family could qualify for a mortgage loan on a typical home. This index calculates affordability based on the national median-priced single family home, the typical family median income, and the prevailing mortgage interest rate to determine if the median income family can qualify for a mortgage on a typical home.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Methodology|url=https://www.nar.realtor/research-and-statistics/housing-statistics/housing-affordability-index/methodology|access-date=2021-03-28|website=www.nar.realtor|date=28 December 2011 |language=en}}</ref> To interpret the indices, a value of 100 means that a family with the median income has exactly enough income to qualify for a mortgage on a median-priced home.<ref name=":0" /> An index over 100 signifies that family earning the median income has more than enough income for a mortgage loan on the median-priced home (assuming they have a 20 percent down payment).<ref name=":0" /> For example, a composite HAI of 120.0 means a family earning the median family income has 120% of the income necessary to qualify for a conventional loan covering 80 percent of a median-priced existing single-family home.<ref name=":0" /> An increase in the HAI shows that this family is more able to afford the median-priced home.<ref name=":0" />

The [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) developed a housing affordability index that attempts to capture the total cost of housing by several factors include employment accessibility, amenities, transportation costs and transit access, quality of schools, etc. In computing the index the obvious cost of rents and mortgage payments are modified by the hidden costs of those choices.<ref>{{cite report|url=http://web.mit.edu/cre/research/hai/aff-index.html|format=.html|title=Measuring Housing Affordability|work=The HAI Affordable Housing Index|publisher=MIT Center for Real Estate|access-date=13 December 2011}}</ref> Other groups have also created amenity based housing affordability indexes.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Fisher|first1=Lynn M.|last2=Pollakowski|first2=Henry O.|last3=Zabel|first3=Jeffrey|date=December 2009|title=Amenity-Based Housing Affordability Indexes|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1111/j.1540-6229.2009.00261.x|journal=Real Estate Economics|language=en|volume=37|issue=4|pages=705–746|doi=10.1111/j.1540-6229.2009.00261.x|s2cid=155007018|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

The [[Center for Neighborhood Technology]] developed the Housing + Transportation (H+T) Affordability Index provides a comprehensive view of affordability that includes both the cost of housing and the cost of transportation at the neighborhood level.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2009-01-01|title=Housing + Transportation Affordability Index|url=https://www.cnt.org/tools/housing-and-transportation-affordability-index|access-date=2021-03-28|website=Center for Neighborhood Technology|language=en}}</ref> CNT notes that the 30% of household income affordability measurementment results in little over half (55%) of U.S. neighborhoods being considered "affordable" for the typical household.<ref name=":1" /> They note that such a measurement fails to take into account transportation costs (such as multiple cars, gas, maintenance), which are usually a household's second-largest expenditure.<ref name=":1" /> When transportation costs are factored into the measurement, the number of affordable neighborhoods nationally drops to 26%, resulting in a net loss of 59,768 neighborhoods that Americans can truly afford.<ref name=":1" /> Per CNT's measurement, people who live in location-efficient neighborhoods that are compact, mixed-use, and have convenient access to jobs, services, transit and amenities tend to have lower transportation costs.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Center for Transit-Oriented Development and Center for Neighborhood Technology|title=The Affordability Index: A New Tool for Measuring the True Affordability of a Housing Choice|url=https://www.brookings.edu/wp-content/uploads/2016/06/20060127_affindex.pdf|website=ReconnectingAmerica.org}}</ref>

===Household income and wealth approaches===
Some analysts believe income is the primary factor{{snd}}not price and availability, that determines housing affordability.<ref>{{cite book
|chapter-url=http://www.uml.edu/centers/cic/Research/Tilly_Research/Housing-Tilly%20chapter-GRBT106-2299G-01-020-037.pdf
|author=Tilly, Chris
|title=The Economic Environment of Housing: Income Inequality and Insecurity
|chapter=10
|date=2 November 2005
|access-date=16 December 2011
|archive-date=7 April 2012
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120407124840/http://www.uml.edu/centers/cic/Research/Tilly_Research/Housing-Tilly%20chapter-GRBT106-2299G-01-020-037.pdf
}}</ref> In a market economy the distribution of income is the key determinant of the quantity and quality of housing obtained. Therefore, understanding affordable housing challenges requires understanding trends and [[Economic inequality#Causes of inequality|disparities in income and wealth]]. Housing is often the single biggest expenditure of low and middle income families. For low and middle income families, their house is also the greatest source of wealth.<ref>{{cite book
|chapter-url=http://www.uml.edu/centers/cic/Research/Tilly_Research/Housing-Tilly%20chapter-GRBT106-2299G-01-020-037.pdf
|author=Tilly, Chris
|title=The Economic Environment of Housing: Income Inequality and Insecurity
|chapter=10
|publisher=Center for Industrial Competitiveness, University of Massachusetts
|location=Lowell, Massachusetts
|date=2 November 2005
|access-date=16 December 2011
|archive-date=7 April 2012
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120407124840/http://www.uml.edu/centers/cic/Research/Tilly_Research/Housing-Tilly%20chapter-GRBT106-2299G-01-020-037.pdf
}}</ref>

Another method of studying affordability looks at the regular hourly wage of full-time workers who are paid only the minimum wage (as set by their local, regional, or national government).<ref>{{Cite web|last=Adamczyk|first=Alicia|date=2020-07-14|title=Minimum wage workers cannot afford rent in any U.S. state|url=https://www.cnbc.com/2020/07/14/minimum-wage-workers-cannot-afford-rent-in-any-us-state.html|access-date=2021-03-28|website=CNBC|language=en}}</ref> This methods attempts to determine if workers at that income can afford adequate housing.

===Differing parameters and limitations in approaches===
Measuring affordable housing is tricky. Different organizations look at different things: some at buying homes, others at renting apartments. Many U.S. studies, for example, only consider the average rent of a two-bedroom apartment, regardless of location or quality. This can make housing look more expensive than it actually is for many people. Additionally, these studies often ignore cheaper options like rooms in houses or illegal conversions, even if they are common. Finally, someone paying off a mortgage might look like they are struggling one month, but be fine the next, further skewing the data. An 2026 opinion poll found 64% of Americans were very concerned about price of housing.<ref name="e413">{{cite web | last1=Daniller | first1=Andrew | last2=Cerda | first2=Andy | last3=Hartig | first3=Hannah | last4=Oliphant | first4=J. Baxter | title=Americans' evaluations of the economy remain negative | publisher=Pew Research Center | date=2026 | url=https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2026/07/23/americans-evaluations-of-the-economy-remain-negative/ | access-date=2026-08-06}}</ref>

==Economics==
[[File:St James Town1.jpg|thumb|Affordable housing, or low income housing, at the [[St. James Town]] neighborhood in [[Toronto|Toronto, Ontario]], Canada]]
{{See also|Urban economics}}

===Factors that affect demand of housing stock===
* demographic changes, increased [[life expectancy]], declining number of people per dwelling, smaller family size, a greater propensity for people to live alone
* young adults delaying forming their own household, changes in desire for home ownership<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.rideforhome.com.au/files/pdf/HousingAffordability.pdf |title=Housing Affordability: and Homelessness|website=www.rideforhome.com.au |access-date=13 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120426051823/http://www.rideforhome.com.au/files/pdf/HousingAffordability.pdf |archive-date=26 April 2012 }}</ref>
* [[Relocation (personal)|relocation]] for example [[urban flight]], [[rural flight]], growing density convergence and regional urbanization
* [[population growth]]<ref name="economist.com">{{cite news |date=26 November 2011 |title=House of horrors, part 2: The bursting of the global housing bubble is only halfway through |newspaper=The Economist |url=https://www.economist.com/finance-and-economics/2013/08/29/house-of-horrors-part-2 |access-date=15 December 2011}}</ref>
* [[net migration rate]] and [[List of sovereign states by immigrant and emigrant population|immigrant population]]<ref name="w888">{{cite journal | last=Sanchis-Guarner | first=Rosa | title=Decomposing the impact of immigration on house prices | journal=Regional Science and Urban Economics | volume=100 | date=2023 | doi=10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2023.103893 | doi-access=free | article-number=103893| bibcode=2023RSUE..100j3893S | hdl=2445/118284 | hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* reduced profitability of other forms of investment as alternatives to [[real estate investing]]{{Citation needed|date=August 2026}}

===Factors that affect supply of housing stock===
* [[real estate development]] rate of housing
* higher gains from unimproved value of land<ref>{{cite web|last1=Smith |first1=Nicholas |last2=Dumieński |first2=Zbigniew |editor-first1=Helen |editor-first2=Charis |editor-last1=Westerman |editor-last2=Palmer |url=https://theconversation.com/a-land-value-tax-could-fix-australasias-housing-crisis-49997|title=A land value tax could fix Australasia's housing crisis|date=9 November 2015 |doi=10.64628/AA.s4fv4ekmn }}</ref>
* availability of housing finance<ref name="André, C. 2010">{{cite report|url=http://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/docserver/download/fulltext/5kmlh5qvz1s4.pdf?expires=1323920702&id=id&accname=guest&checksum=A332B821073ADDF04D35D466588AC744|title=A Bird's Eye View of OECD Housing Markets|author=André, C.|date=28 January 2010|series=OECD Economics Department Working Papers|number=746}}{{Dead link|date=February 2015}}</ref>
* significant taxes, levies and fees by government on new housing
* low interest rates<ref name="André, C. 2010"/>
* mortgage market innovations<ref name="André, C. 2010"/>
* changes in [[planning permission]]s
* land use re[[zoning]]
* changes in [[building code]]s<ref>Listokin, David; Hattis, David B., [http://www.huduser.org/periodicals/cityscpe/vol8num1/ch2.pdf "Building Codes and Housing"], ''Cityscape: A Journal of Policy Development and Research'', Volume 8, Number 1, 2005, U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Policy Development and Research</ref>
* [[impact fee]]s<ref name="d960">{{cite journal | last=Been | first=Vicki | title=Impact Fees and Housing Affordability | journal=Cityscape | publisher=US Department of Housing and Urban Development | volume=8 | issue=1 | year=2005 | issn=1936-007X | jstor=20868573 | pages=139–185 }}</ref>

===Balance between supply and demand===
[[File:Supply-demand-equilibrium.svg|thumb|[[Supply and demand]] curves with price and quantity sold]]
In research, there is an established connection between the supply of housing and the price of housing; housing tends to be more expensive when there is a [[Housing shortage|shortage of housing]] (when the supply does not meet demand).<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-06-05 |title=Housing Affordability & Supply |url=https://www.nar.realtor/research-and-statistics/research-reports/housing-affordability-supply |access-date=2024-04-06 |website=www.nar.realtor |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=US. Housing Supply: Recent Trends and Policy Considerations |url=https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/R/R47617/1 |website=crsreports.congress.gov}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The growing housing supply shortage has created a housing affordability crisis |url=https://www.epi.org/blog/the-growing-housing-supply-shortage-has-created-a-housing-affordability-crisis/ |access-date=2024-04-06 |website=Economic Policy Institute |language=en-US}}</ref> In some countries, the market has been unable to meet the growing demand to supply housing stock at affordable prices. Although demand for affordable housing, particularly rental housing that is affordable for low and middle income earners, has increased, the supply has not.<ref>{{cite web|title=Affordable housing|url=http://www.facs.gov.au/sa/housing/pubs/homelessness/not-for-profithousingsector/Pages/affordable_housing.aspx|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120328070847/http://www.facs.gov.au/sa/housing/pubs/homelessness/not-for-profithousingsector/Pages/affordable_housing.aspx|archive-date=28 March 2012|publisher=Government of Australia}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|date=6 May 2010|title=Housing supply and demand – UK Parliament|url=http://www.parliament.uk/business/publications/research/key-issues-for-the-new-parliament/social-reform/housing-supply-and-demand/|access-date=15 August 2012|publisher=Parliament.uk}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Housing and Urban Policy|url=http://www2.rgu.ac.uk/publicpolicy/introduction/housing.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120717000606/http://www2.rgu.ac.uk/publicpolicy/introduction/housing.htm|archive-date=17 July 2012|access-date=15 August 2012|publisher=.rgu.ac.uk}}</ref><ref name="Mostafa, Anirban 2006 9">{{cite journal|author=Mostafa, Anirban|author2=Wong, Francis K. W.|author3=Hui, Chi Mun Eddie|year=2006|title=Relationship between Housing Affordability and Economic Development in Mainland China – Case of Shanghai|journal=Journal of Urban Planning and Development|volume=132|issue=62|page=9|doi=10.1061/(asce)0733-9488(2006)132:1(62)}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Dunn |first1=Julianne |last2=Brizuela |first2=Isabel |date=2021-09-29 |title=Strong Demand, Limited Supply, and Rising Prices: The Economics of Pandemic-Era Housing |url=https://www.clevelandfed.org/publications/cleveland-fed-district-data-brief/2021/cfddb-20210929-strong-demand-limited-supply-and-rising-prices-the-economics-of-pandemic-era-housing |journal=Cleveland Fed District Data Brief |series=Cleveland Fed District Data Briefs |language=en |issue=20210929 |doi=10.26509/frbc-ddb-20210929|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[YIMBY movement|YIMBYs]] argue building more housing makes housing more affordable.<ref name=Seattle_YIMBYs>{{ cite news | url=http://seattlemag.com/meet-yimbys-seattleites-support-housing-density | title=Meet the YIMBYs, Seattleites in Support of Housing Density - A new movement is saying yes to urban density in all its forms | last=Barnett | first=Erica | work=Seattle Magazine | date=2016-11-01 | access-date=2018-07-05 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161205102620/http://seattlemag.com/meet-yimbys-seattleites-support-housing-density | archive-date=2016-12-05 | url-status=live | quote=Although they span the political spectrum, from far left social-justice activists to hard-core libertarian free marketeers, YIMBYs generally agree that cities should be accessible and affordable for everyone, whether they own a million-dollar mansion or rent a $900-a-month studio, and whether they work as a barista or just moved to Seattle for a new job at Amazon. }}</ref> Potential home buyers are forced to turn to the rental market, which is also under pressure.<ref>{{cite conference
|last1=Yates
|first1=Judith
|author-link1=Judith Yates
|last2=Wulff
|first2=Maryann

</ref> An inadequate supply of affordable housing stock increases demand on the private and social rented sector, and in worse case scenarios, results in increased homelessness rates.<ref name="Schmuecker, Katie 2011">{{cite report|url=http://www.ippr.org/images/media/files/publication/2011/05/Good%20bad%20and%20ugly%20-%20Housing%20demand%202025_1829.pdf|title=The good, the bad and the ugly: Housing demand 2025|author=Schmuecker, Katie|date=March 2011|publisher=Institute for Public Policy Research|access-date=16 December 2011|series=Challenging ideas – Changing policy}}{{dead link|date=January 2018|bot=InternetArchiveBot|fix-attempted=yes}}</ref> [[Homelessness]] rates are correlated with higher rents, especially in areas where rent exceeds 30% of an area's median income.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Research |first=Zillow |date=2018-12-11 |title=Homelessness Rises Faster Where Rent Exceeds a Third of Income |url=https://www.zillow.com/research/homelessness-rent-affordability-22247/ |access-date=2024-04-06 |website=Zillow |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Homelessness and Housing |url=https://www.city-journal.org/article/homelessness-and-housing/ |access-date=2024-04-06 |website=City Journal |language=en}}</ref>

===Factors that affect tenure choices (ex. owner occupier, private rented, social rented)===
* [[Employment rate]]s
** Rising [[unemployment rate]]s increase demand for market rentals, social housing and homelessness.
* Real [[household income]]s
** Household incomes have not kept up with rising housing prices
* Affordability of rents and owner occupation
* [[Interest rate]]s for [[mortgage]]s
** Availability of mortgages
* Levels of confidence in the economy and housing market
** Low confidence decreases demand for owner occupation.<ref name="Schmuecker, Katie 2011" />

===Inequality and housing===
{{See also|Housing inequality}}
A number of researchers argue that a shortage of affordable housing – at least in the US – is caused in part by income inequality.<ref name="Rodda 1994">{{Cite thesis |title=Rich Man, Poor Renter: A Study of the Relationship Between the Income Distribution and Low Cost Rental Housing |first=David T. |last=Rodda |date=1994 |publisher=Harvard University |page=148 |oclc=34635540 }}</ref><ref name="Vigdor 2002">{{cite journal|author= Vigdor, Jacob|title= Does Gentrification Harm the Poor? |journal= Brookings-Wharton Papers on Urban Affairs |volume= 2002 |pages= 133–182 |doi=10.1353/urb.2002.0012 |year= 2002|s2cid= 155028628 }}</ref><ref name="MatlackVigdor2006">{{cite journal |title=Do Rising Tides Lift All Prices? Income Inequality and Housing Affordability |first1=Janna L. |last1=Matlack |first2=Jacob L. |last2=Vigdor |year=2008 |journal=Journal of Housing Economics |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=212–224 |doi=10.1016/j.jhe.2008.06.004 |url=http://www.nber.org/papers/w12331.pdf }}</ref> David Rodda noted that from 1984 and 1991, the number of quality rental units decreased as the demand for higher quality housing increased.<ref name="Rodda 1994" />{{rp|148}} Through [[gentrification]] of older neighbourhoods, for example, in East New York, rental prices increased rapidly as landlords found new residents willing to pay higher market rate for housing and left lower income families without rental units. The [[Ad valorem tax|ad valorem property tax]] policy combined with rising prices made it difficult or impossible for low income residents to keep pace.<ref name=pushedout2009>{{cite report|title=Pushed Out: The Hidden Costs of Gentrification: Displacement and Homelessness |url=http://www.icphusa.org/PDF/reports/ICP%20Report_Pushed%20Out.pdf |year=2009 |publisher=Institute for Children and Poverty |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130806195638/http://www.icphusa.org/PDF/reports/ICP%20Report_Pushed%20Out.pdf |archive-date=6 August 2013 }}</ref>

Lack of affordable housing places a particular burden on local economies. As well, individual consumers are faced with mortgage arrears and excessive debt and therefore cut back on consumption. A combination of high housing costs and high debt levels contributes to a reduction in savings. These factors can lead to decreased investment in sectors that are essential to the long-term growth of the economy.{{Citation needed|date=March 2021}}

The geographic distribution of affordable housing and its respective restrictions provides a disproportionate distribution of benefits to certain economic groups. Research has found that cities are more likely to have zoning restrictions, which effectively limits the expansion of affordable housing units in these areas.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last1=Rodríguez-Pose |first1=Andrés |last2=Storper |first2=Michael |date=February 2020 |title=Housing, urban growth and inequalities: The limits to deregulation and upzoning in reducing economic and spatial inequality |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0042098019859458 |journal=Urban Studies |language=en |volume=57 |issue=2 |pages=223–248 |doi=10.1177/0042098019859458 |bibcode=2020UrbSt..57..223R |s2cid=191923573 |issn=0042-0980|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These zoning restrictions increase in housing prices, forcing the housing developers who create subsidized housing to look towards other options.<ref name=":02" /> Zoning restrictions drive low-income families to live in neighborhoods with reduced opportunities, restricting access to metropolitan economies.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last=Metcalf |first=Gabriel |date=2018-02-01 |title=Sand Castles Before the Tide? Affordable Housing in Expensive Cities |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=59–80 |doi=10.1257/jep.32.1.59 |issn=0895-3309|doi-access=free }}</ref> These patterns of zoning ultimately force the income divide between different socioeconomic groups to widen by creating enclaves of low-income and wealthy neighborhoods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhu |first1=Yushu |last2=Yuan |first2=Yue |last3=Gu |first3=Jiaxin |last4=Fu |first4=Qiang |date=2021-11-23 |title=Neoliberalization and inequality: disparities in access to affordable housing in urban Canada 1981–2016 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02673037.2021.2004093 |journal=Housing Studies |volume=38 |issue=10 |language=en |pages=1860–1887 |doi=10.1080/02673037.2021.2004093 |s2cid=244569247 |issn=0267-3037|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These enclaves dictate the distribution of labor, causing a geographical distribution of industries that disproportionately exclude low-income residents from lucrative industries.<ref name=":12" />

== Affordable housing and urbanization ==

=== Urbanization ===
The majority of people on earth now live in urban areas.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2018 Revision of World Urbanization Prospects {{!}} Multimedia Library – United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs |url=https://www.un.org/development/desa/publications/2018-revision-of-world-urbanization-prospects.html |access-date=2022-03-26 |website=www.un.org}}</ref> There are more than 500 city regions of more than one million inhabitants in the world.<ref>{{Cite web |last=United Nations |date=2016 |title=The World's Cities in 2016 Data Booklet |url=https://www.un.org/en/development/desa/population/publications/pdf/urbanization/the_worlds_cities_in_2016_data_booklet.pdf |website=United Nations}}</ref> Cities become megacities become megalopolitan city regions and even "galaxies" of more than 60&nbsp;million inhabitants. The Yangtze Delta-Greater Shanghai region now surpasses 80&nbsp;million. Tokyo-Yokohama adjacent to Osaka-Kobe-Kyoto have a combined population of 100&nbsp;million. Rapid population growth leads to increased need for affordable housing in many cities.<ref>{{Citation |last1=van Doorn |first1=Lisette |chapter=In the Age of Cities: The Impact of Urbanisation on House Prices and Affordability |date=2019 |title=Hot Property |pages=3–13 |place=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-030-11673-6 |last2=Arnold |first2=Amanprit |last3=Rapoport |first3=Elizabeth|doi=10.1007/978-3-030-11674-3_1 |s2cid=197589134 |doi-access=free }}</ref> The benefits of urbanization include employment opportunities and better living conditions with access to infrastructure, education, healthcare, and recreation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Miranda |date=2019-10-31 |title=The Impact of Urbanization |url=https://www.flashparking.com/blog/the-impact-of-urbanization/ |access-date=2022-08-10 |website=Flash Parking |language=en-US}}</ref> World Bank reports that by 2050 nearly 7 of 10 people in the world will live in cities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Overview |url=https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/urbandevelopment/overview |access-date=2022-08-10 |website=World Bank |language=en}}</ref>  This kind of growth however brings challenges to urban development as cities are tasked with efficiently using resources in accordance with the global demand for affordable housing. The availability of affordable housing in proximity of mass transit and linked to job distribution has become severely imbalanced in this period of rapid regional urbanization and growing density convergence.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McKinsey Global Institute |date=October 2014 |title=A blueprint for addressing the global affordable housing challenge |url=https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/mckinsey/featured%20insights/urbanization/tackling%20the%20worlds%20affordable%20housing%20challenge/mgi_affordable_housing_executive%20summary_october%202014.ashx |website=McKinsey}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jan K. Brueckner, Somik V. Lall |date=July 2014 |title=Cities in Developing Countries: Fueled by Rural-Urban Migration, Lacking in Tenure Security, and Short of Affordable Housing |url=http://real-faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/~duranton/Duranton_Papers/Handbook/Cities_in_developing_countries_fueled_by_rural_urban_migration_lacking_in_tenure_security_and_short_of_affordable_housing.pdf |journal=Handbook of Regional and Urban Economics |volume=5}}</ref>

=== The urban poor and homeless ===
[[File:Mumbai_03-2016_105_Bandra_station_surroundings.jpg|thumb|Slums in Mumbai]]
Globally, it is estimated that 1.6&nbsp;billion people live in inadequate housing conditions.<ref>{{Cite web |title=First-ever United Nations Resolution on Homelessness {{!}} DISD |url=https://www.un.org/development/desa/dspd/2020/03/resolution-homelessness/ |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=www.un.org}}</ref> The majority of that population live in "[[Slum|urban slums]]" which are highly populated, impoverished residential areas consisting of densely packed housing that lack proper shelter and basic necessities such as clean water, food, hygiene facilities, and electricity.<ref name="smartcitiesdive.com">{{Cite web |title=The Emergence of Urban Slums {{!}} Smart Cities Dive |url=https://www.smartcitiesdive.com/ex/sustainablecitiescollective/emergence-urban-slums/119186/ |access-date=2022-08-11 |website=www.smartcitiesdive.com |language=en-US}}</ref> Slums typically form in developing countries as populations migrate from rural to urban areas searching for employment and better living conditions. But due to the higher prices of urban living and a range of other factors such as economic stagnation, migrators find themselves forced to relocate to such slums.<ref name="smartcitiesdive.com"/> The largest slum in the world is Neza-Chalco-Itza in Mexico, housing almost four million people.<ref name="smartcitiesdive.com"/> According to estimates, by 2030 1 in 4 people on the planet will live in a slum or other informal settlement.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Phillip |first=Kanika |date=2017-12-07 |title=The World's Largest Slums: Dharavi, Kibera, Khayelitsha & Neza |url=https://www.habitatforhumanity.org.uk/blog/2017/12/the-worlds-largest-slums-dharavi-kibera-khayelitsha-neza/ |access-date=2022-08-12 |website=Habitat for Humanity GB |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Meanwhile, there are approximately 140 million people worldwide who are homeless, usually as a result of being evicted from slums.<ref>{{Cite web |title=First-ever United Nations Resolution on Homelessness {{!}} DISD |url=https://www.un.org/development/desa/dspd/2020/03/resolution-homelessness/ |access-date=2022-08-12 |website=www.un.org}}</ref> Since slum residents do not own a title or lease to property, they are often evicted from their home by someone with a claim to the land and left without one.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What is a Slum? Definition of a Global Housing Crisis |url=https://www.habitatforhumanity.org.uk/what-we-do/slum-rehabilitation/what-is-a-slum/ |access-date=2022-08-12 |website=Habitat for Humanity GB |language=en-GB}}</ref> The same principle is applied in the United States as people who are unable to afford their mortgage or rent are evicted and left homeless.

==== The State of Homelessness in America ====
In September 2019, the Council of Economic Advisers from the Executive Office of the President of the United States published the report "The State of Homelessness in America". The report found that "[O]ver half a million people go homeless on a single night in the United States" with approximately 65% or 350,000 people living in homeless shelters and 35% – just under 200,000 people – are unsheltered in the streets (living on sidewalks or in parks, cars, or abandoned buildings).<ref name=":04">The Council of Economic Advisers: The State of Homelessness in America. September 2019. Executive Office of the President of the United States.</ref> Almost half (47%) of all unsheltered homeless people are found in the state of California. Rates of sheltered homelessness are highest in Boston, New York City, Washington D.C., with NYC alone containing over one-fifth of all sheltered people in the U.S.<ref name=":04" /> In a framework of [[supply and demand]] the report analyzes the major factors that causes the variation in homelessness across communities. Considering the four major drivers of homeless populations: (i) the higher price of housing resulting from overregulation of housing markets; (ii) the tolerability of sleeping on the street (outside of shelter or housing); (iii) the supply of homeless shelters; and (iv) the characteristics of individuals in a community that make homelessness more likely,<ref name=":04" /> the report concludes with federal policies and programs aimed at reducing homelessness.
[[File:Tenting_in_Los_Angeles_Skid_Row.jpg|thumb|Homeless tents in Los Angeles]]
The first factor contributing to an increase in homelessness is the higher price of housing resulting from the overregulation of housing markets. As stated in President Trump's Executive Order Establishing a White House Council on Eliminating Regulatory Barriers to Affordable Housing, such regulations include: "overly restrictive zoning and growth management controls; rent controls; cumbersome building and rehabilitation codes; excessive energy and water efficiency mandates; unreasonable maximum-density allowances; historic preservation requirements; overly burdensome wetland or environmental regulations; outdated manufactured-housing regulations and restrictions; undue parking requirements; cumbersome and time-consuming permitting and review procedures; tax policies that discourage investment or reinvestment; overly complex labor requirements; and inordinate [[impact fee|impact or developer fees]]." These regulations reduce the supply of housing and as a result increase the price of a home. Given the relationship between higher home prices and homelessness, the report simulated the impact of deregulation on housing in individual metropolitan areas. It showed that if 11 metropolitan areas with significantly supply constrained housing were deregulated, homelessness would fall by 54 percent in San Francisco, by 50 percent in Honolulu, by 40 percent in Oxnard and Los Angeles, by 38 percent in San Diego, by 36 percent in Washington, D.C., and by between 19 and 26 percent in Boston, Denver, New York, Seattle and Baltimore.<ref name=":04" />

The second factor the report provides is the tolerability of sleeping on the street (outside of shelter or housing). Studies show that cities with warmer climates have significantly higher rates of unsheltered homelessness compared to cities with cold climates.<ref name=":04" /> The homeless are more accepting of unsheltered living in areas with warmer conditions, hence why Los Angeles and San Diego have some of the highest unsheltered rates.
[[File:Homeless in New York City..jpg|thumb|Homeless in New York City]]
The third factor that explains variation in homelessness is the supply of substitutes to housing through homeless shelters. "Some places, including New York City, the State of Massachusetts, and the District of Columbia – provide a legal "right to shelter" that promises shelter of some minimum level of quality".<ref name=":04" /> This means that regardless of occupancy, the shelter ensures a certain level of quality. "Thus, as long as the minimum shelter quality is set high enough (i.e., higher than equilibrium quality levels reached in other places), we would expect right-to-shelter places to have a larger supply of homeless shelters."<ref name=":04" /> Since a larger shelter supply entails a higher shelter quality, people who otherwise would not be homeless are found living in shelters because they provide a better alternative. This results in a decrease in the demand for housing and an increase in homelessness.

The fourth and final cause of homelessness is a higher prevalence of individual-level risk factors. These factors include mental health, substance abuse, incarceration, poverty, and social ties.<ref name=":04" /> "According to the 2018 homeless point-in-time count, 111,122 homeless people (20 percent) had a severe mental illness and 86,647 homeless people (16 percent) suffered from chronic substance abuse. Among all adults who used shelter at some point in 2017, 44 percent had a disability."<ref name=":04" /> In addition, "people experiencing homelessness generally have low incomes and relatively weaker social ties."<ref name=":04" /> While the vast majority of people with these issues are not homeless, there is a strong connection to those who are.

The Federal Government provides funding to communities to support homeless assistance programs. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) is the largest source of Federal funds, providing $2.6&nbsp;billion combined via the Continuum of Care (CoC) program and Emergency Solution Grant program alone in 2019.<ref name=":04" /> These two programs support competitive funding to communities for homeless outreach, emergency shelter, transitional housing, rapid rehousing, permanent supportive housing and homelessness prevention. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) provides $1.8&nbsp;billion for programs that serve homeless veterans, in addition to funding from HUD targeted specifically to homeless veterans.<ref name=":04" /> Other smaller sources of funding include the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, the U.S. Department of Education, and the U.S. Department of Labor. State and local governments and private philanthropy provide substantial funding and support for homeless assistance as well.<ref name=":04" />

The Trump Administration implemented a range of policies in conjunction with homeless assistance programs in addressing the four major drivers of homelessness. Most significant was the reformation of the Housing First approach which provides competitive funding to CoC's. While the program maintains a commitment to providing housing with no preconditions to program participants, the 2019 Notice of Funding Availability allowed communities flexibility to impose service participation requirements for participants after they have been stabilized in housing.<ref name=":04" /> Such reforms allow homeless assistance programs help vulnerable homeless individuals become self-sufficient through employment and earning an income.

==Social and environmental impacts==

Social Science Research Network (SSRN). Accessed 31 January 2020.</ref> Lack of affordable housing is considered by many [[urban planning|urban planners]] to have negative effects on a community's overall health.<ref>{{cite report

}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Unaffordable housing can increase the support for [[Redistribution of income and wealth|redistribution]].<ref name="j365">{{cite journal |last1=Furtado|first1=Julia|last2=Flynn|first2=Lindsay B.|title=Housing unaffordability and political preferences among young people in Europe|journal=International Journal of Comparative Sociology|volume=66|issue=4|date=2025|issn=0020-7152|doi=10.1177/00207152241295976|pages=606–632|url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/00207152241295976|access-date=2026-01-31|doi-access=free}}</ref> Homeowners tend to oppose policies which decrease housing prices.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=A direct test of the homevoter hypothesis|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0094119007001179|journal=Journal of Urban Economics|date=2008|issn=0094-1190|pages=155–170|volume=64|issue=1|doi=10.1016/j.jue.2007.11.001|first=Carolyn A.|last=Dehring|first2=Craig A.|last2=Depken|first3=Michael R.|last3=Ward|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

=== Labour market performance and transportation ===
{{main|Workforce housing}}

Lack of affordable housing can make low-cost labor more scarce, and increase demands on transportation systems (as workers travel longer distances between jobs and affordable housing).
"Faced with few affordable options, many people attempt to find less expensive housing by buying or renting farther out from their place of employment, but long commutes often result in higher transportation costs that erase any savings on shelter."<ref name=":5">{{cite report |url=http://www.va-rems.org/connecting_home_and_work.pdf |title=Jobs, Transportation, and Affordable Housing: Connecting Home and Work |author=Pollard, Trip |publisher=Southern Environmental Law Center/Housing Virginia |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120309133328/http://www.va-rems.org/connecting_home_and_work.pdf |archive-date=9 March 2012 |year=2010 }}
</ref> This has been called the "drive 'til you qualify" approach, which causes far-flung development and forces people to drive longer distances to get to work, to get groceries, to take children to school, or to engage in other activities.<ref name=":5" /> A well located dwelling might save significant household travel costs and therefore improve overall family economics, even if the rent is higher than a dwelling in a poorer location.<ref name="qahc.asn.au" /><ref>{{cite news |last=White |first=Shelley |date=15 April 2016 |title=Why commuting costs can make the 'burbs more expensive than living downtown |newspaper=[[The Globe and Mail]] |url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/globe-investor/why-commuting-from-the-burbs-can-be-more-costly-than-living-downtown/article29642363/ |access-date=1 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161231000902/https://www.theglobeandmail.com/globe-investor/why-commuting-from-the-burbs-can-be-more-costly-than-living-downtown/article29642363/ |archive-date=31 December 2016 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Bridge, Gary |title=The New Blackwell Companion to the City |author2=Watson, Sophie |date= 2011 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons}}{{ISBN?}}
</ref> A 2012 study led by [[Pembina Institute]] affirmed that the additional expenses of long-distance commuting often negated the savings associated with lower housing costs.<ref>{{cite web |title=Costs of Living and Commuting in the GTA |url=https://www.pembina.org/reports/live-where-you-go-cost-comparison.pdf |publisher=[[Pembina Institute]] |access-date=1 July 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161010071100/https://www.pembina.org/reports/live-where-you-go-cost-comparison.pdf |archive-date=10 October 2016 |date=July 2012 |url-status=live }}</ref>

In both large metropolitan areas and regional towns where housing prices are high, a lack of affordable housing places local firms at a competitive disadvantage. They are placed under wage pressures as they attempt to decrease the income/housing price gap. Key workers have fewer housing choices if prices rise to non-affordable levels. Variations in affordability of housing between areas may create labour market impediments. Potential workers are discouraged from moving to employment in areas of less affordability. They are also discouraged from migrating to areas of high affordability as the low house prices and rents indicate low capital gain potential and poor employment prospects.<ref>{{cite report |url=http://www.ahuri.edu.au/downloads/NRV3/NRV3_Research_Paper_1.pdf |title=Conceptualising and measuring the housing affordability problem |author1=Gabriel, Michelle |author2=Jacobs, Keith |date=May 2005 |publisher=Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute |page=3 |isbn=1-920941-76-2 |author3=Arthurson, Kathy |author4=Burke, Terry |author5=Yates, Judith |author-link5=Judith Yates |series=National Research Venture 3: Housing Affordability for Lower Income Australians |number=1 }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Lack of affordable housing can make low-cost labour scarcer (as workers travel longer distances).<ref name="Bhatta, Basudeb 42">{{cite book |author=Bhatta, Basudeb |title=Analysis of Urban Growth and Sprawl from Remote Sensing Data |date=2010 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-642-05298-9 |series=Advances in Geographic Information Science |page=42}}</ref>

=== Public health and education ===
"In addition to the distress it causes families who cannot find a place to live, lack of affordable housing is considered by many urban planners to have negative effects on a community's overall health."<ref name="Bhatta, Basudeb 42" /> Improving thermal comfort at home especially for houses without adequate warmth and for tenants with chronic respiratory disease may lead to improved health and promote social relationships.<ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Thomson H, Thomas S, Sellstrom E, Petticrew M|date=28 February 2013|title=Housing improvements for health and associated socio-economic outcomes|url=http://eprints.gla.ac.uk/82620/3/82620.pdf|journal=Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews|issue=2|article-number=CD008657|doi=10.1002/14651858.CD008657.pub2|pmid=23450585 |pmc=12551615 }}</ref> Housing cost increases in American cities have been linked to declines in enrollment at local schools.<ref>{{cite web |title=Deconstructing the Myths: Housing Development Versus School Costs |url=http://www.bos.frb.org/commdev/c%26b/2005/Spring/Housing.pdf |access-date=6 January 2018 |archive-date=19 October 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121019024530/http://www.bos.frb.org/commdev/c%26b/2005/Spring/Housing.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Cleeland |first=Nancy |date=11 June 2006 |title=There Goes the Enrollment |url=https://www.latimes.com/news/education/la-me-enroll11jun11,1,481921.story?coll=la-news-learning |access-date=6 January 2018 |work=Los Angeles Times}}</ref>

The [[American Journal of Public Health]] recognizes homelessness as a public health issue.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Donovan |first1=Shaun |last2=Shinseki |first2=Eric K. |date=2013 |title=Homelessness Is a Public Health Issue |journal=American Journal of Public Health |volume=103 |issue=Suppl 2 |pages=S180|doi=10.2105/AJPH.2013.301727 |pmid=24256062 |pmc=3969122 }}</ref> In a 2013 survey, a lack of affordable housing was the number one in the list of causes of homelessness among families with children and unaccompanied individuals.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Hunger and Homelessness Survey |publisher=The United states Conference of Mayors |year=2014 |publication-date=December 2014 |page=2}}</ref> Studies through the [[The Canadian Journal of Psychiatry|Canadian Journal of Psychiatry]] have shown that access to rapid permanent housing with treatment, rehabilitation, and support services have led to a decrease in shelter and emergency department costs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ly |first1=Angela |last2=Latimer |first2=Eric |date=November 2015 |title=Housing First Impact on Costs and Associated Cost Offsets: A Review of the Literature |journal=The Canadian Journal of Psychiatry |language=en |volume=60 |issue=11 |pages=475–487 |doi=10.1177/070674371506001103 |issn=0706-7437 |pmc=4679128 |pmid=26720505}}</ref>

Affordable Housing is found to reduce the likelihood that a family will be forced to move due to financial challenges such as eviction, foreclosure, or rent increase.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bartlett |first=Sheridan |date=April 1997 |title=The significance of relocation for chronically poor families in the USA |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/095624789700900101 |journal=Environment and Urbanization |language=en |volume=9 |issue=1 |pages=121–132 |doi=10.1177/095624789700900101 |bibcode=1997EnUrb...9..121B |s2cid=154584773 |issn=0956-2478|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A study focusing on the effects of foreclosure on student academic performance within the Boston public school system, found a relationship that suggests foreclosures have a small negative association with individual students' test score and attendance, controlling for the student's previous test score or attendance.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Boston |first=Federal Reserve Bank of |date=2013-11-21 |title=The Effect of Foreclosure on Boston Public School Student Academic Performance |url=https://www.bostonfed.org/publications/research-department-working-paper/2013/the-effect-of-foreclosure-on-boston-public-school-student-academic-performance.aspx |access-date=2022-05-30 |website=Federal Reserve Bank of Boston |language=en}}</ref>  A 1996 technical report also found that teachers that teach students that have had to move with a high frequency have had to include a reduction in instructional pacing and more review to accommodate variation and uncertainty in student learning.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kerbow |first=David |date=October 1996 |title=CRESPAR Report #5: Patterns of Urban Student Mobility and Local School Reform |url=https://jscholarship.library.jhu.edu/handle/1774.2/62864 |journal=Center for Research on the Education of Students Placed at Risk |language=en-US |volume=5}}</ref>

=== Affordable housing and sustainability ===
A new subsection of affordable housing has emerged: sustainable affordable housing. This type of affordable housing incorporates both environmentally friendly building practices and elements such as improved insulation and solar energy to lower both current and future environmental impact.<ref name=":06">{{Cite web |title=Sustainable and Affordable Housing Report|url=https://worldgbc.org/article/sustainable-and-affordable-housing/|access-date=2026-02-24|website=World Green Building Council|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Savio|first=Andrea|date=2025-02-03|title=What is Sustainable Housing?|url=https://globalrealassets.georgetown.edu/insight/what-is-sustainable-housing/|access-date=2026-02-24|website=Steers Global Real Assets|language=en-US}}</ref> This creates environmentally friendly housing for low-moderate income individuals and families with up to 30% lower utility bills.<ref name=":06" /><ref name=":7">{{Cite web |date=2026-02-01|title=The Role of Sustainability and Energy Efficiency in Affordable Housing|url=https://www.ecomena.org/sustainability-key-to-affordable-housing/|access-date=2026-02-24|language=en-US}}</ref> Improving the sustainability of affordable housing units is also found to increase economic value and  comfort.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Olanrewaju|first=AbdulLateef|last2=Tan|first2=Seong Yeow|last3=Abdul‐Aziz|first3=Abdul‐Rashid|date=2018-07-04|title=Housing providers' insights on the benefits of sustainable affordable housing|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sd.1854|journal=Sustainable Development|language=en|volume=26|issue=6|pages=847–858|doi=10.1002/sd.1854|issn=0968-0802|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230212020818/https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sd.1854|archive-date=2023-02-12|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref name=":22">{{Cite journal |last1=Olanrewaju |first1=AbdulLateef |last2=Tan |first2=Seong Yeow |last3=Abdul-Aziz |first3=Abdul-Rashid |date=2018-07-04 |title=Housing providers' insights on the benefits of sustainable affordable housing |journal=Sustainable Development |volume=26 |issue=6 |pages=847–858 |doi=10.1002/sd.1854 |s2cid=158672166 |issn=0968-0802}}</ref>

==== Strategies and approaches ====
A significant amount of research has been done on the topic of making sustainability affordable. One method emphasized is creating disaster-resistant affordable housing units to reduce the impact of climate change-related natural disasters. This method includes using weather-resistant housing materials and placing affordable housing units in disaster-resistant geographical locations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gan|first=Xiaolong|last2=Zuo|first2=Jian|last3=Wu|first3=Peng|last4=Wang|first4=Jun|last5=Chang|first5=Ruidong|last6=Wen|first6=Tao|date=2017-09-20|title=How affordable housing becomes more sustainable? A stakeholder study|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0959652617312180|journal=Journal of Cleaner Production|volume=162|pages=427–437|doi=10.1016/j.jclepro.2017.06.048|issn=0959-6526|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Another proposed method is the use of Frugal Innovation (FI), a cost-saving method involving removing unnecessary and complicating aspects of products and business models to reduce costs.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last=Mbabil Dok-Yen|first=David|last2=Yaw Addai Duah|first2=Daniel|last3=Nii Addy|first3=Michael|date=2023|title=Frugal Innovation a Game Changer to Sustainable Affordable Housing|url=https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/irspsd/11/2/11_13/_article|journal=International Review for Spatial Planning and Sustainable Development|volume=11|issue=2|pages=199–221|doi=10.14246/irspsd.11.2_199|doi-access=free}}</ref> In a review of over 480 publications on FI, David Mbabil Dok-Yen et al. found that FI has the potential to lower affordable housing building costs, which in turn reduces costs for the end consumer.<ref name=":13" /> A different study found cross-laminated timber (CLT) to be a safe and cost effective replacement for steel or concrete in building multi story buildings, which could reduce material costs for builders of apartments or condos.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=van de Lindt|first=John W.|last2=Koliou|first2=Maria|last3=Bahmani|first3=Pouria|date=2023|title=Getting Cross-Laminated Timber into U.S. Design Codes: A Must for Affordable and Sustainable Multifamily Housing|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/48725033|journal=Cityscape|volume=25|issue=1|pages=57–69|issn=1936-007X}}</ref>

==== Assessment and outcomes ====
The evaluation of sustainable affordable housing generally involves several factors, such as environmental performance, economic feasibility, and social outcomes.<ref name=":6" /> The sustainability of these developments is often assessed with metrics such as energy efficiency, long term cost savings, resident well-being, and environmental impact reduction.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Adabre |first=Michael Atafo |last2=Chan |first2=Albert P.C. |date=12 December 2018 |title=The ends required to justify the means for sustainable affordable housing: A review on critical success criteria |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/sd.1919 |journal=Sustainable Development |language=en |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=781–794 |doi=10.1002/sd.1919 |issn=0968-0802|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

One key factor for evaluation is upfront cost. Although sustainable building features often increase initial construction costs, this additional cost is frequently diminished over time through lower utility bills and operational costs.<ref name=":06" /><ref name=":7" /><ref name=":22" /> There are some downsides, however, including the fact that high upfront costs are often a barrier to widespread usage and the extent of savings depends on location, climate, and the specific strategies implemented.

Social outcomes are also a key component of the assessment of sustainable affordable housing. Improved insulation, ventilation, and access to green spaces have been associated with better physical and mental health outcomes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Barton |first=Jo |last2=Rogerson |first2=Mike |date=1 November 2017 |title=The importance of greenspace for mental health |url=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5663018/ |journal=BJPsych international |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=79–81 |doi=10.1192/s2056474000002051 |issn=2056-4740 |pmc=5663018 |pmid=29093955}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=Low indoor temperatures and insulation |date=2018 |work=WHO Housing and Health Guidelines |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535294/ |access-date=2026-04-28 |publisher=World Health Organization |language=en}}</ref>

Finally, environmental impact, including policy and certification systems, such as green building standards, are often used to evaluate and guide sustainable affordable housing projects.<ref>{{Cite web |last=US EPA |first=OLEM |date=2014-09-30 |title=Green Building |url=https://www.epa.gov/smartgrowth/green-building |access-date=2026-04-28 |website=www.epa.gov |language=en}}</ref> As the primary driving factor in sustainable movements, the impact on the environment is one of the most important measurements in the success of sustainable affordable housing projects. In a study on the relationship between sustainable and affordable housing found that setting clearer standards for energy usage and efficiency as well as location would help to reduce environmental stressors like greenhouse gas emissions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chan|first=Albert P. C.|last2=Adabre|first2=Michael Atafo|date=2019-03-15|title=Bridging the gap between sustainable housing and affordable housing: The required critical success criteria (CSC)|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132319300356|journal=Building and Environment|volume=151|pages=112–125|doi=10.1016/j.buildenv.2019.01.029|issn=0360-1323|hdl=10397/103347|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

Despite these efforts, there is still no universally accepted standard for evaluating sustainable affordable housing, leading to differences in how success is measured across different regions and projects.

=== Land values ===
According to a 2022 study, [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|LIHTC]] projects in the United States increase land value in surrounding neighborhoods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Voith |first1=Richard |last2=Liu |first2=Jing |last3=Zielenbach |first3=Sean |last4=Jakabovics |first4=Andrew |last5=An |first5=Brian |last6=Rodnyansky |first6=Seva |last7=Orlando |first7=Anthony W. |last8=Bostic |first8=Raphael W. |date=2022 |title=Effects of concentrated LIHTC development on surrounding house prices |journal=Journal of Housing Economics |language=en |volume=56 |article-number=101838 |doi=10.1016/j.jhe.2022.101838 |s2cid=247788358 |issn=1051-1377|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Public policy==
Policy makers at all levels – global, national, regional, municipal, community associations – are attempting to respond to the issue of affordable housing, a highly complex crisis of global proportions, with a myriad of policy instruments.<ref name="papers.ssrn.com" /> These responses range from stop-gap financing tools to long-term intergovernmental<ref name="McGill-Queen's University Press">{{cite book
 |author      = Hulchanski, David J.
 |chapter-url         = http://www.ppm-ppm.ca/SOTFS/Hulchanski.pdf
 |chapter     = 10. What Factors Shape Canadian Housing Policy? The Intergovernmental Role in Canada's Housing System
 |editor      = Young, Robert
 |editor2     = Leuprecht, Christian
 |title       = Canada: The State of the Federation 2004: Municipal-Federal-Provincial Relations in Canada
 |date        = June 2006
 |series      = Institute of Intergovernmental Relations
 |publisher   = McGill-Queen's University Press
 |access-date  = 15 December 2011
 |archive-url  = https://web.archive.org/web/20120426055747/http://www.ppm-ppm.ca/SOTFS/Hulchanski.pdf
 |archive-date = 26 April 2012
}}</ref> infrastructural changes. There has been an increase among policy makers in affordable housing as the price of housing has increased dramatically creating a crisis in affordable housing.<ref name="Schmuecker, Katie 2011" /> Additionally, the process of weighing the impacts of locating affordable housing is quite contentious and may have [[gentrification|race and class implications]].{{citation needed|date=January 2025}}

Affordable housing policy has political, philosophical, and ethical elements. In the simplest of terms, affordability of housing refers to the amount of capital one has available in relation to the price of the goods to be obtained. Public policies are informed by underlying assumptions about the nature of housing itself. Is housing a basic need, a right, an entitlement, or a public good? Or is it just another household-level [[consumer choice]], a commodity or an investment within the free market system?<ref>{{cite report
 |url        = http://www.unhabitat.org/downloads/docs/3680_5167_1.pdf

}}</ref><ref>{{cite web

</ref> "Housing Policies provide a remarkable litmus test for the values of politicians at every level of office and of the varied communities that influence them. Often this test measures simply the warmth or coldness of heart of the more affluent and secure towards families of a lower socio-economic status."<ref>{{cite book

Evidence from Property Records and Meeting Minutes | journal=American Political Science Review | volume=114 | issue=4 | date=2020 | issn=0003-0554 | doi=10.1017/S0003055420000556 | pages=1213–1229 | url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0003055420000556/type/journal_article | access-date=2026-04-17| url-access=subscription }}</ref>

To combat [[slum]]s, [[homelessness]], and other social and economic impacts of a housing unaffordability, many groups have argued for a "[[right to housing]]". Article 25 of the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] recognizes the right to housing as part of the [[right to an adequate standard of living]].<ref name="Edgar20022">{{Cite book|last=Edgar|first=Bill|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pxFjtTWFJlYC&q=right+to+housing+human+rights|title=Access to housing: homelessness and vulnerability in Europe|author2=Doherty, Joe|author3=Meert, Henk|publisher=[[The Policy Press]]|year=2002|isbn=978-1-86134-482-3|page=17}}</ref> Article 11(1) of the [[International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights]] (ICESCR) also guarantees the right to housing as part of the [[right to an adequate standard of living]].<ref name="Edgar20022" /> Many housing rights groups also attempt to combat social and political issues which relate to access to quality affordable housing such as [[housing discrimination]], [[redlining]], and lack of access to amenities in areas with affordable housing including [[food desert]]s and [[transit desert]]s.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-10-02|title=How Stable, Affordable Housing Can Help Tackle Food
