===Supply-side approaches===
{{see also|YIMBY}}

Policies that reduce housing cost though increased housing supply include favorable land use policies such as [[inclusionary zoning]], relaxation of environmental regulations, and the enforcement of affordable housing quotas in new developments.{{Citation needed|date=March 2021}}

In some countries, such as Canada and the United States, municipal governments began to play a greater role in developing and implementing policies regarding form and density of municipal housing in residential districts, as early as the 1950s.<ref name="McGill-Queen's University Press"/> At the municipal level, promoted policy tools include zoning permissions for diverse housing types or [[Missing Middle Housing]] types such as duplexes, cottages, rowhouses, fourplexes, and [[Garage apartment|accessory dwelling units]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=The 'Missing' Affordable Housing Solution|url=https://www.aarp.org/livable-communities/housing/info-2020/missing-middle-housing-affordability.html|access-date=2021-03-13|website=AARP|language=english}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Wegmann|first=Jake|date=2020-01-02|title=Death to Single-Family Zoning…and New Life to the Missing Middle|journal=Journal of the American Planning Association|volume=86|issue=1|pages=113–119|doi=10.1080/01944363.2019.1651217|issn=0194-4363|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=MRSC – Affordable Housing|url=http://mrsc.org/Home/Explore-Topics/Planning/Specific-Planning-Subjects-Plan-Elements/Affordable-Housing-Ordinances-Flexible-Provisions.aspx|access-date=2021-03-13|website=mrsc.org|archive-date=22 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210122155146/http://mrsc.org/Home/Explore-Topics/Planning/Specific-Planning-Subjects-Plan-Elements/Affordable-Housing-Ordinances-Flexible-Provisions.aspx}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Missing Middle Housing Initiatives across the US|url=https://www.missingmiddlearlington.net/insights/missing-middle-housing-initiatives-across-the-nation|access-date=2021-03-13|website=Missing Middle Arlington|language=en-US}}</ref> Some municipalities have also reduced the amount of [[parking]] that must be built for a new structure to reduce land acquisition and construction costs.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Litman|first=Todd|date=June 5, 2020|title=Parking Requirement Impacts on Housing Affordability|url=https://www.vtpi.org/park-hou.pdf|website=Victoria Transport Policy Institute}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Regional Housing Task Force|url=https://housingtaskforce.mapc.org/strategies|access-date=2021-03-13|website=housingtaskforce.mapc.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=People Over Parking|url=https://www.planning.org/planning/2018/oct/peopleoverparking/|access-date=2021-03-13|website=American Planning Association}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Reduced parking requirements|url=https://www.localhousingsolutions.org/act/housing-policy-library/reduced-parking-requirements-overview/reduced-parking-requirements/|access-date=2021-03-13|website=Local Housing Solutions|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Reducing parking means increasing affordability in eTOD|url=https://etod.cnt.org/Reducing-Parking-Means-Increasing-Affordability-in-eTOD.php|access-date=2021-03-13|website=etod.cnt.org|archive-date=13 June 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210613112557/https://etod.cnt.org/Reducing-Parking-Means-Increasing-Affordability-in-eTOD.php}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Stalled Out: How Empty Parking Spaces Diminish Neighborhood Affordability|url=https://www.cnt.org/sites/default/files/publications/CNT_Stalled%20Out_0.pdf|website=Center for Neighborhood Technology}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=A Map of Cities That Got Rid of Parking Minimums|url=https://www.strongtowns.org/journal/2015/11/18/a-map-of-cities-that-got-rid-of-parking-minimums|access-date=2021-03-13|website=Strong Towns|language=en-US}}</ref> Other common strategies include reducing permitting costs and wait times for new housing, permitting small-lot development, multi-family tax exemptions, density bonuses, preserving existing affordable housing, and transit-oriented development.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Evaluating Affordable Housing Development Strategies|url=https://www.planetizen.com/node/85106/evaluating-affordable-housing-development-strategies|access-date=2021-03-13|website=Planetizen – Urban Planning News, Jobs, and Education|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Housing Innovations Program|url=https://www.psrc.org/hip|access-date=2021-03-13|website=Puget Sound Regional Council|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=The Housing Affordability Toolkit|url=https://housingtoolkit.nmhc.org/#affordability-strategies|access-date=2021-03-13|website=housingtoolkit.nmhc.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Housing Innovations Program (HIP) Complete Housing Toolkit|url=https://www.psrc.org/sites/default/files/hip-toolkit.pdf|website=Puget Sound Regional Council Housing Innovations Program|access-date=13 March 2021|archive-date=9 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709170722/https://www.psrc.org/sites/default/files/hip-toolkit.pdf}}</ref>

Existing housing that is affordable may be used, instead of building new structures. This is called "Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing", or NOAH.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://bankingjournal.aba.com/2017/08/noah-the-new-housing-acronym-you-need-to-learn/|title=NOAH: The New Housing Acronym You Need to Learn|last=Calisle|first=Corey|work=ABA Banking Journal|date=1 August 2017|access-date=15 November 2020}}</ref>

In a [[housing cooperative]] people join on a democratic basis to own or manage the housing facility in which they live. Generally these housing units are owned and controlled collectively by a corporation which is owned and controlled jointly by a group of individuals who have equal shares in that corporation.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|title=National Association of Housing Cooperatives (NAHC) » Buying into a Housing Cooperative|url=https://coophousing.org/resources/owning-a-cooperative/buying-into-a-housing-cooperative/|access-date=2021-07-19|language=en-US|archive-date=19 July 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210719225309/https://coophousing.org/resources/owning-a-cooperative/buying-into-a-housing-cooperative/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-03-23|title=What Is a Co-Op? The Benefits and Drawbacks to Cooperative Housing|url=https://www.realtor.com/advice/buy/the-basics-of-co-op-housing/|access-date=2021-07-19|website=Real Estate News & Insights {{!}} realtor.com|language=en-US}}</ref> In market rate cooperatives owners can accumulate equity and sell their share of the corporation at market rate. In a limited-equity housing cooperative there are restrictions on the profits members can earn from selling their share (such as caps on sale price) to meant to maintain affordable housing.<ref name=":3" />

[[Community land trust]]s are nonprofit corporation that holds land, housing, or other assets on behalf of a neighborhood or community. A community land trust acquires and maintains ownership of the land through a not-for-profit that holds the land in a trust.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Leasing Land for Affordable Housing|url=https://www.lincolninst.edu/publications/articles/community-land-trusts|access-date=2021-07-19|website=LILP|date=21 September 2016 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite web|date=2012-06-21|title=Community Land Trusts (CLTs)|url=https://community-wealth.org/strategies/panel/clts/index.html|access-date=2021-07-19|website=Community-Wealth.org|language=en}}</ref> Homeowners then purchase or build a home on land trust property but do not purchase the land thus reducing costs. If the homeowner sells, they may be limited on what they may sell the home for or the family may earn only a portion of the increased property value with the remainder kept by the trust to preserve affordable housing<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Community land trusts|url=https://www.localhousingsolutions.org/housing-policy-library/community-land-trusts/|access-date=2021-07-19|website=Local Housing Solutions|language=en-US}}</ref> There are over 225 community land trusts in the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|title=StackPath|url=https://groundedsolutions.org/strengthening-neighborhoods/community-land-trusts|access-date=2021-07-19|website=groundedsolutions.org}}</ref>

====Right to build====
An article by [[libertarian]] writer [[Virginia Postrel]] in the November 2007 issue of ''[[Atlantic Monthly]]'' reported on a study of the cost of obtaining the "right to build" (i.e. a [[planning permission]], red tape, bureaucracy, etc.) in different U.S. cities. The "right to build" cost does not include the cost of the land or the cost of constructing the house. The study was conducted by [[Harvard]] economists [[Edward Glaeser]] and Kristina Tobio. According to the chart accompanying the article, the cost of obtaining the "right to build" adds approximately $600,000 to the cost of each new house that is built in San Francisco.  The study, cited, published by Ed Glaeser and Joseph Gyourko, reached its conclusion about the value of the right to build in different localities based on a methodology of comparing the cost of single-family homes on quarter-acre versus half-acre lots to get a marginal land price and then comparing the selling price of homes to construction costs to get a price for the land plus other costs, with the difference between the two being attributed to the cost of zoning and other local government permitting and regulations.<ref>[https://www.theatlantic.com/doc/200711/housing?ca=PoSzloTzAzqq0Pg%2BPB504R6MjpVFf78zhjpE2yeHl78%3D "A Tale of Two Town Houses"], ''Atlantic Monthly'', November 2007</ref>

Many governments put restrictions on the size or cost of a dwelling that people can live in,{{citation needed|date=September 2014}} making it essentially illegal to live permanently in a house that is too small, low-cost or not compliant with other government-defined requirements. Generally, these laws are implemented in an attempt to raise the perceived "standard" of housing across the country. This can lead to thousands of houses across a country being left empty for much of the year even when there is a great need for more affordable housing; such is the case in countries like Sweden, [[Norway]], [[Finland]] and [[Denmark]], where there is a common tradition to have a [[summer house]]. This sometimes raises concerns for the respect of rights such as the [[Property rights (economics)|right to use one's property]].

In the United States, most cities have zoning codes that set the minimum size for a housing unit (often 400 square feet) as well as the number of non-related persons who can live together in one unit, resulting in having "outlawed the bottom end of the private housing market, driving up rents on everything above it."<ref name=Bring_back_boarding_house>{{ Cite news | last=Badger | first=Emily | title=Is It Time to Bring Back the Boarding House? | newspaper=Bloomberg.com | url=https://www.citylab.com/equity/2013/07/it-time-bring-back-boarding-house/6236/ | access-date=2017-11-13 | publisher=CityLab – The Atlantic Monthly Group | date=2013-07-18 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171114022002/https://www.citylab.com/equity/2013/07/it-time-bring-back-boarding-house/6236/ | archive-date=2017-11-14 | url-status=live | quote=Politically, it's a coalition of the greedy and the well-meaning that led to the banning of private-sector affordable housing in our cities," he says. The well-meaning folks were appalled by the living conditions of poor and working-class families. The greedy folks were appalled by the prospect of living next to them. Together, this awkward alliance helped advocate laws that established minimum living conditions not simply for safety but also to define how much space an individual should reasonably be expected to live in.}}</ref> In California in 2021, researchers estimated that parking requirements increase the cost of building affordable housing by up to $36,000 per unit, and up to $75,000 per unit in cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco.<ref name="SJMN_1">{{cite news | url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2021/04/06/fewer-parking-spaces-for-new-homes-shops-it-could-happen/ | title=Fewer parking spaces for new homes, shops? It could happen – Pro-housing groups push reform to mandatory parking minimums | last=Hansen | first=Louis | newspaper=[[San Jose Mercury News]] | date=2021-04-06 | quote=Researchers at UC Berkeley's Terner Center for Housing Innovation found parking requirements can add up to $36,000 to the cost of a single affordable housing unit – more than the cost of using environmentally-friendly materials or paying city development fees. In San Francisco and Los Angeles, parking requirements can add up to $75,000 per unit. }}</ref> Until 2018, in Los Angeles, for an affordable housing development to be allowed to be built, it required a "letter of acknowledgement" from the city councilperson in whose district it would be constructed. This allowed city council members to block affordable housing developments in their district without having to give any reason.<ref name="LAist_1">{{cite news | url=https://laist.com/2018/10/17/la_city_council_members_just_lost_a_way_to_block_affordable_housing_in_their_districts.php | title=LA City Council Members Just Lost A Way To Block Affordable Housing In Their Districts | last=Wagner | first=David | newspaper=[[LAist]] | date=2018-10-17 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103184612/https://laist.com/2018/10/17/la_city_council_members_just_lost_a_way_to_block_affordable_housing_in_their_districts.php | archive-date=2018-11-03 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="LAT_ed1">{{cite news | url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/editorials/la-ed-homeless-housing-letter-lawsuit-20180801-story.html | title=Editorial: L.A. City Council members don't deserve unilateral veto power over homeless projects they don't like  | last=The Times Editorial Board  | newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=2018-08-01  }}</ref>

In 2021, former [[Joe Biden|President Joe Biden]] launched the Emergency Housing Vouchers program (EVH) as part of the [[American Rescue Plan Act of 2021|American Rescue Plan Act]], developed post the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] to assist Americans experiencing [[domestic violence]], homelessness, and [[human trafficking]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Emergency Housing Voucher Program (EHV) |url=https://hcr.ny.gov/ehv |access-date=2025-04-27 |website=Homes and Community Renewal |language=en}}</ref> On March 6, 2025, the [[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development|U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development]] (HUD) issued a letter announcing that funding for the program is expected to end by of 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-04-21 |title=60,000 Americans to lose their rental assistance and risk eviction unless Congress acts |url=https://apnews.com/article/trump-congress-housing-voucher-assistance-funding-cuts-26f9a716af6731e3c6445015488bab3a |access-date=2025-04-27 |website=AP News |language=en}}</ref>

===Demand-side approaches===
One potential means of addressing affordable housing is through public policy instruments that focus on the demand side of the market, programs that help households reach financial benchmarks that make housing affordable. This can include approaches that simply promote economic growth in general{{snd}}in the hope that a stronger economy, higher employment rates, and higher wages will increase the ability of households to acquire housing at market prices. Federal government policies define banking and mortgage lending practices, tax and regulatory measures affecting building materials, professional practices (ex. real estate transactions).<ref name="McGill-Queen's University Press"/>

Decreased demand can contribute to lower rent prices.<ref name="e140">{{cite web |last=Flemming|first=Jack|title='Finally, a renter's market': L.A. rent prices drop to four-year low|website=Los Angeles Times|date=2026-01-28|url=https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-01-28/finally-renters-market-la-rent-prices-drop-to-four-year-low|access-date=2026-01-31}}</ref>

===Subsidy-based approaches===
{{See also|Subsidized housing}}
Subsidies can alleviate housing costs and expenses, while increasing demand for housing. Subsidy-based approaches may take the form of government sponsored rental subsidies, government sponsored rental supplements, tax credits, or housing provided by a non-for-profit.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Types of Housing Subsidies|url=https://tenantsunion.org/rights/types-of-housing-subsidies|access-date=2021-03-31|website=Tenants Union|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=October 2014|title=A blueprint for addressing the global affordable housing challenge|url=https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/McKinsey/Featured%20Insights/Urbanization/Tackling%20the%20worlds%20affordable%20housing%20challenge/MGI_Affordable_housing_Executive%20summary_October%202014.pdf|website=McKinsey Global Institute}}</ref> The purchasing power of individual households can be enhanced through tax and fiscal policies that result in reducing the cost of mortgages and the cost of borrowing. Public policies may include the implementation of subsidy programs and incentive patterns for average households.<ref name="McGill-Queen's University Press"/> For the most vulnerable groups, such as seniors, single-parent families, the disabled, etc. some form of publicly funded allowance strategy can be implemented providing individual households with adequate income to afford housing.

Some forms of subsidies can increase housing supply. In a mutual-aid housing cooperative, a group of families forms a cooperative to collectively build, own, and manage land by participating in the process of constructing the housing for the cooperative.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2018-07-30|title=Solutions to an Unjust Housing System|url=https://shelterforce.org/2018/07/30/solutions-to-an-unjust-housing-system/|access-date=2021-07-19|website=Shelterforce|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Latin America's Co-ops Are an Alternative to Housing Crisis|url=https://tribunemag.co.uk/2020/07/latin-americas-co-ops-are-an-alternative-to-housing-crisis|access-date=2021-07-19|website=tribunemag.co.uk|language=en-GB}}</ref> Each family is responsible for contributing labor towards the construction of the housing complex to reduce costs and members take on responsibilities before, during, and after the construction. The Uruguayan Federation of Mutual Aid Housing Cooperatives (FUCVAM) has completed nearly 500 housing cooperatives housing more than 25,000 families.<ref>{{Cite web|title=South-South Cooperation: international transfer of the FUCVAM model of mutual aid housing cooperatives|url=https://world-habitat.org/world-habitat-awards/winners-and-finalists/south-south-cooperation-international-transfer-of-the-fucvam-model-of-mutual-aid-housing-cooperatives/|access-date=2021-07-19|website=World Habitat}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Ibán Díaz Parra, Pablo Rabasco Pozuelo|date=November 27, 2013|title=¿Revitalización sin gentrificación? Cooperativas de vivienda por ayuda mutua en los centros de Buenos Aires y Montevideo|url=https://revistaseug.ugr.es/index.php/cuadgeo/article/view/1516/1719|journal=Cuadernos Geográficos|volume=52|issue=2|pages=99–118}}</ref>[[File:George Washingthon Hof von oben.jpg|thumb|The George-Washington-Hof is protected public housing in Vienna.]]

===Public, state, or social housing approaches===
{{See also|Public housing}}Public housing is a form of housing tenure in which the property is usually built and owned by a government authority, either central or local. In some countries, public housing is focused on providing affordable housing for low-income earners while in others, such as [[Public housing in Singapore|Singapore]], citizens across a wide range of incomes live in public housing.<ref>{{Cite web|title='But what about Singapore?' Lessons from the best public housing program in the world|url=https://blogs.worldbank.org/sustainablecities/what-about-singapore-lessons-best-public-housing-program-world|access-date=2021-03-31|website=blogs.worldbank.org|date=31 January 2018 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Public Housing {{!}} HUD.gov / U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)|url=https://www.hud.gov/program_offices/public_indian_housing/programs/ph|access-date=2021-03-31|website=www.hud.gov}}</ref> In Vienna, Austria, social housing may be completely government built and run or include a mixture of public land and private-sector construction and management.<ref name="Merrifield">{{Cite web|last1=Merrifield|first1=Will|last2=attorney|title=How European-Style Public Housing Could Help Solve The Affordability Crisis|url=https://www.npr.org/local/305/2020/02/25/809315455/how-european-style-public-housing-could-help-solve-the-affordability-crisis|access-date=2021-04-04|website=NPR.org|date=25 February 2020 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Holeywell|first=Ryan|date=February 2015|title=Governing: The International Issue: Haus Beautiful|url=https://drjdbij2merew.cloudfront.net/GOV/GOV_Mag_Feb13.pdf|website=Governing}}</ref> Combined, the two types of housing represent about 46 percent of the city's housing stock (26% government owned and managed and 20% a public/private partnership) and house people with a wide variety of incomes.<ref name="Merrifield"/><ref name=":2" /> In South Korea the public [[Korea Land & Housing Corporation]] has provided homes to 2.9&nbsp;million households which is 15% of the national total of 19.56&nbsp;million households. This includes 2.7&nbsp;million newly built public housing units and 1.03&nbsp;million rental homes of which 260,000 were purchased or rented by the Land and Housing Corporation.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Welcome to Korea Land & Housing Corporation |url=https://www.lh.or.kr/eng/index.do|access-date=2021-07-25|website=www.lh.or.kr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Herald|first=Korea|date=2013-06-04|title=LH strives to expand supply of affordable housing|url=http://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20130604000841|access-date=2021-07-25|website=The Korea Herald|language=en}}</ref>

===Design-based approaches===
====Containerized housing units====
{{see also|Containerized housing unit}}
[[File:53 foot reefer home.webp|thumb|53-foot [[Refrigerated container|reefer container]] home]]
Containerized housing units are [[pre-fabricated housing]] units [[Shipping container architecture|built out of shipping containers]] or similar containers.  They can be stacked or connected to make a larger home, or to make a block of multi-family housing.
Reefer containers or [[refrigerated container]]s are [[Shipping container|containers]] built to haul refrigerated or frozen products.  Compared to standard shipping containers, they have good [[R-value (insulation)|insulation]] in the walls, ceiling, and floor, so they maintain a more comfortable temperature.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.discovercontainers.com/should-you-use-a-refrigerated-shipping-container-for-your-container-home/ | title=Refrigerated Containers: Good to Build With? – Discover Containers | date=5 February 2018 }}</ref>

====Triple decker triplex====
[[File:Triple decker triplex animation.webm|thumb|Modern [[Three-decker (house)|triple decker triplex]] concept with standing seem [[Thin-film solar cell#Thin film solar on metal roofs|metal roof with thin film solar]]. The left and right side doors go to the 2nd and 3rd floors respectively.]]
[[Triple-decker triplex]] housing is more prominent in the [[New England]] area and became popular in the late 19th century and early 20th century with the [[History of immigration to the United States#1850 to 1930|immigration from Europe]] during that time.  Each floor is separately owned or rented out.  If they are owned like a condo an [[Homeowner association|HOA]] maintains ownership of the outside and yard.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://newenglandhistoricalsociety.com/rise-fall-rebirth-new-england-triple-decker/ | title=The Rise, Fall and Rebirth of the Triple Decker | date=28 November 2017 }}</ref>

====Over-1s====
[[5-over-1]]s down to 1-over-1 buildings have the parking spaces below the living spaces and allow for higher density building, because [[parking lot]]s take up a lot of space and on street parking limits the density of zoning for a particular lot.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://mtcopeland.com/blog/what-are-5-over-1-buildings/ | title=What are 5 over 1 Buildings? Pros and Cons of One-Plus-Fives | date=12 January 2022 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rn5IxF-Nykc | title=- YouTube | website=YouTube }}</ref>

==== Adaptive reuse ====
In the United States, "adaptive reuse" has been proposed by affordable housing experts as a way to increase the supply of affordable housing. As opposed to new construction, adaptive reuse involves the repurposing of old structures into housing or mixed-use developments.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Henderson |first=Susan |date=2024-12-16 |title=Old walls, new homes |url=https://www.cnu.org/publicsquare/2024/12/16/old-walls-new-homes |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=CNU |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Walk-Morris |first=Tatiana |title=How Adaptive Reuse Can Help Solve the Housing Crisis |url=https://www.planning.org/planning/2021/spring/how-adaptive-reuse-can-help-solve-the-housing-crisis/ |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=American Planning Association |language=en}}</ref> This is considered more sustainable than building new because the developed structures already exist as underused, abandoned, or functionally obsolete buildings.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Biro |first=Andrew |date=2024-06-20 |title=6 Examples of Affordable Housing Through Adaptive Reuse |url=https://gbdmagazine.com/affordable-housing-adaptive-reuse/ |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=gb&d magazine |language=en-US}}</ref> Adaptive reuse has also been described as less expensive than new construction.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Firtea |first=Diana |date=2024-07-18 |title=MHN Asks: Can Design Really Reduce Affordable Housing Development Costs? |url=https://www.multihousingnews.com/mhn-asks-can-design-really-reduce-affordable-housing-development-costs/ |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=Multi-Housing News |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=December 13, 2015 |title=Adaptive Reuse is Better than New Construction |url=https://sites.psu.edu/arch311w/2015/12/13/adaptive-reuse-is-better-than-new-construction/ |website=Penn State University}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Adaptive Reuse: Higher ROI Compared to New Construction |url=https://www.ny-engineers.com/blog/how-adaptive-reuse-can-offer-a-higher-roi-than-new-construction |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=www.ny-engineers.com |language=en}}</ref>

According to 2023 estimates, 90 percent of U.S. real estate growth by 2033 will entail the adaptive reuse of existing buildings rather than new construction.<ref>{{Cite web |last=REIS |first=Matthews |date=2023-03-02 |title=Adaptive Reuse: The Benefit for Investors |url=https://www.matthews.com/thought-leadership-benefits-of-adaptive-reuse/ |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=Matthews™ |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Adams |first=Mark |date=2022-12-14 |title=2023 Trends: Back To The Future With Adaptive Reuse |url=https://www.workdesign.com/2022/12/2023-trends-back-to-the-future-with-adaptive-reuse/ |access-date=2025-01-24 |website=Work Design Magazine |language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Self-built (owner-built) housing ====
Low-tech, low-cost, traditionally designed, sustainable, self-built homes can enable individuals to construct affordable, healthy housing using local materials. The process may be assisted by free-to-access plans optimised for single-person construction, that are also easily adapted to a broad variety of locations and climates. An example of this approach is the Tasmanian House project in Australia.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2025-04-12 |title=Architect uploads free plan for owner-builders to use |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-04-13/architect-releases-free-owner-build-plans-to-support-housing/104213884 |access-date=2025-10-22 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Keighran |first=Mandi |date=2025-07-07 |title=Budget Breakdown: How an Architect Built a Family Home in Tasmania for $72K |url=https://www.dwell.com/article/budget-breakdown-tasmanian-house-3-jiri-lev-affordable-home-plans-australia-8da5d447 |access-date=2025-10-22 |website=Dwell}}</ref>

==Affordable housing by country==
{{main|Affordable housing by country}}

Different countries and cities throughout the world have found unique ways to respond to the need for affordable housing. In some provinces within China, for example, local governments have instituted "tradable land quotas." These quotas allow developers to construct new housing units at the outer bounds of the city limits, and, in return, land outside of the city is protected from development. On the other hand, in Los Angeles, the city government recently{{when|date=September 2023}} instituted legislation that allows motels to be transformed into affordable housing units, regardless of zoning regulations. In Brussels, an architectural firm was able to repurpose a soap factory, creating affordable housing units that included one- to 6-bedroom apartments, studios, lofts, and duplexes. These residential units are also energy-efficient, so have both social and environmental benefit.<ref>{{Cite web |title=10 ways cities are tackling the global affordable housing crisis |url=https://www.weforum.org/agenda/2019/06/10-ways-cities-are-tackling-the-global-affordable-housing-crisis/ |access-date=2022-04-25 |website=World Economic Forum |date=6 June 2019 |language=en}}</ref>

While innovative building practices have been incredibly successful in countries such as Nigeria and India, cities in more developed countries have found unique ways to increase affordable housing in dense urban areas through partnerships with private developers. For example, in Germany, cities including Berlin and Hamburg have established partnerships with private developers to construct new affordable housing units. In a 2011 agreement, developers in Hamburg agreed to build 3,500 new housing units per year and 30% of these units would only be available to low and middle income households. To support the developer's work, Hamburg's city government agreed to provide city-owned land and acquire privately owned land on which the units would be constructed. Additionally, Hamburg modified urban planning regulations in locations occupied predominantly by low-income individuals to simplify the process of affordable housing construction. Conversely, in Berlin, the Alliance for Housing Construction, which was established in 2014, brought together Berlin's local government, private landlords, and public utility landlords to make rental units in the city more affordable. Public utility landlords such as non-profit organizations agreed to build 3000 new dwellings each year. Between 300 and 1000 of these units would be provided as "non-serviced rents." Additionally, private landlords agreed to construct 6000 units each year, and between 600 and 1200 of these units would be provided as "non-serviced rents."<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Granath Hansson |first=Anna |date=6 February 2017 |title=City strategies for affordable housing: the approaches of Berlin, Hamburg, Stockholm, and Gothenburg |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/19491247.2017.1278581 |journal=International Journal of Housing Policy |volume=19 |pages=95–119 |doi=10.1080/19491247.2017.1278581 |s2cid=214625694 |via=Virgo|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Affordable housing in Canada
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
{{Living spaces}}

[[File:Vancouver Hotel Martinique 2010.jpg|thumb|right|200px|Hotel Martinique provides social housing in Vancouver. Social housing is one subtype of affordable housing.]]
In Canada, affordable housing refers to living spaces that are [[Affordable housing|financially accessible]] to people with a [[median household income]].<ref name="Bhatta, Basudeb 2010 23">{{cite book |author=Bhatta, Basudeb |title=Analysis of Urban Growth and Sprawl from Remote Sensing Data |date=15 April 2010 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-642-05298-9 |series=Advances in Geographic Information Science |page=23}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Real estate market: Definitions, graphs and data |url=https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/indicators/capacity-and-inflation-pressures/real-estate-market-definitions/ |access-date=2023-04-04 |website=www.bankofcanada.ca |language=en-US}}</ref> Canada ranks among the lowest of the most developed [[Affordable housing by country|countries for housing affordability]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Prices - Housing prices |url=https://data.oecd.org/price/housing-prices.htm |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220811142758/https://data.oecd.org/price/housing-prices.htm |archive-date=August 11, 2022 |access-date=August 14, 2022 |publisher=OECD}}</ref> Housing affordability is generally measured based on a shelter-cost-to-income ratio (STIR) of 30% by the [[Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation]] (CMHC), the national housing agency of Canada. It encompasses a continuum ranging from market-based options like affordable [[rental housing]] and affordable [[home ownership]], to non-market alternatives such as [[Subsidized housing|government-subsidized housing]] ([[emergency shelter]]s, [[transitional housing]], and [[public housing]]).<ref>{{cite web|title=The National Housing Strategy Glossary of Common Terms|url=https://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/nhs/guidepage-strategy/glossary|work=CMHC|date=17 May 2022|access-date=10 June 2024}}</ref>

==Definition==
Definitions of "affordable housing" in Canada vary among governments and organizations, typically referring to housing that costs less than 30% of gross household income or is targeted towards those with greater need, such as households earning below thresholds like $60,000 in certain cities.{{Sfn|Laird|2007}}{{sfn|CMHC|2022}}{{Sfn|Eidelman|Hachard|Slack|2022|page=2}}{{sfn|City of Calgary Deputy Manager|2022}} The Canadian housing continuum ranges from non-market options (including shelters and social housing) to market housing such as private rentals and ownership.{{Sfn|Eidelman|Hachard|Slack|2022|page=2}} [[File:Dilapidated apartment yard in Regent Park (44731511740).jpg|thumb|right|The Regent Park apartments in Toronto's Cabbagetown neighborhood were intended to be community housing, but they have become dilapidated.]]

Social housing in Canada is generally defined as housing that is targeted to low-income households and offered at below-market rents, typically provided by governments or non-profits, and sometimes via rent supplements in private rentals; this aligns with the OECD definition and includes terms like rent-geared-to-income or rent-assisted units.{{sfn|Segel-Brown|2025}} According to a 2025 analysis by the [[Parliamentary Budget Officer]], Canada lacks reliable data on its social housing stock, but the best estimates indicate there are about 600,000 to 700,000 units—a figure that has changed little in the past 30 years. Most of this housing was built before 1994, with ongoing federal support provided through long-term operating agreements.{{sfn|Segel-Brown|2025}}
As of 2024, social and community housing accounted for approximately 3–4% of Canada's housing stock, while most households either own their home or rent at market rates.{{sfn|CMHC|2019}}

As of 2018, the market-based housing system accounted for approximately 80% of Canadian households' housing acquisitions.{{sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2018}} About two thirds of Canadian households are home owners, and one third are renters who rent market-rate and non-market units.{{Sfn|Eidelman|Hachard|Slack|2022}}

To restore affordability, Canada needs to double housing starts from about 250,000 to 430,000–480,000 units per year through 2035.{{sfn|CMHC|2025b}}

== Measuring housing affordability ==
Measuring affordability of housing is complicated by Canada's vast physical and human geography which includes both remote northern communities and affluent urban regions.{{Sfn|Yalnizyan|2010}} A common [[rule of thumb]] is to calculate how much of a household's income is spent on housing expenses each month. For example, if a household spends more on average on housing expenses than each month, then their housing situation may be considered unaffordable.{{Sfn|Hulchanski|1995}} In a 1994 background paper commissioned by the [[Ontario Human Rights Commission]], J. David Hulchanski, the North American editor of the international journal ''Housing Studies'', described how the ratio of housing cost as a percentage of income was 12% from 1900 until the early 1920s, when it was increased to 20%. This increased again to 25% in the 1960s, and by the mid-1980s it reached 30%.{{sfn|Hulchanski|1994}} In Canada, the commonly used 20% rule of thumb was adjusted to 25% in the 1950s. In the 1980s, this was replaced by a 30% rule.{{Sfn|Hulchanski|1995}} When the monthly carrying costs of a home exceed 30–35% of household income, then housing expenses are considered unaffordable. While the 30% rule continues to be used by the CMHC, banks, and mortgage providers, it has been challenged by Hulchanski and others.{{Sfn|Hulchanski|1995}}

A 2011 article recommended tracking indicators like the share of affordable rental units for median earners, wage requirements to rent, demand for assistance, core housing need, shelter use, eviction filings, arrears or foreclosures, and vacancy rates, to better measure Canadian housing insecurity and policy outcomes.{{Sfn|Pomeroy|2011|page=14–5}}

A 2012 [[Macdonald-Laurier Institute]] report argued for 40-year amortization options for young buyers in expensive markets and criticized CMHC's [[mortgage insurance]] for generating substantial federal revenues from first-time and lower-income buyers, while also noting that current affordability metrics are too lenient and should consider net, not gross, income and actual household expenses.{{Sfn|Londerville|2012}}

The City of Calgary describes affordable housing in terms of need. A household is in need of affordable housing when it earns less than $60,000/year and spends over 30% of gross income on the cost of housing.{{sfn|City of Calgary Deputy Manager|2022}} Alternatively, mortgage lending institutions define affordability in terms of potential home buyers considering the relative cost of debt based on interest rates and average household incomes. This measure of affordability is not oriented towards renters.{{Sfn|Laird|2007}}{{rp|4}}[[File:Markham-suburbs aerial-edit2.jpg|thumb|A large proportion of Canadians are housed in market-based suburban developments such as Markham, Ontario]]Accurate measurement of housing affordability is needed to decide if a family qualifies for assistance in housing or for a mortgage to purchase privately. While the 30% rule may be used for the latter, banks and lending agencies might require a much higher Qualifying Income before approving a mortgage.{{Sfn|Royal Bank of Canada|2011}}

=== Shelter-cost-to-income ratio ===
The shelter-cost-to-income ratio (STIR), commonly set at no more than 30% of gross household income, is the most frequent benchmark for housing affordability, but definitions and included costs vary and have notable limitations. STIR often fails to capture the true financial burden on lower-income or diverse households, prompting recognition of its shortcomings by organizations like CMHC.{{sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2019}}

===Housing affordability indexes in market-based housing===
The [[Bank of Canada]]'s [[Housing affordability index|Housing Affordability Index]] (HAI), the [[Royal Bank of Canada]] Housing Affordability Measure,{{Sfn|Royal Bank of Canada|2011}} and the [[National Bank of Canada]]'s Housing Affordability Monitor{{Sfn|Dahms|Ducharme|2022}} are examples of indexes used by financial institutions involved in the real estate market. The HAI is based on housing costs, which includes mortgage payments and utilities, in relation to disposable income of a representative household.<ref>{{cite web |work=Bank of Canada |title=Real estate market: Definitions, graphs and data |url=https://www.bankofcanada.ca/rates/indicators/capacity-and-inflation-pressures/real-estate-market-definitions/ |access-date=17 June 2024|date=n.d.}}</ref> The HAI represents the percentage of disposable income the average Canadian household would need to cover the mortgage and utilities of their home.{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2022}} By December 2023, with increases in mortgage rates and the price of houses, the Bank of Canada reported that affordability was the worst since 1982.<ref>{{cite news |first=Craig |last=Lord|date=13 December 2023|title=Housing affordability at worst levels in 41 years, Bank of Canada index shows|work=Global News|access-date=17 June 2024|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/10167093/housing-affordability-bank-canada-index/}}</ref> Since the beginning of the [[COVID-19 pandemic in Canada|COVID-19 pandemic]] in 2020, house prices saw a significant increase of over 34%.<ref>{{Cite news| last = Armstrong| first = Peter| title = Bank of Canada says housing affordability is about boosting supply, not lowering interest rates| work = CBC News| access-date = 17 June 2024| date = 7 February 2024| url = https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/armstrong-housing-bank-of-canada-macklem-1.7106867}}</ref> By 2023, the low supply of housing including rental units, across Canada also caused rents to soar.<ref>{{Cite news| title = Rent prices soared in 2023 as Canada saw lowest vacancy rate on record| work = CBC News| access-date = 2024-06-17| date = 2024-01-31| url = https://www.cbc.ca/news/business/rent-prices-rose-in-2023-1.7100571}}</ref> By 2022, with an unexpected demand coupled with a diminishing supply of residential real estate along with historically low interest rates{{emdash}}set during the pandemic to stabilize the economy{{emdash}}the price of housing rose sky high in Canada. The ''BBC'' said that Canada faced some "of the worst housing affordability issues in the world." Based on [[OECD]] data, the "disconnect" between the average home price{{emdash}}$817,000{{emdash}}and household incomes is "one of the most dramatic". The price represents over "nine times household income."{{sfn|BBC|2022}}

==Current situation==

===Financialization of housing===
According to research by housing expert Steve Pomeroy, Canada experienced a significant decline in private rental housing between 2011 and 2016 due chiefly to the [[financialization]] of housing, with over 300,000 units disappearing from the market and fewer than 20,000 new subsidized units added.<ref>{{cite report| publisher = Focus Consulting| last = Polmeroy| first = Steve| title = Why Canada needs a non-market rental acquisition strategy| location = Ottawa, Ontario| access-date = 2024-11-21| date = May 2020| url = https://www.focus-consult.com/why-canada-needs-a-non-market-rental-acquisition-strategy/}}</ref> The financialization of housing refers to the use of housing by [[Real Estate Investment Trusts]] (REIT) and [[private equity]] as a profit-making financial instrument.<ref name="Simms_20230116">{{cite news| last = Simms| first = Tom| title = Financialization of housing must be confronted | work = Winnipeg Free Press |via= Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives| location = Winnipeg, Manitoba| access-date = 3 July 2024| date = 16 January 2023| url = https://policyalternatives.ca/publications/commentary/financialization-housing-must-be-confronted}}</ref> Financialized landlords include large corporations such as Avenue Living and MainStreet that engage in en masse purchasing of undervalued rental apartments. These units that were previously affordable for lower income households, are upgraded as higher-end rental units.<ref name="Simms_20230116"/><ref name="Medi_20240630">{{Cite report| last = Medi| first = Lynn| title = Housing policy news: June 2024| work = Canadian Centre for Housing Rights| access-date = 3 July 2024| date = 30 June 2024| url = https://housingrightscanada.com/housing-policy-news-june-2024/}}</ref>

In May and June 2024, during a series of House of Commons hearings on the financialization of housing, Federal Housing Advocate, [[Marie-Josée Houle]], said that it is widespread and increasing, has "very little oversight", and a "negative impact on housing in Canada". According to Houle, who reports to the [[Canadian Human Rights Commission]], it contributes to deteriorating housing conditions and affordability of housing, displacements, and evictions.<ref name="Zapata_20230802">{{Cite news| last = Zapata| first = Karina| title = Housing advocates say big money is transforming rental markets. And Alberta could be a poster child| work = CBC News| access-date = 3 July 2024| date = 2 August 2023| url = https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/calgary/financialization-of-housing-alberta-1.6921645}}</ref>

In a CBC ''[[The Fifth Estate (TV program)|Fifth Estate]]'' episode{{sfn|Malik|Luck|2022}} and accompanying ''[[CBC News]]'' article investigating how Canada had fallen into a "rental crisis", which could affect a third of the Canadian population, they found that one of the major factors considered was the financialization of the rental housing sector.{{sfn|Luck|Pierce|Angelovski|Malik|2022}} The investigation found that municipality and city systems view these practices as an advantageous revenue stream, facilitating these systemic opportunities driven by individual gain, capitalizing on the absence of regulations and market conditions.{{sfn|Nethercote|2020}}{{sfn|Dachis|2023}}{{sfn|Kalman-Lamb|2017}} CBC while examined the issue from the point of view of renters{{emdash}}single parents, large families, pensioners and others on fixed or low incomes, young people starting their careers{{emdash}}who felt that their voices were not being heard.{{sfn|Luck|Pierce|Angelovski|Malik|2022}}{{sfn|Malik|Luck|2022}}

In a ''Fifth Estate'' interview, Calgary-based Michael Brooks—CEO of Real Property Association of Canada (REALPAC), which lobbies the federal government on behalf of Canada's largest commercial real estate companies—said that the private sector was not "primarily in the business of providing a public good," such as affordable housing.{{sfn|Malik|Luck|2022}} The private sector is "self-interested in maintaining and growing their income." They "want to be seen as contributing to the solution and not being part of the problem." Their obligations are to their investors, which includes managing costs.{{sfn|Malik|Luck|2022}} REALPAC members, an association that was established in 1970, comprised $1 trillion in [[assets under management]] across Canada by 2022.{{sfn|Sokic|2022}}

The [[Brookings Institution]] lists [[real estate investment trust]]s (REITS), along with large Canadian banks, and multinational corporations as the "most reliable dividend payers" and recommends that pensioners invest in these financial instruments.{{sfn|Jackson|2022}} During the pandemic, REITs and other financial landlords "thrived" with individual REITs posting 100s of millions in profits in the first three months alone. They benefited from the historically low interest rates backed by the CMHC to buy and sell multi-family residential buildings, refinance debt, do renovations that allowed them to raise rents.{{sfn|August|2021}}

===Residential land use by-laws===
The role of municipalities in housing policy is significant, particularly in setting policies related to zoning, land-use, and in the prevention of homelessness. At times, financial constraints come into play as well, since their primary funding source for housing strategies is often property taxes.{{sfn|Meissner|2022}}{{Sfn|Eidelman|Hachard|Slack|2022}}{{rp|3}}

In response to the federal government's 2023 $4-billion Housing Accelerator Fund, municipalities have been amending land use by-laws to allow for more flexibility in zoning in order to claim federal funding tied to zoning changes.<ref name="Uday_20231028">{{Cite news| last = Rana| first = Uday| title = Can a zoning 'revolution' save Canada from a housing crisis?| work = Global News| access-date = 4 July 2024| date = 28 October 2023| url = https://globalnews.ca/news/10051121/canada-housing-zoning-changes}}</ref>

The provincial and territorial governments provide the most funding for housing and they determine limits on municipal governments. Provinces and territories establish their own regulatory framework for housing and set their own laws which can restrict what municipalities can do.{{Sfn|Eidelman|Hachard|Slack|2022}} However, the federal government provides funding to provinces, territories, and occasionally directly to municipalities through bilateral agreements. A 2022 report by the [[University of Toronto]]'s Institute on Municipal Finance and Governance calls for more co-operation between levels of government to respond to the affordability crisis in housing.{{Sfn|Hachard |Eidelman|Riaz|2022|page=3}}{{Sfn|Meissner|2022}}

In a 2018 ''[[Journal of the American Planning Association]]'' article, four researchers described how the changing role of government in Canada since the 1970s affected affordable housing for those with lower incomes.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}} Public policies since the 1970s favoured more market-based solutions, and as a result the government's role in providing social services was reduced, including in the provision of affordable housing for those with lower incomes.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}} Public policies—such as "[[inclusionary zoning]], density bonuses, and [[housing trust]]s" introduced at that time in some municipalities in the United States to reduce housing affordability pressures for lower income earners—were not adopted in Canada at the same rate.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}} The authors said that in the absence of any adequate policies to balance housing needs of those whose ability to pay is constrained with the market's natural tendency to provide housing to those who can afford to pay, led the growth of developments in central locations where amenities are rich for homebuyers whose incomes were increasingly higher than lower income earners.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}}

Research from the 2018 study showed that there is a "disconnect between evidence and public policy" in terms of urban planning based on promoting increased density and mixed-use zoning in cities like Toronto.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}}{{Sfn|Haider|Moranis|2018}} An unintended negative consequence of these "quintessential tenets of good urban design, has been a decrease in affordable housing.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}}{{Sfn|Haider|Moranis|2018}} The article showed that in mixed-use zones, high-income earners in sectors such as "management, business, technology, and health" experienced greater housing affordability{{emdash}}they spent a smaller percentage of their income on housing even with higher priced housing because their incomes had increased. Housing affordability worsened for those with occupations in manufacturing, trades and cultural and social services. Their incomes had either remained stagnant or decreased over time and/or housing costs had increased.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}}{{Sfn|Haider|Moranis|2018}} While this study focused on Toronto, the findings would be similar in other major census metropolitan areas (CMAs) like Vancouver.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}}

Housing economists have cautioned against attributing housing unaffordability primarily to immigration levels. Following renewed political attention to record immigration rates amid the housing crisis, a January 2024 [[CBC News]] analysis found that economists and housing experts identified high interest rates, increasing construction costs, and municipal red tape slowing housing approvals as concurrent pressures on the housing market.{{sfn|Zimonjic|2024}} [[David Hulchanski|David Hulchanski]], a professor of housing and community development at the [[University of Toronto]], questioned whether policy should require newcomers to settle only where housing supply exists, since immigrants are free to choose where they live.{{sfn|Zimonjic|2024}}

A February 2026 [[Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|CMHC]] study, drawing on data from more than 400 municipalities, found that municipal land-use regulation was independently associated with higher home prices: a 10% increase in a city's regulatory restrictiveness was associated with an approximately 14% increase in house prices, after accounting for population, density, and growth.{{sfn|Once|2026}}{{sfn|CMHC|2026}}

==History==
===Early 20th century===
Following the [[Great Depression]] and [[World War II]] many Canadians lived in inadequate housing as fewer new homes were built, older homes needed repairs, and families lived in over-crowded dwellings.{{sfn|Hulchanski|2009}} The 1935 ''[[Dominion Housing Act]]'' (DHA) established the focus of federal policies on housing programs as market-oriented (as opposed to social welfare-oriented) for decades to come.{{sfn|Hulchanski|1986}}{{rp|19}} For example, the DHA included no subsidized low rental housing; instead it introduced a joint government private lender mortgage loans for the 20% of Canadians who could afford to purchase real estate in the marketplace. During the post-WWII period federal housing policy included using taxation to revitalize the housing market, while also building social housing and subsidizing rental housing in the private sector.{{sfn|Hulchanski|2009}}

In 1946, the federal Wartime Housing Corporation was replaced with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation{{emdash}}now known as [[Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation]] (CMHC){{emdash}}a federal [[Crown corporations of Canada|Crown corporation]]. The CMHC administered the ''[[National Housing Act (Canada)|National Housing Act]]'' providing Canadians with grants, loans to purchase homes in the market system, and with mortgage insurance on credit financing through private lenders.{{sfn|McAfee|2006}} In the late 1940s the federal government provided 75% of funding and subsidies, with the provinces adding 25%, towards public social and rental housing for low-income families.{{sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2014}}

In the 1950s, municipalities received federal grants towards urban renewal projects which included low-rent housing developments, some of which included rent-geared-to-income (RGI) subsidies. With the introduction of the CMHC's Mortgage Loan Insurance, home ownership became more accessible. The federally backed insurance allowed homebuyers and private mortgage providers to take a greater risk on mortgages that had a 25% [[down payment]].{{sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2014}}

From the 1950s to the 1970s, the government built "dedicated affordable rental stock and public housing".{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}}

During the 1960s, Canada's economy grew at a sustained pace.{{Sfn|Yalnizyan|2010}}{{rp|22}} In the mid-1960s, Prime Minister [[Lester Pearson]] said that in a democratic society the goal must be for everyone to have "decent housing."{{sfn|Hulchanski|2009}}{{rp|2}} In the 1970s, public housing policy obligation was based on ensuring all Canadians were adequately housed. Through amendments to the National Housing Act in 1973, 20,000 social housing units were built every year.{{sfn|Hulchanski|2009}}{{rp|2}}

During the [[Premiership of Pierre Trudeau|Premiership of Pierre Elliot Trudeau]], then-Minister of Urban Affairs [[Ron Basford]] introduced the amended ''National Housing Act'' by saying, "When we talk about people's basic needs{{emdash}}the requirements for survival{{emdash}}society and the government obviously have an obligation to assure that these basic needs of shelter are met." Housing strategies focused on "rehousing people into better housing and neighbourhoods."{{sfn|Hulchanski|2010}}

Before 1970, almost all housing policy was federal and only 5% of government programs were dedicated to low-income housing.<ref name="Begin_199901"/> Starting in the early 1970s, for almost two decades there were approximately 16,000 non-profit or co-op homes built or acquired every year.{{sfn|St. Denis|2022}}{{sfn|Hulchanski|2010}} In the next ten years, the number of residential co-operatives dropped to about 1,500 homes a year.{{sfn|St. Denis|2022}} This began to change in the 1970s, as government role was reduced.{{Sfn|Moos|Vinodrai|Revington|Seasons|2018}}

=== 1980s ===
Under the Canadian Constitution, housing policy and programs are the responsibility of the provinces. In practice the federal government, along with the provinces and municipalities, share the responsibility.<ref name="Begin_199901">{{Cite report|first=Patricia |last=Begin|work=Political and Social Affairs Division|date=January 1999|number=PRB99–1E| title = Housing and Parliamentary Action | access-date = 3 July 2024| url = https://publications.gc.ca/Collection-R/LoPBdP/modules/prb99-1-homelessness/housing-e.htm}}</ref>

Starting in the 1980s, federal housing policies changed and more households across Canada began to experience housing affordability pressures, including those who own the residences in which they live and those who rent. Under the premiership of [[Brian Mulroney]] significant cuts to federal housing programs were initiated, effectively ending many national initiatives for affordable housing. In 1984, the federal government began cutting back on social housing.{{sfn|Hulchanski|2009}}{{rp|2}}{{efn|In the late 1980s, housing policy debates in the United Kingdom shifted away from discussion of housing need to more market-oriented analyses of affordability (Whitehead 1991:12).}}

Around that time, the concept of "core housing need" was developed by the [[Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation]] as a basis for evaluating those eligible for federal funding under the 1986 Global Agreements on Social Housing, an agreement between the federal and provincial/territorial governments regarding administration and cost sharing of social housing programs under the ''National Housing Act'' and the ''CMHC Act''.{{sfn|Pomeroy|2011}}{{sfn|Pomeroy|2017a}} A household is considered to be in core housing need if it meets certain criteria{{emdash}}if it falls below acceptable standards of affordability, adequacy, or suitability and if the cost of housing exceeds 30% or more of its before-tax household income.{{Citation needed|date=April 2023}}

There was a consistent increase in housing affordability problems starting in the early 1980s in "all regions and major cities" and for almost all social classes of Canadian households, according to a 2004 article in the ''Housing Studies'' journal.{{Sfn|Moore|Skaburskis|2004}} Affordability problems were "highly concentrated" in low-income households, particularly in households led by women.{{Sfn|Moore|Skaburskis|2004}}

In the late 1980s, there was a major shift in housing policies, which included amendments to taxation that benefitted those who could afford homeownership. At the same time, the federal government withdrew from funding projects for social and affordable housing resulting in a dramatic decline in affordable housing stock.{{sfn|Gaetz|Gullier|Richter|2014|page=10–11}} There was a "massive investment" in building houses and condominiums and a dramatic decline in purpose-built rental apartment units.{{sfn|Gaetz|Gullier|Richter|2014|page=10–11}} Investors purchased some condos for rental units but rents were priced at the "higher end of market"{{sfn|Gaetz|Gullier|Richter|2014|page=10–11}} and were affordable only for households with higher incomes.

=== 1990s ===
During the 1990s, there was a devolution of new responsibilities, including affordable housing, from provincial governments to municipal governments without adequate revenue tools.{{Sfn|Canadian Federation of Municipalities|2011}} Since the early 1990s, the responsibility of providing support for affordable housing, and a number of other social issues related to the environment, [[Indigenous peoples in Canada|Indigenous Peoples]] ([[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]], [[Inuit in Canada|Inuit]], and [[Métis]]), public health and security, had been down-loaded with no increase in sources of funding.{{Citation needed|date=April 2023}}

In the 1990s, although the price of houses remained "remarkably stable," [[income inequality]] increased and housing affordability problems became more prevalent and more severe.{{Sfn|Moore|Skaburskis|2004}} Throughout the decade, the federal government was focused on cutting the federal [[Deficit spending|deficit]], and began to transfer responsibility to supply social housing for those in need{{emdash}}including low-income housing{{emdash}}to the provinces and territories.{{Sfn|Hulchanski|2009}} The provinces and territories transferred some of these responsibilities to municipalities without providing corresponding financial resources.{{Sfn|Canadian Federation of Municipalities|2011}}

By 1991, Canadian public policy on the affordability of housing was more aligned with the concept of need than [[Housing in the United Kingdom|in the United Kingdom]] in the 1980s, for example, where the concept of affordability was more market-oriented.{{Sfn|Whitehead|1991}}{{efn|In the United Kingdom for example since the late 1980s, housing policy debates shifted away from discussion of housing need to more market-oriented analyses of affordability (Whitehead 1991-12).}}

By 1996, the federal government revoked the [[Canada Assistance Plan]] of 1966, which made it mandatory that people whose income was inadequate to meet basic needs (including the [[working poor]]) have access to an established appeals procedures in the provinces and territories regarding social assistance.{{Sfn|Hick|1998}} In the same year, the federal government transferred responsibility for most existing federal housing program to the provinces.{{Sfn|Hulchanski|2009}}{{sfn|Kothari|2009}}{{rp|9}}

Between 1993 and 2003, while federal government revenues increased 12% and the provinces and territories increased 13%, municipalities' revenues only increased by 8%.{{Sfn|Canadian Federation of Municipalities|2011}} From 1993 to 2004, federal and provincial fiscal transfers to municipalities decreased from 25 cents per dollar of municipal revenue to 16 cents, representing a decrease of 37% while their responsibilities had increased resulting in a fiscal imbalance.{{Sfn|Canadian Federation of Municipalities|2011}}

Also in the 1990s, [[real estate investment trust]]s (REITs), hedge funds, private equity firms, and publicly listed real estate firms entered the urban rental market in large North American cities, and later on nationally and in other anglophone countries like the United Kingdom, Australia, and Ireland; for the next 15 years they expanded exponentially.{{sfn|Nethercote|2020}} REITs emerged in Canada when the ''Canadian Income Tax Act'' in 1995 allowed REITs to qualify as closed-end trusts,<ref>{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1142/S0219091506000793| issn = 0219-0915| volume = 09| issue = 3| pages = 441–462| last = Assaf| first = Ata| title = Canadian REITs and Stock Prices: Fractional Cointegration and Long Memory| journal = Review of Pacific Basin Financial Markets and Policies| access-date = 2022-04-29| date = September 2006| url = https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0219091506000793| url-access = subscription}}</ref> with the first REIT established in Canada being in 1997 in Toronto. In the 15 years between 2000 and 2015, the ownership of Toronto apartments was increasingly concentrated among REITs, institutional investors, private equity funds and some large family-owned firms.{{sfn|August|Walks|2018}}{{sfn|Nethercote|2020}}

=== 2000s ===
Since 2000 the cost of renting increased by more than 20%.{{sfn|Federation of Canadian Municipalities|2012}}

To support affordable housing in 2001, the [[Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation]] introduced Canada Mortgage Bonds, with a focus on low-cost interest rates and mortgages.{{sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2014}}

The Affordable Housing Initiative (AHI), operating from 2001 to 2011, was an intergovernmental multilateral housing initiative on affordable housing in Canada.{{sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2011d}} The federal government, working through the CMHC, provided funding for the supply of new affordable rental housing under the Affordable Housing Program with CA$1 billion from 2001 to 2008 (to be matched by provinces and territories).{{efn|The federal government promised to invest an additional CAD$1.9 billion from 2008 to 2013 for housing and homelessness programs for low-income Canadians.}} The federal government placed the AHI within the Affordable Housing Framework 2011–2014 to improve "access to affordable, sound, suitable and sustainable housing."{{Sfn|Canada's Economic Action Plan|2011}} The Framework acknowledged that a wide range of solutions was required to respond to the diversity of affordable housing program needs and priorities specific to each jurisdiction. Under the Framework, it was reiterated that the responsibility for the design and delivery of affordable housing programs lay with the provinces and territories. The provinces and territories would be given flexibility in how to invest federal funds that were to be matched by provinces and territories, if the overall intended outcome was reached. The goal was "to reduce the number of Canadians in housing need by improving access to affordable housing that is sound, suitable and sustainable" Examples of initiatives that could be undertaken under the Framework included "new construction, renovation, homeownership assistance, rent supplements, shelter allowances, and accommodations for victims of family violence."{{Sfn|CMHC|2011a}}

A 2003 ''TD Economic'' report recommended that government initiatives should focus on raising market incomes at the lower end, as the number of low-income households was too high. The report raised concerns about low-income households that were subject to provincial and federal claw backs and tax backs, for example, on back to work and the federal-provincial [[National Child Benefit]] (NCB).{{Sfn|TD Economics|2003}} The report said that decreasing the number of low income household would be more effective than the inefficient, expensive, publicly funded expenditure-based or tax-based incentives to increase the number of affordable rental units.{{Sfn|TD Economics|2003}}

The TD report concluded that municipalities need a more sustainable funding arrangement, and provinces need to play a more active role in affordable housing, becoming leaders within the [[Affordable Housing Framework]] agreement.{{Sfn|TD Economics|2003}}

By 2004, 1.7 million Canadians experienced housing affordability issues.{{Sfn|Laird|2007}}{{rp|4}}

{{As of |2006}}, the CMHC directed those needing subsidized housing for low-income households to the municipal government.{{Sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2006}} In 2011 the [[Canadian Federation of Municipalities]] called for better coordination between the three levels of government as the expanded responsibilities were either "unfunded or underfunded."{{Sfn|Canadian Federation of Municipalities|2011|page=1}}

The number of rental units declined starting in 2005.{{Sfn|Federation of Canadian Municipalities|2012}}

The [[2006 Canadian federal budget]] "provided $300 million for affordable housing in the territories."{{Sfn|Government of Canada|2011}}

By 2007, affordability of housing was a problem for low and middle income Canadians.{{Sfn|Laird|2007}}{{rp|4}} Canadians in the lowest quintile who were in renters households were 18 times more likely than the average household to experience affordability problems.{{Sfn|Laird|2007}}{{rp|4}}{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2006a}}

With historically low interest rates, and readily available debt and mortgage financing in 2007, Canada's housing market was in a period of strong growth. Affordable housing was a relative measure.{{Sfn|Laird|2007}} At the same time private affordable rental stock across Canada was low. In many cities the vacancy rate for affordable rental units was less than 1%.{{Sfn|Laird|2007}}{{rp|36}}

According to reports in 2006 and 2010, rising income inequality has been cited as a contributing factor.{{Sfn|Yalnizyan|2010}}{{Sfn|Drummond|Tulk|2006}}

From 2009 through 2014, the federal government budgeted $388 million a year for the housing sector.{{sfn|Pomeroy|2017}}

The [[2009 Canadian federal budget]] allocated funds for the period covering 2009–2011: renovation and energy retrofits to social housing ($1 billion); to build housing for low-income seniors ($400 million); to build social housing for persons with disabilities ($75 million); to support social housing in the North ($200 million); low-cost loans to municipalities to improve housing-related infrastructure ($2 billion) as part of Canada's Economic Action Plan.

=== 2010s ===
{{As of|2010}}, housing prices and construction costs rose dramatically in Canada as they did elsewhere in the world.{{Sfn|Yalnizyan|2010}}

There was a modest improvement in housing affordability across Canada in the third quarter of 2011 after two consecutive quarters of deterioration. Part of this was due to decreased costs in home ownership resulting from lower mortgage rates.{{Sfn|Royal Bank of Canada|2011}}

By 2012, the rising inequality gap had presented a significant challenge for Canadian households who were "priced out" of rental and ownership housing markets.{{Sfn|Shapcott|2012}} By that year, there was a slight deterioration in housing affordability, according to the [[Royal Bank of Canada]] (RBC).{{Sfn|Royal Bank of Canada|2012}}{{efn|RBC measures erosion, deterioration and/or improvements in affordability of housing in terms of levels of ease or difficulty for Canadians to carry the costs of home ownership comparing price, mortgage rate, utilities and taxes and income while also considering fundamentals such as supply-and-demand and market slowdown. Vigorous housing demand raises prices if supply has not kept pace. RBC also examines soft factors such as weather; mild weather, for example, motivates consumer demand for housing (RBC 2012-08).}}

Many parts of the country that year also reported that key workers—teachers, nurses, police officers, construction workers and others—who earned reasonably good income from their professions, were finding it increasingly difficult to afford the high cost of housing."{{Sfn|Shapcott|2012}} According to a 2012 report by the [[Federation of Canadian Municipalities]], one third of Canadians were renters. The construction and rehabilitation of affordable rental units did not kept pace with the number of affordable rental units lost to demolition, urban intensification projects and the more profitable conversion to condominiums. Fewer than 10% of new housing starts by 2012 were rental units.{{Sfn|Federation of Canadian Municipalities|2012}} The FCA found that the shortage of available rental housing is worsening at the same time that more Canadians are being priced out of home ownership.{{Sfn|Federation of Canadian Municipalities|2012}}

In 2012, while Canada had a strong real estate market{{Sfn|Canadian Press|2012}} many Canadian households faced [[housing insecurity]].

At the 2018 National Housing Conference hosted by the CMHC, concerns were raised about a stark increase in the financialization of the housing sector that had extended into the private rental market.{{sfn|Markovich|2018}}{{rp|6}} Canadian Federation of Apartment Associations disagreed with the premise, and described conference featured speakers as "progressives."{{sfn|Canadian Federation of Apartment Associations|2019}} Issues included the rise of "amateur landlords," condominiums, [[Airbnb]], [[short-term rental]]s, increased rents, and problems with evictions. Multiple-residential buildings are being purchased as housing assets to generate wealth at a time when rental units are in short supply.{{sfn|Markovich|2018}}{{rp|6}}

The [[2022 Canadian federal budget|2022 federal budget]], released on April 7, called for a review of tax treatment for large corporate trusts that use residential real estate as financial investment instruments. This review would examine the impact of housing as an asset class on Canadian homebuyers and renters.{{sfn|Sun Life Global Investments Tax & Estate Planning Team|2022}} The budget also included $1.5 billion for [[housing cooperative]]s as part of the solution to the affordable housing crisis.{{sfn|St. Denis|2022}} From the early 1990s to 2020, 25 of the biggest financial landlords{{emdash}}including REITs{{emdash}}consolidated about 330,000 rental suites representing 20% of Canada's "private, purpose-built stock of rental apartments."{{sfn|August|2021}} As of 2021, REITs and other financial landlords benefit from preferential tax treatment, which Martine August described as state subsidies. August has called on the CMHC to stop providing financial landlords with "preferential mortgage lending rates", which are effectively subsidies to firms that are not providing public good. She also calls on the federal government to disallow financial landlords form accessing National Housing Strategy loans and grants since these firms "eliminate affordable housing as a business strategy."{{sfn|August|2021}}

=== 2020s ===
The 2020 report on the 2018 Survey revealed that 1,644,900 Canadian households or 11.6% were in core housing need,{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2020}} compared to 12.7% reported in the [[2016 Canadian census]].{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2017}} In 2016, the Canadian regions with the most households experiencing core housing need included [[Nunavut]] at 36.5%, [[Northwest Territories]] at 15.5%, [[Ontario]] at 15.3%, and [[Yukon]] at 15.2%.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2017}} The 2016 Census also showed that the highest rates of core housing need in metropolitan areas were [[Toronto]] at 19.1% and [[Vancouver]] at 17.6%.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2017}}

By May 2021, the price of housing increased with a "rapid acceleration," the supply of housing and mortgage rates were at historic lows and the demand increased, with economists at the [[Royal Bank of Canada]] and the [[Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce]] raising concerns that speculators were entering the market, pricing young and lower income families out of affordable housing.{{sfn|Hagan|Hertzberg|2021}} With 424 housing units per 1,000 people, Canada ranks lowest of the [[G7|G7 nations]]{{efn|Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK and the United States are members of the G7, an organisation of the seven largest economies, that play a dominant role in the international financial system and trade.}} in "average housing supply per capita" compared to France, which has 540 units per 1,000{{emdash}}the largest housing supply per capita. Within Canada, the available housing supply inventory is the lowest on record.{{sfn|Hagan|Hertzberg|2021}} It reflects a chronic insufficiency of home supply. From 2016 to 2021, the population of Canada increased to about 37 million with the arrival of 1.8 million new residents who often prefer to live in the "downtowns and distant suburbs of large cities."{{sfn|Gordon|2022}}

The [[COVID-19 pandemic in Canada|COVID-19 pandemic]] exacerbated housing pressures including the unpredicted preference for housing type and geographic location.{{sfn|Perrault|2021}} During the pandemic, in February 2022, it was reported that the Canadian housing market was experiencing an unexpected boom with record-breaking high prices, combined with historically low interest rates and a decreasing supply of real estate. In both 2020 and 2021 real estate sales records were broken. By the end of 2021, the MLS Home [[Price index|Price Index]] was a record  25.3% higher than 2020.{{sfn|Drudi|2022}} During the pandemic, inter-provincial migration was also strong and continued into 2022, which also contributed to high prices.{{sfn|Drudi|2022}}

In the [[2022 Canadian federal budget|2022 federal budget]], "A Plan to Grow Our Economy and Make Life More Affordable", released on April 7, the federal government responded to concerns about the role of the speculative market in sky-high real estate prices. A two-year ban on "foreign buyers" was introduced.{{sfn| Younglai|2022}}<ref>{{Cite news |last=Gordon |first=Julie |date=2021-12-21 |title=Canada should temporarily ban foreign home buyers, rezone cities - housing minister |language=en |work=Reuters |url=https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/canada-should-temporarily-ban-foreign-home-buyers-rezone-cities-housing-minister-2021-12-21/ }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-01-01 |title=Consolidated federal laws of Canada, Prohibition on the Purchase of Residential Property by Non-Canadians Act |url=https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-25.2/page-1.html |website=Department of Justice Canada}}</ref> However, the ban was restricted to purchases without plans to develop housing in 2023 federal budget, on the grounds of stimulating housing construction.<ref>{{Cite web |last=McDowell |first=Connor |date=2023-03-29 |title=Canada repeals some bans on foreigners buying property |url=https://tnc.news/2023/03/29/foreigners-property/ |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Research and observations ==
Eighty per cent of Canadians are served by market-based housing, which includes individual home ownership and private rental housing.{{Sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|nd}} In the market-based housing system, individuals finance their own housing, independent of government assistance.

A 2019 Royal Bank of Canada RBC Economics report on home affordability said that, in 9 of the 14 market areas they track, a majority of Canadian families are able to purchase an average home.{{Sfn|Royal Bank of Canada|2019}} The most affordable markets are Saint John, St. John's, Regina, Quebec City and Halifax, while the least affordable markets are Vancouver, Toronto, and Victoria.

[[Statistics Canada]] reported that, while Canada's "[[real gross domestic product]] (GDP) per capita increased by roughly 50% between 1980 and 2005," and the workforce increased educational attainment and work experience during this same period and median earnings among the top 20% of full-time full-year employees grew by 17.9%, among those in the bottom one-fifth of the distribution median earnings decreased by 13.3%."{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2006}} Full-time full-year median earnings of Canadians edged only slightly higher from $41,348 in 1980 to $41,401 in 2005.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2006}}

Ryerson City Building Institute's research and policy manager Graham Haines in Toronto said in 2017 that Canadian policymakers had focused almost exclusively on promoting home ownership since the late 1990s creating a pattern of building housing units, like [[Condominium|condos]], for investors rather than the end users{{emdash}}the renters. By "letting the market do what the market wants," Canada neglected the needs of its population, Haines wrote.
