This resulted in a decades-long decline in the supply of [[Purpose-built village|purpose-built]] rental apartments as developers preferred to build condominiums especially with favourable tax policies and incentives in place. Haines said that as millennials reach an age where they are ready to become homebuyers they may well be competing for the same condominiums as seniors who want to downsize.{{sfn|Press|2017}} Haines called for public policy changes that favour the construction of appropriate rental units that are affordable for those who will be using them, recognizing that rent will be a significant part of the real estate sector in Canada.{{sfn|Press|2017}}

In a 2020 ''Housing Studies'' article, Megan Nethercote, a Vice Chancellor's research fellow at [[RMIT University]], investigated the financialization of rental housing in the private real estate market. She expressed her concern regarding the paucity of literature on the provision of social or affordable housing provision, despite the significance of the expansion of the private rental sector on affordable housing. REITs are highly recommended as among the most reliable payers of dividends for their investors, particularly for pensioners and others who need safe investments. During the pandemic REITs thrived as they benefit from low mortgage rates and other CMHC grants and loans, and experienced significant growth in the private rental market in crisis.{{sfn|Nethercote|2020}} They convert older apartments to condos or higher rental units, and housing experts evaluate success of their business model is based on eliminating affordable rental housing.

In its 2016 second quarter report [[Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation]] warned housing prices are [[Overvaluation|overvalued]] in 9 Canadian markets, with [[Vancouver]] at high risk.
Strong evidence of "problematic conditions" also continue to exist in [[Toronto]], [[Calgary]], [[Saskatoon]] and [[Regina, Saskatchewan|Regina]], while in [[Ottawa]] "problematic conditions" are weak.{{Sfn|Marr|2016}}

By Q3 2021, 37.1% of disposable income was needed to pay for housing costs, which represents an increase of 5.2 points in 2021, the highest ratio since 2008.{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2022}} In 2008, the average home prices were much lower than in 2021 and the interest rates were 5 points higher than the Bank of Canada's 2021 rate, which was near zero.{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2022}}

==Affordable housing for Indigenous communities==
Housing is said to be one of a number of [[social determinants of health]] (SDH), along with poverty, employment, income, education, social support networks, physical environments, early child development, gender and social capital, that prevent [[Indigenous peoples in Canada]] ([[First Nations in Canada|First Nations]], [[Inuit]], and [[Métis]]) from achieving [[health equity]] with other Canadians.{{sfn|Kolahdooz|Nader|Yi|Sharma|2015}} According to a 2015 [[meta-analysis]] by a team of [[University of Alberta]] and [[Memorial University of Newfoundland|Memorial University]] researchers, sources in their systematic review indicated that [[Indigenous peoples in Alberta]] were more likely to have a "limited affordability for dwellings" and to "live in dwellings with inappropriate housing conditions and private spaces."{{sfn|Kolahdooz|Nader|Yi|Sharma|2015}} As of 2016, First Nations, Inuit, and Metis households lived in "inadequate and insufficient" housing; this was recognized as a critical problem across Canada.{{sfn|Richmond|Cook|2016}}

Prior to the 1950s, [[Inuit]] lived semi-nomadic lives, moving from hunting camps to fishing camps. In the 1950s, federal government agencies promised Inuit quality housing to convince them to move into permanent [[Hamlet (place)|hamlets]] across what was then part of the [[Northwest Territories]].{{sfn|Igloliorte|2014}} During the Qikiqtani Truth Commission undertaken by the Qikiqtani Inuit Association, Inuit testified repeatedly that the promises of quality housing were not kept.{{sfn|Igloliorte|2014}} The government did not consult with Inuit in regards to "appropriate and affordable housing."{{sfn|Igloliorte|2014}} The first federal rent-to-own housing program began in 1959 as The Eskimo Housing Loan Program, which offered low-cost 16' x 16' Rigid Frame poorly constructed buildings with no reflection of Inuit lifestyle, that were quickly called "matchbox" houses.{{sfn|Igloliorte|2014}} The payment plan was for 7 to 10 years at $15 monthly.{{sfn|Qaqqaq|2021a}} Even at this price these houses were unaffordable as most "Inuit subsisted on hunting and seasonal employment."{{sfn|Igloliorte|2014}} With the collapse of the Loan Program in 1965, new complex rental systems administered
by housing councils were introduced.{{sfn|Igloliorte|2014}} As of 2021, in [[Nunavut]] there were 5,600 public housing units with rents geared to income managed by the Nunavut Housing Corporation (NHC) with more than 20,000 tenants.{{sfn|Qaqqaq|2021a}} This is one facet of the way in which Nunavut has been addressing housing issues.{{sfn|Qaqqaq|2021a}} Nunavut's housing challenges are complex and are dealt with using "multi-faceted approaches." This includes "trauma-informed policies and programs" which are necessary to respond to "[[intergenerational trauma]] from forced relocation and [[Canadian Indian residential school system|residential schools]]" which impact "socio-economic conditions in Nunavut."{{sfn|Qaqqaq|2021a}} In a 2021 podcast, [[Mumilaaq Qaqqaq]], a former MP for Nunavut, described the three-week tour to Nunavut hamlets to report on the housing crisis first hand.{{sfn|Qaqqaq|2021b}} She reported on multi-generational families living in over-crowded, drafty, mould-ridden houses that had not been repaired or renovated in years.{{sfn|Qaqqaq|2021a}}

Following in-depth media reports critical on the lack of action on the part of the federal government, a comprehensive study of Indigenous housing in Canada was commissioned resulting in the 1992 report, ''A Time for Action: Aboriginal and Northern Housing''. The report said that about 50% of 70,000 houses on reserve houses were "unfit" as residences and called for the "immediate construction of 21,700 new homes." The report said that 6,700 homes needed to be replaced, while about 44,500 houses "required substantial repairs." The cost at that time was estimated at $2.1 billion.{{sfn|Belanger|2016}}

Following 18 months of talks on improving access to housing, employment, health services, and education, the Government of Canada, First Ministers of the Provinces, Territorial Leaders, and the leaders of five national Aboriginal organizations signed a series of agreements in 2005, known as the [[Kelowna Accord]] with a five-year $5-billion plan to "improve the lives of First Nations, Métis and Inuit."{{sfn|CBC News|2006b}} It would have included $1.6 billion for housing. Housing on reserves is considered a federal responsibility due to treaty rights. In the first budget during the [[Premiership of Stephen Harper]], who did not endorse the Accord made with the Whigs, the 2006 budget allocated only $150 million to finance housing, education, clean water, and other services for First Nations, Métis, and Inuit.{{sfn|CBC News|2006a}} The Harper government, instead, introduced a "market-based solution" to the housing crisis on reserves in 2008{{emdash}}the First Nations Market Housing Fund{{emdash}}to help individual First Nations households purchase homes on reserves with a goal of "25,000 privately owned dwellings by 2018". This action marked an effort to further emphasize the privatization of indigenous housing that had been initiated in the mid-1980s. Its aim was to lessen the federal government's role and responsibilities in housing matters for indigenous communities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Collings |first=Peter |date=2005 |title=Housing Policy, Aging, and Life Course Construction in a Canadian Inuit Community |journal=Arctic Anthropology |volume=42 |issue=2 |pages=50–65 |doi=10.1353/arc.2011.0037 |jstor=40316646 |pmid=21847837 |s2cid=16417468 |issn=0066-6939}}</ref> In 2008, the federal government allocated a one-time investment of $300 million without consulting the First Nations about the introduction of a new housing concept. From 2008 to 2015 the fund grew to $344 million through non-housing investments. Administrative costs, stipends, and travel expenses total about $3.6 million per year, and over eight years, only 99 homes were built, indicating that the market-based solution was a [[Market failure|failure]]. [[Pierre Poilievre]] was the minister responsible for the CMHC at that time, the agency that managed the Fund. [[Bernard Valcourt]], then Minister of Aboriginal Affairs, was also involved.{{sfn|Beeby|2015}}

==Home ownership in Canada==
{{Further|Land ownership in Canada}}
In 1981 the rate of home ownership in Canada was 62.4%,{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012|page=9}} after dropping to an all-time low of 60% in 1999, it increased to 63.9% in 2000;{{Sfn|RE/MAX Canada|2021}} to 68.4% in 2006,{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012|page=9}} and  68.55% in 2021.{{Sfn|RE/MAX Canada|2021}}

Since the 1990s, there was a rapid increase in the price of residential real estate,{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012|page=9}} so the increase in home ownership also resulted in an increase in mortgage debt.{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012|page=11}} According to a 2012 Bank of Canada (BOC) report,  the BOC's affordability measure (AFF), which was based on the "ratio of monthly mortgage payments to disposable income (DI)", was "consistently favourable by historical standards" starting in the late 1990s.{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012|page=11}} According to [[Mark Carney]]—the Governor of the [[Bank of Canada]]  from 2008 to 2013—the demand for housing in Canada was consistent with housing supply.{{Sfn|Carney|2011}} Carney warned in 2011, that even though measures of housing affordability in Canada were favorable in most cases—with some housing markets already severely unaffordable even at current rate—interest rates were at a record low. He raised concerns that Canadian household debt was high and therefore vulnerable to increases in mortgage interest rates which could cause housing affordability fall to "its worst level in 16 years."{{Sfn|Carney|2011}} Affordability in the real estate market was increased partly because of labour market conditions that supported increased income and the low interest rates.{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012|page=11}} The banking sector benefitted from the "strong credit growth" and higher loads of indebtedness that these homebuyers incurred from 2001 to 2011. However, concerns were raised about the very high household indebtedness which had reached c. 150% of debt-to-income ratio by 2012.{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012}}

As of early 2020, about a third of all homes in Ontario and British Columbia were owned by investors also known as multiple-residential property owners. In Nova Scotia and New Brunswick investors own 40% of all residential housing units.{{sfn|Altstedter|2022}} Concerns have been raised that while the investors group provide a significant portion of rental housing supply but may also be responsible for the rapid escalation of residential properties. Scrutiny of this buyers group increased during the COVID-19 pandemic as the housing supplies reached crucial lows.{{Sfn|STOREYS|2022}} The CHSP April 2022 data revealed that in urban areas, the median income of renters was $25,000 compared to FTHBs whose median income was twice as much, $50,000, in larger census metropolitan areas (CMAs) across Canada.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2022}}

About one third of Canadians rent their homes. Ontario and British Columbia have a higher rate of residential property rentals.{{Sfn|RE/MAX Canada|2021}}

During the COVID-19 pandemic, housing supplies{{emdash}}particularly affordable housing{{emdash}}dropped to historical lows.{{Sfn|STOREYS|2022}} The average price of a home in Canada increased 17.1% to $779,000 in Q4 2021 compared to Q4 2020, according to a Royal LePage survey.{{Sfn|BNN Bloomberg|2022}}

A 13 January 2022 [[Bank of Canada]] report examined three types of buyers in Canada,  first-time home buyers (FTHBs), repeat homebuyers, and investors or multiple residential property owners.{{Sfn|Khan|Xu|2022}} The CHSP April 2022 data revealed that in urban areas, the median income of renters was $25,000 compared to FTHBs whose median income was twice as much, $50,000, in larger census metropolitan areas (CMAs) across Canada.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2022}} Nineteen per cent of the down payment towards purchase of the first home was gifted by a family member.{{Sfn|BNN Bloomberg|2022}} Residential property owners are described as "repeat buyers" when they buy a new home while selling their old one; multiple residential property owners are described as "investors" if they purchase a new residence, potentially for rental income, while keeping their old one.{{Sfn|Holliday|2022}} Investors or multiple residential property owners, who may be individuals or entities, own properties as an investment including rental income, as a recreational property which may be as a source of rental income.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2022}} The report describes investors as older, higher-income, and more indebted.{{Sfn|Khan|Xu|2022}} According to the Bank of Canada report based on mortgage data, since 2014, FTHBs have been the largest group of homebuyers in Canada, representing about 50% of all mortgaged home purchases; repeat homebuyers represented 31%, and investors represented 19% since 2014.{{Sfn|Khan|Xu|2022}} During the pandemic, FTHBs represented 47% in June 2021, compared to 53% in 2015.{{Sfn|Holliday|2022}} The Bank of Canada reported a "rapid increase" in mortgage home purchases by all three groups, but the most pronounced increase was in the investors group.{{Sfn|Khan|Xu|2022}}

According to Statistics Canada's Canadian Housing Statistics Program (CHSP) data for 2019 and 2020 on home ownership reported on 12 April 2022, which compared first-time home buyers (FTHBs) and multiple residential property owners, the latter own about a third of all residential properties in Canada. Of these the top 10% wealthiest represent 25% of residential housing value.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2022}} While investors provide a significant part of the rental housing supply, they may also exacerbate the "so-called boom-bust cycles in housing markets" causing economic instability.{{Sfn|Khan|Xu|2022}}

==Affordability problem==
[[File:Office towers March 2010.jpg|thumb|Homeless man living in a bus shelter in downtown Toronto (2010)]]
The mayors of Canada's largest cities declared the lack of affordable housing a national housing disaster in 1998. The federal government responded by announcing cost-shared conditional federal-provincial initiatives to construct affordable housing, worth $1 billion. However, during this period of tax cutting and debt reduction initiatives, the devolution of federal responsibilities to the provinces, without an accompanying transfer of funds, made it impossible for the provinces to contribute their share for affordable housing projects. Provinces were focused on reducing government size and increasing provincial tax cuts.{{Sfn|Yalnizyan|2004}}

The United Nations [[Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights]] issued a highly critical and detailed report on Canada's social policies in its 1998 review of Canada's compliance with these rights particularly about disastrous levels of homelessness. It concluded "that while Canada has a long history of housing successes, the housing cuts starting in the late 1980s have effectively prevented Canada from meeting its international housing obligations."{{Sfn|Hulchanski|2005}}{{sfn|Kothari|2009}}{{Sfn|Poverty and Human Rights Centre|2007}} Similar concerns were raised in their 2016 follow up report, which called for respect for the right to adequate housing. The Committee raised concerns about the housing crisis and the lack of a national housing strategy and funding, inadequate housing subsidies, the shortage of housing supply, and evictions and called for action on a number of issues. This included increase resources for housing at the federal and provincial levels, increase the supply of social and affordable units "substantially"; protect renters from evictions specifically in accordance with international laws regarding homelessness. The committee recommended that the federal government adopt a national strategy on homelessness.{{sfn|UN Committee|2016}}

All mortgages provided by federally regulated institutions where the down payment is 25% or less, are required under the federal Bank Act, to carry mortgage insurance, according to a 2005 ''Canadian Business'' journal article.{{Sfn|Taylor|2005}} In 2004, this represented 45% of all home buyers, or 500,000 Canadian households at a total cost of $1.6 billion for mortgage insurance which was paid to the CMHC, the Crown corporation that provides mortgage insurance. Based on the CMHC's 2004 annual report, mortgage insurance premiums collected totaled $1.1 billion while $51 million in claims were paid out, which represents less than 5% payout. From 1994 through 2004, CMHC paid out at approximately 45% which is much lower than most other kinds of insurance. The 2005 ''Canadian Business'' article cautioned that the CMHC's mortgage insurance program was the most "lucrative line of insurance in Canada."{{Sfn|Taylor|2005}} CMHC's government-backed mortgage insurance purchased at a flat, upfront fee for mortgage insurance through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation is obligatory for home buyers with down of less than 20% of the home's value."{{Sfn|CBC News|2012}}

in 2006, 5.5% of Canadians, 1.7 million people of a total population of 31 million were under-housed or non-housed.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2006a}}

In Canada's market based housing system, in 2010 the federal government intervened only when affordability of housing was stressed to the point home ownership became inaccessible even to individuals with full-time employment.{{Sfn|Yalnizyan|2010}}

A [[Conference Board of Canada]] 2010 report entitled "Building From the Ground Up: Enhancing Affordable Housing in Canada" argued that the shortage of affordable housing was "having a detrimental effect on Canadians' health, which, in turn, reduces their productivity, limits our national competitiveness, and indirectly drives up the cost of health care and welfare." Stress, asthma, and diabetes are connected to inadequate housing.{{Sfn|Conference Board of Canada|2010|page=1}}

There are concerns about aggressive marketing that began in the mid-1990s making secured personal lines of credit (PLCs) (often secured by housing assets) much more widely available. By 2011 secured PLCs represented 50% of consumer debt. This places many households in a vulnerable exposed situation if housing prices drop, mortgage rates rise, or their income decreases.{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012}}

Concerns over high Canadian [[household debt]] levels led to changes to mortgage regulations announced June 2012 by Finance Minister Jim Flaherty. The federal government lowered the maximum amortization period for a government-insured mortgage from 30 to 25 years. The upper limit Canadian homeowners could borrow against their home equity was lowered from 85% to 80%.{{Sfn|CBC News|2012}}

The federal government's CMHC stated in 2021 that $2,225 per month constitutes "affordable" housing in [[Greater Montreal]]. This led to condemnation from both [[New Democratic Party]] and [[Conservative Party of Canada|Conservative]] MPs. CMHC said that its principal goal was to stimulate new housing construction, not keep prices low.{{Sfn|Bergeron|2021}}

===Core housing need===
In 1986, CMHC entered into Global and Operating Agreements under the ''[[National Housing Act (Canada)|National Housing Act]]'' and the CMHC Act, with the provinces and territories regarding administration and cost sharing of social housing programs. The core housing need concept was developed and adopted as an eligibility criterion to target households who were in need and as a basis to allocate federal funds through CMHC to participating provinces and territories. A household is considered to be in core housing need by CMHC if it meets certain criteria{{emdash}}if it falls below acceptable standards of affordability, adequacy, or suitability and if the cost of housing exceeds 30% or more of its before-tax household income.{{Sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2006}}

Households are considered to have a housing affordability problem by CMHC if they have to spend 30% or more of total before-tax household income on shelter expenses.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2009}} Shelter expenses include "rent and any payments for electricity, fuel, water and other municipal services" for renters and "mortgage payments (principal and interest), property taxes, and any condominium fees, along with payments for electricity, fuel, water and other municipal services" for home owners.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2009}}

Data on core housing need is collected by Statistics Canada through the Canadian Housing Survey.

In 2006, [[Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation]] (CMHC) deemed that 20% of Canadian households (1.7 million households) fall within the core housing need. These households could not find adequate and suitable housing without spending 30% or more of their pre-tax income. CMHC found that a disturbing 656,000 households (7%) spent at least half of their before-tax income on shelter in 1996, up from 422,000 households, or 5%, in 1991. While accounting for only 35% of all households, almost 70% of those in core need were renters.{{Sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2006}}

In 2011, about 1.5 million Canadian households or 12.5% of Canadian households were in core housing need,{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2017}} and various levels of governance in Canada were exploring policy solutions to assist challenges faced by the low-income renter and homeowner overburdened with shelter costs.{{Sfn|Pomeroy|2011}}

The 2020 report on the 2018 Survey revealed that 1,644,900 Canadian households or 11.6% were in core housing need.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2020}} Only 6.5% of homeowners experienced core housing needs compared to renter households, where 23% were likely to live in core housing need.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2020}} Twenty one per cent of renters did not live in core housing need.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2020}}

Core housing need does not measure progress against some measurable indicator.{{Sfn|Pomeroy|2011|page=1}}

==Public policy==

===National Housing Strategy===
In November 2017, the federal government expanded its role in housing with the introduction of the '''National Housing Strategy''' ('''NHS''') (NHS), with a human rights-based approach to housing.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Human Rights-Based Approach to Housing |url=https://www.placetocallhome.ca/human-rights-based-approach-to-housing |access-date=2023-04-04 |website=A Place to Call Home |language=en}}</ref>{{Sfn|Eidelman|Hachard|Slack|2022|page=3}}{{efn|The [[Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation]] (CMHC), a Crown corporation, with a mandate to "promote housing affordability and choice," reports to the federal [[Minister of Housing and Diversity and Inclusion|Department of Housing and Diversity and Inclusion]]}}  The NHS's goal was "to ensure everyone in Canada has access to housing that meets their needs and that they can afford".<ref name=":0" />

Prior to the NHS's launch, housing initiatives were introduced and funded by the federal, provincial, territorial and municipal governments, along with civil society organizations (including the charitable sector).{{sfn|Kothari|2009}}{{rp|8–9}} In 2016, the federal [[Minister of Families, Children and Social Development]] said that strategies for a national affordable-housing strategy were being considered.{{Sfn|Kneebone|Wilkins|2016}} Through this first NHS, the Government of Canada promised to spend $40 billion over the next decade on housing,{{sfn|St. Denis|2022}} funding that would go to build 100,000 new affordable units, repair 300,000 affordable units, and to cut homelessness by 50%.{{Sfn|Canadian Association Of Retired Persons|2017}}<ref name="RadioCanada_20240412">{{Cite web| work= ICI Radio Canada| title = Federal government launches new housing strategy| access-date = 3 July 2024| date = 12 April 2024 | url = https://ici.radio-canada.ca/rci/en/news/2064444/federal-government-launches-new-housing-strategy}}</ref>

Before 2017, Canada was the only [[G8]] nation that lacked a national housing strategy.{{Sfn|Shapcott|2012}}{{Sfn|Shapcott|2012a}}{{sfn|Kothari|2009}}{{rp|7}}{{Sfn|Canadian Association Of Retired Persons|2017}}{{Sfn|National Housing Strategy|n.d.}}<ref name="FINA_2009">{{Cite web| title = Committee Report No. 6 - FINA (40-2) - |work=Standing Committee on Finance (FINA) House of Commons of Canada| access-date = 3 July 2024|date=2009| url = https://www.ourcommons.ca/documentviewer/en/40-2/FINA/report-6/page-285}}</ref>{{rp|285}}

In November 2017, Canada's 2017{{endash}}2027 housing plan, One major outcome of the four-month-long Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC)-led consultation process{{emdash}}which included representatives responsible for housing at the federal, provincial, and territorial level{{emdash}}was a call for a National Housing Strategy that would "help vulnerable groups obtain secure, affordable housing".<ref>{{Cite report| title = What we heard: shaping Canada's National Housing Strategy|work=Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation via The Conference Board of Canada |date=2016|access-date=3 July 2024|url=https://assets.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/sf/project/placetocallhome/pdfs/nhs-what-we-heard-report-en.pdf}}</ref>

In April 2019, the ''National Housing Strategy Act'' was passed in Parliament as part of the ''2019 Budget Implementation Act'', setting out the Government of Canada's housing policy. Based on a human rights-based approach to housing, the federal policy "recognize(s) that the right to adequate housing is a fundamental human right affirmed in [[international law]]."<ref name=":0" />{{Sfn|van den Berg|2019}}  It also commits Canada to further the progressive realization of the [[right to adequate housing]]. This right is recognized in the [[International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights]] (ICESCR).

By 2022, the first NHS introduced in 2017, was valued at more than $75 billion over ten years, funding programs through loans and grants such as the Community Housing Initiative, Reaching Home, Canada Housing Benefit, First-time home buyer programs, the Rental Construction Financing Initiative (RCFI), the National Housing Co-Investment Fund (NHCI), and the Rapid Housing Initiative (RHI).<ref name="Lee_20220301">{{Cite news|first=Marc |last=Lee|title = What happened to the National Housing Strategy?| work = Policy Note| access-date = 3 July 2024| date = 1 March 2022| url = https://www.policynote.ca/national-housing-strategy/}}</ref>

The second National Housing Strategy (NHS) was launched in April 2024 with a budget of over CDN$82 billion.<ref name="RadioCanada_20240412"/> This included the 2024 Housing Accelerator Fund.

The government's investment in social housing is seen as a critical step to address the pressing needs of low-income households and to reduce homelessness in Canada. However, lack of affordable housing is becoming an increasingly serious problem in many urban areas of the country, and government's policy like NHS that was supposed to increase affordable non-market housing is used as a tool for funding corporate developers to build market rental housing with low-interest loans without any obligations to ensure housing rights of the largely affected population through rental control measures, annually building affordable housing units through a percentage of their profit from using the low-interest loans or converting a certain percentage of their market housing units in a development to non-market housing units.<ref name="Lee_20220301"/>

As an unintended consequence in the process of providing affordable housing, NHS ended up supporting private developers for building market rental housing and turning Canadian homes into financial assets by generously providing low-interest loans. In 2023, the Canadian government's spending on housing was small, and only accounted 0.1% to 0.2% of the country's GDP. It is also projected to decrease as a proportion of GDP in the future. Critics have also observed that despite its establishment many years ago, there has been no comprehensive strategy or a significant implementation plan for the creation of dedicated non-market housing.<ref name="Lee_20220301"/>

The Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) is one of the main federal organizations responsible for administering the various programs and initiatives of NHS. It was supposed to efficiently administer [[seed funding]], co-investment fund, the innovation fund, the federal lands initiative, and rental construction financing, as well as expanding the mortgage loan insurance to include market properties and flexibilities for affordable housing.

=== Affordable Housing Fund ===
On November 21, the 2023, the federal program formerly known as the '''National Housing Co-investment Fund''' ('''NHCF''') was renamed the Affordable Housing Fund.<ref>{{Cite web| title = Affordable Housing Fund| access-date = 3 July 2024| url = https://www.cmhc-schl.gc.ca/professionals/project-funding-and-mortgage-financing/funding-programs/all-funding-programs/affordable-housing-fund}}</ref> The Fund offers low-cost CMHC loans for developers engaged in affordable housing projects.{{Sfn|Luck|2021}} There was an increase in funding for affordable housing in the spring federal budget and in the fall of 2021, which included an additional $2.7 billion for the NHCF. The NHCF budget allocated $250 million to target housing for domestic violence survivors. As of 2021, the national [[non-profit association]] advocacy group, the [[Canadian Housing and Renewal Association]], said that while more federal funding for community housing is the right step, the CMHC loan approval process is too slow.{{Sfn|Luck|2021}}

===Housing Accelerator Fund===
{{anchor|Housing Accelerator Fund}}
The federal government's $4-billion Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF), launched in May 2023, is part of Canada's second National Housing Strategy (NHS).<ref name="Uday_20231028"/> The HAF offers an additional $5 billion in infrastructure grants for provinces and territories, to encourage municipalities to implement pro-housing policies, with a main focus on the "missing-middle" homes such as duplexes, triplexes, and small apartment buildings.<ref name="Relman_20240703">{{Cite news| last = Relman| first = Eliza| title = Canada's bold plan to make housing more affordable is showing signs of working — and could be a model for the US| work = [[Business Insider]]|date=3 July 2024| access-date = 3 July 2024| url = https://www.businessinsider.com/canada-housing-crisis-prices-rents-real-estate-infrastructure-funding-2024-6}}</ref> The targeted pro-housing policies focus primarily on the "missing-middle" homes such as duplexes, triplexes, and small apartment buildings.<ref name="Relman_20240703"/> Launched in May 2023, the Housing Accelerator Fund (HAF) is a $4 billion initiative from the Government of Canada that will run until 2026–27.<ref name="Uday_20231028"/>

=== Build Canada Homes ===
{{see also|Build Canada Homes}}

==Affordability by province==

===Alberta===
Calgary’s housing affordability varies sharply by income. In 2016, 78% of households met their needs in the market, 3% received government support, and 19% needed affordable housing.{{sfn|City of Calgary|2016}} By 2022, about 84,000 households (20%) earned under $60,000 and spent over 30% of income on housing; 42,000 spent over 50%, and more than 3,200 people were homeless.{{sfn|City of Calgary Deputy Manager|2022}}

Despite high incomes and comparatively affordable ownership costs, Calgary has been described as Canada’s least-affordable city for low-income residents.{{sfn|Calgary Economic Development|2021}}{{sfn|School of Public Policy|2017}} Only 3.6% of Calgary housing was non-market in 2022.{{sfn|City of Calgary Deputy Manager|2022}} Financialized landlords’ subsidized retrofits have also contributed to rent increases beyond low-income tenants’ means.<ref name="Medi_20240630"/>

===Ontario===
The non-profit Housing Services Corporation delivers programs for the affordable housing sector in Ontario.{{sfn|Housing Services Corporation|2022}} It was created under the Housing Services Act, 2011 to replace the [[Social Housing Services Corporation (SHSC)]] which was operational from 2002 until 2012.

The SHSC was created in 2002 following the devolution of responsibility for over 270,000 social housing units from the province to the municipalities to "provide Ontario housing providers and service managers with bulk purchasing, insurance, investment and information services that add significant value to their operations."{{Sfn|Social Housing Services Corporation|2007}}

Over 20% of home owners residing in Ontario had housing affordability issues as of 2006.{{Sfn|Statistics Canada|2006}} A 2010 survey by the Ontario Non-Profit Housing Association revealed that the number of households on affordable housing waiting lists was at an "all-time high of 141,635".{{Sfn|Shapcott|2010}}

Through partnerships with the government, private investors became interested again in investing in multi-family rental housing in the 1990s.{{sfn|August|Walks|2018}}{{sfn|Nethercote|2020}} CAPREIT was established in 1997 becoming Canada's first REIT. As more REITs were created, more multi-family rental housing were owned by these institutions.{{sfn|August|Walks|2018}}{{sfn|Nethercote|2020}} By 2015, CAPREIT was Toronto's biggest landlord with about 11, 000 rental units. In the fifteen years between 2000 and 2015, the ownership of Toronto apartments was increasingly concentrated among REITs, institutional investors, private equity funds and some large family-owned firms.{{sfn|August|Walks|2018}}{{sfn|Nethercote|2020}}

On 29 January 2020, a motion to declare a housing and homeless emergency in Ottawa was passed unanimously by Ottawa City Council, becoming the first Canadian city to declare such an emergency. Faced with an urgent need for more affordable housing, new housing subsidies, and more assistance to those who are chronically homeless, to people who need supportive housing for a number of reasons{{emdash}}including those with disabilities or serious injuries{{emdash}}the city called on all levels of government to respond.{{Sfn|Britneff|2020}} The municipality provides 56% of funding for programs related to housing and homelessness, and the federal and provincial governments provide the remainder.{{Sfn|Britneff|2020}}

The price of the average home in most cities and towns in Canada increased by double digits. In Toronto, the increase was 15% breaching the "$1 million mark for the first time" in February 2021.{{sfn|Hagan|Hertzberg|2021}}

According to Reuters, by October 2022, the shortage of construction workers in Canada was a major factor in responding to housing shortage challenges, particularly in Ontario, British Columbia and Quebec.<ref name="Reuters_20221006">{{Cite news| title = Labour shortage to restrict Canadian housing supply -CMHC| work = Reuters| access-date = 2022-11-26| date = 2022-10-06| url = https://www.reuters.com/world/americas/labour-shortage-restrict-canadian-housing-supply-cmhc-2022-10-06/}}</ref> According to a June 2022 CMHC report, the labour shortage could contribute to making housing less affordable. The CMHC report said that in order to make housing affordable in Canada by 2030, millions of new homes had to be built.<ref name="Reuters_20221006"/>

The "More Homes Built Faster Act", which was introduced in November 2022 in response to Ontario's housing supply problems, raised concerns as it would make sweeping changes to a number of statutes.<ref>{{cite web  |date= 28 November 2022 |work= Legislative Assembly of Ontario |title= Bill 23, More Homes Built Faster Act, 2022|script-title= |trans-title= |page= |url=https://www.ola.org/en/legislative-business/bills/parliament-43/session-1/bill-23|access-date=March 14, 2023 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Crombie_20221114">{{Cite news| last1 = Crombie |first1=David| last2 = Hall| first2 = Barbara| last3 = Sewell| first3 = John| title = Three former mayors of Toronto on why the More Homes Built Faster Act disempowers municipalities — and needs a serious rethink before proceeding| work = The Toronto Star| access-date = November 26, 2022 | date = November 14, 2022 | url = https://www.thestar.com/opinion/contributors/2022/11/14/three-former-mayors-of-toronto-on-why-the-more-homes-built-faster-act-disempowers-municipalities-and-needs-a-serious-rethink-before-proceeding.html}}</ref>

===British Columbia===
[[File:Man sleeping on Canadian sidewalk.jpg|thumb|
Unhoused man in Vancouver]]
[[Vancouver]] had the least affordable housing market in Canada by 1980; the average home cost 5.7 times the average family income.{{efn|Statistics Canada, 1983a, table 7; Statistics Canada, 1983b, table 19.}}{{Sfn|O'Toole|2007}}{{rp|16–17}} O' Toole calculated that given the high interest rates in 1980, "an average family would have to devote more than 70 percent of its income to pay off a mortgage on an average home in 30 years."{{Sfn|O'Toole|2007}} According to a report in ''[[The Economist]]'', a factor contributing to Vancouver's high property prices may be Canadian laws which enable foreigners to buy Canadian property—possibly for purposes of [[tax evasion]] or [[money laundering]]—while shielding their identities from tax authorities, a practice which is known as [[snow washing]].{{Sfn|Economist|2018}}

The governor of the [[Bank of Canada]] noted that affordability of housing has been eroded as wealthy [[Asian people|Asian]] [[investor]]s seeking [[diversification (finance)|diversification]] and [[hard asset]]s purchase housing in Vancouver. Consequently, "[t]he average selling price of a home in Vancouver is now nearly 11 times the average Vancouver family's household income, a multiple similar to those seen in [[Hong Kong]] and [[Sydney]]—cities that have also become part of a more [[globalized]] [[real estate market]]."{{Sfn|Bank of Canada|2012}}

The 2006–2010 redevelopment of Vancouver's [[Woodward's building]] combined social and market housing, and has been credited with revitalizing [[Gastown]] in the [[Downtown Eastside]].{{sfn|City of Vancouver|2011}}{{sfn|Narvey|2010}}{{sfn|Maschaykh|2015}}

[[Randal O'Toole]] of the [[Fraser Institute]] argued that the [[GVRD|Greater Vancouver Regional District]]'s 1996 "Livable Region Strategic Plan" prioritized curbing [[urban sprawl]] and protecting green space over affordability, contributing to the region's high housing costs.{{sfn|O'Toole|2007}}{{sfn|O'Toole|2007a}}
[[File:Downtown Vancouver July 2011 (1).jpg|thumb|High-rise apartments in Vancouver]]
{{as of|2012}} Vancouver was the most stressed area in the province in terms of affordability of housing in Canada.{{Sfn|Royal Bank of Canada|2012}} In 2012, Vancouver was ranked by [[Demographia]] as the second-most unaffordable in the world, rated as even more severely unaffordable in 2012 than in 2011.{{Sfn|Cox|Pavletich|2012}}{{Sfn|Bula|2007}}{{Sfn|Demographia|2006}}{{Sfn|Royal Bank of Canada|2006}} The city has adopted various strategies to reduce housing costs, including [[housing cooperative|cooperative housing]], legalized [[secondary suite]]s, increased density and [[smart growth]]. As of April 2010, the average two-level home in Vancouver sold for a record high of $987,500, compared with the Canadian average of $365,141.{{Sfn|Business in Vancouver|2010}}

In June 2016, the youth-advocacy group [[Generation Squeeze]] declared housing affordability in British Columbia a "Code Red."{{sfn|Woodward|2016}}

In 2016, the [[BC government]] announced a $516 million investment in 68 new affordable housing projects to build 2,900 units across the province, targeting renters with incomes that were low to moderate. This included 68 projects with 1441 units in [[Lower mainland]] and [[Fraser Valley]], 774 units on [[Vancouver Island]] and the [[Gulf Islands]], 256 units in [[Thompson Country|Thompson]]-[[Okanagan]], and the rest to [[British Columbia Coast|Coast]], [[Kootenays]], [[Cariboo]], and North/Northeast.{{Sfn|Larsen|2016}}

===Nunavut===
The capital of [[Nunavut]] faces an extreme affordability challenge mainly due to the supply side. In 2010 [[Iqaluit]] had the most expensive rental market in Canada: a two-bedroom apartment cost $2,365 a month in Iqaluit compared to $1,195 in Vancouver.{{Sfn|Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation|2011c}}{{rp|13}} In 2018, over 10,000 Nunavut residents were without housing of their own, translating to a deficit of 3,500 housing units.{{Sfn|Christensen|2021}}

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Affordable housing in Silicon Valley
======================================================================

{{Update|reason=Needs updates with Regional Housing Needs Allocation, Housing elements, and more recent data|date=April 2025}}
[[File:Aerial view of Silicon Valley.jpg|thumb|Silicon Valley]]
[[File:California map showing Santa Clara County.png|thumb|Santa Clara County is generally considered to be the center of Silicon Valley.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/place/Silicon-Valley-region-California|title=Silicon Valley {{!}} region, California, United States|website=Encyclopedia Britannica|language=en|access-date=2019-10-16}}</ref>]]

[[File:Housing prices to personal income ratios.webp|thumb|300px|[[Housing in the United States|Housing prices]] to [[Personal income in the United States|personal income]] ratios by [[Metropolitan area|metro area]]

{{legend-line|#1DB100 solid 3px|[[Denver metropolitan area|Denver]]}}
{{legend-line|#FFD932 solid 3px|[[New York metropolitan area|New York]]}}

{{legend-line|#970E53 solid 3px|[[Boston Metropolitan Area|Boston]]}}

[[Silicon Valley]], a region located in the southern part of the [[San Francisco Bay Area]], is one of the most expensive regions to live in the United States, and many residents lack access to [[affordable housing]]. In 2018, the median home price across the area was $1.18 million, the highest of the 100 largest metro areas in the U.S.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.kiplinger.com/tool/real-estate/T010-S003-home-prices-in-100-top-u-s-metro-areas/index.php|title=Home Prices in 100 Top U.S. Metro Areas|website=www.kiplinger.com|access-date=2019-10-15}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{cite web|website=Joint Venture Silicon Valley|year= 2019|title= 2019 Silicon Valley Index|url=https://jointventure.org/download-the-2019-index}}</ref>  There have been local efforts to address affordable housing, as well as state measures in response to housing issues across California (see [[California housing shortage]]).

Silicon Valley does not have concrete boundaries, and is defined differently by different organizations. Thus, housing initiatives and data often come from specific cities, counties, or metro areas, rather than the entire region. Statistics referencing the "Silicon Valley" refer to Joint Venture Silicon Valley's 2019 Index, which includes all of Santa Clara and San Mateo counties, as well as select cities in Alameda and Santa Cruz counties.<ref name=":0" />

== Cost and availability of affordable housing ==
In 2018, the median rental rate in Silicon Valley was $2,911, the highest of any major metropolitan region in the United States.<ref name=":0" /> At $3.20 per square foot, the San Jose metro area has the second highest rental rate per square foot in the United States, behind San Francisco at $3.42.<ref name=":0" /> In comparison, the median rental rate per square foot in New York was $2.67; in Las Vegas, it was $1.20.<ref name=":0" /> The 2018 median home price in Silicon Valley was $1.18 million, a 21% increase from 2017.<ref name=":0" /> Almost 90% of low income renters in the San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara metro area were cost burdened in 2017, meaning they spent more than 30% of their income on housing.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=https://reports.nlihc.org/gap/2017/ca|title=California|date=2019-03-13|website=[[National Low Income Housing Coalition]]|access-date=2019-10-15}}</ref> Over a third of mid-income renters were cost burdened as well.<ref name=":1" />

In the San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara metropolitan area, there are 30 available and affordable housing units for every 100 extremely low-income households below 30% of the area median income. There are 43 available and affordable units for every 100 low income households below 50% of the area median income.<ref name=":1" /> The average monthly inventory of homes for sale in Silicon Valley has seen a major decline in past years: in 2011, there were around 7,000 homes for sale each month; in 2018, there were just over 3,000.<ref name=":0" />

In California, local governments work with the state government to develop a Regional Housing Need Allocation, the number of housing units that should be created in an area to meet its housing needs. {{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}Between 2015 and 2018, Silicon Valley cities permitted 85% of units needed to reach the goal for residents in the Above Moderate Income category, or residents who make above 120% of the area median income.{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}{{Update inline|date=April 2025}} However, for very low income, low income, and moderate income residents, there has been far less housing production; 5%, 6%, and 2% of the need has been met for those groups, respectively.<ref name=":0" />

== Intersection of jobs and housing ==
A major cause of high housing costs in Silicon Valley is expansive job growth without adequate housing production.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2018/02/07/silicon-valleys-spectacular-job-growth-creates-harsh-environment-many-residents-report/|title=Silicon Valley's spectacular job growth creates 'harsh environment' for many residents, report says|date=2018-02-07|website=The Mercury News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-19}}</ref> In 2018, close to 36,000 new jobs were created in the area (34% of which were tech jobs); only 8,400 new residential units were issued permits.<ref name=":0" />

=== Corporate housing investments ===
Several Silicon Valley companies have taken steps to aid the area's housing shortage.

In January 2019, a group called The Partnership for the Bay's Future announced a $500 million investment in affordable housing in Silicon Valley.<ref name=":3">{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/01/24/business/bay-area-affordable-housing-zuckerberg.html|title=$500 Million Pledge in Bay Area Supports Affordable Housing|last=Flitter|first=Emily|date=2019-01-24|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-10-20|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The project was spearheaded by the [[Chan Zuckerberg Initiative]], founded by Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg and his wife Priscilla Chan. Other supporters include Morgan Stanley, Kaiser Permanente, Facebook and Genentech. The group will create an investment fund to preserve current housing and build new units, as well as a policy fund to support governments and other groups in affordable housing endeavors.<ref name=":3" />

In June 2019, Google announced that it would invest $1 billion to aid the housing shortage in Silicon Valley. Their plan includes working with local government to lease company-owned land to developers, and creating a $750 million investment fund to incentivize affordable housing construction.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/18/technology/google-1-billion-housing-crisis.html|title=Google Pledges to Invest $1 Billion to Ease Bay Area Housing Crisis|last1=Wakabayashi|first1=Daisuke|date=2019-06-18|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-10-20|last2=Dougherty|first2=Conor|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In October 2019, Facebook announced that they would also be investing $1 billion in California housing.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/22/technology/facebook-1-billion-california-housing.html|title=Facebook Pledges $1 Billion for California Housing|last=Dougherty|first=Conor|date=2019-10-22|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-10-22|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref> The money will be used in several different ways. Facebook will partner with the California state government and spend $250 million to build mixed-income housing on state land. $150 million will support affordable housing development, particularly for the homeless, through the Partnership for the Bay's Future. Facebook will produce over 1,500 mixed-income units on $225 million of their own land in Menlo Park, and they will spend $25 million to build housing for teachers throughout Silicon Valley. The remaining $350 million will be spent depending on the success of each project.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://newsroom.fb.com/news/2019/10/facebook-commits-1-billion-to-address-housing-affordability/|title=Facebook Commits $1 Billion and Partners with the State of California to Address Housing Affordability {{!}} Facebook Newsroom|date=22 October 2019|language=en|access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref>

In November 2019, Apple announced a $2.5 billion investment in California housing.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.apple.com/newsroom/2019/11/apple-commits-two-point-five-billion-to-combat-housing-crisis-in-california/|title=Apple commits $2.5 billion to combat housing crisis in California|website=Apple Newsroom|language=en-US|access-date=2019-11-29}}</ref> Apple will create a $1 billion investment fund for affordable housing, and another $1 billion mortgage assistance fund to aid first-time homebuyers in California. They will also make $300 million worth of company-owned land available for affordable housing production, create a $150 million fund to support affordable housing specifically in the Bay Area, and donate $50 million to Destination: Home, a non-profit that addresses homelessness in Silicon Valley.

=== Since 2015 ===
Since 2015, there have been reports of a changing environment in the housing market. Job growth in Silicon Valley has been slowing since 2015, and 2018 saw the lowest rate of job growth since the Great Recession.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/02/13/job-growth-slowing-in-silicon-valley/|title=Job growth slowing in Silicon Valley|date=2019-02-13|website=The Mercury News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-20}}</ref> The rate of population growth has also been decreasing since 2015, and more people are moving out of the area than moving into it.<ref name=":0" /> Since April 2018, the median sale price of homes in Santa Clara County has been dropping; neighboring San Mateo County has not had the same steady downward trend, but median home sale prices were lower in August 2019 than their peak in January 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.zillow.com/captchaPerimeterX/?url=%2fsanta-clara-county-ca%2fhome-values%2f&uuid=d9607cd0-f385-11e9-8550-09d013d95a5e&vid=|title=Santa Clara County Home Prices & Values|last=|first=|date=|website=www.zillow.com|archive-url=|archive-date=|access-date=2019-10-20}}</ref> [[The Mercury News]] reported that in March 2019, the median home sale price for all nine counties of the Bay Area dropped for the first time in seven years.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/04/29/long-running-streak-of-rising-bay-area-home-prices-broken/|title=Snap! Record upward climb of Bay Area home prices broken|date=2019-04-29|website=The Mercury News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-20}}</ref> Furthermore, the average monthly inventory of homes for sale in Silicon Valley increased 15% from 2017 to 2018.<ref name=":0" /> Real estate agents report an increasing number of middle-aged and elderly residents selling their homes and moving to more affordable locations, and although this has not made the housing market "affordable", it is causing changes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/05/09/success/silicon-valley-real-estate-market-home-prices/index.html|title=Silicon Valley's real estate market is finally cooling off. Sort of|last=Bahney|first=Anna|website=CNN|date=9 May 2019|access-date=2019-10-20}}</ref><ref name=":4" />

== Zoning ==
A proposed solution to affordable housing has been to change zoning laws to allow increased density, although critics, often long-time residents, frequently oppose such measures and say they will worsen the already-bad traffic in the area.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|url=http://www.ocregister.com/5-ways-to-solve-californias-housing-crisis|title=5 ways to solve California's housing crisis|date=2018-04-13|website=Orange County Register|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2018/02/09/no-one-likes-bay-area-traffic-but-getting-us-out-of-our-cars-is-a-challenge/|title=No one likes Bay Area traffic, but getting us out of our cars is a challenge|date=2018-02-09|website=The Mercury News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://extras.mercurynews.com/blame/|title=Who caused the Bay Area's housing shortage?|website=extras.mercurynews.com|access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref>

In 2018, Palo Alto passed a number of changes to zoning laws with the goal of incentivizing housing production, both market-rate and subsidized.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://siliconvalleyathome.org/palo-alto-city-council-passes-landmark-changes-to-incentivize-housing-development/|title=Palo Alto: City Council Passes Landmark Changes to Incentivize Housing Development|date=2018-12-06|website=SV@Home|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-15}}</ref> Since then, the city council passed the first completely affordable housing development since 2013, a 59 unit apartment complex targeting low-income residents.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.paloaltoonline.com/news/2019/01/14/affordable-housing-project-wins-approval-in-palo-alto|title=First affordable-housing project in seven years wins approval|last=Sheyner|first=Gennady|website=www.paloaltoonline.com|date=15 January 2019 |language=en|access-date=2019-10-15}}</ref>

== Policy recommendations ==
Public transportation is often cited as an important feature in producing affordable housing{{citation needed|date=April 2022}} {{By whom|date=April 2022}}. Experts suggest investing in affordable housing as a whole, including better connecting the 27 different transit agencies in the Bay Area, as well as strategically building affordable housing close to public transportation routes.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/03/01/how-to-solve-the-housing-crisis-silicon-valley-leaders-hash-it-out/|title=How to solve the Bay Area housing crisis? Silicon Valley leaders hash it out|date=2019-03-01|website=The Mercury News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref> Affordable housing proponents also suggest making the permitting process easier for developers to get through, and subsidizing affordable housing construction or reducing fees.<ref name=":5" />

The California Housing Partnership, a statewide nonprofit, issues housing reports for counties across the state and works with local organizations to develop county-specific recommendations. Their April 2018 report suggested that Santa Clara County set aside more units in new developments for very low- and low-income families, focus more on the homeless population, change policies that create barriers for housing developers, and look further into the development of [[Secondary suite|accessory dwelling units]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://1p08d91kd0c03rlxhmhtydpr-wpengine.netdna-ssl.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Santa-Clara-2018-HNR.pdf|title=Santa Clara County's Housing Emergency and Proposed Solutions|last=|first=|date=|website=California Housing Partnership|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191022191533/https://1p08d91kd0c03rlxhmhtydpr-wpengine.netdna-ssl.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Santa-Clara-2018-HNR.pdf |archive-date=2019-10-22 |access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref>

== Affordable housing initiatives by city ==

=== San Jose ===
San Jose plans to build over 6,000 rental units in 2019, a 283% increase from the number of units built last year.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2019/09/13/bay-area-sees-increase-in-apartment-construction-in-face-of-national-decline/|title=Bay Area increases apartment construction despite national decline|date=2019-09-13|website=The Mercury News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-15}}</ref> The city has also recently passed a bill to subsidize the production of high rise buildings in the downtown area, although it is a controversial move that critics say will benefit developers but harm workers.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mercurynews.com/san-jose-city-council-debates-granny-flats-affordable-housing-and-high-rises|title=San Jose City Council votes to extend downtown high-rise fee waiver|date=2019-09-24|website=The Mercury News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-15}}</ref>

The city's first ever affordable housing complex for previously homeless residents, Second Street Studios, opened in August 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://abc7news.com/5489162/|title=San Jose opens first affordable housing complex for the homeless|date=2019-08-24|website=ABC7 San Francisco|language=en|access-date=2019-10-16}}</ref>

San Jose was one of few cities in America to have [[Rent control in the United States|rent control]] laws, which were adopted by the city in 1979.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sanjoseca.gov/index.aspx?NID=1355|title=Apartment Rent Ordinance|last=|first=|date=|website=SanJoseCA.gov|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121208232416/http://www.sanjoseca.gov/index.aspx?NID=1355 |archive-date=2012-12-08 |access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref> A statewide rent control bill was signed into law by governor Gavin Newsom in October 2019.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.natlawreview.com/article/california-s-new-statewide-rent-control-what-you-need-to-know|title=California's New Statewide Rent Control – What You Need to Know|website=The National Law Review|language=en|access-date=2019-10-22}}</ref>

With the growth of Silicon Valley, the [[San Jose, California|City of San Jose]] has been tasked by the [[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development|California Department of Housing and Urban Development]] to build 23,775 units of low-income housing by 2031. Of those 23,775 units, 15,088 will be designated for extremely low-income and very low-income households. The remaining 8,687 units will be designated for low-income households.<ref>{{Cite web |title=2023-2031 Draft Housing Element {{!}} City of San José |url=https://www.sanjoseca.gov/your-government/departments-offices/planning-building-code-enforcement/planning-division/citywide-planning/housing-element/2023-2031-draft-housing-element |access-date=2023-05-23 |website=www.sanjoseca.gov |language=en}}</ref>

In Spring of 2020, the [[San Jose City Council]] approved the McEvoy and Dupont Apartments to be built in downtown San Jose. Combined, the McEvoy and Dupont will have 365 affordable units designated for working individuals and families. Both towers will receive a LEED Platinum rating and built using mass timber, an innovative sustainability technique.<ref>{{Cite web |title=McEvoy Apartments {{!}} Future {{!}} Property Portfolio {{!}} FCH |url=https://www.firstcommunityhousing.org/mcevoy-apartments |access-date=2023-05-23 |website=firstcommhousing |language=en}}</ref>

On May 18, 2023, the San Jose City Council approved a plan to issue approximately $120 million in housing revenue bonds. These bonds will be used to finance two projects: the Charles and Tamien Station. The Charles is a 97-unit apartment complex for households earning incomes of 30% to 50% of the area median income. Tamien Station will contain 134 units for households earning 30% to 60% of the area median income.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Geha |first=Joseph |date=2023-05-18 |title=San Jose supporting hundreds of affordable apartments |url=https://sanjosespotlight.com/san-jose-supporting-hundreds-of-affordable-apartments/ |access-date=2023-05-23 |work=[[San José Spotlight]] |language=en-US}}</ref>

To improve the approval process for developers, the City of San Jose plans to launch a streamline permitting process to reduce the time needed to secure permitting approval. In many surrounding cities, permitting may take several years, while San Jose projects may potentially be permitted in as few as six months.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Eckholm |first=Cara |date=2023-02-06 |title=Opinion: San Jose, the metropolis of the future? How a 'forgettable' city may become a national model |url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2023-02-06/san-jose-housing-development-urban-planning-nimbyism |access-date=2023-05-23 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Sunnyvale ===
A 100% affordable housing complex known as "Block 15" is set to begin construction in downtown Sunnyvale in 2020. The 90-unit building will house low-income and extremely-low-income residents, with 23 units set aside for those with developmental disabilities.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.svvoice.com/affordable-housing-relief-ahead-for-sunnyvale/|title=Affordable Housing Relief Ahead for Sunnyvale|date=2019-05-14|website=The Silicon Valley Voice|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.mercurynews.com/sunnyvale-community-briefs-for-the-week-of-oct-18|title=Sunnyvale community briefs for the week of Oct. 18|date=2019-10-13|website=The Mercury News|language=en-US|access-date=2019-10-16}}</ref>
