The term "[[affordable housing]]" refers to housing that is considered economically accessible for individuals and families whose [[household income]] falls at or below the Area Median Income (AMI), as evaluated by either national or local government authorities through an officially recognized [[housing affordability index]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bhatta |first=Basudeb |title=Analysis of urban growth and sprawl from remote sensing data |date=2010 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-642-05298-9 |series=Advances in geographic information science |location=Berlin Heidelberg}}</ref> However, in the United States, the term is mostly used to refer to housing units that are deed restricted (for typically at least 30 years) to households considered Low-Income (80% of AMI), Very Low-Income (50% of AMI), and Extremely Low-Income (30% of AMI). These units are often constructed by [[non-profit]] "affordable housing developers" who use a combination of private money and government subsidies. For-profit developers, when building market-rate developments, may include some "affordable" units (often 10-30%), if required as part of a city's [[inclusionary zoning]] mandate.

Housing has consistently been the largest expenditure within the average American family's [[financial plan]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Caporal |first=Jack |date=2020-01-23 |title=American Households' Average Monthly Expenses {{!}} The Motley Fool |url=https://www.fool.com/money/research/average-monthly-expenses/ |access-date=2025-01-27 |website=www.fool.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Bennett |first=Karen |date=2024-12-10 |title=The Average American Household Budget |url=https://www.bankrate.com/banking/savings/average-household-budget/ |access-date=2025-01-27 |website=Bankrate |language=en-US}}</ref> Housing expenses have also traditionally outpaced income growth, especially impacting those who rent their residences.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pattillo |first=Mary |date=2013 |title=Housing: Commodity versus Right |journal=Annual Review of Sociology |volume=39 |pages=509–531 |doi=10.1146/annurev-soc-071312-145611 |jstor=43049647 |issn=0360-0572}}</ref> Following the [[Great Recession|Great Recession in 2008]], there has been a substantial decline in the rate of home ownership, leading to increases in foreclosures and short sales.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |title=Racial and Ethnic Disparity in Homeownership Continues Even Among Highly Educated |url=https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2022/11/homeownership-by-young-households-below-pre-great-recession-levels.html |access-date=2025-01-27 |website=Census.gov |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-01-31 |title=Homeownership Rate Dips in Fourth Quarter Amid Housing Affordability Woes |url=https://www.nahb.org/blog/2024/01/homeownership-rate-dips-in-fourth-quarter |access-date=2025-01-27 |website=www.nahb.org |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-08-05 |title=Lowest Homeownership Rate for Younger Householders in Four Years |url=https://www.nahb.org/blog/2024/08/lowest-homeownership-rate-in-four-years |access-date=2025-01-27 |website=www.nahb.org |language=en-US}}</ref> This, in turn, has driven a surge in the number of individuals and families opting to rent homes, causing greater rental expenses.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rohe |first=William M. |date=2017-05-04 |title=Tackling the Housing Affordability Crisis |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/10511482.2017.1298214 |journal=Housing Policy Debate |language=en |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=490–494 |doi=10.1080/10511482.2017.1298214 |s2cid=157724490 |issn=1051-1482|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

According to the 2024 American Community Survey one-year estimates, median gross rent, including utilities, rose by 2.7 percent in inflation-adjusted terms, from $1,448 in 2023 to $1,487 in 2024.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Cost of Homeownership Continues to Rise |url=https://www.census.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025/acs-1-year-estimates.html |publisher=United States Census Bureau |date=September 11, 2025 |access-date=September 8, 2026}}</ref> The median share of income paid toward rent remained 31 percent.<ref>{{cite web |title=Housing Costs: 2024 ACS |url=https://www.census.gov/library/visualizations/2025/demo/housing-costs-2024.html |publisher=United States Census Bureau |date=September 11, 2025 |access-date=September 8, 2026}}</ref>

The [[National Low Income Housing Coalition]] (NLIHC) released its annual report, ''Out of Reach: The High Cost of Housing'' in June 2023, showing a disparity between people's earnings and the cost of modest rental housing across the U.S. It emphasizes how rising rents, coupled with the end of [[COVID-19 pandemic]]-era support programs, are intensifying financial instability for low-income renters. The report's key figure, the "Housing Wage," reveals the hourly earnings necessary for full-time workers to afford [[Fair market rent|fair market]] rental homes without exceeding 30% of their incomes. Nationally, the 2023 Housing Wage is $28.58 per hour for a modest two-bedroom home and $23.67 per hour for a one-bedroom home. The findings emphasize that housing remains unaffordable for workers across various job types and income levels. Sixty percent of workers earn less than the hourly wage required for a two-bedroom home, and nearly 50% earn less than the one-bedroom Housing Wage.<ref name="National Low Income Housing Coalition-2023">{{Cite book |title=Out of Reach: The High Cost of Living |date=June 14, 2023 |publisher=National Low Income Housing Coalition}}</ref>

Some of the main issues which lead to the need for affordable housing are [[Homelessness in the United States|homelessness]], the housing affordability crisis,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Freeman |first1=Lance |last2=Schuetz |first2=Jenny |date=2017 |title=Producing Affordable Housing in Rising Markets: What Works? |journal=Cityscape |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=217–236 |jstor=26328307 |issn=1936-007X}}</ref> and historic [[Housing discrimination in the United States|housing discrimination]] against people of color. The reported effects of affordable housing range from improved health and educational outcomes to reduced homelessness.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=2004-07-01 |title=The Challenge of slums: global report on human settlements, 2003 |journal=Choice Reviews Online |volume=41 |issue=11 |pages=41–6602–41-6602 |doi=10.5860/choice.41-6602 |doi-broken-date=1 July 2025 |hdl=2099/1595 |issn=0009-4978|hdl-access=free }}</ref> A series of legislative steps have been taken to address different aspects of housing policy in the United States, including the [[National Housing Act of 1934]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Gotham |first=Kevin Fox |date=2000 |title=Racialization and the State: The Housing Act of 1934 and the Creation of the Federal Housing Administration |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.2307/1389798 |journal=Sociological Perspectives |language=en |volume=43 |issue=2 |pages=291–317 |doi=10.2307/1389798 |jstor=1389798 |s2cid=144457751 |issn=0731-1214|url-access=subscription }}</ref> [[Housing Act of 1937]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Harner |first=Paul E. |date=1987 |title=Implied Private Rights of Action under the United States Housing Act of 1937 |journal=Duke Law Journal |volume=1987 |issue=5 |pages=915–944 |doi=10.2307/1372694|jstor=1372694 }}</ref> [[Housing Act of 1949]],<ref>{{Cite journal |date=1949 |title=Provisions of the Housing Act of 1949 |journal=Monthly Labor Review |volume=69 |issue=2 |pages=155–159 |jstor=41831843 |issn=0098-1818}}</ref> and [[Fair Housing Act of 1968]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Massey |first=Douglas S. |date=2015 |title=The Legacy of the 1968 Fair Housing Act |journal=Sociological Forum |volume=30 |issue=S1 |pages=571–588 |doi=10.1111/socf.12178 |jstor=43654407 |pmid=27034538 |pmc=4808815 |issn=0884-8971}}</ref> Together, these acts represent a progression of federal housing policy, from facilitating [[mortgage insurance]] and creating public housing options to emphasizing the importance of affordable and equitable housing opportunities, while also addressing discrimination and promoting [[fair housing]] practices. Government policies and programs, such as [[Subsidized housing in the United States|subsidized housing]], tax incentives, and [[inclusionary zoning]], coupled with innovative solutions like tenant protections, [[Mixed-income housing|mixed-income developments]], and [[Homeownership in the United States|homeownership programs]], have contributed to shaping the affordable housing landscape in the U.S.

In 2025, [[U.S. News & World Report|''U.S. News & World Report'']] published a list of cities with affordable housing offering some 1br apartments in the range of $500-$600 per month.<ref> https://realestate.usnews.com/places/rankings/cheapest-places-to-live</ref>

== Housing discrimination and equity ==

=== Homelessness ===
{{main|Homelessness in the United States}}
[[File:Tenting in Los Angeles Skid Row.jpg|thumb|Tents of homeless people on the sidewalk in [[Skid Row, Los Angeles]]]]
Central to public discourse on housing affordability is the conversation surrounding advocacy for unhoused and homeless individuals. The evolution of homelessness within the U.S. has been characterized by significant changes not only in perceived solutions, but also in the gradual politicization of statewide provisioning for unhoused and displaced persons. Homelessness first emerged as a national issue in the early 1870s, although the term originally referred to "itinerant 'tramps' traversing the country in search of work,"<ref>[https://www.nationalacademies.org/hmd/reports/2018/permanent-supportive-housing.aspx "Permanent Supportive Housing: Evaluating the Evidence for Improving Health Outcomes Among People Experiencing Chronic Homelessness."] NCBI, National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 11 July 2018</ref> attributing the solution to homelessness as one of employment and job provision rather than affordable and accessible housing.

The advent of "[[Muckraker|muckraking]]" journalism, led by reform-focused journalists in the early 1900s [[Progressive Era]] who were focused on exposing corruption and "the realities of the American people" to the public, helped shed new light on the issue of homelessness and displacement. Particularly notable is the work of Danish photojournalist [[Jacob Riis]], most known for his series "[[How the Other Half Lives]]." Riis's photography work revealed the deplorable living conditions of those occupying U.S. slums and tenements, drawing more public attention towards the issue of homelessness.<ref>Riis, Jacob A., et al. "Jacob Riis: Revealing 'How the Other Half Lives' Riis and Reform." Riis and Reform – Jacob Riis: Revealing "How the Other Half Lives" | Exhibitions – Library of Congress, 14 Apr. 2016, www.loc.gov/exhibits/jacob-riis/riis-and-reform.html.</ref> This awareness helped to usher in the "Modern Era" of the housing movement, as advocates and [[Civil and political rights|civil rights activists]] attempted to address the low supply of affordable housing, a worsening recession, and continued [[Gentrification in the United States|gentrification]] of inner city spaces.<ref>"The Evolution of Homelessness throughout History." ABC7 News, ABC News, 9 Nov. 2020, abc7amarillo.com/features/invisible/the-evolution-of-homelessness-throughout-history.</ref>

The homelessness experience for individuals simultaneously coping with severe [[Mental illnesses|mental disorders]] is often intrinsically tied to the extended "institutional circuit"<ref name="PhD">PhD, Kim Hopper, et al. "Homelessness, Severe Mental Illness, and the Institutional Circuit." Psychiatric Services, vol. 48, no. 5, May 1997, pp. 659–665.,  {{doi|10.1176/ps.48.5.659}}.</ref> intended to function as a solution to residential instability. In a 1995 research study that interviewed applicants for a [[homeless shelter]] judged to be severely mentally ill in [[Westchester County, New York]], researchers found that shelters functioned as "part of a more extended institutional circuit, as a temporary source of transitional housing, as a surrogate for exhausted support from kin, and as a haphazard resource in essentially nomadic lives."<ref name="PhD" /> This perpetuation of short-term countermeasures to homelessness, all while de-prioritizing long-term options for stable and appropriate housing, raises the issue of whether shelters and existing institutional models are fully addressing the needs of mentally ill clients who have been displaced or houseless.

With the existing reliance on community shelters to accommodate mentally ill clients, the reinforcement of housing as a public need is also coupled by the de-institutionalization of mental illnesses previously addressed in custody and asylum.<ref>Yohanna, Daniel. "Deinstitutionalization of People with Mental Illness: Causes and Consequences." Journal of Ethics | American Medical Association, American Medical Association, 1 Oct. 2013, journalofethics.ama-assn.org/article/deinstitutionalization-people-mental-illness-causes-and-consequences/2013-10.</ref> The rise of the 1960s [[civil rights movement]] led to more public demands for severely mentally ill patients to be removed from the "deplorable environments" perpetuated by mental hospitals, asylums, and the like. Legal restrictions on institutionalization have pointed towards placing the responsibility of care on a largely decentralized mental care system.

=== Redlining ===
{{main|Redlining}}

After the [[Great Depression in the United States|Great Depression]] and the subsequent wave of home [[foreclosure]]s, the federal government created new organizations to make affordable home mortgages more accessible. These agencies included the [[Home Owners' Loan Corporation]] (HOLC) and [[Federal Housing Administration]] (FHA). HOLC and FHA conducted extensive evaluations of neighborhoods to assess their investment risk, a practice known as "[[redlining]]," which took into consideration the racial composition of residents.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Swope |first1=Carolyn B. |last2=Hernández |first2=Diana |last3=Cushing |first3=Lara J. |date=2022 |title=The Relationship of Historical Redlining with Present-Day Neighborhood Environmental and Health Outcomes: A Scoping Review and Conceptual Model |journal=Journal of Urban Health |language=en |volume=99 |issue=6 |pages=959–983 |doi=10.1007/s11524-022-00665-z |pmid=35915192 |pmc=9342590 |issn=1099-3460}}</ref>

Redlining led to the systematic denial of various services, particularly [[mortgage loan]]s, insurance, and other financial services, to people in specific neighborhoods based on their [[Race (human categorization)|racial]] or [[Ethnicity|ethnic]] composition. This practice has had a long-lasting impact on housing affordability and access to homeownership for minority communities in the United States. Redlining became widespread in the 1930s and continued for several decades but was officially banned with the passage of the [[Fair Housing Act]] in 1968 and the [[Community Reinvestment Act]] in 1977.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lovett |first=Laura L. |date=2020 |title=Eugenic Housing: Redlining, Reproductive Regulation, and Suburban Development in the United States |journal=WSQ: Women's Studies Quarterly |volume=48 |issue=1–2 |pages=67–83 |doi=10.1353/wsq.2020.0019 |s2cid=219466684 |issn=1934-1520}}</ref> The discriminatory practice of redlining used by governments made it extremely difficult for residents of redlined neighborhoods to accumulate [[Wealth inequality in the United States|wealth]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Korver-Glenn |first=Elizabeth |date=2018 |title=Compounding Inequalities: How Racial Stereotypes and Discrimination Accumulate across the Stages of Housing Exchange |journal=American Sociological Review |volume=83 |issue=4 |pages=627–656 |doi=10.1177/0003122418781774 |jstor=48588563 |s2cid=149810113 |issn=0003-1224}}</ref>

Although redlining is no longer a formal practice, its legacy continues to influence patterns of housing discrimination, disparities in homeownership rates, and access to housing and community resources for minority populations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mills |first=Alison |date=2018-03-27 |title=The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America |journal=Berkeley Planning Journal |volume=29 |issue=1 |doi=10.5070/bp329138440 |issn=1047-5192|doi-access=free }}</ref> The 2023 ''Out of Reach'' report by the [[National Low Income Housing Coalition]] highlights a substantial housing cost disparity for people of color, particularly women of color. The report's key figure, the "Housing Wage," reveals the hourly earnings necessary for full-time workers to afford fair market rental homes without exceeding 30% of their incomes. Nationally, while the median wage of a full-time white worker surpasses the one-bedroom Housing Wage by $2.23, full-time Black and Latino workers fall short by approximately $0.73 and $1.84, respectively. The disparity worsens for women of color, with Black and Latina female workers earning median wages that are $3.96 and $5.47 less than the one-bedroom Housing Wage, respectively.<ref name="National Low Income Housing Coalition-2023" />

Additionally, an ecologic study published by ''SSM – Population Health'' in 2021 found a strong correlation between past instances of redlining and ongoing instances of discriminatory [[lending]] practices in [[Milwaukee County, Wisconsin|Milwaukee County]]. More specifically, the researchers identified a direct link between redlining and adverse mental and [[physical health]] outcomes within the city. The observed pattern of increased lending discrimination corresponding with declining health indicates that [[structural racism]], evident in historical and contemporary lending disinvestment, serves as a predictor for poor health outcomes in the deeply [[Racial segregation in the United States|segregated]] neighborhoods of Milwaukee.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lynch |first1=Emily E. |last2=Malcoe |first2=Lorraine Halinka |last3=Laurent |first3=Sarah E. |last4=Richardson |first4=Jason |last5=Mitchell |first5=Bruce C. |last6=Meier |first6=Helen C.S. |date=2021 |title=The legacy of structural racism: Associations between historic redlining, current mortgage lending, and health |journal=SSM – Population Health |language=en |volume=14 |article-number=100793 |doi=10.1016/j.ssmph.2021.100793 |pmc=8099638 |pmid=33997243}}</ref>

== Government policies and programs ==

=== Subsidized housing ===
{{main|Subsidized housing in the United States}}

Various government policies and programs have been put in place to address affordable housing. One such program is the [[Section 8 (housing)|Section 8 Housing Choice Voucher Program]], which the [[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development|U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development]] (HUD) uses to provide rental assistance vouchers to eligible low-income households. The program offers financial aid to households with an annual gross income not surpassing 50% of [[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development|HUD]]'s [[median income]] criteria. HUD mandates that 75% of newly enrolled households should fall at or below 30% of the area's median income. Eligibility considers various factors such as household income, size, composition, citizenship status, assets, and essential expenses like healthcare and childcare.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Housing Choice Voucher Section 8 Housing Program – TDHCA |url=https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/section-8/#:~:text=HUD |website=www.tdhca.state.tx.us}}</ref> In the United States, the widely accepted standard for identifying households with extremely low incomes is either income at or below the [[federal poverty guideline]] or 30% of the area median income (AMI), whichever is higher.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mallach |first=Alan |date=2020-04-02 |title=A Review of "Introduction to housing (second edition)", Edited by Katrin B. Anacker, Andrew T. Carswell, Sarah D. Kirby and Kenneth R. Tremblay |journal=International Journal of Housing Policy |volume=20 |issue=2 |pages=302–307 |doi=10.1080/19491247.2020.1749416 |bibcode=2020IJHP...20..302M |s2cid=219060930 |issn=1949-1247}}</ref>

An [[Empirical research|empirical research study]] aimed at gauging the impact of government-subsidized housing in mitigating homelessness concluded that these housing initiatives did not effectively prioritize individuals at the highest risk of experiencing homelessness.<ref name="Early-1998" /> Consequently, a mere expansion of current housing programs administered by the [[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development|HUD]] is unlikely to significantly reduce the homeless population. This study published in the ''[[Journal of Policy Analysis and Management]]'' proposes an adjustment to [[Section 8 (housing)|Section 8]] programs. It suggests the restructuring of these programs by decreasing subsidies for each income bracket, removing those with relatively higher incomes from the eligibility criteria, and reallocating the resulting savings to provide subsidies to the most economically disadvantaged individuals who face a significantly higher risk of homelessness.<ref name="Early-1998">{{Cite journal |last=Early |first=Dirk W. |date=1998 |title=The Role of Subsidized Housing in Reducing Homelessness: An Empirical Investigation Using Micro-Data |journal=Journal of Policy Analysis and Management |volume=17 |issue=4 |pages=687–696 |doi=10.1002/(SICI)1520-6688(199823)17:4<687::AID-PAM5>3.0.CO;2-M |jstor=3325719 |issn=0276-8739}}</ref>

While [[Subsidized housing in the United States|subsidized housing]] is often intended to reduce [[Homelessness in the United States|homelessness]], the implementation of surveillance within subsidized housing has been shown to intensify the effects of poverty.<ref name="Hughes-2020">{{Cite journal |last=Hughes |first=Cayce C |date=2020-12-03 |title=A House but Not a Home: How Surveillance in Subsidized Housing Exacerbates Poverty and Reinforces Marginalization |journal=Social Forces |volume=100 |issue=1 |pages=293–315 |doi=10.1093/sf/soaa108 |issn=0037-7732}}</ref> An analysis based upon in-depth interviews with 67 low-income Black mothers living in subsidized housing in [[Houston|Houston, Texas]] found that property owners and [[landlord]]s often disproportionately surveil minority tenants. The surveillance that these mothers describe within their residences results in a lack of privacy within the home, increases the likelihood of eviction, and intensifies their financial struggles.<ref name="Hughes-2020" />

=== Inclusionary zoning ===
{{main|Inclusionary zoning}}
{{See also|Low-Income Housing Tax Credit}}

The United States government uses various [[inclusionary zoning]] regulations to require or incentivize developers to include a certain percentage of affordable housing units in new residential developments.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Youqin |last2=Ren |first2=Jianyu |date=2022-01-13 |title=Moving Toward an Inclusive Housing Policy?: Migrants' Access to Subsidized Housing in Urban China |journal=Housing Policy Debate |volume=32 |issue=4–5 |pages=579–606 |doi=10.1080/10511482.2021.1996430 |s2cid=245942802 |issn=1051-1482}}</ref> Incentives include density bonuses, tax credits, fee waivers, and deferral programs.<ref name="Schuetz 2012 32–36">{{cite encyclopedia |last1=Schuetz |first1=J. |chapter=Inclusionary Zoning to Support Affordable Housing |date=2012 |encyclopedia=International Encyclopedia of Housing and Home |pages=32–36 |publisher=Elsevier |doi=10.1016/b978-0-08-047163-1.00242-3 |isbn=978-0-08-047171-6 |last2=Meltzer |first2=R.}}</ref> Inclusionary zoning policies aim to promote [[Socioeconomics|socioeconomic]] diversity within communities and ensure that affordable housing is integrated into areas with a mix of income levels.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/resrep22075 |title=Inclusionary Housing: Creating and Maintaining Equitable Communities |last=Jacobus |first=Rick |date=2019 |publisher=Lincoln Institute of Land Policy}}</ref>

[[Inclusionary zoning|Inclusionary housing]] policies were initially designed to counteract the impact of "[[exclusionary zoning]]" practices that reinforced economic and [[racial segregation]]. These inclusionary policies use the [[Financial market|private market]], often enabling the establishment of new affordable units without heavy reliance on public funding. Because the creation of affordable units under an inclusionary zoning policy hinges on the construction of market-rate housing, it is most effective in areas with active construction or expected new development, where it is likely to generate a substantial number of affordable homes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Inclusionary zoning |url=https://localhousingsolutions.org/housing-policy-library/inclusionary-zoning/ |website=Local Housing Solutions |language=en-US}}</ref>

One inclusionary zoning program put in place by the United States government to encourage the development and rehabilitation of affordable rental housing is the [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit]] (LIHTC) program. Through this program, developers receive [[tax credit]]s in exchange for agreeing to rent a portion of their units to low-income tenants at reduced rates.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Leviner |first=Sagit |date=2004 |title=Affordable Housing and the Role of the Low Income Housing Tax Credit Program: A Contemporary Assessment |journal=The Tax Lawyer |volume=57 |issue=4 |pages=869–904 |jstor=20772495 |issn=0040-005X}}</ref> Eligibility for these tax credits necessitates that the proposed development either encompasses new construction or involves substantial refurbishment of residential units. The specific amount of credits a development may obtain depends on the overall depreciable capital improvements and the available funding a state has to cover the entire development cost.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Housing Tax Credits FAQs |url=https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us/multifamily/faqs-htc-app-review.htm |website=www.tdhca.state.tx.us}}</ref>

The [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|LIHTC]], established in 1986, stands as a groundbreaking departure from the typical structure of supply-side housing programs, which primarily relied on [[Subsidized housing in the United States|subsidizing]] low-income housing. As of 2010, this innovative approach yielded the construction of 1.5&nbsp;million low-income housing units.<ref name="Desai-2010">{{Cite journal |last1=Desai |first1=Mihir |last2=Dharmapala |first2=Dhammika |last3=Singhal |first3=Monica |date=2010 |title=Tax Incentives for Affordable Housing: The Low Income Housing Tax Credit |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/649832 |journal=Tax Policy and the Economy |language=en |volume=24 |issue=1 |pages=181–205 |doi=10.1086/649832 |s2cid=167657010 |issn=0892-8649|url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, while the [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|LIHTC]] has expanded to provide the most new affordable housing in the United States, the program has received many criticisms and calls for its elimination.

One such criticism is that the effectiveness of the [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|LIHTC]] program in providing affordable housing depends on the motivations of various market participants. Currently, major [[corporation]]s are the primary investors in [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|LIH credits]], and their incentives may be influenced not only by the [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|LIHTC]] program itself but also by related programs, like [[Community Reinvestment Act]] (CRA) regulatory obligations.<ref name="Desai-2010" />

In terms of benefits of the [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|LIHTC]] program, a 2011 analysis published in the ''Housing Policy Debate'' journal found that increases in the use of tax credits are linked to reductions in [[racial segregation]] in [[metropolitan area]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Horn |first1=Keren M. |last2=O'Regan |first2=Katherine M. |date=2011 |title=The low income housing tax credit and racial segregation |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10511482.2011.591536 |journal=Housing Policy Debate |language=en |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=443–473 |doi=10.1080/10511482.2011.591536 |s2cid=154635214 |issn=1051-1482|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This means that LIHTC projects do not tend to lead to increased segregation, even in areas with elevated poverty levels.

== Innovative solutions and community initiatives ==

=== Tenant protections ===
Tenant protections are legal measures and regulations designed to safeguard the rights and interests of tenants in the rental housing market.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tach |first1=Laura |last2=Emory |first2=Allison Dwyer |date=2017 |title=Public Housing Redevelopment, Neighborhood Change, and the Restructuring of Urban Inequality |journal=American Journal of Sociology |volume=123 |issue=3 |pages=686–739 |doi=10.1086/695468 |s2cid=149298544 |issn=0002-9602}}</ref> An example of tenant protections is [[rent regulation]], which includes [[Rent control in the United States|rent control]] and rent stabilization policies. Both of these protections are used to regulate and limit the amount landlords can increase rent for tenants in certain properties; however, they have distinct origins and guidelines.<ref name="rentguidelinesboard.cityofnewyork.us">{{Cite web |title=Rent Control FAQ – Rent Guidelines Board |url=https://rentguidelinesboard.cityofnewyork.us/resources/faqs/rent-control/#difference |website=rentguidelinesboard.cityofnewyork.us}}</ref>

[[Rent control in the United States|Rent control]] allows landlords to increase rents, with limitations such as an annual increase cap and an upper limit known as the "maximum base rent," adjusted periodically to align with operating costs.<ref name="rentguidelinesboard.cityofnewyork.us" /> Assessing the impact of rent control on its ability to promote stability for individuals residing in rent-controlled units has predominantly shown positive outcomes. Nevertheless, the evidence regarding its effectiveness in promoting economic opportunities or diminishing racial disparities is inconclusive.<ref name="Rajasekaran-2019">{{Cite journal |last1=Rajasekaran |first1=Prasanna |last2=Treskon |first2=Mark |last3=Greene |first3=Solomon |date=January 2019 |title=Rent Control: What Does the Research Tell Us about the Effectiveness of Local Action? |journal=Research to Action Lab}}</ref>

Rent stabilization laws restrict rent increases, but they are typically less stringent than rent control. These laws include rights to lease renewal and constraints on annual rent increases, which are recalculated each year.<ref name="Rajasekaran-2019" /> Despite their differences, rent stabilization has become more prevalent than rent control. For example, in New York City in 2021, there were 16,400 rent-controlled apartments compared to 1,048,860 rent-stabilized apartments.<ref name="Rajasekaran-2019" />

[[Just-Cause Eviction|Just cause eviction]] laws are also tenant protections, given they prevent landlords from evicting tenants without valid reasons, such as non-payment of rent or lease violations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jackson |first=Thomas |date=2017-12-01 |title=Evicted: Poverty and Profit in the American City |journal=Journal of American History |volume=104 |issue=3 |pages=820–822 |doi=10.1093/jahist/jax411 |issn=0021-8723}}</ref> Approximately 44 million households, constituting around one-third of all households in the United States, are renters. Annually, about 2.7&nbsp;million of these renting households face potential [[Eviction in the United States|eviction]] through legal procedures.<ref name="Graetz-2023">{{Cite journal |last1=Graetz |first1=Nick |last2=Gershenson |first2=Carl |last3=Hepburn |first3=Peter |last4=Porter |first4=Sonya R. |last5=Sandler |first5=Danielle H. |last6=Desmond |first6=Matthew |date=2023-10-10 |title=A comprehensive demographic profile of the US evicted population |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |language=en |volume=120 |issue=41 |article-number=e2305860120 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2305860120 |doi-access=free |issn=0027-8424 |pmc=10576155 |pmid=37782792|bibcode=2023PNAS..12005860G }}</ref> Data linking eviction court records to the 2006 - 2015 [[American Community Survey]] show a significant disparity: despite Black Americans making up an average of 18.6% of all renters, they represent 51.1% of those under threat of eviction and 43.4% of those actually evicted. In contrast, while White Americans comprise over half of all renters at 50.5%, they constitute only 26.3% of those facing eviction and 32.0% of those evicted.<ref name="Graetz-2023" /> [[Just-Cause Eviction]] laws are especially crucial in contexts where certain groups, such as Black Americans in this case, face a higher risk of eviction despite being a smaller percentage of the renting population.

=== Mixed-income developments ===
[[File:Via Sol Apartments, Saint Louis Park.jpg|thumb|A new apartment building under construction in St. Louis Park, Minnesota, called Via Sol by PLACE (Projects Linking Art, Community and Environment). The development project is a "mixed-use, mixed-income creative community" along the Highway 7 frontage road near the Southwest Light Rail (SWLRT) Wooddale Station, with 217 apartment units, renewable energy sources, and 220 parking spaces.]]
One innovative solution for housing affordability is [[Mixed-income housing|mixed-income developments]], which are housing projects that include a blend of units at various rent or price levels, designed to create [[Socioeconomics|socioeconomically]] diverse communities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fraser |first1=James C. |last2=Chaskin |first2=Robert J. |last3=Bazuin |first3=Joshua Theodore |date=2013 |title=Making Mixed-Income Neighborhoods Work for Low-Income Households |journal=Cityscape |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=83–100 |jstor=41959112 |issn=1936-007X}}</ref> These residences might be mixed within the same hallway, placed in distinct buildings, or situated on separate floors or wings within a single building. Additionally, city blocks or neighborhoods can be deemed mixed-income when they encompass a variety of housing options affordable to individuals spanning various income brackets.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Developing mixed income housing |url=https://localhousingsolutions.org/refine/developing-mixed-income-housing/ |website=Local Housing Solutions |language=en-US}}</ref>

The term "mixed-income" varies across locations, reflecting diverse ratios of affordable and market-rate units along with differing [[income bracket]]s defining affordability in such developments. Various subsidy programs, such as [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|Low Income Housing Tax Credits]] and project-based vouchers, are often combined to cater to the needs of lower-income households, dependent on the specific community and housing assistance type.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Laura |first1=Tach |last2=Pendall |first2=Rolf |last3=Derian |first3=Alexandra |date=January 2014 |title=Income Mixing across Scales Rationale, Trends, Policies, Practice, and Research for More Inclusive Neighborhoods and Metropolitan Areas |journal=The Urban Institute}}</ref>

Allocating more units for higher-income residents in mixed-income spaces has been shown to enhance maintenance and amenities, fostering [[economic diversity]] by competing with market-rate developments.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brophy |first1=Paul C. |last2=Smith |first2=Rhonda N. |date=1997 |title=Mixed-Income Housing: Factors for Success |journal=Cityscape: A Journal of Policy Development and Research |volume=3 |issue=2}}</ref> However, research challenges the assumption that integrating lower-income and higher-income households significantly strengthens social connections within these developments, indicating limited interaction across income groups and no substantial changes in the economic status of assisted housing families.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Levy |first1=Diane K. |last2=McDade |first2=Zach |last3=Bertumen |first3=Kassie |date=2013 |title=Mixed-Income Living: Anticipated and Realized Benefits for Low-Income Households |journal=Cityscape: A Journal of Policy Development and Research |volume=15 |issue=2}}</ref>

== Affordable housing initiatives by city ==

=== San Diego ===
{{See also|California housing shortage}}

[[San Diego]]'s housing crisis is largely driven by a shortage of housing units. According to the [[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development|Housing and Urban Development]], total housing costs are affordable if they meet or are below 30% of annual income.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Hamidi |first1=Shima |last2=Ewing |first2=Reid |last3=Renne |first3=John |date=3 May 2016 |title=How Affordable Is HUD Affordable Housing? |url=https://pdxscholar.library.pdx.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1086&context=trec_reports |journal=Housing Policy Debate |volume=26 |issue=3 |pages=437–455 |doi=10.1080/10511482.2015.1123753 |s2cid=73663740|url-access=subscription }}</ref> According to the [[American Community Survey]] of 2016, 54.8% of renters in [[San Diego]] pay 30% or over of their income toward rent and housing costs every month.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ACS 2016 (1-Year Estimates) |url=https://www.socialexplorer.com/tables/ACS2016/R11533394 |access-date=2019-03-06 |website=Social Explorer}}</ref> Even with an estimated 84,000 vacant housing units,<ref>{{Cite web |last=U.S. Census Bureau |title=Selected Housing Characteristics 2013–2017 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates |url=https://factfinder.census.gov/faces/tableservices/jsf/pages/productview.xhtml?pid=ACS_17_5YR_DP04&prodType=table |archive-url=https://archive.today/20200214011026/https://factfinder.census.gov/faces/tableservices/jsf/pages/productview.xhtml?pid=ACS_17_5YR_DP04&prodType=table |archive-date=2020-02-14 |access-date=2019-03-06 |website=American Factfinder}}</ref> a significant number of people choose to live outside of county lines, where housing costs are lower. About twenty percent of [[San Diego]] workers live outside the county, notably in [[Riverside County]], where median home costs can be as much as $195,400 cheaper.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Service |first=City News |date=18 April 2018 |title=San Diego County To Study Affordable Housing Solutions |url=http://www.kpbs.org/news/2018/apr/18/san-diego-county-to-study-affordable-housing/ |access-date=2019-03-06 |website=KPBS Public Media}}</ref> However, where housing costs may be lower, these workers are now facing longer commutes. The combination of housing costs and transport costs means that as many as 45% of the population working in [[San Diego]] face poverty.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A Renewed Struggle for the American Dream: PRRI 2018 California Workers Survey |url=https://www.prri.org/research/renewed_struggle_for_the_american_dream-prri_2018_california_workers_survey/ |access-date=2019-03-06 |website=PRRI|date=28 August 2018 }}</ref>

Homelessness is a huge challenge also stemming from this lack of affordable housing. San Diego's Regional Task Force on the Homeless counted 4,912 homeless individuals in the City of San Diego alone, with 8,576 homeless persons in the [[San Diego]] region.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Regional Task Force on the Homeless |date=May 17, 2018 |title=2018 WeAllCount Annual Report San Diego County |url=https://www.rtfhsd.org/get-involved/weallcount/}}</ref> Multiple propositions have been made to abate the problem. In 2018, California voted on Proposition 10, which would have lifted state regulations on [[Rent regulation|rent control]] and allowed local jurisdictions to set their own policies. Proposition 10 did not pass.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Proposition 10 {{!}} Official Voter Information Guide {{!}} California Secretary of State |url=http://www.voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/10/ |access-date=2019-03-06 |website=www.voterguide.sos.ca.gov}}</ref> More recently, in March 2019, the [[San Diego City Council]] voted and approved a reform to parking standards on housing units near public transit with the goal of reducing housing costs associated with mandated parking spots and relieve traffic by encouraging residents to use [[Public transport|public transit]].<ref>{{cite press release |title=Mayor Faulconer's Parking Reforms Win City Council Approval |publisher=City of San Diego |date=4 March 2019 |url=https://www.sandiego.gov/mayor/news/releases/mayor-faulconer%E2%80%99s-parking-reforms-win-city-council-approval}}</ref>

==== Initiatives ====
[[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development|The Department of Housing and Urban Development's]] [[Section 8 (housing)|Section 8]] programs help low income citizens find housing by paying the difference between the market price of a home and 30% of the renter's income.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hamidi |first1=Shima |last2=Ewing |first2=Reid |last3=Renne |first3=John |title=How Affordable is HUD Affordable Housing? |url=http://nlihc.org/sites/default/files/How-Affordable-Is-HUD-Affordable-Housing.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170516152222/http://nlihc.org/sites/default/files/How-Affordable-Is-HUD-Affordable-Housing.pdf |archive-date=2017-05-16 |access-date=2018-11-03}}</ref> According to the San Diego Housing Commission, [[Section 8 (housing)|Section 8 housing vouchers]] are the city's largest affordable housing program and were responsible for helping to fill 14,698 homes in the 2014–2015 fiscal year.<ref>{{cite web |title=San Diego Housing Commission Rental Assistance |url=http://www.sdhc.org/Rental-Assistance |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180616105850/http://www.sdhc.org/Rental-Assistance/ |archive-date=2018-06-16 |access-date=2018-11-03 |publisher=San Diego Housing Commission}}</ref> The San Diego Housing Commission currently owns 2,221 affordable housing units and plans to expand that number in the future to meet the growing demand.<ref>{{cite web |title=Affordable Housing Programs |url=http://www.sdhc.org/Affordable-Housing |publisher=San Diego Housing Commission}}</ref>

In 2009, the San Diego Housing Commission implemented a finance plan that created 810 more units of affordable rental housing through leveraging the equity of its owned properties. The conversion of city-owned buildings into low-income affordable housing was made possible by an agreement made with the [[United States Department of Housing and Urban Development|Department of Housing and Urban Development]] in September 2007. The cost of rent and availability of these units for residents will remain consistent, as the city has put in place provisions to make them affordable for at least 55 years. Additionally, because of a concern that the people who need these housing units might be crowded out, the units are only available to residents with an income cap of 80% of the [[San Diego]] median.<ref>{{cite web |title=Creating Affordable Housing |url=http://www.sdhc.org/Affordable-Housing/Creating-Affordable-Housing |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180614194953/http://www.sdhc.org/Affordable-Housing/Creating-Affordable-Housing/ |archive-date=2018-06-14 |access-date=2018-11-03 |publisher=San Diego Housing Commission}}</ref>

In 2017, the new Atmosphere apartment building in downtown [[San Diego]] drew attention when it announced that it would be offering 205 apartments to low-income residents.<ref name="San Diego Union Tribune">{{cite news |last1=Molnar |first1=Phillip |title=Living in downtown San Diego with a Balcony- for $525 a month |newspaper=San Diego Union Tribune |url=http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/business/real-estate/sd-fi-atmosphere-affordable-housing-20170531-story.html}}</ref> Residents pay their portion of rent through [[Section 8 (housing)|Section 8 vouchers]], and many of the apartments are available only to families who make 30% or less of the median income of the city.<ref>{{cite web |date=2015-03-25 |title=A New Atmosphere in San Diego |url=http://www.csh.org/2015/03/a-new-atmosphere-in-san-diego/ |access-date=28 November 2017 |publisher=Corporation for Supportive Housing}}</ref> The new housing project aimed to provide a low-rent area for residents who work downtown but who are unable to live near their workplace because of the high costs.<ref name="San Diego Union Tribune" />

In 2021, [[Gavin Newsom|Governor Newsom]]'s $110&nbsp;billion California Comeback Plan, which included the passing of Senate Bills 8, 9, and 10, was an attempt to help mitigate the current housing crisis. By extending housing production while avoiding displacement of existing tenants and increasing access to zoning for multi-units these bills aim to increase state provisioning and facilitate the development of denser housing.<ref name="California Governor-2021">{{Cite web |date=2021-09-16 |title=Governor Newsom Signs Historic Legislation to Boost California's Housing Supply and Fight the Housing Crisis |url=https://www.gov.ca.gov/2021/09/16/governor-newsom-signs-historic-legislation-to-boost-californias-housing-supply-and-fight-the-housing-crisis/ |access-date=2021-12-14 |website=California Governor |language=en}}</ref> The idea behind the California Comeback Plan is to boost [[California housing shortage|California's housing supply]] by removing barriers to [[Multifamily residential|multi-family units]] and [[Secondary suite|accessory dwelling units]].<ref name="California Governor-2021" />

=== San Francisco ===
{{See also|San Francisco housing shortage}}

Affordable housing and [[Homelessness in the San Francisco Bay Area]] represents an ongoing part of public discourse, especially as the [[San Francisco Bay Area|Bay Area]] population has increased to house about 20% of the [[California|State of California]]'s population – the regional population is expected to increase from 7.2&nbsp;million to 9.3&nbsp;million by 2040.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Bay Area in 2040 |url=https://mtc.ca.gov/sites/default/files/2-The_Bay_Area_In_2040.pdf |access-date=2022-04-19 |website=mtc.ca.gov |publisher=Metropolitan Transportation Commission}}</ref> Major cities including Los Angeles and San Francisco frequently cite increases to the homeless population as a result of reductions in [[Real estate economics|housing supply]], while the limitations to affordable housing are also exacerbated by issues of [[gentrification]] and [[redlining]], growing residential sprawl within residential communities, and the prevalence of the [[housing bubble]] that keeps rent prices consistently high.<ref>"The History of Homelessness in the United States." Permanent Supportive Housing: Evaluating the Evidence for Improving Health Outcomes Among People Experiencing Chronic Homelessness., U.S. National Library of Medicine, 11 July 2018, www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519584/.</ref> While local governance bodies such as the Zoning Adjustment Board (ZAB) have worked to introduce reforms to policies such as [[single-family zoning]] in an effort to improve housing affordability, the growing homeless population within the [[San Francisco Bay Area|Bay Area]] also points to shortfalls in addressing the intersection of homelessness with issues of [[Mental disorder|mental illness]], anti-homeless sentiments and [[racial discrimination]].

=== New York City ===
{{main|New York City housing shortage}}
{{See also|New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development}}

New York City has a shortage of affordable housing resulting in overcrowding and homelessness. New York City attracts thousands of new residents each year and housing prices continue to climb. Finding affordable housing affects a large portion of the city's population including low-income, moderate-income, and even median income families.<ref name="Subsidized Housing 2011">[http://furmancenter.org/files/publications/SHIPReportFinal.pdf "State of New York City's Subsidized Housing: 2011."] New York: [[Furman Center for Real Estate and Urban Policy]], The Institute for Affordable Housing.</ref>  Since 1970, income has remained relatively stagnant while rent has nearly doubled for [[Demographics of New York (state)|New Yorkers]].<ref name="Subsidized Housing 2011" /> Consequently, 48.7% of householders spend more than 30% of their income on rent.<ref name="Subsidized Housing 2011" /> Several federal and state initiatives have targeted this problem, but have failed to provide enough affordable, inclusive, and sustainable housing for New York City residents. The demand for affordable housing in New York City remains high: 2.5 million applications were submitted for 2,600 available affordable apartments in 2016.<ref>Erin Durkin. [https://web.archive.org/web/20220114010705/https://www.nydailynews.com/new-york/2-5m-people-applied-nyc-2-600-affordable-housing-units-article-1.2633482 Over 2.5 million people applied for just 2,600 available affordable housing units this year], ''New York Daily News'', May 11, 2016</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Australian property market
======================================================================

{{Short description|Real estate market in Australia}}
The '''Australian property market''' comprises the trade of land and its permanent fixtures located within [[Australia]]. It is dominated by residential property and forms a central part of the national economy, with housing serving as the main store of household wealth and the construction and sale of dwellings accounting for a substantial share of economic activity and employment.<ref name="HunterRBA2024">{{cite web |last=Hunter |first=Sarah |title=Housing Market Cycles and Fundamentals |publisher=Reserve Bank of Australia |date=16 May 2024 |url=https://www.rba.gov.au/speeches/2024/sp-ag-2024-05-16.html}}</ref> The market is characterised by a concentration of population and value in the major capital cities, a housing stock weighted towards detached houses, and high levels of owner-occupation alongside a large private rental sector.<ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" /><ref name="AHURI328" /> Underlying demand for housing is shaped chiefly by population growth, which is rapid by international standards and driven largely by immigration, and by the average number of people living in each household. Supply responds more slowly, so prices and rents tend to adjust in the meantime.<ref name="HunterRBA2024" />

Australian housing has drawn sustained attention for the long-run rise in prices relative to incomes, which has made affordability a recurring economic and political issue, and for one of the highest levels of household debt among advanced economies, most of it owed against housing.<ref name="APRA2025DTI" /> Real house prices changed little for much of the twentieth century before entering a sustained upward trend from the 1950s, rising particularly strongly from the mid-1990s after the financial deregulation of the 1980s opened mortgage lending to greater competition and treated housing increasingly as an investment asset.<ref name="d941" /><ref name="AHURI328" /> There has been a disagreement among researchers about the main causes of higher prices, variously emphasising interest rates, population growth and immigration, constraints on the supply of new housing, and tax settings favouring property investment, and about whether the market constitutes a [[Australian property bubble|housing bubble]].<ref name="SaundersTulip2019" />

== History ==
The Australian property market has been studied over the long run mainly through historical house prices for Sydney and Melbourne, which reach back to 1880 and have been joined onto modern data to form a continuous record running to the present.<ref name="d941" /> In the seventy years from 1880 to the mid-1950s, real house prices changed little, with several periods of significant decline, before beginning a sustained upward trend. From the early 1970s real prices rose by an average of about 3 per cent a year, and the cycle that began in the mid-1990s produced rises of around 6 per cent a year. Across this period, the market moved through cycles tied to each of the major economic cycles, the two most pronounced being the boom of the 1880s with the 1890s depression that followed, and the boom that ran from the mid-1990s into the 2000s.<ref name="d941">{{cite web | last=Stapledon | first=Nigel | title=A History of Housing Prices in Australia 1880-2010 | website=Search eLibrary | date=2010-11-18 | url=https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=1711224 | access-date=2026-06-09}}</ref>

From the end of the Second World War to the mid-1970s, the market operated within a heavily regulated environment of low, controlled interest rates, with home finance channelled largely through building societies, alongside relatively cheap and abundant land. From the 1970s, and more sharply through the financial [[deregulation]] of the 1980s, this changed: the banking and mortgage system was opened to greater competition and to international capital, lending conditions were relaxed, and housing increasingly came to be treated as an investment asset as well as shelter, a shift often described as the financialisation of housing.<ref name="AHURI328">{{cite report |last1=Burke |first1=Terry |last2=Nygaard |first2=Christian |last3=Ralston |first3=Liss |title=Australian home ownership: past reflections, future directions |publisher=Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute |series=AHURI Final Report No. 328 |date=May 2020 |doi=10.18408/ahuri-5119801 |url=https://www.ahuri.edu.au/research/final-reports/328|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

From 2000, prices entered a period of exceptional growth, with real median house prices in the capital cities roughly doubling between 2000 and 2010. Australia largely avoided the house-price falls seen elsewhere during the 2007 to 2008 global financial crisis. Growth was more uneven over the following decade: real prices fell and then flattened in the early 2010s, recovered to about 2017, and dipped again to 2020 amid tighter lending standards. Real prices then rose sharply from late 2020 through 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, before falling by about 11 per cent in 2023 as mortgage rates climbed steeply, and resuming mild growth from mid-2023. From the mid-2010s the market also became less uniform across the country, with Adelaide, Brisbane and Perth recording stronger growth while Melbourne lagged.<ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025">{{cite report |last1=Abelson |first1=Peter |last2=Joyeux |first2=Roselyne |title=Housing Rents and Prices in Australia 2000-25: Facts, Explanations and Outcomes |publisher=Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, Crawford School of Public Policy, Australian National University |series=TTPI Working Paper 22/2025 |date=December 2025 |url=https://crawford.anu.edu.au/sites/default/files/2025-12/WP%20-%20Housing%20Rents.pdf}}</ref>

== Market structure ==
The structure of the Australian property market can be described by the make-up of the housing stock and by how that stock is held. Dwellings range from detached houses to higher-density townhouses and apartments, while occupants hold their housing either as owners, who may live in the dwelling or let it to tenants, or as renters.

===Dwelling types===
By 2025 Australia had around 11.4 million residential dwellings. Detached houses remained the most common dwelling type, comprising about 71 per cent of the stock in 2024, with semi-detached dwellings and townhouses making up around 13 per cent and apartments about 16 per cent.<ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" /> The apartment share has grown over time, from roughly 14 per cent of dwellings in 2010 to 16 per cent in 2021, continuing a longer-term trend in building approvals towards higher-density housing such as townhouses and units.<ref>{{cite news |last=Mulligan |first=Mark |title=Apartments, townhouses continue to drive Australian building approvals |work=The Sydney Morning Herald |date=4 May 2015 |url=https://www.smh.com.au/business/the-economy/apartments-townhouses-continue-to-drive-australian-building-approvals-20150504-1mzb3y.html |access-date=2026-06-13}}</ref> Between 2015 and early 2025 the dwelling stock grew by about 17 per cent, marginally faster than the population, while average household size edged down from about 2.6 to 2.54 persons.<ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" /> Turnover in the market typically averages around 6 per cent of dwellings a year.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.rba.gov.au/publications/smp/boxes/2014/nov/a.pdf |title=Housing Prices, Turnover and Borrowing |access-date=2015-10-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150707064210/http://www.rba.gov.au/publications/smp/boxes/2014/nov/a.pdf |archive-date=2015-07-07 }}</ref>

=== Ownership ===
[[Owner-occupancy|Owner-occupation]] has been a defining feature of Australian housing since the mid-twentieth century. The home-ownership rate rose strongly in the postwar decades and has since remained high by international standards, holding broadly around two-thirds of households.<ref name="AHURI328" /><ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" /> That stable headline figure, however, masks a marked decline in ownership among younger households, for whom rising prices have made home purchase harder to attain.<ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" /> Owners of residential property fall into two groups: owner-occupiers, who live in the dwelling, and [[investors]], who let properties to tenants.

Owner-occupiers have consistently formed the larger group, accounting for more than 60 per cent of total housing demand across the states and territories, though the investor share varies by region, ranging from around 22 per cent in Tasmania to about 38 per cent in New South Wales.<ref name="MaReedLiang2019">{{cite journal |last1=Ma |first1=Le |last2=Reed |first2=Richard |last3=Liang |first3=Jian |title=Separating owner-occupier and investor demands for housing in the Australian states |journal=Journal of Property Investment & Finance |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=215-232 |date=2019 |doi=10.1108/JPIF-07-2018-0045}}</ref> Whether negative or positive gearing is more advantageous depends on prevailing tax settings and interest rates; negative gearing is most effective when interest rates are low and property values are rising, so that the expected capital gain outweighs the holding loss.<ref name="EBSCO-NG">{{cite web |title=Negative gearing |website=EBSCO Research Starters |url=https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/business-and-management/negative-gearing |access-date=2026-06-13}}</ref><ref name="RBA-QA-2019">{{cite web |title=Question & Answer Session: Property, Debt and Financial Stability |publisher=Reserve Bank of Australia |date=20 March 2019 |url=https://www.rba.gov.au/speeches/2019/sp-ag-2019-03-20-q-and-a-transcript.html |access-date=2026-06-13}}</ref> Studies have found that investor activity rises as expected [[capital growth]] increases, with investors willing to accept lower rental yields, and that rising prices tend to draw in buyers seeking [[capital gains]] rather than rental return.<ref name="MaReedLiang2019" /><ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" /> Owner-occupier first-home buyers have increasingly depended on family financial support, sometimes called the "[[Bank of Mum and Dad|bank of mum and dad]]", to meet deposit requirements.<ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" />

=== Residential rental market===
{{main|Australian residential rental market}}
Renting accounts for a substantial share of Australian housing, with roughly a quarter to a third of households renting their home. The proportion renting privately rose from about 20 per cent in 1999–2000 to 26 per cent in 2019–20, while the share renting from state and territory social housing authorities fell from around 6 per cent to about 3 per cent over the same period.<ref name="ABS250522">{{cite web |title=Housing Occupancy and Costs |url=https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/people/housing/housing-occupancy-and-costs/latest-release |website=Australian Bureau of Statistics |access-date=19 September 2022}}</ref>

From 2022, advertised rents rose sharply, increasing by about 12 per cent over the year, the strongest rise in 14 years, while the national vacancy rate fell to around 1 per cent, a situation widely described as a rental crisis.<ref name="Guardian140722">{{cite news |last1=Taylor |first1=Josh |title='A landlord's market': rents hit record highs across Australia's capital cities |url=https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2022/jul/14/a-landlords-market-rents-hit-record-highs-across-australias-capital-cities |access-date=22 September 2022 |work=The Guardian |date=14 July 2022}}</ref> Contributing factors cited at the time included some landlords selling to owner-occupiers, the use of dwellings for short-term letting such as [[Airbnb]], a limited supply of social housing, and pandemic-related shifts such as smaller household sizes and movement to regional areas.<ref name="ABC210922">{{cite news |title=Australia's runaway rents |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-09-21/australia-is-in-the-grip-of-its-worst-rental-crisis/101453246 |access-date=22 September 2022 |publisher=Australian Broadcasting Commission |date=21 September 2022}}</ref>

The severity of the crisis is contested. Analysis of official data distinguishes advertised rents, which cover only the small flow of newly listed properties and rose steeply, from the rents actually paid across the whole stock, which rose more modestly because most tenants remained on existing agreements; advertised rents have been around a third higher than rents paid market-wide.<ref name="Phillips2025">{{cite report |last=Phillips |first=Ben |title=Australian Rental Cost Trends |publisher=POLIS: The Centre for Social Policy Research, Australian National University |date=2025 |url=https://polis.cass.anu.edu.au/files/docs/2025/6/Rental-Trends-Paper_0.pdf}}</ref> Measured against incomes, rents have broadly kept pace over the longer term, though affordability pressures fall most heavily on lower-income households, for whom rent can absorb 40 per cent or more of income, and are concentrated in outer suburban, coastal and remote areas rather than inner cities.<ref name="Phillips2025" /><ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" />

== Regional variations ==

The Australian property market is non-uniform, with high variation observed across the major cities and regional areas.<ref>[http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/mf/6416.0 6416.0 - Residential Property Price Indexes: Eight Capital Cities, Jun 2015]</ref>

=== Sydney ===
Sydney is Australia's largest and most expensive capital city housing market. Its dwellings are spread across distinct submarkets that differ sharply in price and tenure: the northern and eastern regions are the most expensive and have higher rates of owner-occupation, while the more affordable western and inner-western regions have larger shares of rental and investor-owned housing.<ref name="BanguraLee2022">{{cite journal |last1=Bangura |first1=Mustapha |last2=Lee |first2=Chyi Lin |title=Housing price bubbles in Greater Sydney: evidence from a submarket analysis |journal=Housing Studies |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=143-178 |date=2022 |doi=10.1080/02673037.2020.1803802|hdl=1959.4/unsworks_73361 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> At the 2016 census around 29 per cent of Greater Sydney dwellings were investor-owned, with rented dwellings making up about 35 per cent of housing in Western Sydney compared with roughly 19 per cent in the east.<ref name="BanguraLee2022" /> By mid-2025 Sydney's median house price was the highest of any capital at around $1.46 million, having risen about 29 per cent in real terms over the preceding decade, while unit prices grew far more slowly.<ref name="AbelsonJoyeux2025" />

===Melbourne===
Melbourne was historically Australia's second most expensive capital city by median dwelling value, but was overtaken by Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth during the mid-2020s.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.commbank.com.au/articles/newsroom/2025/10/housing-market-changes-gear.html|title=House prices change gear with Sydney closing in on $2m|publisher=Commonwealth Bank of Australia|date=23 October 2025|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref> Melbourne's home values grew more slowly than those of other major capitals following the COVID-19 pandemic, with prices recording a small decline in 2024 before stabilising. By early 2026, Melbourne's median dwelling value was around $854,000 according to PropTrack, with values still below their March 2022 peak.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.commbank.com.au/articles/newsroom/2026/01/australian-home-prices-record-high.html|title=Australian home prices hit record high in 2025|publisher=Commonwealth Bank of Australia|date=January 2026|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref>

===Brisbane===
Brisbane experienced strong price growth through the early 2020s, with its median house price first surpassing $1 million in 2025.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.commbank.com.au/articles/newsroom/2026/01/australian-home-prices-record-high.html|title=Australian home prices hit record high in 2025|publisher=Commonwealth Bank of Australia|date=January 2026|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref>  [[Cotality]] (formerly CoreLogic) recorded dwelling value growth of approximately 84 per cent between 2020 and 2026, making Brisbane the country's second most expensive capital after Sydney on a median dwelling basis.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://propertyupdate.com.au/the-latest-median-property-prices-in-australias-major-cities/|title=The latest median property prices in Australia's major cities|publisher=Property Update|date=May 2026|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref>

===Perth===
Perth's property market underperformed the national average for much of the 2010s following the end of the mining boom, but recorded the strongest annual growth of any capital city between 2023 and 2025, with dwelling values rising more than 24 per cent in some twelve month periods.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://propertyupdate.com.au/everything-you-need-to-know-about-the-state-of-australias-property-markets-in-charts/|title=The state of Australia's property markets in charts, April 2026|publisher=Property Update|date=April 2026|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref> Strong demand has been attributed to interstate migration, resources sector activity, and the city's relative affordability compared with the east coast capitals.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ibtimes.com.au/australias-two-speed-housing-market-cools-sydney-melbourne-prices-slip-2026-1867579|title=Australia's two-speed housing market cools as Sydney, Melbourne prices slip in 2026|publisher=International Business Times Australia|date=April 2026|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref>

===Adelaide===
Adelaide's property market recorded sustained price growth from 2020 onward, with dwelling values rising approximately 77 per cent over five years.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://propertyupdate.com.au/the-latest-median-property-prices-in-australias-major-cities/|title=The latest median property prices in Australia's major cities|publisher=Property Update|date=May 2026|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref>  The city's median house price exceeded Melbourne's during 2024, having previously been one of the most affordable capital cities. CoreLogic head of research Eliza Owen attributed the strength of the Adelaide market to low listing volumes and buyer demand from higher-income households.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.indailysa.com.au/news/in-depth/2025/01/08/adelaide-house-prices-keep-growing-as-sydney-melbourne-decline|title=Adelaide house prices keep growing as Sydney, Melbourne decline|work=InDaily|date=8 January 2025|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref>

===Hobart===
After being one of Australia's strongest performing capital city markets in the late 2010s, Hobart's growth slowed considerably during the Reserve Bank's interest rate rises of 2022 to 2024, with values remaining largely flat over the period.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.propertyology.com.au/2025-property-market-outlook/|title=2025 Property Market Outlook|publisher=Propertyology|date=2025|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref> Hobart contained several of the country's most affordable capital city suburbs by 2025, with median house values under $450,000 in localities including Gagebrook, Herdsmans Cove and Bridgewater.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cotality.com/au/insights/articles/housing-rebound-defies-affordability-strain-as-2025s-standout-suburbs-revealed|title=Best of the Best 2025|publisher=Cotality|date=December 2025|access-date=11 May 2026}}</ref>

== Drivers and influences ==
=== Population and immigration ===
Population growth, much of it driven by immigration, adds to underlying demand for housing. The Productivity Commission's 2004 inquiry into first home ownership found that growth in immigration since the mid-1990s had been an important contributor to housing demand, particularly in Sydney and Melbourne, while noting the difficulty of quantifying the effect of short-stay migrants such as overseas students.<ref name="PC2004">{{cite report |author=Productivity Commission |title=First Home Ownership |publisher=Productivity Commission |series=Inquiry Report No. 28 |date=2004 |url=https://www.pc.gov.au/inquiries/completed/first-home-ownership/report |access-date=2026-06-22}}</ref> Reserve Bank modelling of the mid-2000s immigration surge similarly estimated that the rise in population growth lowered rental vacancies and raised both rents and housing prices.<ref name="SaundersTulip2019" />

The extent to which immigration has driven more recent increases in prices and rents is contested. A peer-reviewed study covering 2006 to 2016 estimated that immigration raised housing prices by a meaningful but limited amount, accounting for roughly a fifth of price growth over the period, with larger effects on house prices than on units.<ref name="MoallemiMelser2020">{{cite journal |last1=Moallemi |first1=Morteza |last2=Melser |first2=Daniel |title=The impact of immigration on housing prices in Australia |journal=Papers in Regional Science |volume=99 |issue=3 |pages=773-786 |date=2020 |doi=10.1111/pirs.12497 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Several studies published in 2025 argued that immigration was not the primary cause of the affordability pressures of the 2020s, pointing instead to constraints on housing supply, tax settings favouring investors, and low interest rates. A study by the [[University of South Australia]] found no statistically significant link between international student numbers and rising rents over 2017 to 2024,<ref name="UniSA2025">{{Cite news |date=2025-03-20 |title='Thrown under the bus': Study concludes international students not to blame for rising rents |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-03-21/australia-rent-crisis-not-international-students-fault-study/105076290 |access-date=2025-09-12 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU}}</ref> and a 2025 Reserve Bank paper concluded that rapid growth in student numbers had not substantially raised rents or inflation.<ref name="RBA2025students">{{Cite news |last=Hutchens |first=Gareth |date=2025-07-24 |title=International students have not driven rents and inflation substantially higher, RBA says |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-07-24/international-students-did-not-drive-rents-inflation-higher-rba/105562616 |access-date=2025-09-12 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU}}</ref> Modelling by KPMG suggested that sharply reducing migration could even raise house prices over time. In a scenario limiting population growth to natural increase, it estimated that a smaller labour force would push up wages and that the resulting shortage of construction workers would constrain new housing supply by more than lower population growth reduced demand, leaving house prices modestly higher over a decade than under continued migration.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Commins |first=Patrick |date=2025-09-09 |title=Slashing migration would actually lead to higher house prices in Australia. Here's why |url=https://www.theguardian.com/business/2025/sep/10/slashing-migration-would-actually-lead-to-higher-house-prices-in-australia-heres-why |access-date=2025-09-12 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

=== Interest rates and monetary policy ===
Interest rates have large and clearly identified effects on Australian housing prices and construction, according to modelling published by the Reserve Bank of Australia, which also found that the effect of monetary policy on the wider economy operates largely through its effect on housing.<ref name="SaundersTulip2019">{{cite report |last1=Saunders |first1=Trent |last2=Tulip |first2=Peter |title=A Model of the Australian Housing Market |publisher=Reserve Bank of Australia |series=Research Discussion Paper 2019-01 |date=March 2019 |url=https://www.rba.gov.au/publications/rdp/2019/2019-01.html}}</ref> The same research estimated that a sustained fall in real mortgage rates of one percentage point would, holding rents constant, raise housing prices by around 8 per cent after two years, with larger effects over the longer run. Of the roughly threefold rise in real dwelling prices since 1982, the modelling attributed the greater part to the long decline in real mortgage rates, which fell from a peak of about 6 per cent in the 1980s to around 3 per cent, rather than to growth in rents.<ref name="SaundersTulip2019" />

=== Land supply and planning ===
The responsiveness of housing supply to prices, and the role of land-use regulation, are debated. Reserve Bank modelling found that home building does increase when prices rise, estimating that each 1 per cent increase in the number of dwellings lowers housing costs by around 2.5 per cent. The same research concluded that planning and land-development rules slow new housing but do not hold it back completely, and that the rules tend to loosen when there is enough money to be made from building.<ref name="SaundersTulip2019" /> Separate Reserve Bank research attributed a large part of the gap between house prices and construction costs to zoning, estimating that planning restrictions raised detached house prices in Sydney by around 73 per cent relative to the cost of supply, with smaller but still substantial effects in the other major cities, and that this effect had grown as restrictions bound more tightly against rising demand.<ref name="KendallTulip2018">{{cite report |last1=Kendall |first1=Ross |last2=Tulip |first2=Peter |title=The Effect of Zoning on Housing Prices |publisher=Reserve Bank of Australia |series=Research Discussion Paper 2018-03 |date=March 2018 |url=https://www.rba.gov.au/publications/rdp/2018/2018-03.html}}</ref> Other research has questioned whether relaxing planning rules reliably increases supply: a study of Australia's largest listed developers found they held landbanks equivalent to many years of sales, including large quantities of already-approved land, and timed construction to market conditions rather than building out as quickly as planning permitted.<ref name="Murray2020">{{cite journal |last=Murray |first=Cameron K. |title=Time is money: How landbanking constrains housing supply |journal=Journal of Housing Economics |volume=49 |article-number=101708 |date=2020 |doi=10.1016/j.jhe.2020.101708}}</ref>

=== Household debt and lending standards ===
Australian households carry high levels of debt by international standards, most of it owed against housing. According to the prudential regulator, aggregate household debt rose from around 155 per cent of disposable income to about 180 per cent over the two decades to 2025, a level well above many comparable economies.<ref name="APRA2025DTI">{{cite report |author=Australian Prudential Regulation Authority |title=Activating debt-to-income limits as a macroprudential policy tool |publisher=Australian Prudential Regulation Authority |date=27 November 2025 |url=https://www.apra.gov.au/news-and-publications/activating-debt-income-limits-macroprudential-policy-tool}}</ref> The build-up has been linked to financial deregulation in the 1990s, which eased access to credit, and to the long decline in interest rates, which allowed larger loans to be serviced at a similar cost; housing debt makes up roughly three-quarters of the total.<ref name="IMF2019">{{cite report |last1=Loukoianova |first1=Elena |last2=Wong |first2=Yu Ching |last3=Hussiada |first3=Ioana |title=Household Debt, Consumption, and Monetary Policy in Australia |publisher=International Monetary Fund |series=IMF Working Paper WP/19/76 |date=April 2019 |url=https://www.imf.org/en/Publications/WP/Issues/2019/04/05/Household-Debt-Consumption-and-Monetary-Policy-in-Australia-46689}}</ref>

Regulators have periodically tightened lending standards to contain these risks. The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority introduced limits on investor lending in 2014 and on interest-only lending in 2017, and from late 2014 required lenders to assess new mortgages against an interest-rate buffer to ensure borrowers could withstand higher rates.<ref name="APRA2025DTI" /> The Reserve Bank has assessed that, despite high debt levels, the household sector is generally resilient, with borrowing concentrated among higher-income households better able to service it; it estimated that even under a 30 per cent fall in housing prices, around nine in ten borrowers would retain positive equity, while noting that highly indebted and lower-income borrowers remain the most vulnerable.<ref name="RBAFSR2025">{{cite report |author=Reserve Bank of Australia |title=Financial Stability Review – April 2025: Resilience of Australian Households and Businesses |publisher=Reserve Bank of Australia |date=April 2025 |url=https://www.rba.gov.au/publications/fsr/2025/apr/resilience-of-australian-households-and-businesses.html}}</ref>

== Affordability ==
[[File:MelbourneHousing2013.JPG|thumb|Melbourne House prices to income ratio, 1965 to 2013]]
In the late 2000s, housing prices in [[Australia]], relative to average incomes, were among the highest in the world. As at 2011, house prices were on average six times average household income, compared to four times in 1990.<ref>{{cite web |title=The facts on Australian housing affordability |website=[[The Conversation (website)|The Conversation]] |url=http://theconversation.com/the-facts-on-australian-housing-affordability-42881}}</ref> This prompted speculation that the country was experiencing a [[real estate bubble]], like many other countries.<ref>[https://newmatilda.com/2008/10/21/there-recession-brewing-our-housing-bubble Is There a Recession Brewing in Our Housing Bubble?]</ref>

A 2025 industry analysis estimated that Australia needs to build an average of 225,400 new dwellings annually to 2034 in order to meet both new and historic housing demand.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-26 |title=More Houses Sooner: Australian Housing Demand & Timber Use Scenarios To 2034 |url=https://fwpa.com.au/report/more-houses-sooner/ |access-date=2025-06-04 |website=FWPA |language=en-AU}}</ref>

A Centre for International Economics report commissioned by the [[Housing Industry Association]] estimated that in the period 2023-2024, the total outlay required by a purchaser for a typical house and land package in a [[Greenfield land|greenfield]] estate in capital cities of Australia to range from {{Currency|638047|AUD}} for Adelaide to {{Currency|1252365|AUD}} for Canberra.
