This was estimated at 20% more by the California LAO.{{  r | LAO_C&C | p=13 | q=Construction labor is about 20 percent more expensive in California metros than in the rest of the country.}}<ref name=OCR_unions>{{cite news | last=Saltsman | first=Michael | title=Unions' fight against affordable housing | url=http://www.ocregister.com/2016/06/05/unions-fight-against-affordable-housing/ | access-date=2017-11-07 | newspaper=The Orange County Register | date=June 5, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171108020252/http://www.ocregister.com/2016/06/05/unions-fight-against-affordable-housing/ | archive-date=2017-11-08 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.bizjournals.com/sanfrancisco/blog/2016/10/housing-development-bay-area-oakland-labor-unions.html | title=Housing development's latest enemy: Bay Area construction unions  | last=Li | first=Roland | newspaper=San Francisco Business Times  | date=October 26, 2016 | access-date=2018-01-07 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170629161123/https://www.bizjournals.com/sanfrancisco/blog/2016/10/housing-development-bay-area-oakland-labor-unions.html | archive-date=2017-06-29 | url-status=live | quote=Angered by some developers' attempts to use cheaper non-union labor, Bay Area construction unions have filed appeals challenging projects' approvals and allied themselves with community groups who oppose the projects for different reasons. Labor groups are also fighting policies that supporters say would help address the region's housing crisis, such as more use of modular housing and streamlined project approvals. It's a high-stakes game: Unions say the appeals give them leverage to pressure developers to commit to using union labor and to hire locally.}}</ref> Multiple studies have estimated the contribution of prevailing wage requirements to total construction cost to be between a 0% and 37% percent increase, with a study finding a 0% cost increase (taking into account increased worker productivity and savings from decreased public subsidies) and all other studies finding at least a 9% cost increase.{{ r | LAT_PW | p=1 | q=No one knows how much prevailing wage increases the costs of homebuilding — but unions and developers are interested in the answer – It's hard to determine how much more paying prevailing wages adds to the cost of building homes. Consider the difficulty in finding two housing projects with different wage scales, but built at the exact same time and in the same place, at the same size and with the same materials. That's the challenge facing any researcher attempting to gauge the impact of prevailing wage. Here are some estimates on how prevailing wage affects California residential construction costs: Author 	Percent Cost Increase UC Berkeley 9% to 37% The California Institute for County Government 11% National Center for Sustainable Transportation 	15% San Diego Housing Commission 9% Beacon Economics 46% Smart Cities Prevail 0%*  *No cost impact, especially when taking into account increased worker productivity and savings from decreased public subsidies }}

Material costs are higher due to building codes and standards requiring better quality materials and higher energy efficiency.{{ r | LAO_C&C | p=13 | q=California's building codes and standards also are considered more comprehensive and prescriptive, often requiring more expensive materials and labor. For example, the state requires builders to use higher quality building materials—such as windows, insulation, and heating and cooling systems—to achieve certain energy efficiency goals.}}

=== Insurance costs ===
''[[CalMatters]]'' detailed in August 2024 how rising home insurance costs in the state were impacting landlords and renters. Renters are also being encouraged to take out renter's insurance policies to hedge against losing their possessions to natural disasters like fire in some parts of the state.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sumagaysay |first=Levi |date=2024-08-13 |title=Californians: Your rent may go up because of rising insurance rates |url=https://calmatters.org/economy/2024/08/california-insurance-crisis-hits-renters/ |access-date=2024-08-18 |work=CalMatters |language=en-US |quote=This is where the insurance crisis could worsen the housing crisis, according to some experts. Increased insurance costs for properties other than single-family homes are starting to affect the rental market — in a state where almost half of residents are renters — and could compound the state's housing problems, they say.}}</ref>

== Effects ==

=== Affordability ===
[[File:Median Housing Prices by Metro Area.webp|thumb|Median Housing Prices by Metro Area]]
[[File:Median rent by metro area 2.webp|thumb|Median rent by metro area]]This shortage has driven home prices and rents to extremely high levels.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-affordable-housing-transit-zoning-20190526-story.html|title=A little-noticed zoning twist is set to spark a home-building boom in L.A.|last=Khouri|first=Andrew|date=May 26, 2019|work=[[Los Angeles Times]]|access-date=2019-05-28}}</ref> In 2017, the median price of a home in California was more than 2.5 times the median in the U.S. as a whole, and in California's coastal urban areas, the shortage was greater than the inland areas, as demonstrated by the median prices of homes in those respective markets: $1.3M in San Francisco, $1M in San Jose, and $600k in Los Angeles, while only $250k in Fresno.<ref name=Median_bay_area_prices>{{ cite news | last=Scheinin  | first=Richard | title=As housing supply shrinks, San Francisco, San Jose and Oakland are nation's three most competitive markets | url=http://www.mercurynews.com/2017/11/16/as-the-housing-supply-shrinks-san-francisco-san-jose-and-oakland-are-the-nations-three-most-competitive-markets/ | access-date=2017-11-19 | publisher=Bay Area News Group | date=November 16, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171117072933/http://www.mercurynews.com/2017/11/16/as-the-housing-supply-shrinks-san-francisco-san-jose-and-oakland-are-the-nations-three-most-competitive-markets/ | archive-date=2017-11-17 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=Median_socal_prices>{{cite news | last=Romero | first=Dennis | title=A Middle-of-the-Road L.A. Home Now Costs Nearly $600,000 | url=http://www.laweekly.com/news/los-angeles-median-home-price-has-reached-nearly-600000-8061540 | access-date=2017-11-19 | newspaper=LA Weekly | date=March 27, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170611211748/http://www.laweekly.com/news/los-angeles-median-home-price-has-reached-nearly-600000-8061540 | archive-date=2017-06-11 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=Fresno_home_prices>{{cite news | last=Lee | first=Bonhia | title=How much do you have to make to buy a home in Fresno? | url=http://www.fresnobee.com/news/business/article166343727.html | access-date=2017-11-19 | newspaper=The Fresno Bee | date=August 9, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170810053507/http://www.fresnobee.com/news/business/article166343727.html | archive-date=2017-08-10 | url-status=live }}</ref> In the rental market, California now has the lowest vacancy rate the state has ever seen, at 3.6%;<ref name=SFChron_homeless_crisis>{{cite news | url=http://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/California-s-homelessness-crisis-moves-to-the-12182026.php | title=California's homelessness crisis expands to country | last1=Fagan | first1=Kevin | last2=Graham | first2=Alison | newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle | date=September 8, 2017 | access-date=2017-12-12 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170911021612/http://www.sfchronicle.com/news/article/California-s-homelessness-crisis-moves-to-the-12182026.php | archive-date=2017-09-11 | url-status=live | quote=With the county's rental vacancy rate hovering around 1 percent — California's is 3.6 percent, an all-time low for the state —  }}</ref> and while the median rent throughout the state for a two-bedroom apartment is $2,400, the median rent in coastal urban areas is even higher, surpassing $4,000 per month in San Francisco.{{ r | SJMN_HC_worse2 | p=1 | q=Across the state, the median rental price for a two-bedroom apartment is about $2,400, the third highest in the country. But statewide figures water down how absurd the situation is getting in urban coastal markets, where the vast majority of Californians live. The median rent for a two-bedroom apartment in San Francisco reached more than $4,000 this year.}}

In 2023, the [[housing market in San Diego]] shows that nearly 60% of homes have listing prices above $1 million. The median home price in the city is $910,000, making it the fourth highest among the 30 largest U.S. cities.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://fox5sandiego.com/news/local-news/san-diego/san-diego-among-cities-where-majority-of-homes-cost-over-1m-study/ |last=Coakley | first= Amber |title=San Diego among cities where majority of homes cost over $1M: study |work=fox5sandiego.com |date=Jul 12, 2023 |access-date=Sep 5, 2023   |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230713230110/https://fox5sandiego.com/news/local-news/san-diego/san-diego-among-cities-where-majority-of-homes-cost-over-1m-study/ |archive-date=July 13, 2023}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cbs8.com/article/news/local/paradise-at-a-price/nearly-60-of-homes-for-sell-in-san-diego-are-over-1m/509-0061dbb2-7a93-47a8-9d07-85122bfe2794 |last=De La Fe | first= Rocio |title=Report: Nearly 60% of homes for sale in San Diego are over $1 million |work=cbs8.com |date=Jul 13, 2023 |access-date=Sep 5, 2023   |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230714115033/https://www.cbs8.com/article/news/local/paradise-at-a-price/nearly-60-of-homes-for-sell-in-san-diego-are-over-1m/509-0061dbb2-7a93-47a8-9d07-85122bfe2794 |archive-date=July 14, 2023}}</ref> The average monthly rent in San Diego has risen to $3,175, placing it as the third-highest in the nation, only $7 less than that of San Francisco.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.kpbs.org/news/local/2023/07/11/san-diego-now-has-the-3rd-highest-rent-prices-in-the-nation |last=Carroll | first= John |title=San Diego now has the 3rd highest rent prices in the nation |work=kpbs.org |date=Jul 11, 2023 |access-date=Sep 6, 2023   |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230813142541/https://www.kpbs.org/news/local/2023/07/11/san-diego-now-has-the-3rd-highest-rent-prices-in-the-nation |archive-date=August 13, 2023}}</ref>

Housing affordability has declined over the last three decades; {{as of|2018|lc=y}}, less than a third of Californians could afford a median-priced home; in job centers such as the San Francisco Bay Area, that number is less than a quarter. (Nationally, more than half of American households can afford the median-priced American home.)<ref name=Housing_Affordability_Index>{{cite web |url=https://www.car.org/marketdata/data/haitraditional/ |title=Housing Affordability Index – Traditional |publisher=California Association of Realtors |access-date=2018-06-16|quote=C.A.R.'s Traditional Housing Affordability Index (HAI) measures the percentage of households that can afford to purchase the median priced home in the state and regions of California based on traditional assumptions.}}</ref> Housing unaffordability also leads to crowding, defined as more than one adult per room of a dwelling (counting two children as one adult). Californians are four times as likely to live in crowded housing as the average American, and this holds across every type of housing—renters, owners, those with and without children.{{ r | LAO_C&C | p=29-31 }}

When comparing the rental rates of Los Angeles and the average rate across the United States one can see just how much higher the city is compared to the rest of the country. While in 2017 the average rental rate in the United States was $1,357, in comparison the average rental rate in Los Angeles in 2017 was $2,284, almost a $1,000 average increase.{{citation needed|date=May 2019|reason=}}

=== Displacement and environmental impact ===

As a result, workers have moved to more affordable inland locations which requires longer commutes. {{As of|2018}}, the three cities in the United States with the largest share of [[super commuter]]s—workers spending an hour and a half or more each way to get to and from their jobs—are [[Stockton, California|Stockton]], [[Modesto, California|Modesto]] and [[Riverside, California|Riverside]].<ref name="Bennet 2018">{{cite web | last=Bennet | first=Sydney | title=Rise of the Super Commuters | website=Rentonomics | date=April 24, 2018 | url=https://www.apartmentlist.com/rentonomics/increase-in-long-super-commutes/ | access-date=2018-06-16}}</ref>{{ r | NYT_supercommuters_1 | p=1 | q=And that has given Stockton one of the nation's highest concentrations of "extreme commuters" who travel 90 or more minutes to work. Long commutes are, of course, not unique to Northern California. The number of commuters who travel 90 or more minutes to work is almost 3 percent nationwide. But the phenomenon is even more evident in the Bay Area, where the numbers rose to nearly 5 percent from 3 percent in just three years, according to an analysis of census data by the Brookings Institution. In Stockton, 8 percent of commuters travel 90 minutes or more. }} Workers have been displaced outside of the state as well; from 2007 to 2016, California saw net out-migration among all groups making under $110,000 a year, largely to [[Sun Belt]] states like [[Arizona]], [[Nevada]] and [[Texas]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Uhler |first1=Brian |last2=Garosi |first2=Justin |title=California Losing Residents Via Domestic Migration [EconTax Blog] | website=Legislative Analyst's Office | date=February 21, 2018 | url=http://lao.ca.gov/LAOEconTax/Article/Detail/265 | access-date=2018-06-16}}</ref> New market-rate production can help ease rent pressures, however, if the development is too small it may increase displacement and exclusion pressures for low-income households. Developing at least 100 units of new subsidized housing help alleviate those pressures in most markets. This number may be larger in superstar cities such as San Francisco.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chapple |first1=Karen |last2=and Song |first2=Taesoo |date=2025-01-02 |title=Can New Housing Supply Mitigate Displacement and Exclusion?: Evidence from Los Angeles and San Francisco |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01944363.2024.2319293 |journal=Journal of the American Planning Association |volume=91 |issue=1 |pages=1–15 |doi=10.1080/01944363.2024.2319293 |issn=0194-4363}}</ref>

Longer commutes and increased traffic caused by [[Urban sprawl|suburban sprawl]] due to housing shortages concentrated in job centers increase greenhouse gas emissions. Because of California's mild climate and heavily renewable [[energy mix]], transportation is the largest category of emissions in the state.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.arb.ca.gov/cc/inventory/data/data.htm |title=California Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventory |date=June 6, 2017 |author=California Air Resources Board |access-date=2018-06-16 |archive-date=June 13, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190613172152/https://www.arb.ca.gov/cc/inventory/data/data.htm }}</ref> When Californians emigrate to [[List of U.S. states by carbon dioxide emissions|states with higher per-capita greenhouse gas emissions]], they drive more, consume more energy for air conditioning, and use more fossil fuel-dependent electricity generation.<ref name=JUE_2010-05>{{ cite journal | last1=Glaeser |first1=Edward | author-link1=Edward Glaeser | last2=Kahn | first2=Matthew | author-link2=Matthew Kahn | date=2010-05-01 | title=The greenness of cities: Carbon dioxide emissions and urban development | url=http://papers.nber.org/papers/w14238.pdf | journal=Journal of Urban Economics | volume=67 | issue=3 | pages=404–418 |doi=10.1016/j.jue.2009.11.006 | access-date=2020-04-23 | quote=We find that the lowest emissions areas are generally in California and that the highest emissions areas are in Texas and Oklahoma. There is a strong negative association between emissions and land use regulations. By restricting new development, the cleanest areas of the country would seem to be pushing new development towards places with higher emissions. | url-access= }}</ref> Scarce, low-density housing is directly at odds with California's climate goals.{{ r | NYT_CA_CO2 | p=1 | q=The idea is to foster taller, more compact residential neighborhoods that wean people from long, gas-guzzling commutes, reducing greenhouse-gas emissions. ... Transportation accounts for one-third of the nation's carbon-dioxide emissions and recently surpassed power plants as its largest contributor to global warming. ... The Urban Land Institute concluded that policies to promote compact growth — such as building taller apartments around transit centers or adding more housing downtown — could help cut vehicle travel 20 to 40 percent. ...the combination of high housing costs and rising commute times threatens to keep the state from achieving its ambitious target of cutting emissions 40 percent below 1990 levels by 2030. }}<ref name=LAT_2017-03-06>{{ cite news | url=https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-housing-climate-change-goals-20170306-story.html | title=California won't meet its climate change goals without a lot more housing density in its cities | last=Dillon | first=Liam | newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=2017-03-06 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240111060401/https://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-housing-climate-change-goals-20170306-story.html |archive-date= Jan 11, 2024 }}</ref> <blockquote>"You can't be pro-environment and anti-housing, ... You can't be anti-sprawl and anti-housing. This is something that has not been very well understood." – [[Marlon Boarnet]], chair of the Department of Urban Planning and Spatial Analysis at [[USC Price School of Public Policy|USC]].{{ r | LAT_2017-03-06 }}</blockquote>

Scientists at the [[Renewable and Appropriate Energy Laboratory]] at the [[University of California, Berkeley]] recently found that [[infill development]], that is utilizing existing vacant urban structures for future housing or commercial use, has the potential to reduce [[CO2|CO<sub>2</sub>]] emissions; more so than any other option. Simply put, creating a denser housing structure limits the amount of travel time from work to home and back, thus limiting CO<sub>2</sub> emissions drastically. At governor [[Gavin Newsom]]'s first legislative session, he pledged to make the housing crisis one of his top priorities. One such solution is the More Homes Act, which overrides restrictive zoning requirements by implementing small to midsize apartment buildings near major job and transit centers.<ref>{{Cite news|last1=Wiener|first1=Scott|last2=Kammen|first2=Daniel|date=2019-03-25|title=Opinion {{!}} Why Housing Policy Is Climate Policy |url-access=subscription |language=en-US|work=The New York Times|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/03/25/opinion/california-home-prices-climate.html|access-date=2020-11-18|issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Bergöö|first1=Bettina|title=We Must Invest in Climate-Ready Affordable Housing Now|url=https://www.nrdc.org/experts/bettina-bergoo/we-must-invest-climate-ready-affordable-housing-now|access-date=2020-11-18|website=NRDC|date=June 30, 2020 |language=en |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210125115840/https://www.nrdc.org/experts/bettina-bergoo/we-must-invest-climate-ready-affordable-housing-now |archive-date= Jan 25, 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=HCD Policy: Housing and Climate Change|url=https://www.hcd.ca.gov/policy-research/specific-policy-areas/housing-climate-change.shtml|access-date=2020-11-18|website= California Department of Housing and Community Development  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201130231650/https://www.hcd.ca.gov/policy-research/specific-policy-areas/housing-climate-change.shtml |archive-date= Nov 30, 2020 }}</ref>

=== Poverty ===

When the cost of housing is factored into the poverty rate, as the [[United States Census Bureau|Census Bureau]] now does in its releases of the "Supplemental Poverty Measure,"<ref>{{ cite web | url=https://www.census.gov/topics/income-poverty/supplemental-poverty-measure/about.html | title=Supplemental Poverty Measure | publisher=United States Census Bureau | date=March 16, 2017 | access-date=2018-01-04 | quote=The official poverty measure, which has been in use since the 1960s, estimates poverty rates by looking at a family's or an individual's cash income. The new measure is a more complex statistic incorporating additional items such as tax payments and work expenses in its family resource estimates. Thresholds used in the new measure are derived from Consumer Expenditure Survey expenditure data on basic necessities (food, shelter, clothing and utilities) and are adjusted for geographic differences in the cost of housing.}}</ref> California's poverty rate lists as the highest in the nation, (and has since 2011, when the Census Bureau first started releasing poverty by this measure) currently at 20.4%, or just over 1 in 5 people.{{ r | SJMN_poverty | p=1 | q=When the cost of living is factored in, the Golden State has the highest poverty rate in the country. ... California has been the poorest state in the nation under the vastly more sophisticated "supplemental" poverty measure since the alternative statistic was created... The Census uses data dating to 2011 to calculate the cost of living, so even the improved poverty rate could be underestimating how big a drain housing has been on California's poor. }}<ref>{{ cite news | last=Huang | first=Josie | title=California's housing costs are driving its No. 1 poverty ranking | url=https://www.scpr.org/news/2017/09/12/75575/california-s-housing-costs-are-driving-its-no-1-po/ | access-date=2017-11-07 | publisher=Southern California Public Radio | date=September 12, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171005045133/https://www.scpr.org/news/2017/09/12/75575/california-s-housing-costs-are-driving-its-no-1-po/ | archive-date=2017-10-05 | url-status=live }}</ref> The [[Public Policy Institute of California]] estimates that if the housing costs in California matched those for the nation overall, California's poverty rate would instead be 14 percent.{{ r | SJMN_poverty | p=1 | q=One method: What would poverty look like if everyone in California had cheaper rents? Researchers at the Public Policy Institute of California, which has developed its own California-specific alternative poverty measure, tried to simulate an answer to that question. Researchers there ran a model of the state's poverty rate with every Californian bearing a cost of living similar to that in Fresno County, where a family of four making about $25,000 a year would not be considered poor. The result? The overall poverty rate drops dramatically (from about 21 percent to 14 percent)... }}

=== Homelessness ===
{{Main|Homelessness in California}}
[[File:Homeless in san francisco mission district California (6086987323).jpg|thumb|A homeless person sleeps on the sidewalk next to a limousine in the Mission area of San Francisco.]]
California in 2017 was home to an oversized share of the nation's homeless: 22%, for a state whose residents only make up 12% of the country's total population.{{ r | CA_Housing_Future | p=1 | q=California is home to 12 percent of the nation's population, but a disproportionate 22 percent of the nation's homeless population. }}<ref name=SacBee_homeless>{{cite news | url=https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article168107042.html | title=How California's housing crisis happened | last=Hart | first=Angela | newspaper=The Sacramento Bee | date=August 21, 2017 | access-date=2018-01-28 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171001045844/http://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article168107042.html | archive-date=2017-10-01 | url-status=live | quote=California is home to 12 percent of the U.S. population, but 22 percent of its homeless people. Cities that have seen dramatic rent increases, such as San Francisco and Los Angeles, attribute their spikes in homelessness directly to a state housing shortage that has led to an unprecedented affordability crisis.}}</ref> ''[[The Sacramento Bee]]'' notes that large cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco both attribute their increases in homeless to the housing shortage.<ref name=SacBee_homeless />{{ r | Kushel_homeless | p=1 | q=Some assume that homelessness is so common on the West Coast because people move here when they become homeless, but data do not support this. Most people experience homelessness close to where they lost their housing. ... Instead, the high rate of homelessness can be attributed to the lack of affordable housing in these regions. The West Coast suffers from rising costs of rental housing,...}} [[Homelessness in California|Homeless persons in California]] now number 135,000 (a 15% increase from 2015).<ref name=SFChron_homeless_crisis />

A study by the California Housing Partnership found that from 2016 to 2017 homelessness increased by 47 percent in Sacramento County (home to the state's capital, [[Sacramento California|Sacramento]]), 36 percent in Alameda County, and 13 percent in Santa Clara County.{{ r | SF_Chron_BA_crisis | p=1 | q=Studying the same time frame as Next 10 did, the Partnership found ... and enormous increases in homelessness. The homeless numbers are particularly shocking. As far away as Sacramento County, homelessness increased by a whopping 47 percent from 2016 to 2017. In Alameda County, homelessness skyrocketed by 36 percent over the course of the same year. In Santa Clara County, homelessness rose by 13 percent. }}

In 2024 California ranked first in the nation for number of homeless residents - with nearly a quarter of the total homeless population residing in the state.<ref name="cal_homeless25">{{cite web |last1=Kendall |first1=Marisa |title=New homelessness data: How does California compare to the rest of the country? |url=https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2025/01/hud-pit-count-2024/ |website=CalMatters |date=January 6, 2025 |access-date=12 April 2025 |ref=cal_homeless25}}</ref>

A study by [[Wharton School]] economists Desin Lin and [[Susan Wachter]] in 2019 concluded that the average marginal effect of regulation on housing prices in California is an increase of approximately 3% (with the average California city as the regulatory reference point). When referenced to the average level of regulation in the U.S., the total regulatory effect is estimated to be four times larger. It estimated that Los Angeles is the city where housing prices are most impacted by regulations and that if it relaxed all of its land use regulations to the levels of least regulated cities, the drop in housing prices would be approximately 25 percent.<ref>{{citation |last1=Lin |first1=Desin |title=The Effect of Land Use Regulation on Housing Prices: Theory and Evidence from California |date=2019-04-04 |url=https://realestate.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/LinWachter19_04042019.pdf |quote=The average marginal effect of regulation on housing prices through all channels is about 3% in California (with the average California city as the regulatory reference point) which consists of 4.38%, 0.32% and -1.73% from the production, the amenity and the GE channels respectively (or 3.24% and 0.27% from the net production and amenity channels). The housing price responses through the amenity and the GE channels to a unit increase in regulation are small (0.32% and -1.73% respectively). If referenced to the average level of regulation in the US, the total regulatory effect will be 4 times larger. |last2=Wachter |first2=Susan |page=2,3}}</ref><ref>{{citation |last1=Lin |first1=Desin |title=The Effect of Land Use Regulation on Housing Prices: Theory and Evidence from California |date=2019-04-04 |url=https://realestate.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2019/04/LinWachter19_04042019.pdf |quote=Our estimated effects show that Los Angeles is the city whose housing prices are most impacted by regulation. In our calculations, if land use regulation in LA were to be decreased to the level observed in the least regulated cities, housing prices would decline by approximately 25%. |last2=Wachter |first2=Susan |page=29}}</ref>

=== Economy ===

A 2017 study<ref name=JoME_study>{{ Cite journal | doi=10.1016/j.jmoneco.2017.11.001 | title=Tarnishing the golden and empire states: Land-use restrictions and the U.S. economic slowdown | journal=Journal of Monetary Economics | volume=93 | last3=Prescott | first3=Edward | last2=Ohanian | first2=Lee | last1=Herkenhoff | first1=Kyle | date=November 9, 2017 | pages= 89–109| s2cid=109928994 | url=http://www.nber.org/papers/w23790.pdf }}</ref> by [[Nobel Laureate]] in economics [[Edward C. Prescott|Edward Prescott]], Lee Ohanian (senior fellow at the [[Hoover Institution]]), and Kyle Herkenhoff, estimates that if California were to roll back its land use regulations to where they stood in 1980, the state's GDP could permanently increase by almost $400 billion (a [[Economy of California|14% increase]]).<ref name=WSJ_land-use_GDP_effect /> "If every state rolled back land regulations to 1980 levels, [total US] GDP could rise by as much as $1.8 trillion [9%]."<ref name=WSJ_land-use_GDP_effect>{{cite news | url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/what-in-the-sam-hill-are-cows-doing-on-sand-hill-road-1512171702 | title=What in the Sam Hill Are Cows Doing on Sand Hill Road? They're eating the priciest grass in America, thanks to California's out-of-control land-use rules. | last2=Prescott | first2=Edward | last1=Ohanian | first1=Lee | newspaper=[[The Wall Street Journal]] | date=December 1, 2017 | access-date=2018-05-23 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180106194545/https://www.wsj.com/articles/what-in-the-sam-hill-are-cows-doing-on-sand-hill-road-1512171702 | archive-date=2018-01-06 | url-status=live | quote=If California rolled back its land rules to where they stood in 1980, our research estimates that the state's population could ultimately grow to 18% of the country. U.S. gross domestic product could permanently increase by about 2%, or $375 billion. If every state rolled back land regulations to 1980 levels, GDP could rise by as much as $1.8 trillion.}} Note: This article is behind a paywall.</ref>{{ r | CityLab_Obama | p=1 | q=A recent study co-authored by Nobel Prize–winning economist Edward Prescott, Kyle Herkenhoff of the University of Minnesota, and Lee Ohanian of the University of California, Los Angeles, shows that although land-use restrictions can and do stifle overall economic productivity, they have also kept geographic inequality between states from growing worse. The study looks at the effects of land-use policy on the 48 contiguous U.S. states over the six-plus decades between 1950 and 2014. It compares the effects of tight land-use restrictions in California and New York to Texas, the state with the most relaxed restrictions of those studied, as well as five other broad groups of states: the South; the Rust Belt; the Northeast/Mid-Atlantic region; the Midwest region; and the Pacific/Mountain region. The study finds that tighter land-use restrictions in California and New York have created a vast spatial misallocation of resources. The authors' analysis reveals that reverting urban land regulations from 2014 levels back to 1980s levels would vastly improve productivity. If all U.S. states moved just halfway from their current regulation levels to the current Texas level, both productivity and economic output nationwide would be roughly 12 percent higher. }}

A [[McKinsey Quarterly|McKinsey Global Institute]] report estimates that the housing shortage is costing the California economy between $143 and $233 billion dollars per year, from lost construction activity (at least $85 billion annually), lower consumption of consumer goods because of high housing costs (at least $53 billion annually) and the costs of providing services to the increased number of homeless persons (at least $5 billion per year).{{ r | McKinsey_3.5_by_2025 }}<ref name=Pasadena_Star>{{cite news | url=https://www.pasadenastarnews.com/2017/01/04/california-needs-to-build-a-staggering-number-of-homes-and-we-are-way-behind/ | title=California needs to build a staggering number of homes and we are way behind  | last=Smith | first=Kevin | newspaper=Pasadena Star-News | date=January 4, 2017 | access-date=2018-01-22 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180123060042/https://www.pasadenastarnews.com/2017/01/04/california-needs-to-build-a-staggering-number-of-homes-and-we-are-way-behind/ | archive-date=2018-01-23 | url-status=live | quote=The McKinsey Global Institute estimates that California's housing shortage is costing the state $143 billion to $233 billion in lost economic output, primarily from consumption that's crowded out by high housing costs and lost construction activity.}}</ref>{{ r | SJMN_HC_worse2 | p=1 | q=The McKinsey Global Institute found that housing shortages cost the economy between $143 billion and $233 billion annually, not taking into account second-order costs to health, education and the environment. Much of that is due to households spending too much of their incomes on the rent or mortgage and not enough on consumer goods. }}{{ r | CalMatters_housing_primer | p=1 | q=See the section titled: "The housing crisis has major repercussions for the economy" for the graphic which separates out construction, consumer, and homeless spending. }}

== Quantifying the shortage ==
=== Estimated under-supply of housing units ===
{{Chart|definition=Persons per housing unit for California and for the United States since 1940.chart|data=Persons per housing unit for California and for the United States since 1940.tab
 |thumb=yes|width=400px

}}

The [[California Legislative Analyst's Office]] 2015 report "California's High Housing Costs – Causes and Consequences" estimates that for the state to have kept housing prices no more than 80% higher than the median for the U.S. as a whole (the price differential which existed in 1980, as opposed to the >150% differential which exists today), California would have needed to add approximately 210,000 new housing units each year over the past three decades (1980–2010), rather than the 120,000 / year which were built. Their midpoint estimate of underbuilding for the last three decades is 90,000 units per year, resulting in an estimated shortage of 2.7 million housing units (20%) by 2010.{{ r | LAO_C&C | p=21 | q=Between 1980 and 2010, California's major metros added about 120,000 new housing units each year. Our analysis suggests that between 190,000 units per year and 230,000 units per year were needed to keep California's housing cost growth in line with cost escalations elsewhere in the U.S. Our midpoint estimate—which represents our single best guess at California's housing need—is slightly above 210,000 units per year.}}

Since 2010, the state's construction of new housing units has averaged well below 90,000 units per year.<ref name=LA_Times_housing_still_not_enough /> It took a drop after the 2008 [[Great Recession]], but has increased to about 90,000 / year in 2016.<ref name=LA_Times_housing_still_not_enough>{{cite news | last=Khouri | first=Andrew | title=Housing construction is on the rise in California, but it's still not enough | url=http://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-housing-population-growth-20170501-htmlstory.html | access-date=2017-11-05 | newspaper=Los Angeles Times | date=May 1, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510163629/http://www.latimes.com/business/la-fi-housing-population-growth-20170501-htmlstory.html | archive-date=2017-05-10 | url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="bloom 2019-2-11">{{cite news|title=America Isn't Building Enough New Housing|work=Bloomberg Businessweek|first= Peter|access-date=February 11, 2019|date=February 11, 2019|last=Coy|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-02-11/america-s-housing-market-isn-t-building-enough-new-homes}}</ref>

In September 2017, a team of economists from [[UCLA Anderson School of Management|UCLA Anderson Forecast]], led by Jerry Nickelsburg, predicted that "it would take 20 percent more housing to achieve a 10 percent reduction in prices. Such a reduction throughout California would bring costs down roughly to 2014 levels..."<ref name=SF_chronicle_UCLA_economists_forecast>{{cite news | url=https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Severe-housing-shortage-for-Bay-Area-state-12235869.php | title=Report: To cut housing prices 10 percent, California needs 20 percent more units | last=Fimrite | first=Peter | newspaper=San Francisco Chronicle | date=September 27, 2017 | access-date=2018-02-21 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171004032359/https://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Severe-housing-shortage-for-Bay-Area-state-12235869.php | archive-date=2017-10-04 | url-status=live }}</ref> In a 2018 UCLA Anderson Forecast report, economist Nickelsburg estimated the shortage at 3 million units.{{ r | CityLab_Chiland_1 | p=1 | q=Nickelsburg estimates that across the state, more than 3 million new houses and apartments would need to be constructed. }}

In October 2017, lieutenant governor and gubernatorial candidate [[Gavin Newsom]] said that California should set a goal to produce 3.5 million new homes by 2025.<ref name=NPR_2021-06-08>{{ cite news | url=https://www.npr.org/sections/money/2021/06/08/1003982733/squalor-behind-the-golden-gate-confronting-californias-homelessness-crisis | title=How California Homelessness Became A Crisis | last=Rosalsky | first=Greg | newspaper=[[NPR]] | date=2021-06-08 | quote=A 2016 study by McKinsey Global Institute estimated that California needs 3.5 million new housing units by 2025 to deal with its chronic housing shortage. Yet new housing construction has only slowed since then, despite Gov. Gavin Newsom's campaign promise to lead an effort to produce those 3.5 million units. }}</ref>{{ r | McKinsey_3.5_by_2025 }} This would require a quadrupling of the current rate of building to almost 400,000 units per year, a rate the state has not experienced since 1954.<ref name=Newsom_3.5M_by_2025>{{cite news | url=http://www.latimes.com/politics/essential/la-pol-ca-essential-politics-updates-newsom-calls-for-california-to-nearly-1508790304-htmlstory.html | title=Gavin Newsom calls for California to nearly quadruple its annual housing production | last=Dillon | first=Liam | newspaper=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=October 23, 2017 | access-date=2018-06-01 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180202220514/http://www.latimes.com/politics/essential/la-pol-ca-essential-politics-updates-newsom-calls-for-california-to-nearly-1508790304-htmlstory.html | archive-date=2018-02-02 | url-status=live }}</ref> {{ r | LAT_Newsom_threat | p=1 | q=As a candidate, Newsom called for the building of 3.5 million new homes in the state by 2025, an amount that would more than quadruple the current rate of production. }}<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.latimes.com/opinion/story/2019-08-30/gavin-newsom-fair-share-housing-southern-california|title=Editorial: Gavin Newsom tells Southern California to plan for housing. A lot more housing|date=2019-09-02|website=Los Angeles Times|language=en-US|access-date=2019-09-04}}</ref>

In April 2018, state Senator [[Scott Wiener]], author of several bills to reduce the housing shortage, estimated it at 4 million units.<ref name=leg_bill_killed>{{cite news | url=http://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-big-housing-bill-dies-20180417-story.html | title=California lawmakers killed one of the biggest housing bills in the country | last=Dillon | first=Liam | newspaper=Los Angeles Times | date=April 17, 2018 | access-date=2018-04-23 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180423183815/http://www.latimes.com/politics/la-pol-ca-big-housing-bill-dies-20180417-story.html | archive-date=2018-04-23 | url-status=live | quote=Wiener said the bill would help the state reduce a shortage of homes he has estimated at 4 million.}}</ref>

In a 2019 paper, economists [[Enrico Moretti]] and [[Chang-Tai Hsieh]] analyzed the U.S. housing market and found that if Americans had consistently built housing commensurate with demand, the city of [[San Francisco]] would have two million housing units (rather than the 400,000 it has today) and a population of four million people (as opposed to its actual 2022 population of around 815,000), and the greater [[San Francisco Bay Area|Bay Area]] would have five times the population it has today.<ref name="Lowrey">{{cite news |last1=Lowrey |first1=Annie |author1-link=Annie Lowrey |title=The U.S. Needs More Housing Than Almost Anyone Can Imagine |url=https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/archive/2022/11/us-housing-gap-cost-affordability-big-cities/672184/ |access-date=4 December 2022 |work=The Atlantic |date=November 21, 2022}}</ref>

In 2023, ''[[CalMatters]]'' graphed the various estimates of the housing shortage against actual housing production, showing improvements in production in the last decade but a significant gap remaining between the estimates of what would be needed to address the shortage.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Christopher |first=Ben |date=2023-05-15 |title=California is losing population and building new houses. When will home prices come down? |url=http://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/california-exodus-housing-cost/ |access-date=2024-08-09 |work=CalMatters |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Increase in housing production needed ===
Experts say that California needs to double its current rate of housing production (85,000 units per year) just to keep up with expected population growth and prevent prices from further increasing, and needs to quadruple the current rate of housing production over the next 7 years in order to for prices and rents to decline.{{ r | KQED_housing_5 | p=1 | q=The state housing department estimates that we need to build 180,000 new housing units a year to keep prices stable. Over the past 10 years, we've averaged less than half of that. }}{{ r | LAT_HS | p=1 | q=Ben Metcalf, the state's top housing official, has said the affordability problems are as bad as they've ever been in California's history. And the state is expected to add an additional 6.5 million people over the next two decades. The primary driver of the affordability problem is a lack of home building. Developers in California need to roughly double the 100,000 homes they build each year to stabilize housing costs, according to the McKinsey study and reports from the state Department of Housing and Community Development and nonpartisan Legislative Analyst's Office. }}{{ r | McKinsey_3.5_by_2025 }}{{ r | CA_Housing_Future }}{{ r | LAO_C&C | p=21 | q=Between 1980 and 2010, California's major metros added about 120,000 new housing units each year. Our analysis suggests that between 190,000 units per year and 230,000 units per year were needed to keep California's housing cost growth in line with cost escalations elsewhere in the U.S. (Our midpoint estimate—which represents our single best guess at California's housing need—is slightly above 210,000 units per year. }}{{ r | SJMN_5_ways | p=1 | q=California ranks dead last in home construction on a per capita basis in recent years, said Jonathan Woezel, lead author of the much-cited McKinsey Global Institute report on the state's housing crisis. Is there a solution to this crisis? Yes, the experts say. Provided Californians are willing to ease local and state barriers to development, build more high-density and affordable housing and — at least one economist dared to say — scale back Prop. 13. In short, the state must build 3.5 million more homes by 2025, the McKinsey report concluded. That's roughly 350,000 units a year over the next seven years, versus an average of just 85,000 homes a year over the last seven years. "This is a fixable problem," Woezel said. "This is not impossible." }}{{ r | SFC_Danville_AH | p=1 | q=While Danville can take a bow for going outside its comfort zone, this project illustrates how long a road California must travel to reach its goal of building 180,000 units annually — the total it must hit just to keep pace with demand. }}

In 2018, California ranked 49th among the United States in housing units per resident.{{ r | VOX_sb827 | p=1 | q=California is in the midst of crippling housing crisis. The state's population has steadily grown, but it hasn't been building new places for people to live at anything close to the same rate.
