======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Inclusionary zoning
======================================================================

{{Short description|Laws mandating a percentage of affordable units in new housing projects}}
{{Unreliable sources|date=July 2024}}
{{Globalize|date=July 2026}}
'''Inclusionary zoning''' ('''IZ''') is a type of [[urban planning]] intervention<ref name="ahuri_iz">{{cite web
|url=https://www.ahuri.edu.au/analysis/brief/what-inclusionary-zoning-and-how-does-it-help-deliver-affordable-housing
|title=What is Inclusionary zoning, and how does it help deliver affordable housing
|date=2023-08-29
|publisher=Australian Housing and Urban Research Institute
}}</ref> with the aim of increasing the supply of [[affordable housing]]. It is sometimes enacted through a [[local ordinance]] or [[development plan]] requiring (or providing incentives for) a percentage of units in [[real estate development]] be affordable by people with low to moderate incomes.

It is named in contrast to [[exclusionary zoning]], which is [[zoning]] requirements (such as [[single-family zoning]] or minimum parcel or house sizes) that result in exclusion of low-income residents.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|title=Exclusionary Zoning
|url=https://www.merriam-webster.com/legal/exclusionary%20zoning |encyclopedia=Merriam-Webster
}}</ref> Inclusionary zoning is the [[urban planning]] counterpart to 'affordable' housing. 'Affordable' housing has a specific meaning in [[Australia]] and the United States.<ref name="ip_affordable_housing">{{cite web
|url=https://inflectionpoints.work/articles/against-affordable-housing
|publisher=Inflection Points 
|title=Against ‘Affordable’ Housing
|author1=Dominic Behrens
|author2=Ethan Gilbert
|date=2026-05-16
}}</ref>  In the US, "affordable housing developers" are non-profits which build 100% of their units as affordable, but need significant taxpayer subsidies for this model to work.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}} While inclusionary zoning allows municipalities to build 'affordable' housing with no financial cost, they have an opportunity cost which is not a small subsidy.<ref name="ip_affordable_housing"/>
  
The bulk of economic evidence indicates inclusionary zoning, without well-calibrated incentives, substantially restricts new housing supply and reduces overall affordability.<ref name="mock2023"/><ref name="bento2009"/><ref name="means2015"/> The typical inclusionary zoning ordinance in [[California]] reduces annual new residential construction by 31.8%, and the cost of generating an affordable unit through IZ is approximately $800,000{{efn|In excess rents paid by other market rate renters, who are on average lower income<ref name="kouchekinia2026"/>{{rp|25}} }}.<ref name="kouchekinia2026">{{cite web
|title=Inclusionary Zoning and Housing Supply Evidence from California’s Palmer Fix
|author=Noah Kouchekinia
|publisher=University of California
|date=June 2026
|url=https://bpb-us-e2.wpmucdn.com/sites.uci.edu/dist/b/5302/files/2026/06/IZ_Kouchekinia.pdf
}}</ref> This is more than the cost of directly subsidizing housing in [[California]], which is estimated to be $441,000.<ref>Reid et al., 2026</ref><ref name="kouchekinia2026"/>{{rp|25}}

Alternatives to unfunded inclusive zoning with the aim of improving housing affordability include funded (or "bonus") inclusionary zoning, providing [[rent control|rent controls]], [[public housing]], [[Subsidized_housing#Rent_subsidies|rent subsidies]],  or [[YIMBY|allowing more housing]].

== Background ==
{{Globalize|date=July 2026}}

Non-profit affordable housing developers build 100% of their units as affordable, but need significant taxpayer subsidies for this model to work.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}} Inclusionary zoning allows municipalities to have new affordable housing constructed without explicit taxpayer subsidies.<ref name=":1" /> In order to encourage for-profit developers to build projects that include affordable units, cities often allow developers to build more total units (a "density bonus") than their zoning laws currently allow so that there will be enough profit generating market-rate units to offset the losses from the below market-rate units and still allow the project to be financially feasible.<ref name=":1" />

Inclusionary zoning can be mandatory or voluntary, though the great majority of units have been built as a result of mandatory programmes.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Castro|first=Julián|year=2013|title=Inclusionary Zoning and Mixed-Income Communities|url=https://www.huduser.gov/portal/periodicals/em/spring13/highlight3.html|journal=Evidence Matters|volume=Spring 2013|via=Office of Policy Development and Research (PD&R) U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development|archive-date=2016-11-17|access-date=2016-11-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161117064654/https://www.huduser.gov/portal/periodicals/em/spring13/highlight3.html|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Encyclopedia of the City|last=Caves|first=R. W.|publisher=Routledge|year=2004|isbn=9780415252256|pages=373}}</ref>  There are variations among the set-aside requirements (percentage of units set-aside for low-income residents), affordability levels (what income level is considered "low-income"), and length of time the unit is deed-restricted as affordable housing.<ref name=":1" />

In practice, these policies involve placing [[deed]] restrictions on 10–30% of new houses or apartments in order to make the cost of the housing affordable to lower-income households. The mix of "[[affordable housing]]" and "market-rate" housing in the same neighborhood may be seen as beneficial by city planners and sociologists.<ref>{{cite book
|last1=Duany |first1=Andres
|last2=Plater-Zyberk |first2=Elizabeth
|last3=Speck |first3=Jeff
|date=2000
|title=Suburban Nation: The Rise of Sprawl and the Decline of the American Dream
|publisher=North Point Press
|location=New York
|isbn=978-0-86547-557-1
|url=https://archive.org/details/suburbannationri00duan
}}</ref> Another goal of inclusionary zoning is to build mixed-income communities, rather than having poor households concentrated in specific city neighborhoods.<ref name=":1" />

Most inclusionary zoning is enacted at the municipal or county level; when imposed by the state, as in [[Massachusetts Comprehensive Permit Act: Chapter 40B|Massachusetts]], it has been argued that such laws usurp local control. In such cases, developers can use inclusionary zoning to avoid certain aspects of local zoning laws.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

== History ==
During the mid- to late-20th century, new [[suburb]]s grew and expanded around American cities as [[middle-class]] house buyers, supported by federal [[loan]] programs such as [[United States Department of Veterans Affairs|Veterans Administration]] housing loan guarantees, left established neighborhoods and communities. These newly populated places were generally more economically homogeneous than the cities they encircled. Many [[suburbs|suburban communities]] enacted local ordinances, often in zoning codes, to preserve the character of their municipality. One of the most commonly cited exclusionary practices is the stipulation that lots must be of a certain minimum size and houses must be set back from the street a certain minimum distance. In many cases, these housing ordinances prevented affordable housing from being built, because the large plots of land required to build within the code restrictions were cost-prohibitive for modestly priced houses. Communities have remained accessible to wealthier citizens because of these ordinances, effectively shutting the low income families out of desirable communities. Such zoning ordinances have not always been enacted with conscious intent to exclude lower income households, but it has been the unintended result of such policies.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

Supporters of inclusionary zoning point out that low income households are more likely to become economically successful if they have [[middle class]] neighbors as peers and role models.{{citation needed|name=July 2026|date=July 2026}} When effective, inclusionary zoning reduces the concentration of poverty in [[slum]] districts where [[social norm]]s may not provide adequate models of success.{{citation needed|name=July 2026|date=July 2026}} Education is one of the largest components in the effort to lift people out of poverty; access to high-quality  [[Public school (government funded)|public schools]] is another key benefit of reduced segregation.{{citation needed|name=July 2026|date=July 2026}} Statistically, a poor child in a school where 80% of the children are poor scores 13–15% lower compared to environments where the poor child's peers are 80% middle class.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.gamaliel.org/DavidRusk/keynote%2010-5-05.pdf |title=Gamaliel |access-date=2006-02-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061004075530/http://www.gamaliel.org/DavidRusk/keynote%2010-5-05.pdf |archive-date=2006-10-04 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Income requirements for the "affordable" housing differ among jurisdictions where inclusive zoning is implemented. In [[California]], 16% of the population could afford the median-priced home during 2005.<ref>[http://www.car.org/index.php?id=MzUyODE= CAR]{{Dead link|date=September 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

== Potential Benefits ==
{{more detail needed}}

Expanding affordable housing may give poor and working families would access to a range of opportunities, including good employment opportunities, good schools, comprehensive transportation system and safe streets.<ref>Brown, K. (2001). EXPANDING AFFORDABLE HOUSING THROUGH INCLUSIONARY ZONING: LESSONS FROM THE WASHINGTON METROPOLITAN AREA (1st ed.). The Brookings Institution Center on Urban and Metropolitan Policy.</ref>

Some [[affordable housing]] advocates seek to promote the policies in order to ensure that housing is available for a variety of income levels in more places.  These supporters hold that inclusionary zoning produces needed affordable housing and creates income-integrated [[community|communities]].{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

Inclusionary zoning may alleviate the problem of inadequate supply of Affordable Housing{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

Affordable housing may avoid economic and racial segregation, which helps reducing crime rate, failing schools and improving social stability{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

Affordable housing requires relatively small amount of explicit subsidies required for adopting IZ as a market-based tool.<ref>Brunick, N., Goldberg, L., & Levine, S. Large Cities and Inclusionary Zoning (1st ed.). Business and Professional People for the Public Interest.</ref>{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

== Criticism ==

The bulk of the existing academic evidence indicates that mandatory IZ (without incentives), substantially restricts new housing supply, making affordability worse.<ref name="mock2023">{{cite journal
|last1=Mock
|first1=Rozalyn
|last2=Willis-Jackson
|first2=Megan
|last3=Wang
|first3=Robert
|last4=de Benedictis-Kessner
|first4=Justin
|last5=Bilmes
|first5=Linda
|last6=Iammartino
|first6=Brian
|date=January 2023
|title=Can Inclusionary Zoning Be an Effective Housing Policy in Greater Boston? Evidence from Lynn and Revere
|journal=HKS Working Paper
|issue=RWP23-006
|ssrn=4343923
|doi=10.2139/ssrn.4343923}}</ref><ref name="bento2009">{{cite journal
|last1=Bento
|first1=Antonio
|last2=Lowe
|first2=Scott
|last3=Knaap
|first3=Gerrit-Jan
|last4=Chakraborty
|first4=Arnab
|date=2009
|title=Housing Market Effects of Inclusionary Zoning
|journal=Cityscape
|volume=11
|issue=2
|pages=7–26
|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/20868701
|jstor=20868701}}</ref><ref name="means2012">{{cite journal
|last1=Means
|first1=Tom
|last2=Stringham
|first2=Edward Peter
|date=2012
|title=Unintended or Intended Consequences? The Effect of Below-Market Housing Mandates on Housing Markets in California
|journal=Journal of Public Finance and Public Choice
|volume=30
|issue=1–3
|pages=39–64
|url=https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=2638698
}}</ref>

Inclusionary zoning may only have low production of affordable housings, which produced approximately 150,000 units over several decades in the [[United States]].<ref>{{Cite book|title=Inclusionary Housing in International Perspective: Affordable Housing, Social Inclusion, and Land Value Recapture|last1=Calavita|first1=Nico|last2=Mallach|first2=Alan|publisher=Lincoln Institute of Land Policy|year=2010}}</ref> Other schemes, such as [[Housing choice voucher program|Housing Choice Vouchers]] (which assists approximately two million households) and the [[Low-Income Housing Tax Credit|LIHTC]] program have produced over two million affordable homes{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

Inclusionary zoning may result in unstable production of affordable housing that highly affected by local housing-market conditions.<ref>{{cite report
|last1=Schwartz |first1=Heather L.
|last2=Ecola |first2=Liisa
|last3=Leuschner |first3=Kristin J.
|last4=Kofner |first4=Aaron
|date=2012-06-01
|title=Is Inclusionary Zoning Inclusionary? A Guide for Practitioners
|number=TR-1231
|publisher=[[RAND Corporation]]
|location=Santa Monica, CA
|url=https://www.rand.org/content/dam/rand/pubs/technical_reports/2012/RAND_TR1231.pdf
}}</ref>

There is very little research on outcomes for participants in these programs.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}} Although these affordable housing programs, by definition, offer lower-cost units that municipalities promote as inclusive, the deed restrictions imposed on participants in these programs result in additional economic disparities and other hardships not faced by market-rate homeowners.<ref>Perry, A. (2022, May 24). The money pit-falls of Boulder's permanently affordable housing [Guest opinion]. Daily Camera.
</ref>

Some advocates state that Inclusionary Zoning can have the opposite effect and actually reduce affordable housing in a community. For example, in Los Angeles, California, inclusionary zoning apparently accelerated gentrification, as older, unprofitable buildings were razed and replaced with mostly high-rent housing, and a small percentage of affordable housing; the net result was less affordable housing. In New York, NY, inclusionary zoning allows for up to a 400% increase in luxury housing for every unit of affordable housing and for an additional 400% luxury housing when combined with the liberal use of development rights. Critics have stated the affordable housing can be directed to those making up to $200,000 through the improper use of an Area Median Income, and used as political tools by organizations tied to various politicians. New York City communities such as Harlem, the [[Lower East Side]], Williamsburg, Chelsea and Hell's Kitchen have experienced significant secondary displacement through the use of Inclusionary Zoning.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

[[Real estate|Real Estate]] industry detractors note that inclusionary zoning levies an [[indirect tax]] on developers, so as to discourage them from building in areas that face supply shortages.  Furthermore, to ensure that the affordable units are not resold for profit, deed restrictions generally fix a long-term resale [[price ceiling]], eliminating a potential benefit of home ownership.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

[[Free market]] advocates oppose attempts to fix given social outcomes by government intervention in [[market (economics)|market]]s.  They argue inclusionary zoning constitutes an onerous [[land use]] regulation that exacerbates housing shortages.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

Homeowners sometimes note that their property values will be reduced if low income families move into their community. Others counter consider their concerns thinly-concealed [[classism]] and racism.{{Citation needed|date=August 2023}}

Local residents in [[Massachusetts]] begun a lawsuit fighting affordable housing projects.<ref>{{cite news
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090228083839/http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2004/01/29/developer_aims_to_turn_tables_on_opponents/
|title=Developer aims to turn tables on opponents
|author=Christine McConville
|date=2004-01-29
|website=boston.com
|url=http://www.boston.com/news/local/massachusetts/articles/2004/01/29/developer_aims_to_turn_tables_on_opponents/
|url-status=dead
|archive-date=2009-02-28
}}</ref>

Other legal battles have occurred in California, where many cities have implemented inclusionary zoning policies that typically require 10 percent to 15 percent of units to be affordable housing.<ref name=":0" /> The definition of affordable housing includes both low-income housing and moderate-income housing. In California, low-income housing is typically designed for households making 51 percent to 80 percent of the median income, and moderate-income housing is typically for households making 81 percent to 120 percent of the median income.<ref name=":0" /> Developers have attempted to fight back these requirements by challenging local inclusionary zoning ordinances through the court legal system. In the case ''Home Builders Association of Northern California v. City of Napa'', the California First District Court of Appeal upheld the inclusionary zoning ordinances of City of Napa that require 10 percent of units of the new development project to be moderate income housing against the Home Builders Association that challenged the City of Napa.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://landuselaw.wustl.edu/home_build.htm|title=HOME BUILDERS ASSOCIATION OF NORTHERN CALIFORNIA v. CITY OF NAPA|website=landuselaw.wustl.edu|access-date=2016-11-14|archive-date=2018-05-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180509090138/http://landuselaw.wustl.edu/home_build.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref> Cities have also attempted to impose inclusionary requirements on rental units. However, the [[Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act]] prohibits cities in California from imposing limitation on rental rates on vacant units.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.leginfo.ca.gov/cgi-bin/displaycode?section=civ&group=01001-02000&file=1954.50-1954.535|title=CA Codes (civ:1954.50-1954.535)|website=www.leginfo.ca.gov|access-date=2016-11-15|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304070038/http://www.leginfo.ca.gov/cgi-bin/displaycode?section=civ&group=01001-02000&file=1954.50-1954.535|archive-date=2016-03-04}}</ref> Subsequently, developers have won cases, such as ''Palmer/Sixth Street Properties, L.P. v. City of Los Angeles (2009)'', against cities that imposed inclusionary requirements on rental units, as the state law supersedes local ordinances.<ref>{{Citation|title=Palmer/Sixth Street Properties, Lp v. City of Los Angeles|date=July 22, 2009|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar_case?case=13699056597329107094&hl=en&as_sdt=6&as_vis=1&oi=scholarr|access-date=2016-11-15}}</ref>

Citizen groups and developers have also sought other ways to strengthen or defeat inclusionary zoning laws. For example, the [[Popular initiative|initiative]] and [[referendum]] process in California allows citizen groups or developers to change local ordinances on affordable housing by popular vote. Any citizens or interest groups can participate in this process by gathering at least the required number of signatures so that the measure proposed can qualify to be on the ballot; once enough signatures are submitted and the ballot measure is cleared by election officials, the ballot measure is typically placed on the ballot for the upcoming election.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/ballot-measures/initiative-and-referendum-status/|title=Initiative and Referendum Qualification Status {{!}} California Secretary of State|website=www.sos.ca.gov|access-date=2016-11-15}}</ref> One recent case is Proposition C in [[San Francisco]]. This ballot measure was placed on the ballot for the June 2016 California primary election. Passed in June 2016, this proposition amends the city's charter to increase the requirement for affordable housing for development projects of 25 units or more.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sfgov.org/elections/sites/default/files/Documents/BSC/2016%20June/6-Final%20digest-Inclusionary%20Housing%20Requirements%20%28Charter%20Amendment%29.pdf|title=Final digest-Inclusionary Housing Requirements (Charter Amendment)|date=March 4, 2016|website=sfgov.org|publisher=City and County of San Francisco, Department of Elections|access-date=2016-11-14|archive-date=2017-02-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170215072507/http://sfgov.org/elections/sites/default/files/Documents/BSC/2016%20June/6-Final%20digest-Inclusionary%20Housing%20Requirements%20%28Charter%20Amendment%29.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

The clash between these various interests is reflected in [https://ssrn.com/abstract=1676277 this study] published by the [[Libertarianism|libertarian]]-leaning [[Reason Foundation]]'s public policy [[think tank]], and the response of a
[https://web.archive.org/web/20060125022909/http://www.nonprofithousing.org/actioncenter/campaigns/download/IH_countering_critics.pdf peer review] of that research. Local governments reflect and in some cases balance these competing interests. In California, the League of Cities has created [http://www.cacities.org/index.jsp?zone=ilsg&previewStory=2230 a guide] to inclusionary zoning which includes a section on the [https://web.archive.org/web/20070928104213/http://www.cacities.org/resource_files/20555.Part%20III.pdf pros and cons] of the policies.

=== From economists ===
Economists state that IZ functions as a [[price control]] on a percentage of units and has similar negative effects as other price controls ([[rent control]]) being that it discourages the supply of new housing.{{ r | Powell}}  It can also be understood similar to [[impact fees]] as an "inclusionary tax" on market-rate units which raises the prices of new non-price-controlled units in that development and thereby diminishes the financial incentive to create new housing.<ref name=Powell>{{cite journal |last1=Powell |first1=Benjamin |last2=Stringham |first2=Edward |date=2005 |title=The Economics of Inclusionary Zoning Reclaimed: How Effective are Price Controls? |url=https://ssrn.com/abstract=1674474 |journal=[[Florida State University Law Review]] |volume=33 |issue= |pages=471–499 |doi= |access-date=2023-08-07}}</ref>

== Differences in ordinances ==
Inclusionary zoning ordinances vary substantially among municipalities. These variables can include:

* Mandatory or voluntary ordinance. While many cities require inclusionary housing, many more offer zoning bonuses, expedited permits, reduced fees, cash subsidies, or other incentives for developers who voluntarily build affordable housing.
* Percentage of units to be dedicated as inclusionary housing. This varies quite substantially among jurisdictions, but appears to range from 10 to 30%.
* Minimum size of development that the ordinance applies to. Most jurisdictions exempt smaller developments, but some require that even developments incurring only a fraction of an inclusionary housing unit pay a fee (see below).
* Whether inclusionary housing must be built on site. Some programs allow housing to be built nearby, in cases of hardship.
* Whether fees can be paid in lieu of building inclusionary housing. Fees-in-lieu allow a developer to "buy out" of an inclusionary housing obligation. This may seem to defeat the purpose of inclusionary zoning, but in some cases the cost of building one affordable unit on-site could purchase several affordable units off-site.
* Income level or price defined as "affordable," and buyer qualification methods. Most ordinances seem to target inclusionary units to low- or moderate-income households which earn approximately the regional median income or somewhat below. Inclusionary housing typically does not create housing for those with very low incomes.
*Whether inclusionary housing units are limited by price or by size (the [[City of Johannesburg Metropolitan Municipality|City of Johannesburg]]  for example provides for both options)<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=https://www.joburg.org.za:443/documents_/Pages/Key%20Documents/policies/Development%20Planning%20%EF%BC%86%20Urban%20Management/Citywide%20Spatial%20Policies/City-Wide-Spatial-Policies.aspx|title=Inclusionary Housing Incentives, Regulations and Mechanisms|website=www.joburg.org.za|language=en-ZA|access-date=2019-06-24}}</ref>
* Appearance and integration of inclusionary housing units. Many jurisdictions require that inclusionary housing units be indistinguishable from market-rate units, but this can increase costs.
* Longevity of price restrictions attached to inclusionary housing units, and allowable appreciation. Ordinances that allow the "discount" to expire essentially grant a windfall profit, similar to what market-rate owners would get.  Municipalities dislike this because it would mean they would have to create more affordable units. Instead, participants in these programs subsidize themselves, relieving municipalities of the financial burden to keep these programs running. However, placing the brunt of the work and subsidies on the people in these programs raises questions. It can trap individuals in public housing programs, making it nearly impossible for them to move out until they pass away. If they could not afford market-rate housing 15 years ago, staying in a unit that restricts appreciation becomes a significant barrier to leaving public housing.<ref>Powder Days Hansman, Heather. Powder days: Ski bums, ski towns and the future of chasing snow. Harlequin, 2021.</ref>  In addition, requiring participants to do maintenance and take on all other homeowner liabilities on a home that is economically similar to a rental (since there is limited appreciation minus HOA fees, interest, taxes, etc.) can add further housing related stress.  
* Whether housing rehabilitation counts as "construction," either of market-rate or affordable units. Some cities, like New York City, allow developers to count rehabilitation of off-site housing as an inclusionary contribution.
* Which types of housing construction the ordinance applies to. For example, high-rise housing costs more to build per square foot (thus raising compliance costs, perhaps prohibitively), so some ordinances exempt it from compliance.

=== Locations of housing ===

IZ policies may not effectively disperse low-income units throughout the region.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=E. Kontokosta|first=Constantine|year=2015|title=Do inclusionary zoning policies equitably disperse affordable housing? A comparative spatial analysis|journal=Journal of Housing and the Built Environment|volume=30|issue=4|pages=569–590|via=Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht|doi=10.1007/s10901-014-9430-5|bibcode=2015JHTRW..30..569K |s2cid=154139083}}</ref> In Suffolk County, there is a spatial concentration of IZ units in poor neighbourhoods.<ref name=":2" /> 97.7% of the IZ units were built in only 10% of the [[census tract]] from 1980 to 2000, which is the area with the lowest-income neighbourhood coupled with clustering of minorities.<ref name=":2" /> Housing policies are controlled by local government rather than regional government in [[Suffolk County, New York]], which may not consider inter-municipality distribution of low-income households.<ref name=":2" /> Density bonuses given to property developers for the provision of IZ units have intensified the concentration of affordable units in poor neighborhood (Ryan & Enderle as cited in Mukhija, Das, Regus et al., 2012).<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last1=Mukhija|first1=Vinit|last2=Das|first2=Ashok|last3=Regus|first3=Lara|last4=Tsay|first4=Sara Slovin|date=2015-03-15|title=The Tradeoffs of Inclusionary Zoning: What Do We Know and What Do We Need to Know?|journal=Planning Practice & Research|volume=30|issue=2|pages=222–235|doi=10.1080/02697459.2015.1008793|s2cid=154913907|issn=0269-7459}}</ref>

== Usage ==

=== Use in Johannesburg, South Africa ===
On 21 Feb 2019, the [[City of Johannesburg Metropolitan Municipality|City of Johannesburg]] Council approved its "Inclusionary Housing Incentives, Regulations and Mechanisms 2019".<ref name=":4" /> The policy is the first of its kind in [[South Africa]] and provides four options for inclusionary housing (including price limited, size limited or negotiated options) where at least 30% of dwelling units in new developments of 20 units or more, must be inclusionary housing.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cliffedekkerhofmeyr.com/en/news/publications/2019/Real/real-estate-alert-18-march-the-city-of-johannesburg-inclusionary-housing-policy-2019.html|title=Cliffe Dekker Hofmeyr - The City of Johannesburg Inclusionary Housing Policy, 2019|website=www.cliffedekkerhofmeyr.com|access-date=2019-06-24}}</ref>

=== Use in the United States ===
More than 200 communities in the [[United States]] have some sort of inclusionary zoning provision.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.northpark.edu/umin/tts/IHMythsFacts.pdf |title=North Park |access-date=2006-02-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070926232102/http://www.northpark.edu/umin/tts/IHMythsFacts.pdf |archive-date=2007-09-26 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Mandatory inclusionary housing (MIH) laws introduced in 2016 require that 20-30% of residential floor area in new developments and some renovations to be "permanently affordable for low-and moderate-income New Yorkers". The units may be offered for rent or for sale.<ref name="ahuri_iz"/>

[[Montgomery County, Maryland]], is often held to be a pioneer in establishing inclusionary zoning policies. It is the sixth wealthiest county in the United States, yet it has built more than 10,000 units of affordable housing since 1974, many units door-to-door with market-rate housing.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.bpichicago.org/rah/pubs/ci_issue_brief4.pdf |title=BPI Chicago |access-date=2006-02-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060420035739/http://www.bpichicago.org/rah/pubs/ci_issue_brief4.pdf |archive-date=2006-04-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

All municipalities in the state of [[Massachusetts]] are subject to that state's General Laws Chapter 40B, which allows developers to bypass certain municipal zoning restrictions in those municipalities which have fewer than the statutorily defined 10% affordable housing units. Developers taking advantage of Chapter 40B must construct 20% affordable units as defined under the statute.<ref>See[[Massachusetts Chapter 40B]]</ref>

All municipalities in the state of [[New Jersey]] are subject to judicially imposed inclusionary zoning as a result of the [[New Jersey Supreme Court]]'s [[Mount Laurel Decision]] and subsequent acts of the New Jersey state legislature.<ref>See [http://www.state.nj.us/dca/coah/fha.shtml ''New Jersey Fair Housing Act'']</ref>

A 2006 study, found that 170 jurisdictions in California had some form of inclusionary housing.<ref>[http://calruralhousing.org/publications/265-affordable-by-choice-trends-in-california-inclusionary-housing-programs California rural housing]</ref>  This was a 59% increase from 2003, when only 107 jurisdictions had inclusionary housing.<ref>[http://calruralhousing.org/publications/46-inclusionary-housing-in-ca-30-years-of-innovation California rural housing]</ref>  In addition, state law requires that 15% of the housing units produced in redevelopment project areas must be affordable. At least 20% of revenue generated from a redevelopment project must be contributed to low-income and moderate-income housing.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Guide to California Planning|last1=Fulton|first1=William|last2=Shigley|first2=Paul|publisher=Solano Press Books|year=2012|isbn=9781938166020|location=Point Arena, CA|pages=221, 305, and 332}}</ref> However, [[Jerry Brown|Governor Jerry Brown]] passed AB 1X 26 that dissolved all redevelopment agencies on February 1, 2012.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

However, [[Los Angeles]], California's inclusionary zoning ordinance for rental housing was invalidated in 2009 by the [[California Courts of Appeal|California Court of Appeal for the Second Appellate District]] because it directly conflicted with a provision of the state's [[Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act]] of 1996 which specifically gave all landlords the right to set the "initial rental rate" for new housing units.<ref>''Palmer/Sixth Street Properties, LP v. City of Los Angeles'', 175 Cal. App. 4th 1396 (2009).</ref>

[[Madison, Wisconsin]]'s inclusionary zoning ordinance respecting rental housing was struck down by Wisconsin's 4th District Court of Appeals in 2006 because that appellate court construed inclusionary zoning to be rent control, which is prohibited by state statute.  The [[Wisconsin Supreme Court]] declined the city's request to review the case. The ordinance was structured with a sunset in February 2009, unless extended by the Common Council.  The Common Council did not extend the inclusionary zoning ordinance and therefore it expired and is no longer in effect.{{citation needed|date=July 2026}}

=== Use in Australia ===

Inclusionary zoning has been implemented to some degree in various states, especially in [[South Australia]] and [[New South Wales]]. Some policies are also in place in the [[Australian Capital Territory]] and [[Victoria (State)]].<ref name="ahuri_iz"/>

The [[City of Sydney]] has mandated affordable housing in specified zones through the City West Scheme.<ref name="ahuri_iz"/>

=== Use in the United Kingdom ===

There is a long established inclusionary planning system (Section 106 agreements) in the UK.<ref name="ahuri_iz"/>

== Types of inclusionary zoning ==

''Voluntary or Mandatory Inclusionary Housing? Production, Predictability, and Enforcement''. 1st ed., Business and Professional People for the Public Interest (BPI), 2004.</ref>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Missing middle housing
======================================================================

{{Short description|Lack of medium density housing in North America}}
[[File:Housing starts.webp|thumb|upright=1.6|Housing starts in the United States, 1959–2021 {{legend-line|blue solid 2px|[[Single family home]]}} {{legend-line|green solid 2px|[[Multifamily residential]]}} {{legend-line|red solid 2px|[[Duplex (building)|2-4 unit residential]]}}]]

'''Missing middle housing''' refers to a lack of [[medium-density housing]] in the [[North America]]n context. 
The term describes an [[urban planning]] phenomenon in [[Canada]], the [[United States]], [[Australia]] and more recent developments in industrialized and newly industrializing countries due to [[zoning]] regulations favoring social and/or racial separation over shared living arrangements, and the prevalence of cars allowing [[Car dependency|car-dependent]] [[Urban sprawl|suburban sprawl]].<ref>Jay Cockburn, Anne Benaroya: [https://99percentinvisible.org/episode/the-missing-middle/ ''The Missing Middle''], podcast series ''99% Invisible'', May 17th 2022</ref>

Medium-density housing is characterized by a range of multi-family or clustered [[housing]] types that are still [[Human scale#Human scale in architecture|compatible in scale]] and heights with single-family or transitional neighborhoods.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Parolek|first=Daniel|title=Missing Middle Housing: Thinking Big and Building Small to Respond to Today's Housing Crisis|publisher=Island Press|year=2020|location=Washington DC|pages=15}}</ref>
Multi-family housing facilitates [[Walkability|walkable]] neighborhoods and affordable housing, and provides a response to changing demographics.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|last=Parolek|first=Daniel|title=Missing Middle Housing: Thinking Big and Building Small to Respond to Today's Housing Crisis|publisher=Island Press|year=2020|location=Washington DC|pages=7–8}}</ref>

Instead of focusing on the number of units in a structure, density can also be increased by building types such as [[duplex (building)|duplexes]], [[rowhouse]]s, and [[courtyard apartment]]s.

The term "missing middle housing" was coined by architect Daniel Parolek in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Missing Middle Housing: Thinking Big and Building Small to Respond to Today's Housing Crisis (Webcast)|url=https://www.strongtowns.org/eventspage/2020/8/11/missing-middle-housing-parolek|access-date=2021-01-03|website=Strong Towns|date=11 August 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":5" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.planetizen.com/node/75901|title='Missing Middle Housing' Website to Fill the Gap Between Supply and Demand|website=Planetizen - Urban Planning News, Jobs, and Education|language=en|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Missing Middle Housing|url=https://opticosdesign.com/missing-middle-housing/|access-date=2021-01-03|website=Opticos Design|language=en-US}}</ref>
[[File:MMH Diagram w Labels logo 2020 short Opticos Design.jpg|center|800x800px|Missing Middle Housing Diagram by Dan Parolek of Opticos Design]]
Many forms of what is now described as "missing middle" housing were built before the 1940s, including two-flats in Chicago; [[Terraced house|rowhouses]] in Brooklyn, Baltimore, Washington, D.C., and Philadelphia; two-family homes or "[[Three-decker (house)|triple-decker]]" homes in Boston, Worcester; and [[bungalow court]]s in California.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://nextcity.org/features/view/cities-affordable-housing-design-solution-missing-middle|title=Will U.S. Cities Design Their Way Out of the Affordable Housing Crisis?|website=nextcity.org|language=en|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref> Post-WWII, housing in the United States trended significantly toward single-family with zoning making it difficult to build walkable medium-density housing in many areas and, therefore, reducing the supply of the now "missing" middle.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nar.realtor/articles/missing-middle-housing|title=Missing Middle Housing|website=www.nar.realtor|date=18 May 2016 |language=en|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal|last=Wegmann|first=Jake|date=2020-01-02|title=Death to Single-Family Zoning…and New Life to the Missing Middle|journal=Journal of the American Planning Association|volume=86|issue=1|pages=113–119|doi=10.1080/01944363.2019.1651217|issn=0194-4363|doi-access=free}}</ref>

[[File:1911 NE 22 - Irvington HD - Portland Oregon.jpg|thumb|upright=1.6|A historic four-plex in [[Portland, Oregon]]]]

==History==
[[File:Scab streetcar led by police - San Francisco Street Car Strike 1907.jpg|thumb|left|Police escorting a [[strikebreaker|scab]]-driven streetcar during the [[San Francisco Streetcar Strike of 1907]]. A number of [[Streetcar strikes in the United States|streetcar strike]]s broke out in the United States during the early 20th century.]]
[[Image:1st Ave Seattle 1900.jpg|upright=1.4|right|thumb|Looking up 1st Ave in [[Seattle]] from Pioneer Square, 1900]]
[[File:Hamburger's Department Store seen from down a very busy street, ca.1890-1899 (CHS-154.1).jpg|thumb|left|A busy [[Los Angeles]] street in the 1890s showing the roads as public space not dominated by one mode of transport]]

At the end of the 19th and beginning of the 20th century, Canadian and American cities with few exceptions, most notably New York and Chicago which already had many tall buildings, were not dramatically different in form from their European counterparts. They had a relatively small physical footprint compared to their population size, and buildings were largely 3–7 stories tall surrounded by a relatively modest ring of [[streetcar suburb]]s.<ref name="auto1">{{Cite journal|date=1990-07-09|title=Self-Building and the Social Geography of Toronto, 1901-1913: A Challenge for Urban Theory |journal=Transactions of the Institute of British Geographers|language=en|volume=15|pages=387–402|last1=Harris|first1=Richard|issue=4 |doi=10.2307/622848 |jstor=622848 |bibcode=1990TrIBG..15..387H }}</ref>
Most city dwellers who were in the lower to middle-income brackets lived in dense urban environments within a practical distance of their workplace.

The less well-off typically lived on either the upper floors of multi-unit residential buildings, as most did not have [[elevator]]s, or in [[tenement]]s. Merchants frequently lived in a residential unit above their store. Those who were better-off may have lived in a rowhouse or terrace, and starting toward the end of the 19th century, perhaps in a streetcar suburb still relatively close to the city centre.<ref name="auto1"/> Overall, the typical arrangement of urban spaces was one where communities were serviced by small-scale owner-operated shops and transport to non-walkable destinations was done by [[History of cycling infrastructure|bicycle]], [[bus]], [[Tram|streetcar]], or [[Rapid transit|train]].<ref name="auto1"/>

Traditionally those in the highest income brackets had typically lived in large houses outside of, but often near to, the city. They travelled to the city originally by horse [[carriage]] and later by [[Car|automobile]].<ref name="auto1"/> For most people, the need to live close to their job significantly limited spatial social stratification beyond [[economic class]]. This situation collapsed in the wake of explosive expansion of post-war [[Urban sprawl|suburban sprawl]], which enabled [[white flight]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2017|title=Measuring the geography of opportunity. |journal=Human Geography|language=en|volume=41pp=3|last1=Lens|first1=M.C.}}</ref>

[[Image:LevittownPA.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.4|Aerial view of [[Levittown, Pennsylvania]], {{circa|1959}}]]

The early to mid-twentieth century implementation of the suburb was thoroughly informed by this social context, and it was not uncommon for policymakers to inappropriately conflate small residential unit size, poverty, and crime with the traditional urban form; while simultaneously idealizing "rural" and upper class style estate living as its cure-all. The new car suburb was an affordable imitation of upper-class housing which became possible at such a vast scale when, after the war, factories could be turned over from producing [[History of Chrysler#Postwar government programs|military vehicles to consumer cars]], helping to reduce the nominal price of a private automobile.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1998|title=Invisible Cities: Lewis Mumford, Thomas Adams, and the Invention of the Regional City, 1923-1929  |journal=Business and Economic History|language=en|volume=27|pages=3|last1=Lens|first1=M.C.}}</ref>

Originally in the US, the legal rule was that "all persons have an equal right in the highway, and that in exercising the right each shall take due care not to injure other users of the way".<ref>Miller McClintock for the Chicago Association of Commerce, "Report and Recommendations of the Metropolitan Street Traffic Survey", p. 133, quoted by Norton, ''Fighting Traffic'', on p. 289.</ref> Pro-automobile interests advocated for the removal of non-drivers from the road, and particularly targeted pedestrians with the invention and criminalization of "[[Jaywalking#Origin of the term|jaywalking]]".<ref>{{Cite book |last=Norton |first=Peter D. |title=Fighting Traffic: The Dawn of the Motor Age in the American City |date=2008 |publisher=MIT Press |location=Cambridge, Mass. |pages=78–79 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Norton |first=Peter D. |date=2007 |title=Street Rivals: Jaywalking and the Invention of the Motor Age Street |journal=Technology and Culture |language=en |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=331–359 (342) |doi=10.1353/tech.2007.0085|s2cid=144015588 }}</ref><ref name="Vanderbilt 2009">{{Cite web |last=Vanderbilt |first=Tom |date=2009-11-02 |title=In Defense of Jaywalking |url=https://slate.com/human-interest/2009/11/a-defense-of-jaywalking.html |access-date=2022-05-27 |website=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate Magazine]] |language=en}}</ref> Importantly Federal, State, and Provincial governments undertook massive [[Interstate Highway System#Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956|highway building programmes]] and also directly subsidized the purchasing of new suburban homes ([[Levittown]] being the prototype).<ref>{{cite news |last1 = Stromberg |first1 = Joseph |title = Highways Gutted American Cities. So Why Did They Build Them? |url = https://www.vox.com/2015/5/14/8605917/highways-interstate-cities-history |work = Vox |date = May 11, 2016 |access-date = May 10, 2019 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190425175726/https://www.vox.com/2015/5/14/8605917/highways-interstate-cities-history |archive-date = April 25, 2019 |url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last = Miller |first = Johnny |date = February 21, 2018 |title = Roads to Nowhere: How Infrastructure Built on American Inequality |url = http://www.theguardian.com/cities/2018/feb/21/roads-nowhere-infrastructure-american-inequality |access-date = April 3, 2021 |website = The Guardian |location = London |language = en |archive-date = April 4, 2021 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210404202301/https://www.theguardian.com/cities/2018/feb/21/roads-nowhere-infrastructure-american-inequality |url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last1 = Nall |first1 = Clayton |last2 = O'Keeffe |first2 = Zachary P. |title = What Did Interstate Highways Do to Urban Neighborhoods? |magazine = What Did Interstate Highways Do to Urban Neighborhoods? |date = 2018 |page = 30 |url = http://www.nallresearch.com/uploads/7/9/1/7/7917910/urbanhighways.pdf |access-date = March 17, 2022 |archive-date = April 3, 2021 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20210403042929/http://www.nallresearch.com/uploads/7/9/1/7/7917910/urbanhighways.pdf |url-status = live }}</ref>

These government policies helped to make cars a practical choice and fostered the wholesale adoption of the car by the middle classes by the 1960s and helped to create the conditions for a decline in the quality, availability, and financial viability of [[public transport]]ation.<ref>{{cite news |last1 = Stromberg |first1 = Joseph |title = The Real Reason American Public Transportation Is Such a Disaster |url = https://www.vox.com/2015/8/10/9118199/public-transportation-subway-buses |work = Vox |date = August 10, 2015 |access-date = May 10, 2019 |archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190510182647/https://www.vox.com/2015/8/10/9118199/public-transportation-subway-buses |archive-date = May 10, 2019 |url-status = live }}</ref> Increasingly the prestige and influence of New York and Chicago, with their high land prices and abundant skyscrapers, fostered a sense among many Canadian and Americans that "real cities" have tall buildings, and a "[[Downtown#Origins|downtown]]" dominated by them, meanwhile European cities remained relatively medium-rise, dense, and pluricentric.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2014|title=Skyscrapers: The City and the Megacity |journal=Theory, Culture & Society|language=en|volume=31 |pages=267–271|last1=Parker|first1=M|issue=7–8 |doi=10.1177/0263276414547776 }}</ref>

With this in mind, it is possible to understand the factors considered most important by policy makers in the mid-twentieth century context and how they pursued policies which would no longer allow for the previously dominant medium-density building types. The resulting policies radically reformed cities into ones that typically have a unicentric urban core which is dominated by tall buildings built to be reliant on office uses with the area often referred to as the [[central business district]] (CBD). This new "urban core" of stacked office uses is typically surrounded by swathes of [[Suburb|sub-urban]] and [[Peri-urbanisation|peri-urban landscapes]] dominated by [[Single-family zoning|single-family homes]] with [[Lawn#United States|gardens]] serviced by the private automobile, [[Power center (retail)|car-centric retail destinations]], and vast highway networks.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2001|title=The Geography of North American Cities and Suburbs, 1900-1950: A New Synthesis. |journal=Journal of Urban History|language=en|volume=27|pages=262|last1=Harris|first1=R.|last2=Lewis|first2=R.|doi=10.1177/009614420102700302 |s2cid=129312108 }}</ref>

== Impacts ==
[[File:Traditional rowhouses, Locust Point, Baltimore (100 0509).jpg|thumb|An example of historic [[row houses]] in [[Baltimore]] with characteristics of medium-density housing ]]

=== Longer commuting patterns ===
The loss of flexible middle-density development serviced by affordable and widely used public transportation has resulted in high [[Commuting|commute times]] for commuters, which have remained stubbornly unaffected by further investment in new road capacity due to the nature of [[Induced demand#In transportation systems|induced demand]], a practical limit on the space required to move large volumes of people in relatively large vehicles, and greatly increased costs for both the vehicle owner and government due to the inherent inefficiency compared to previous modes of transport.<ref name=wood94>{{cite book |first1=Derek |last1=Wood |author2=Standing Advisory Committee on Trunk Road Assessment |name-list-style=amp |title=Trunk Roads and the Generation of Traffic |year=1994 |publisher=HMSO |location=London |isbn=0-11-551613-1 |page=242 |url=https://www.bettertransport.org.uk/sites/default/files/trunk-roads-traffic-report.pdf}}</ref><ref name=cairns98>{{cite book |last1=Cairns |first1=Sally |last2=Hass-Klau |first2=Carmen |last3=Goodwin |first3=Phil |name-list-style=amp|title=Traffic Impact of Highway Capacity Reductions: Assessment of the Evidence |year=1998 |publisher=Landor Publishing |location=London |isbn=1-899650-10-5 |page=261}}</ref><ref name=cairns03>{{cite journal |last1=Cairns |first1=Sally |last2=Atkins |first2=Stephen |last3=Goodwin |first3=Phil|name-list-style=amp |title=Disappearing traffic? The story so far |journal= Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers - Municipal Engineer|year=2002 |volume=151 |issue=1 |url=http://contextsensitivesolutions.org/content/reading/disappearing-traffic/resources/disappearing-traffic/ |pages=13–22 |doi=10.1680/muen.2002.151.1.13|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Other problems include difficulty for low-income residents to find affordable accommodation within a reasonably affordable and practical commute of their place of employment.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}

=== Negative environmental impacts ===
Car-centric cities are less climate-friendly due to impacts relating to inefficient use of resources, volume of paved area contributing to flood risk, and potential loss of natural habitats to human development.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Guangdong |last2=Fang |first2=Chuanglin |last3=Li |first3=Yingjie |last4=Wang |first4=Zhenbo |last5=Sun |first5=Siao |last6=He |first6=Sanwei |last7=Qi |first7=Wei |last8=Bao |first8=Chao |last9=Ma |first9=Haitao |last10=Fan |first10=Yupeng |last11=Feng |first11=Yuxue |last12=Liu |first12=Xiaoping |date=2022-03-25 |title=Global impacts of future urban expansion on terrestrial vertebrate diversity |journal=Nature Communications |language=en |volume=13 |issue=1 |pages=1628 |doi=10.1038/s41467-022-29324-2  |doi-access=free|issn=2041-1723 |pmc=8956596 |pmid=35338145 |bibcode=2022NatCo..13.1628L }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Feng |first1=Qiu |last2=Gauthier |first2=Pierre |date=2021-04-24 |title=Untangling Urban Sprawl and Climate Change: A Review of the Literature on Physical Planning and Transportation Drivers |journal=Atmosphere |language=en |volume=12 |issue=5 |pages=547 |doi=10.3390/atmos12050547 |bibcode=2021Atmos..12..547F |doi-access=free |issn=2073-4433}}</ref>

=== Loss of small retail ===
Without middle-density development to support them, cities have lost retailers not operating with substantial economies of scale. [[Small business|"Mom and pop shops"]] are replaced by [[big-box store]]s.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}

=== Loss of third spaces ===
Cities without middle density have also seen the loss of [[third place]]s, places where people spend time which is neither their private residence nor their place of work.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Finlay |first1=Jessica |last2=Esposito |first2=Michael |last3=Kim |first3=Min Hee |last4=Gomez-Lopez |first4=Iris |last5=Clarke |first5=Philippa |date=November 2019 |title=Closure of 'third places'? Exploring potential consequences for collective health and wellbeing |journal=Health & Place |volume=60 |article-number=102225 |doi=10.1016/j.healthplace.2019.102225 |issn=1873-2054 |pmc=6934089 |pmid=31622919}}</ref> These places are important for recreation, meeting neighbours, for adults to make friends, and for community organization. The loss of these third places and small businesses is due to the need of both to rely on proximity to a large number of people for whom visiting them is easy, can be spontaneous, and would not require a special trip.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}} Some have characterized the replacement of these "third places", where historically people of all backgrounds in the neighbourhood gathered organically, by relatively fewer spaces where people must choose to drive, as a source of social filtering and potential source of [[social alienation]].{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}

Some have suggested the loss of genuine "third spaces" as a contributing factor to a perceived reduction in a sense of [[Belongingness|belonging]], [[Group cohesiveness|inter-group social cohesion]], and a rise in generalized [[loneliness]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2019|title=Closure of 'third places'? Exploring potential consequences for collective health and wellbeing |journal=Health & Place|language=en|volume=60|pages=3|last1=Finlay|first1=Jessica|last2=Esposito|first2=Michael|last3=Kim|first3=Min Hee|last4=Gomez-Lopez|first4=Iris|last5=Clarke|first5=Philippa|article-number=102225 |doi=10.1016/j.healthplace.2019.102225 |pmid=31622919 |pmc=6934089 }}</ref>

=== Environmental racism ===
According to the environmental geographer Laura Pulido, the historical processes of suburbanization and urban decentralization have contributed to contemporary [[environmental racism]].<ref>{{cite journal |author=Pulido, Laura |title= Rethinking Environmental Racism: White Privilege and Urban Development in Southern California |journal=Annals of the Association of American Geographers |volume=90 |number=1 |date=Mar 2000 |pages=12–40 |url= http://www.geog.umn.edu/faculty/squires/courses/BSE3001/PulioEnvironmentalRacismWhitePrivilege.pdf |doi= 10.1111/0004-5608.00182|bibcode= 2000AAAG...90...12P |hdl= 10214/1833 |s2cid= 38036883 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

==Causes==
The polarization of Canadian and American cities into ones dominated by low- and high-density development with little in-between, has been due to implementing strict single-use land-use zoning laws at a municipal level which prioritizes these use types while making new medium-density illegal. This, combined with shifts in [[transportation planning]] at all levels, had helped to create a development paradigm which takes the private motor vehicle as its default mode of transportation, and only after that, considering other modes like walking, cycling, buses, streetcars, and subways. Public transport, where it still exists, has typically also built within this paradigm of car dependency. For example, [[GO Transit]] rail services in the [[Greater Toronto Area]] is one of the few commuter-rail services in either Canada or the United States, but is designed for commuters to drive to parking lots with a train platform where the rail service will take passengers to the CBD in the morning and return them to the parking lot in the afternoon, service has been unidirectional and only operated during rush hour.<ref name="GO Transit Facts">{{Cite web |title=Info to GO |publisher=GO Transit |url=http://www.gotransit.com/public/en/aboutus/GO%20Info%20To%20Go_EN_Jan%202017.pdf |date=January 2017 |access-date=10 March 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170312071143/http://www.gotransit.com/public/en/aboutus/GO%20Info%20To%20Go_EN_Jan%202017.pdf |archive-date=12 March 2017 }}</ref>

==Possible solutions==
[[File:1721 N. Kingsley.jpg|thumb|A [[bungalow court]] development where several small homes surround a central garden]]

Missing middle housing offers a greater choice in housing types that still blend into existing single-family neighborhoods, create more affordable housing options, and help reach sustainability goals.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last=H Ojah Maharaj|first=Shrimatee|date=2020|title=Factors Affecting the Supply of "Missing Middle" Housing Types in Walkable Urban Core Neighborhoods|journal=Muma Business Review|volume=4|pages=001–015|doi=10.28945/4544|issn=2640-6373|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=The Houses that Can't be Built in America - The Missing Middle| date=8 March 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CCOdQsZa15o|language=en|access-date=2021-07-05}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Missing Middle Housing: Diverse choices for walkable neighborhood living|url=https://missingmiddlehousing.com/|access-date=2021-02-13|website=Missing Middle Housing|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=What is "missing middle"? - Housing|url=https://housing.arlingtonva.us/missingmiddle/about/|access-date=2021-02-13|website=housing.arlingtonva.us}}</ref> Missing middle housing units are usually smaller units than single-family homes because they share a lot with other homes, which results in lower per-unit land costs and, therefore, lower housing costs.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Schuetz|first=Alex Baca, Patrick McAnaney, and Jenny|date=2019-12-04|title='Gentle' density can save our neighborhoods|url=https://www.brookings.edu/research/gentle-density-can-save-our-neighborhoods/|access-date=2021-02-13|website=Brookings|language=en-US}}</ref> Missing middle housing types are also one of the cheapest forms of housing to produce because they are typically low-rise, low parking and wood-frame construction, which avoids expensive concrete podiums.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web|title=Finding Affordability in the Missing Middle|url=https://wc-studio.com/journal/2019/11/23/finding-affordability-in-the-missing-middle|access-date=2021-02-14|website=WC STUDIO architects|date=25 November 2019 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite web|publisher=Sacramento Area Council of Governments|date=2018-12-03|title=Housing Policy Toolkit|url=https://www.sacog.org/sites/main/files/housing_policy_toolkit_appendix_included_2018-12-3.pdf|website=www.sacog.org}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=The "Missing Middle" Affordable Housing Solution {{!}} Modern Cities|url=https://www.moderncities.com/article/2017-jan-the-missing-middle-affordable-housing-solution-page-3|access-date=2020-04-26|website=www.moderncities.com |date=13 January 2017 }}</ref> Because the construction and building materials are comparatively less complicated than larger mid- and high-rise structures, a larger pool of small-scale and local home builders can participate in the creation of this form of housing.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> To support municipal budgets, the denser and more efficient use of land and infrastructure may be financially productive for municipalities with more people paying taxes per acre for less infrastructure than large lot single-family homes.<ref name=":6" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=5 Ways To Make the Missing Middle Less Missing|url=https://www.strongtowns.org/journal/2019/7/19/5-ways-to-make-the-missing-middle-less-missing|access-date=2020-04-26|website=Strong Towns|date=19 July 2019 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Litman|first=Todd|date=April 21, 2021|title=Understanding Smart Growth Savings|url=https://www.vtpi.org/sg_save.pdf|website=Victoria Transport Policy Institute}}</ref>

Increasing missing middle housing options may allow families of different sizes, types, and incomes to access quality housing. Missing middle housing tends to become naturally affordable housing as it ages, and provides a level of density that supports the shops, restaurants, and transit that are associated with walkable neighborhoods.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Advancing Racial Equity Through Land-Use Planning|url=https://www.planning.org/pas/memo/2021/may/|access-date=2021-05-31|website=American Planning Association}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Revisiting Single-Family Zoning: Creating Options for a More Affordable Housing Supply|url=https://www.lgc.org/newsletter/revisiting-single-family-zoning-creating-options-for-a-more-affordable-housing-supply/|access-date=2021-02-13|website=Local Government Commission|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.planetizen.com/blogs/107442-dont-miss-middle-critical-role-moderate-priced-housing-affordability|title=Don't Miss the Middle: The Critical Role of Moderate-Priced Housing to Affordability|website=Planetizen - Urban Planning News, Jobs, and Education|language=en|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref> Walkable neighborhoods may then support sustainability, health, and affordability goals by reducing reliance on personal vehicles.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2016-04-01|title=Does urban sprawl hold down upward mobility?|journal=Landscape and Urban Planning|language=en|volume=148|pages=80–88|doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2015.11.012|issn=0169-2046|doi-access=free|last1=Ewing|first1=Reid|last2=Hamidi|first2=Shima|last3=Grace|first3=James B.|last4=Wei|first4=Yehua Dennis|bibcode=2016LUrbP.148...80E }}</ref> This would promote active transportation, reduce sprawl, reduce pollution, and reduce transportation costs by lessening the need for personal vehicles.<ref name=":7" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kim|first1=Eun Jung|last2=Kim|first2=Jiyeong|last3=Kim|first3=Hyunjung|date=February 2020|title=Does Environmental Walkability Matter? The Role of Walkable Environment in Active Commuting|journal=International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health|volume=17|issue=4|page=1261|doi=10.3390/ijerph17041261|issn=1661-7827|pmc=7068548|pmid=32075326|doi-access=free |bibcode=2020IJERP..17.1261K }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Charron|first=David|title=Analysis {{!}} Walkable neighborhoods provide health, environmental and financial benefits|language=en-US|newspaper=Washington Post|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/where-we-live/wp/2017/10/09/walkable-neighborhoods-provide-health-environmental-and-financial-benefits/|access-date=2021-02-13|issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=5 Questions for Architect Daniel Parolek About Missing Middle Housing|url=https://www.aarp.org/livable-communities/housing/info-2016/missing-middle-housing-daniel-parolek.html|access-date=2021-02-13|website=AARP|language=english}}</ref>

Missing middle housing options may allow seniors to downsize without leaving their neighborhood. For example, accessory dwelling units can enable multi-generation households to have privacy while all living on the same property.<ref>{{Cite journal|first1=Phoebe S.|last2=Liebig|first2=Teresa|last1=Koenig|first3=Jon|last3=Pynoos|date=2006-11-21|title=Zoning, Accessory Dwelling Units, and Family Development Office of Policy Development and Research|title=Accessory Dwelling Units: Case Study|url=https://www.huduser.gov/Publications/PDF/adu.pdf|website=HUD USER}}</ref><ref name="aarp.org">{{Cite web|title=ADUs Offer Options for Homeowners to Age in web|last=Stanton|first=Melissa|title=Multifamily, intergenerational housing|url=https://www.aarp.org/livable-communities/housing/info-2016/a-home-within-a-home.html|access-date=2021-02-13|website=AARP|language=english}}</ref>  Missing middle housing may enable a wider range of families to achieve homeownership by offering a wider range of housing options and prices.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-10-14|title=Reasons to Invest in Missing Middle Housing: A Call to Action for Cities and Developers|url=https://opticosdesign.com/blog/reasons-to-invest-in-missing-middle-housing-a-call-to-action-for-cities-and-developers/|access-date=2021-02-13|website=Opticos Design|language=en-US}}</ref> Additionally, missing middle housing types such as accessory dwelling units can support mortgages through the rents of those secondary units.<ref>{{Cite housing at a wide range of prices for a range of family types.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The 'Missing' Affordable Housing Solution|url=https://www.aarp.org/livable-communities/housing/info-2020/missing-middle-housing-affordability.html|access-date=2021-02-13|website=AARP|language=english}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Five Some property rights advocates believe that widely permitting missing middle housing expands property rights by allowing property owners more choice in how to use their property.<ref>{{Cite web|title=It's Time to Abolish Single-Family Zoning|url=https://www.theamericanconservative.com/urbs/its-time-to-abolish-single-family-zoning/|access-date=2021-02-13|website=The American Some equity advocates feel that permitting more diverse housing choices, such as missing middle housing, may reduce historic and modern inequities that keep less affluent people out of certain ===Transit-oriented development (TOD)===
{{Multiple image|direction=vertical|align=right|upright=1.6|image1=ArlingtonTODimage3.jpg|caption1=An aerial view of the [[Rosslyn-Ballston corridor]] in [[Arlington County, Virginia|Arlington, Virginia]]. The high density, mixed use development is concentrated within ¼–½ mile from the [[Rosslyn (WMATA station)|Rosslyn]], [[Court House (WMATA station)|Court House]] and [[Clarendon (WMATA station)|Clarendon]] [[Washington Metro]] stations (shown in red), with limited density outside that area.}}Increasingly from the 1990s onwards, [[transit-oriented development]] (TOD) has been put forward by many urban planners as a way to create more medium-density development. The idea is that creating communities of mixed-use development around public transport nodes will help to recreate demand for public transport and help to re-urbanize Canadian and American municipalities. TOD developments in Canada and the United States are typically near a public transport node, made of large plots with between one and a few buildings on them owned by one to a few owners and, typically, tall buildings and or buildings of intermediate size with a mixture of uses permitted within them predominating. Uses often include shops at the ground floor with residential and office uses interspersed throughout the upper floors.

Some critics of the way the TOD concept has been implemented in Canada and the United States point out that the large TODs fail to engage in placemaking and the result is relatively large highly controlled characterless places not unlike the suburbs and strip malls they are meant to replace.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2013|title=Planning, place-making and building consensus for transit-oriented development: Ogden, Utah case study|journal=Journal of Transport Geography |language=en|volume=32|pages=65–76|last1=Dorsey|first1=Bryan|doi=10.1016/j.jtrangeo.2013.08.010 |bibcode=2013JTGeo..32...65D }}</ref> These critics say that the problem is with trying to zone for what planners think a city looks like; rather than creating the transport and legal conditions to allow it to take shape organically.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2017|title=Measuring TOD around transit nodes - Towards TOD policy|journal=Transport Policy|language=en|volume=56|pages=96–111|last1=Singh|first1=Yamini Jain|last2=Lukman|first2=Azhari|last3=Flacke |first3=Johannes|last4=Zuidgeest|first4=Mark|last5=Van Maarseveen|first5=M.F.A.M.|doi=10.1016/j.tranpol.2017.03.013 |url=https://research.utwente.nl/en/publications/c12314fc-284d-477b-a5b6-d22f0bbfa746 }}</ref>

===Nested Intensity Zoning===
However, [[Zoning#Japan|urban planning in Japan]] uses a zoning system and has not lost middle-density housing. Instead of single-use zoning, zones are defined by the "''most'' intense" use permitted. Uses of lesser intensity are permitted in zones where higher intensity uses are permitted but higher intensity uses are not allowed in lower intensity zones.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |date=January 2003 |title=Introduction to Land use Planning System in Japan |url=http://www.mlit.go.jp/common/000234477.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140913101110/http://www.mlit.go.jp/common/000234477.pdf |archive-date=September 13, 2014 |access-date=June 7, 2022 |publisher=[[Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism]]}}</ref> This results in nested zoning, where the higher intensity zones are inclusive of related lower intensity ones. Zoning districts in Japan are classified into twelve use zones.<ref name="auto"/> Each zone determines a building's shape and permitted uses. A building's shape is controlled by zonal restrictions on allowable building coverage ratios, [[floor area ratio]]s, height (in absolute terms and in relation to adjacent buildings and roads), and minimum residential unit size. These controls are intended to allow adequate light and ventilation between buildings and on roads, and to ensure a decent quality of housing. In this system, rather than trying to plan for how and where to create dedicated districts of medium-density housing, planners are left to focus on creating the conditions necessary to encourage land owners to intensify the use of their plots, and ensuring new areas of medium density that arise have the amenities they need to be successful.

[[File:Contemporary japanese homes - panoramio.jpg|328px|left|thumb|Examples of medium density single detached houses in Japan. Note the absence of cars, car facilities, or private gardens and the use of substantial balconies, strategic window placement, and considerable house size.]]When discussing medium-density housing, it is important to explore the differences between the approach this type of zoning uses with respect to single-detached housing compared to that traditionally used in the United States and Canada. In the United States and Canada, single-detached homes typically require ''large'' [[Setback (land use)|setbacks]] for off-street car parking and yards/gardens; while single detached homes in Japan are in many cases similarly large single detached houses but on small plots taking up virtually the entirety of the plot fronting directly on to the street with no requirement for off-street car parking; instead assuming a reliance on public transport rather than cars to meet daily needs. Roads in these areas are slow and drivers are aware they must legally share responsibility for mutual safety with all the other types of road users equally. [[File:A girl running at the street in Osaka, Japan; May 2013.jpg|thumb|right|A girl running on a street in Osaka; it is common to see children walking and playing with their friends in the street or taking the metro by themselves unsupervised in Japan.<ref>{{cite news |last1 = Hoy |first1 = Selena |title = Why Are Little Kids in Japan So Independent? |url = https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2015-09-28/in-japan-small-children-take-the-subway-and-run-errands-alone |work = Bloomberg |date = September 28, 2015 |access-date = June 21, 2023 }}</ref>]]This type of single detached house can achieve medium housing density while fostering a sense of community, municipal fiscal viability, and good residential amenity. This is achieved while maintaining privacy and access to sunlight by regulating the direction of windows, the use of very small setbacks, much higher maximum building coverage ratios, higher [[floor area ratio]]s, and other considerations discussed in the previous paragraph. It is also worth noting that Japanese houses offer, on average, larger living spaces than that of many wealthy European countries which have not lost their medium-density housing.<ref>{{Cite web| title=Living space - Definitions and methodology | url=https://www.oecd.org/els/family/HC2-1-Living-space.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170216091401/http://www.oecd.org/els/family/HC2-1-Living-space.pdf | archive-date=2017-02-16}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web| title=Low-income neighbourhoods in Britain - The gap between policy ideas and residents' realities | url=https://www.jrf.org.uk/sites/default/files/jrf/migrated/files/poverty-neighbourhood-resident-experience-full.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210411133921/https://www.jrf.org.uk/sites/default/files/jrf/migrated/files/poverty-neighbourhood-resident-experience-full.pdf | archive-date=2021-04-11}}</ref> This approach to not require car parking provision or private yards/gardens in areas with high degrees of good connectivity is seen as desirable because: access to common outdoor green space is seen as sufficient for these needs or, at the very least, an acceptable tradeoff for the convenience of improved connectivity; the provision of sprawling lower-value land-uses like private car parking and residential garden spaces in such locations is viewed as a poor [[return on investment]] by developers eager to maximize living space and plot utilization; urban planners who are eager to avoid the imprudent use of limited public funds with respect to the large nominal and operational costs of public transportation, water, power, roads, etc. which usually increase over distances, while access costs for users do not; and urban planners seeking to avoid wasteful and shortsighted [[opportunity cost]]s.

This approach to zoning gives the landowner more flexibility in using the land while still precluding harmful or inappropriate development and maintaining the benefit of remaining predictable and easy to understand. The result is that when demand changes, like with new public transport investment, land-owners are able to, on an individual basis, redevelop their land to meet demand in a manner that can be reactive to local demand and distributes risk for the local community;  for example the failure of a medium-sized building to find tenants may have a relatively small impact, whereas a large one failing to do so may hamper development of other types in the same community. This type of zoning may also help to foster a more organic and local character to communities, especially over time.

===Form-based code (FBC)===
[[File:Missing Middle Housing Types - 51852913074.png|thumb|Examples of missing middle housing types]]
A '''[[form-based code]]''' (FBC) is a means of regulating land development to achieve a specific urban form. Form-based codes foster predictable built results and a high-quality public realm by using physical form (rather than separation of uses) as the organizing principle, with less focus on [[land use]], through municipal regulations. An FBC is a regulation, not a mere guideline, adopted into city, town, or county law and offers an alternative to conventional zoning regulation.<ref>{{cite web|title=Form-Based Codes Defined|url=http://formbasedcodes.org/definition|website=Form Based Codes Institute}}</ref>

Missing-middle housing comes in a variety of building types and densities but may be characterized by location in a walkable context, lower perceived density, small building footprints, smaller homes, reasonably low amounts of parking, simple construction, and focus on community.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Parolek|first=Daniel|title=Missing Middle Housing: Thinking Big and Building Small to Respond to Today's Housing Crisis|publisher=Island Press|year=2020|location=Washington DC|pages=14–25}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://missingmiddlehousing.com/about/characteristics|title=Characteristics|website=Missing Middle Housing|language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://americas.uli.org/attainable-housing/|title=Attainable Housing: Challenges, Perceptions and Solutions|website=ULI Americas|language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://thefield.asla.org/2018/09/18/missing-middle-housing/|title=Missing Middle Housing|date=2018-09-18|website=The Field|language=en|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref> Forms of missing middle housing may include side-by-side duplexes, stacked duplexes, bungalow courts, accessory dwelling units (carriage houses, basement apartments, etc.), fourplexes, multiplexes, townhomes, courtyard apartments, and live/work units.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://missingmiddlehousing.com/types|title=The Types|website=Missing Middle Housing|language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cnu.org/our-projects/missing-middle-housing|title=Missing Middle Housing|date=2015-06-12|website=CNU|language=en|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref>

These building types typically have a residential unit density in the range of 16 to 30 units per acre but are often perceived as being less dense because they are smaller in scale.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blogs.stthomas.edu/realestate/2013/06/11/cnu-21-missing-middle-housing/|title=CNU 21: Missing Middle Housing|last1=Agnew|first1=Spencer|website=University of St. Thomas}}</ref> Because of its scale, missing middle housing may mix into single-family neighborhoods, act as an end-grain of a single-family housing block, act as a transition between higher density housing and single-family housing, or act as a transition from a [[Mixed-use development|mixed-use]] area to a single-family area.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9KLls6Vk-GM&feature=youtu.be&t=1281|title=Missing Middle Housing: Responding to the Demand for Walkable Urban Living|last=Salt Lake City Television|date=26 June 2016|website=Youtube}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last=Parolek|first=Daniel|title=Missing Middle Housing: Thinking Big and Building Small to Respond to Today's Housing Crisis|publisher=Island Press|year=2020|location=Washington DC|pages=26–29}}</ref> The resulting density may support broader community desires, including walkable retail, amenities, public transportation, and increased "feet on the street".<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://metroscape.imspdx.org/missing-middle-housing|title=Finding the Middle: Overcoming Challenges to Building Missing Middle Housing – Metroscape|language=en-US|access-date=2020-04-26}}</ref>

===Gentle density===
{{See also|Gentle density}}
Gentle density calls for a variety of housing types such as terraces, townhouses, low-rise apartments and dual-occupancy in well-serviced areas that makes use of existing infrastructure and public transport connections.<ref name="ABC"/>
