======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Urban planning in China
======================================================================

{{short description|none}}
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Shanghaipedmall.jpg|300px|thumb|[[Pedestrian mall]] (Shanghai, PRC)]] -->
[[File:Chongqing center.jpg|alt=skyline of chonqing city center|thumb|315x315px|Skyline of the [[Chongqing]] city center, one of the largest cities in both China and the world.]]
'''Urban planning in the People's Republic of China''' is currently characterized by a top-down approach, high density urban development and [[Urbanization in China|extensive urbanization]]. The country's [[urban planning]] philosophies and practices have undergone multiple transitions due to governance and economic structure changes throughout the nation's extensive history. The [[Proclamation of the People's Republic of China|establishment of the People's Republic of China]] in 1949 marks the beginning of three recent historical stages of urban planning philosophies and practice which represent a divergence from traditional Chinese urban planning morphologies and are broadly categorized as socialist, hybrid and global cities.<ref name="Hahn">Hahn, Thomas. 2006. [http://hahn.zenfolio.com/f64817197/ China Urban Planning materials 中国近代城市化图片资料]. Accessed on 17 May 2009</ref>

*Traditional City - walled cities, for example, Xi'an and Beijing's [[Forbidden City]].  Traditional cities, were planned in a manner similar to that of present-day, as they were also directly affected by the philosophies, governance and economies of their time.  Traditional cities are often planned in accordance with archaic concepts of [[geomancy]], [[Feng-shui]], ''[[I-Ching]]''.  ''The [[Rites of Zhou]]'' dating to approximately (1100–256 BC)<ref name=WhitehandGu>Whitehand, J.W.R. and Gu, Kai. (2006). Research on Chinese urban form: retrospect and prospect. Progress in Human Geography 30(3), 2006, pp. 337–355.</ref> serve to emphasize the importance of such philosophies, the cardinal directions and harmony between the human and natural realms.<ref name =Krupp>Krupp, E. C. (2002). Skywise and Streetsmart. Sky & Telescope. 103.6 (June 2002): 78(3).</ref> China's history is rich with examples of early planning philosophies and practices evidenced by traditional cities such as, but not limited to [[Chang'an]] ([[Xi'an]]) ({{Lang|zh-cn|西安}}), [[Beijing]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|北京}}), [[Nanjing]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|南京}}) and [[Luoyang]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|洛阳}}).
*Socialist City - (1950–1980) Planning efforts focused to increase the percentage of blue-collar workers, create affordable housing, urban communes, work unit (''danwei'' {{Lang|zh-cn|单位}}), discrete enclosures, broad, central avenues and large squares and Soviet-style exhibition halls. Examples include: [[Harbin]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|哈尔滨}}) and [[Beijing]].
*Hybrid City - (1860–Present) Planning that incorporating western planning and design principles meshed with traditional Chinese street grids and architectural principles. These were often the first cities to develop modern infrastructures networks and include cities such as [[Shanghai]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|上海}}), [[Shenyang]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|沈阳}}) and [[Tianjin]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|天津}}).
*[[Global City]] - (1990–Present) Planning aimed to encourage strategic economic development of a region for the purposes of global economic participation as a key node in the globalized market; coined and conceptualized by [[Saskia Sassen]].  Global cities are characterized by international familiarity, participation in international events and global affairs, densely populated metropolitan areas, Central Business Districts (CBD) housing key financial, corporate headquarters and national services, extensive public transportation systems, internationally networked airports, large-scale commercial and industrial zones and multiple urban cores. Examples include [[Beijing]], [[Shanghai]], [[Hong Kong]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|香港}}), [[Guangzhou]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|广州}}) and more recently [[Shenzhen]] ({{Lang|zh-cn|深圳}}).<ref name=frieldmann>Frieldmann, J. 1995. Where We Stand: Decade of World City Research, in Knox P and Taylor P J (eds). World Cities in a World System. Cambridge: Cambridge UP 21-47(p.15).</ref><ref name=Sassen>Sassen, Saskia. 2001. Global cities and global city regions: a comparison, in Scott, A(ed). Global city regions, trends, theory and policy. Oxford: OUP 78-95.</ref><ref name=Scott>Scott, A. J. (ed.) (2001) Global City-Regions, Oxford: Oxford University Press Sennett, R. 1990 The Conscience of the Eye, the Design and Social Life of Cities, London: Norton & Company</ref>

==History==
{{main|Ancient Chinese urban planning}}
[[File:Chengzhou Diagram.jpg|thumb|right|250px|The diagram of [[Chengzhou]]'s [[ancient Chinese urban planning|idealized layout]] from the 1175 [[Song dynasty|Song]]-era ''Xinding Sanlitu'', based on the ''[[Kaogongji]]'' descriptions of an ideal capital]]
China provides one of many examples of how archaic philosophies and their resulting planning decisions have had a profound impact on not only the spatial organization, but the culture of cities and nations of the distant past and present.<ref name=WhitehandGu/><ref name=Krupp/><ref name=Ortuzar/> Planning in China originates previous to that of the very early dynastic times, for example, "the most influential study of an ideal layout for a royal capital" was recorded in the ''[[Artificers' Record]]'' ({{translit|zh|Kaogongji}}) during the Western Han dynasty (206 BC{{ndash}}9 AD) and is thought to have been a replacement for a lost section of the ''[[Rites of Zhou]]'' created during the Zhou dynasty (1100-256BC).<ref name=WhitehandGu/><ref name=Krupp/> Further, the Rites of Zhou indicate that the origins of the most basic of urban planning philosophies in China are of a more archaic nature relating to concepts of [[geomancy]], [[Feng Shui]] and ''[[I Ching]]''.<ref name=Krupp/> The planners of ancient China "imposed an orthogonal and cardinal regimen on the districts, temples, places and streets of its capital cities at least as early as the Zhou dynasty (1122-221 B.C.)" and that the ''[[Rites of Zhou]]'' confirm the importance cosmologically based philosophies such as directional orientation and symmetry.<ref name=WhitehandGu/><ref name=Krupp/>  Santiago Ortuzar indicates that such basic rural and urban planning philosophies may have originated more than 7000 years ago in the Neolithic villages, for example, the [[Hemudu culture]] settlements in Zhejiang province. [[Banpo]], a village outside of Xi'an dating to 4500 or 3000 B.C. provides an example of early urban activity centres as 45 dwellings still remain in what could be easily considered high density for the building materials of the time. The traditional walled cities, such as Xi'an were planned in the 7th century AD as the first Chinese capital city under the [[Sui dynasty]]. The construction of which was preceded by a regional survey to ensure the flow of water, resources and a strategic location for reasons of health, natural balance and safety; an exercise planners today practice on a daily basis. Xi'an's city walls during the seventh century AD enclosed approximately 80,000 ha and housed an estimated half a million people; an accomplishment even the most prominent European cities failed to achieve until the 19th century; furthering their historical and present value making them entirely relevant to recent planning paradigm shifts of both the East and Western.<ref name=Ortuzar/>

It is perhaps best to follow the example of Santiago Ortuzar, Professor of Urban Planning, School of Architecture
Central & Mayor Universities, Santiago, Chile, who analyzes traditional urban planning in China by separating urban tradition and urban antiquity; two highly integrated aspects of [[urban morphology]] as their origins in Eastern planning are different.<ref name =Ortuzar>Ortuzar, Santiago. (1997). Letter from China: a perspective on Chinese cities. Australian Planner, 34(4), 1997, pp. 195-199.</ref>

===Urban antiquities===
Human settlements in China are considerably older than those of the West{{citation_needed|date=August 2026}}, as Neolithic villages in the lower plains of the [[Yangtze River]] are approximately 7,500-7,000 years old. [[Banpo]], an early village located on the outskirts of [[Xi'an]], discovered in 1953, may have preceded Xi'an by 1,500 years or more and dates to approximately 5,000 BC. The village, while partially excavated presents considerable evidence of early planning efforts in China as its layout reveals "various land uses (zoning) were allocated and where several activities took place" and further represents "a clear indication of a conscious decision to separate the perilous outside world with a secure internal space" in fashion similar to present towns, cities and global city municipal zoning. Some 45 dwellings and various other structures used for food storage and animal pens compose the site. Further from these structures were work areas, several timber-fired kilns and a cemetery consisting of 250 tombs.  Various types of pottery, bone and timber tools were also recovered from the site; reinforcing the spatial usage patterns derived from the layout, remains and other site data.  The grouping of such objects in archaeological context further reinforces the level of "sophistication both in terms of spatial and human organisation that can only be classified as a settlement inhabited by a cohesive social group composed of urban dwellers" approximately 5,000 years ago.  A second village near Beijing dating to 2,400BC further confirms that similar discoveries such as Banpo "are not isolated examples" of early and intentional urban planning in China.<ref name=Ortuzar/>

Chinese settlements, while later than those of the Nile Valley, Indus, Euphrates and Tigris river basins "are undoubtedly some of the worlds first in terms of human evolution and urban character".<ref name =Mumford>Mumford, L. 1961. The city in history Penguin Books, London.</ref> Ortuzar furthers this statement by indicating that there is "a long urban tradition which stretches far back in time. It has continued to remain uninterrupted for several thousands of years from the very origin of towns until the contemporary city. Few nations can exhibit such continuity over a long period of time".<ref name=Ortuzar/>

===Urban tradition===
Urban tradition is usually intimately related to urban antiquity. However, in the context of China, it has its own set of attributes in relation to urban planning, design and the social realm. China's population is classified as being approximately 55-60% rural, and in contrast to the majority of western countries, rural inhabitants are not thinly distributed over the landscape on individual land tracts.  Rural inhabitants "live grouped together" in hamlets creating an absence of parcel bound dwellings in the countryside. This settlement pattern has existed in China for thousands of years for various purposes including defense from "attacks by bandits, local chieftains and other enemies came together in hamlets. There were practical reasons too, such as the boring of wells to assure themselves of sufficient clean water".  This situation appeared much later in European history for similar reasons.  Rural Chinese live in small scale urban settlements of "about 500 to 700 persons each" with men traveling daily by horseback or bicycle to a nearby plot of land, while women either accompany their husbands to the fields or attend children or the household.  Services, entertainment and social activities are agglomerated in the larger urbanized hamlets that are often planned to service roughly twenty-five surrounding settlements.  The resulting geographic and planned patterns of such settlements respond "to regional criteria of urban distribution, something rarely occurring in other cultures".  The resulting patterns of living in one area and working in another is considered to be a social characteristic that many Chinese peasants have continued as they gradually urbanize into global city regions and other more urbanized and planned environments.  In contrast, European peasants did not begin to urbanize in a similar manner until the advent of modern transportation during the beginning of the Industrial Revolution and arrived in urban areas with little or no urban experience due to the disbursed settlement patterns of the West.  Ortuzar furthers, that the urban tradition in China has been ever-present "as its origins can be traced back to the early ages of development; one which is not necessarily bound to the size of towns, nor to the level or degree of urbanization achieved".<ref name=Ortuzar/>

===Modern time===
[[File:Large boulevard - panoramio.jpg|thumb|A large boulevard in Shanghai]]
In 1949, the year that the People's Republic of China was founded, less than 10% of the population in mainland China was urban.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=203}} Few cities at that time could be considered modern.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=203}} The early PRC took a cautious approach to urbanization, with its national development strategy citing the principle of "controlling large cities, developing small cities cautiously."<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=51}}

Throughout the [[Mao Zedong]] era, Chinese state planners designed urban areas with an explicit purpose of developing a socialist citizenry, including through the construction of work units called ''[[danwei]]'', which provided housing, jobs, food, health care, and other elements of the [[iron rice bowl]] on-site.<ref name=":13">{{Cite book |last=Simpson |first=Tim |title=Betting on Macau: Casino Capitalism and China's Consumer Revolution |date=2023 |publisher=[[University of Minnesota Press]] |isbn=978-1-5179-0031-1 |series=Globalization and Community series |location=Minneapolis}}</ref>{{Rp|page=24–25}} In the view of state planners, the design of the ''danwei'' would help promote [[Proletariat|proletarian]] consciousness.<ref name=":13" />{{Rp|page=24}} Planners also emphasized the development of public squares and spaces across China.<ref name=":Curtis&Klaus" />{{Rp|page=110}} In Beijing, [[Tiananmen]] was re-developed from an insular imperial quarter to a larger public space viewed as consistent socialist political.<ref name=":Curtis&Klaus" />{{Rp|page=110}} Over the 1950s, the [[Tiananmen Square|square]] was quadrupled in size.<ref name=":Curtis&Klaus" />{{Rp|page=110}}

During the period of the First [[Five-year plans of China|Five Year Plan]] (1953–1957), China's urban planning was heavily influenced by the Soviet Union's experience.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Hou |first=Li |title=Building for oil: Daqing and the Formation of the Chinese Socialist State |date=2021 |publisher=[[Harvard University Asia Center]] |isbn=978-0-674-26022-1 |edition= |series=[[Harvard-Yenching Institute]] monograph series |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts |pages=}}</ref>{{Rp|page=68}} Soviet urban planners first came to the PRC in 1949 and returned in 1952 and 1955.<ref name=":Curtis&Klaus">{{Cite book |last1=Curtis |first1=Simon |title=The Belt and Road City: Geopolitics, Urbanization, and China's Search for a New International Order |last2=Klaus |first2=Ian |publisher=[[Yale University Press]] |isbn=9780300266900 |location=New Haven and London |publication-date=2024 |doi=10.2307/jj.11589102 |jstor=jj.11589102}}</ref>{{Rp|page=110}} Soviet experts helped write China's national standards and guidelines and Soviet text books and regulations were translated into Chinese.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=68}} In the early part of the 1950s, city plans also followed the socialist city planning principles from the [[Stalinist architecture#Moscow Master Plan (1935)|1935 Moscow Master Plan]].<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=68}} These principles included maintaining the old city core as administrative areas while building industry on the periphery with green space and residences between the two.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=68}} Planning for factories and workers' housing in this period included strong central axes, [[green belt]]s, symmetrical building placement, parameter blocks, and monumental entrances.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=69}} Residential buildings were built in a historicist style with traditional Chinese roofs.<ref name=":1" />{{Rp|page=69}}

Inspired by [[Soviet urban planning ideologies of the 1920s#Disurbanist school|Soviet disurbanism]], China built satellite towns around industrial centers.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|pages=11-12}} Industrial-focused satellite towns include seven built by Shanghai in the late 1950s, among which were [[Minhang, Shanghai|Minghang]] (mechanical and electrical), [[Anting]] ([[Automotive industry in China|automotive]]), Jinshanwei (petrochemicals), and [[Wusong]] ([[Steel industry in China|steel]]).<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|pages=51-52}}

Urban migration stayed below 20%, with city planning primarily supporting urban industries and limiting opportunities for migrating into cities from rural areas.<ref name="1949-2000">{{Cite journal|last=Ma|first=Laurence J C|date=September 2002|title=Urban Transformation in China, 1949 – 2000: A Review and Research Agenda|journal=Environment and Planning A|volume=34|issue=9|pages=1545–1569|doi=10.1068/a34192|s2cid=145093393 |issn=0308-518X}}</ref> In 1958, [[The Great Leap Forward]] shifted the country's focus towards industrialization. Rural people were moved to factory jobs and city dwellings en masse, straining infrastructure. The country recovered slowly.

In 1963, Mao called for "Learning from Daqing in industry, and from [[Learn from Dazhai in agriculture|Dazhai in agriculture]]" and this concept became a national directive.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=52}} The development of [[Daqing]] was promoted as a model for industrialisation and town-building.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=52}}

During the [[Cultural Revolution]] (1966 – 1976), urban residents are encouraged or forced to leave for the countryside. Many historical sites were damaged or destroyed during the "Destroy the [[Four Olds]]" movement from 1966 to 1968. Subsequently, massive counter-urbanization known as the [[Down to the Countryside Movement]] took place, greatly dampening the process of urbanization in China.

Eventually, in 1979, formal urban planning efforts in China were restored and promoted due to the adoption of reform and open policy, causing consistent urban growth.<ref name="1949-2000"/>  The economic boom ushered in by [[Deng Xiaoping]] increased funding to major city planning works, including urban revitalization and renewal projects.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gao|first=George|date=September 2015|url=http://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2015/11/12/in-china-1980-marked-a-generational-turning-point/|title=In China, 1980 marked a generational turning point|publisher=Pew Research Center}}</ref> Chinese planners in the early [[Reform and opening up|Reform and Opening Up]] period redesigned cities both to accommodate the increasing urban population and increasing economic growth through light industry that produced consumer goods.<ref name=":122" />{{Rp|page=355}} This process changed urban areas from a focus on production to more livable cities.<ref name=":122" />{{Rp|page=355}} Architecture of this era was influenced by a re-connection with global designs, including noteworthy examples such as [[I. M. Pei]]'s the Beijing Xiangshan Hotel.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|url=https://www.britannica.com/art/Chinese-architecture/Stylistic-and-historical-development-since-1912|title=Chinese architecture - Stylistic and historical development since 1912|encyclopedia=Britannica}}</ref>

In 1989, China enacted its first planning law.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last=Lin |first=Zhongjie |title=Constructing Utopias: China's New Town Movement in the 21st Century |date=2025 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-779330-5 |location=New York, NY}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=77}} It established that provincial and municipal governments had responsibility for defining planning areas, preparing urban plans, designating land use, issuing building permits, and enforcing development controls.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=77}} In its impact on policy, the law facilitated urban and rural integration, expanding city boundaries to include a large amount of rural land, and provided a basis for new town development.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=77}}

Shanghai established China's first [[Shanghai Urban Planning Exhibition Center|city planning exhibition hall]] in 2000.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=24}} City planning exhibition halls later became common in major cities and new towns in China.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=24}} These exhibit halls showcase planning models and design drawings in an effort to promote development and increase civic pride.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=24}}

"Themed towns" in China adopt Western-style architecture and urban designs.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=29}} Among the most significant examples of this approach is Shanghai's [[One City, Nine Towns]] initiative, which began in 2001.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=29}}

During the 1990s and the early 2000s, environmental modeling and zoning concepts became important elements of city planning and management in China.<ref name=":03" />{{Rp|page=44}} During the subsequent [[General secretaryship of Xi Jinping|Xi Jinping administration]], these techniques were further emphasized.<ref name=":03" />{{Rp|page=44}}

Following the start of the [[Eleventh five-year plan (China)|Eleventh Five-Year Plan]] in 2006, China introduced a series of policies designed to encourage the development of [[Sustainable city|sustainable cities]].<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=200}}

The pace of urbanization in China accelerated in 2008.<ref name=":022">{{Cite book |last=Jin |first=Keyu |title=The New China Playbook: Beyond Socialism and Capitalism |date=2023 |publisher=Viking |isbn=978-1-9848-7828-1 |location=New York |author-link=Keyu Jin}}</ref>{{Rp|page=167}}

The discourse of [[ecological civilization]] has influenced the planning and development of [[Eco-cities in China|eco-cities]], low-carbon cities, and [[Sustainable city|green cities]] in China.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=23}} In 2013, [[General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party]] [[Xi Jinping]] promoted the [[sponge city]] concept, a construction and design approach to dealing with heavy rainfall through promoting rainwater infiltration, stagnation, storage, purification, utilization, and discharge.<ref name=":122" />{{Rp|page=382}} It includes the use of permeable materials in buildings, roads, and open public spaces as well as remediation of natural features such as wetlands or lakes which were blocked or filled during earlier stages of development.<ref name=":122" />{{Rp|page=382}} China's [[Government of China|central government]] mandates that by 2030, 80% of China's urban space must include sponge city adaptations and must recycle at least 70% of rainfall.<ref name=":Curtis&Klaus" />{{Rp|page=173}}

Between 2013 and 2018, Seaside City in [[Sichuan]], China's first fully 'privatised city', was constructed under the aegis of developer Chairman Huang and is home to over 120,000 people.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/w3ct03bx|title=Emperor Complex|author=David Borenstein|date=2019-12-02|publisher=BBC Sounds}}</ref>

Under the 2014 [[National New-Type Urbanization Plan]], the Chinese state sought to increase urban-rural coordination by incorporating rural planning as part of municipal governments' planning processes.<ref name=":03">{{Cite book |last=Rodenbiker |first=Jesse |title=Ecological States: Politics of Science and Nature in Urbanizing China |last2= |first2= |date=2023 |publisher=[[Cornell University Press]] |isbn=978-1-5017-6900-9 |series=Environments of East Asia |location=Ithaca, NY}}</ref>{{Rp|page=8}} New-type urbanization has since become a central theme of urban planning and development in China.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Hu |first=Richard |title=Reinventing the Chinese City |date=2023 |publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] |isbn=978-0-231-21101-7 |location=New York}}</ref>{{Rp|page=13}} The 2014 The National New-Type Urbanization plan requires 20% of municipal regions to be zoned as ecological protection areas.<ref name=":03" />{{Rp|page=8}}

The [[Thirteenth five-year plan (China)|Thirteenth Five-Year Plan]] (covering 2016–2020) highlighted nineteen [[City clusters in China|city clusters]] to be developed and strengthened pursuant to a geographic layout referred to as two horizontals and three verticals (''liang heng san zong'').<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=206}} The highlighted clusters included the [[Jing-Jin-Ji|Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region]], the [[Yangtze Delta|Yangtze River delta region]], and the [[Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macao Greater Bay Area|Greater Bay area]].<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=206}} Development of these clusters includes establishing regional coordination mechanisms, sharing development costs and benefits, collaborative industrial development, and shared governance approaches to ecological issues and [[Environmental policy in China|environmental protection]].<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=208}}

Before the 2020s, the majority of urban growth generally consisted of outward expansion from city centers, mostly into former farmland.<ref name=":122">{{Cite book |last=Harrell |first=Stevan |title=An Ecological History of Modern China |publisher=[[University of Washington Press]] |year=2023 |isbn=9780295751719 |location=Seattle}}</ref>{{Rp|page=355}}

The [[Fourteenth five-year plan|Fourteenth Five-Year Plan]] (covering the period 2021 to 2025) directs the development of more centralized cities and the avoidance of [[urban sprawl]].<ref name=":Curtis&Klaus" />{{Rp|pages=114–115}} The plan calls for acceleration of urban renewal to develop "human-centric cities."<ref name=":Curtis&Klaus" />{{Rp|page=115}} The plan's related Climate Change Special Plan emphasizes ecologically oriented urban planning, including through means like [[Urban green space|urban green rings]], public transportation, and bicycle lanes and walking paths.<ref name=":Curtis&Klaus" />{{Rp|page=114}}

New towns in China typically have common design elements including wide avenues, large green spaces between tall buildings, shopping malls, and gated residential neighborhoods in a design approach with prioritizes scale and speed.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=21}}

==Planning system==
===Legislation===
The laws in regard to urban and rural planning in the People's Republic of China (mainland) include ''Urban and Rural Planning Law'' ({{Lang|zh-cn|中华人民共和国城乡规划法}}) and its relevant laws, acts and codes.

===Administrative system===
At the national level, urban and rural planning in mainland China has been mainly administrated by the following departments since 1979:

* (1979 - 1982) State Administration of Urban Construction ({{Lang|zh-cn|国家城市建设总局}})
* (1982 - 1988) Ministry of Urban-Rural Construction and Environmental Protection ({{Lang|zh-cn|城乡建设环境保护部}})
* (1988 - 2008) Ministry of Construction ({{Lang|zh-cn|建设部}})
* (2008 - 2018) [[Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development]] (MOHURD, {{Lang|zh-cn|住房和城乡建设部}})
* (2018 - ) [[Ministry of Natural Resources of the People's Republic of China|Ministry of Natural Resources]] (MNR, {{Lang|zh-cn|自然资源部}})

At the municipal level, the department concerned is often called "Natural Resources Bureau" ({{Lang|zh-cn|自然资源局}}) or "Planning and Natural Resources Bureau" ({{Lang|zh-cn|规划和自然资源局}}) varying with the city.

===Types of plans===
In mainland China, the statutory planning system defined in the ''Urban and Rural Planning Law'' is as follows:

====Old system====
; Urban system planning
* National urban system planning ({{Lang|zh-cn|全国城镇体系规划}})
* Provincial urban system planning ({{Lang|zh-cn|省域城镇体系规划}})
; City planning
* City master plan ({{Lang|zh-cn|城市总体规划}})
*: including different types of specialized plans
* Detailed plans
** Regulatory plan ({{Lang|zh-cn|控制性详细规划}})
**: Known as "statutory plan" ({{Lang-zh|s=法定图则|t=法定圖則}}) in Shenzhen; introduced from Hong Kong.
** Site plan ({{Lang|zh-cn|修建性详细规划}})
; Town planning
* Town master plan ({{Lang|zh-cn|镇总体规划}})
*: In China, a towns is subordinate to a county or a district, and a county or a district is subordinate to a city or a municipality.
* Detailed plans
** Regulatory plan ({{Lang|zh-cn|控制性详细规划}})
** Site plan ({{Lang|zh-cn|修建性详细规划}})
; Rural planning
* Township plan ({{Lang|zh-cn|乡规划}})
* Village plan ({{Lang|zh-cn|村庄规划}})

Plans which are formulated by urban planning departments but not defined in the ''Urban and Rural Planning Law'', known as non-statutory planning, include strategic plans and renovation plans, etc..

====New system====
{{Main|Territorial spatial planning}}

The planning system has been undergoing a reform since the establishment of the Ministry of Natural Resources (MNR) and the shift of urban planning administration from MOHURD to MNR. Since 2019, urban planning managed by the urban planning department, [[land-use planning]] managed by the land management administration, as well as other specialized planning of different levels of jurisdictions, have been gradually merged into an integrated "[[territorial spatial planning]]" ({{Lang|zh-cn|国土空间规划}}) system consisting of five levels and three types. The "five levels" are national, provincial, municipal, county, and township levels in correspondence with the [[administrative divisions of China]]. The "three types" include master planning, detailed planning, and specialized planning.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.scio.gov.cn/xwfbh/xwbfbh/wqfbh/39595/40528/zy40532/Document/1655483/1655483.htm|title=国土空间规划按层级和内容分为"五级三类"|publisher=国务院新闻办公室网站|date=2019-05-27|language=|access-date=2019-12-15|archive-date=2019-07-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190701051744/http://www.scio.gov.cn/xwfbh/xwbfbh/wqfbh/39595/40528/zy40532/Document/1655483/1655483.htm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

{| class="wikitable" style="text-align: center; margin: auto;"
|+ The planning system with "Five Levels & Three Types"<ref>{{Cite book|author=吴次芳 叶艳妹 吴宇哲 丘文泽|title=国土空间规划|publisher=地质出版社|year=2019|isbn=9787116114852|language=zh}}</ref>
! Level !! Master planning !! Detailed planning !! Specialized planning
|-
| National || National territorial spatial planning || - || Specialized planning
|-
| Provincial || Provincial territorial spatial planning || - ||  Specialized planning
|-
| Municipal || Municipal territorial spatial planning || rowspan="3"|(Within [[urban growth boundary|UGB]]) Detailed planning<br />(Beyond UGB) Village planning || Specialized planning
|-
| County || County territorial spatial planning || Specialized planning
|-
| Town/Township || Town/township territorial spatial planning || -
|}
Master plans are the most important document in the urban planning system, and are statutory documents.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=147}} The master planning tool entails conceptualizing a built environment from inception, rationalizing land use with a blueprint, designing a comprehensive mobility network, allocating recreational spaces and open areas, and regulating building practices.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=12}} Development control plans are subordinate to master plans.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=147}}

Major entities involved in the planning of new cities in China include [[China Academy of Urban Planning and Design]] (CAUPD) and [[Tongji University]].<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=13}}

===Development control===
In practice, urban and rural planning in China is managed through the examination and approval of "one proposal & three permits" ({{Lang|zh-cn|一书三证}}), namely:

* Written proposal of location ({{Lang|zh-cn|建设项目选址意见书}}, required only for allotted land free of charge in urban areas)
* Land use permit ({{Lang|zh-cn|建设用地规划许可证}}, applied in urban areas)
* Building permit ({{Lang|zh-cn|建设工程规划许可证}}, applied in urban areas)
* Rural construction and planning permit ({{Lang|zh-cn|乡村建设规划许可证}}, applied in rural areas)
The concept of "ecological control line" is a regional development strategy first implemented in Hong Kong and then used elsewhere, such as Shenzhen, where 50% of the land is protected from development.<ref name=":02" />{{Reference page|page=60}}

==Criticism and reform==
It has been pointed out that the current policy of copying existing, "old", western cities or established Asian cities such as [[Singapore]] means missing out on opportunities for radical new thinking regarding city planning that are arising from the unprecedented speed of the current Chinese urbanization. For instance, it has been suggested that putting the entire road network underground can be a viable solution when dense cities are being built "from scratch".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.thepolisblog.org/2012/04/building-compact-really-compact.html |title=polis: Building Compact. Really Compact! |publisher=Thepolisblog.org |date=2012-04-25 |accessdate=2012-11-07}}</ref>

An important theme in urban planning reform discourse is the idea of "integrating multiple plans into one" (''duo gui he yi'').<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=200}} This concept focuses on integrating multiple types of plans (such as urban-rural plans, ecological and environmental plans, and others) into a single plan structure at one administrative level (such as the city level or the county level).<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=200}} Integrating multiple plans into one aims to consolidate planning approaches into a single blueprint and thereby achieve more consistent long-term implementation.<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=200}} Reforms in this regard were first experimented with in the development of [[Pudong New Area]].<ref name=":0" />{{Rp|page=200}}

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Urban planning in communist states
======================================================================

{{Short description|none}}
{{More citations needed|date=July 2019}}
{{Infobox
|above=Urban planning in socialist countries
|image1=[[Image:Communist Romania apartment blocks.jpg|500px]]
|caption1=The skyline of many cities became dominated by standardized apartment blocks, [[Bucharest]]
|image2=[[Image:Paneláky Košík.jpg|500px]]
|caption2=[[Prague]], the Košík housing estate.
}}
Urban planning in the [[Soviet Bloc]] countries during the [[Cold War]] era was dictated by ideological, political, social as well as economic motives.

This thinking was reflected in the urban design of all [[communist countries]]. Most socialist systems exercised a form of centrally controlled development and simplified methods of construction already outlined in the Soviet guidelines at the end of the Stalinist period. The communist planning resulted in virtually identical city blocks being erected across many nations, even if there were differences in the specifics between each country.<ref name="gazeta">{{cite web |url=http://sosnowiec.gazeta.pl/gazetasosnowiec/1,93867,6329503,Wielka_plyta_wytrzyma_jeszcze_wiele_lat.html |title=Wielka płyta wytrzyma jeszcze wiele lat |publisher=[[Gazeta Wyborcza]] Sosnowiec |date=2009-02-28 |access-date=17 February 2014 |author=Michał Wybieralski, Ewa Mikulec |trans-title=The Panel building technology can last years}}</ref>

{{anchor|Commie block}}These uniform apartment blocks, ubiquitous over communist countries, have become known as "commie blocks".<ref>Stephan Ehrig, ''Neubau Atmospheres. East German Cultural Remediations of Modernist Architecture'', 2025 [https://www.google.com/books/edition/Neubau_Atmospheres/6X-DEQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22commie+blocks%22+-wikipedia&pg=PA230 p. 230] </ref><ref>[https://digital.wpi.edu/downloads/2j62s825j Revised Affordable Housing for the Modern Family], a project for affordable housing in Worcester, Massachusetts, [[Worcester Polytechnic Institute]], 2022-2023</ref> 

Soviet-style cities are often traced to Modernist ideas in architecture such as those of [[Le Corbusier]] and his plans for [[Paris]]. The housing developments often featured [[tower block]]s, [[Residential building series|standardized and mass-produced]] using [[structural insulated panel]]s within a short period of time.

==Beginnings of urban planning in communist countries==
[[File:Berlin karlmarxallee kl.jpg|thumb|[[Karl-Marx-Allee]] in [[East Berlin]], built between 1952 and 1960]]{{Main|Housing construction in the Soviet Union}}
Many eastern European countries had suffered physical damage during World War II and their economies were in a very poor state. There was a need to reconstruct cities which had been severely damaged due to the war. For example, [[Warsaw]], Poland, had been practically razed to the ground under the [[planned destruction of Warsaw]] by German forces after the 1944 [[Warsaw Uprising]]. The centre of [[Dresden]], Germany, had been totally destroyed by the 1945 Allied [[Bombing of Dresden in World War II|bombardment]]. [[Stalingrad]] had been largely destroyed and only a small number of structures were left standing.

The financial resources of eastern European countries, after nationalization of industry and land, were under total government control. All development and investment had to be financed by the state. In line with their commitment to communism, the first priority was building industry.
[[File:East Berlin in 1989.jpg|left|thumb|[[East Berlin]] in 1989]]
Therefore, for the first ten to fifteen years, most resources were directed towards the development of industry and the reconstruction of destroyed cities. In most cases, this reconstruction was executed without any urban planning for several reasons. Firstly, reconstruction had to start immediately as there was not enough time to develop a detailed plan. Secondly, the man-power and expertise for developing urban plans in great numbers were not available.

Oftentimes, destroyed cities were not rebuilt as they were before. Rather, entirely new cities were constructed along the principles of Soviet Socialism. However, the historically significant structures in some large cities were rebuilt. Experts worked to make the restoration resemble the original as much as possible. For example, the old city centre in Warsaw, the [[Zwinger (Dresden)|Zwinger]] in Dresden, and many historic buildings in Budapest were restored to their pre-war beauty.<ref>Diefendorf J.M. – Urban Reconstruction in Europe after World War II – Urban Studies, Volume 26, Number 1, February 1989, pp. 128-143</ref>

In the late 1940s, the USSR developed a new type of high-rise. The first such buildings were built in Moscow: [[Main building of Moscow State University|Moscow State University]], [[Kotelnicheskaya Embankment Building]], [[Kudrinskaya Square Building]], [[Hilton Moscow Leningradskaya Hotel]], [[Hotel Ukraina (Moscow)|Hotel Ukraina]], [[Ministry of Foreign Affairs (Russia)|Ministry of Foreign Affairs]], [[Ministry of Construction of Heavy Industry|Ministry of Heavy Industry]]. These were duplicated in some other countries, the main examples being the [[Palace of Culture and Science]] in [[Warsaw]] and the [[House of the Free Press]] in Bucharest. The [[Karl-Marx-Allee|Stalin Allee]] (subsequently named [[Karl-Marx-Allee]]) in [[East Berlin]] was also flanked by buildings having the same Stalinist style, though their concept was different from the Moscow high-rises. These buildings are mainly examples of a new architectural style, but did not involve urban planning to a significant extent, and there is no visible conceptual link between these buildings and their surroundings.

== Urban development in the 1960s and 1970s ==
[[File:Õhuvaade Väike-Õismäe asumile.png|thumb|An oval shape [[microdistrict]] of [[Väike-Õismäe]] built in 1970s, [[Tallinn]], [[Estonia]]]]
In big cities, few new housing units were constructed and the existing units were overcrowded. Around 1960, the USSR changed its policy and began an extensive program of construction of new apartment buildings, with the introduction of [[Khrushchevka]] and the subsequent introduction of [[Brezhnevka]]. This trend was immediately followed by all communist countries in Eastern Europe. The development of new neighborhoods in order to extend the housing capacity of cities required an extensive urban planning effort. In most cities, new development took place on the outskirts of the existing cities, incorporating suburbs or undeveloped land into the city. In cities in which slums existed, the slums were redeveloped with modern housing units.
[[File:Kabul downtown.jpg|thumb|Downtown Kabul during the 1970s in [[Communist Afghanistan]].]]
While the actual design and construction of the apartment buildings is not part of the urban planning exercise, the height and type of the buildings, the density of the buildings and other general characteristics were fixed by the planning exercise. Besides, the entire development of the infrastructure had to be planned. This included the transportation system and the roads, water supply, sewerage, power supply, shopping centers, schools and other infrastructure. Flood control was also a concern for cities located in flood prone areas. The planning also covered the industrial zones where new industries were to be located.

In some parts, urban problems were raised also due to other infrastructure, mainly to the development of waterways. The construction of reservoirs on big rivers in the proximity of cities created new waterfronts which had to be developed. This happened mainly in the Soviet Union, but also in other countries. Also some urban planning was required in the downtown districts where new official buildings were constructed. An example is the development of the area of the congress hall attached to the previous royal palace in the center of Bucharest.

[[File:Каменные джунгли.jpg|thumb|Standard buildings in Moscow, the late 1990s – early 2000s<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.eirz.ru/vostok/novokosino.html|title = &#91;.m&#93; masterhost - профессиональный хостинг сайтаwww.eirz.ru}}</ref>]]

=== Romania ===
{{Main|Systematization (Romania)}}

In time, large-scale demolitions and enormous reconstruction projects of hamlets, villages, towns, and cities, in whole or in part, began to take shape. One of the largest and most ambitious of these developments began in 1974 with the goal of turning Romania into a "multilaterally developed [[Socialism|socialist]] society". Urban planning, in Romania, began early on as displaced rural Romanians started [[Urbanization|flocking to the cities]]. With a "blank canvas" of land, the [[Romanian Communist Party|communist regime]] hoped to create hundreds of urban industrial centers via investment in schools, medical clinics, housing, and industry.

[[File:Orasul Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej vedere aeriana.jpg|thumb|The town of [[Onești]] in the [[Western Moldavia|Moldavia region]] of Romania in the 1960s. The different architectural styles of the apartment blocks: pentagonal quartal (the nearest plan, with romanic vaults), blocks with prefabricated panels (4 floors) and blocks build with continuous concrete casting in sliding formworks (9 floors)]]
Although the systematization plan extended, in theory, to the entire country, initial work centered in [[Moldavia]]. It also affected such locales as [[Ceaușescu]]'s own native village of [[Scorniceşti]] in [[Olt County]]: there, the Ceauşescu family home was the only older building left standing. The initial phase of systematization largely petered out by 1980, at which point only about 10 percent of new housing was being built in historically rural areas.

Given the lack of budget, in many regions systematization did not constitute an effective plan, good or bad, for development. Instead, it constituted a barrier against organic regional growth. New buildings had to be at least two stories high, so peasants could not build small houses. Yards were restricted to 250 square meters and private agricultural plots were banned from within the villages. Despite the obvious negative impact of such a scheme on [[subsistence agriculture]], after 1981 villages were mandated to be agriculturally self-sufficient.

[[File:Apartment blocks in Astra, Brasov, Romania.jpg|thumb|left|2017 photo of Astra, [[Brașov]] (1970s). This area was specifically developed for the workers of [[Roman (vehicle manufacturer)|Autocamioane Brașov]]]]

In the mid-1980s the concept of systematization found new life, applied primarily to the area of the nation's capital, [[Bucharest]]. Nearby villages were demolished, often in service of large-scale projects such as a canal from Bucharest to the [[Danube]] – projects which were later abandoned by Romania's post-communist government. Most dramatically, eight square kilometers in the historic center of Bucharest were leveled. The demolition campaign erased many monuments including 3 monasteries, 20 churches, 3 synagogues, 3 hospitals, 2 theaters and a noted [[Art Deco]] sports stadium. This also involved evicting 40,000 people with only a single day's notice and relocating them to new homes, in order to make way for the grandiose [[Centrul Civic]] and the immense [[Palace of the People (Romania)|Palace of the People]], a building second in size only to the [[The Pentagon|Pentagon]].

Urban planning, especially the destruction of historic churches and monasteries, was protested by several nations, especially [[Hungarian People's Republic|Hungary]] and [[West Germany]], each concerned for their [[national minorities]] in [[Transylvania]]. Despite these protests, Ceauşescu remained in the relatively good graces of the [[United States]] and other Western powers almost to the last, largely because his relatively independent political line rendered him a useful counter to the [[Soviet Union]] in [[Cold War]] politics.

==North Korea==
[[File:North Korea - Pyongyang (5015251483).jpg|thumb|220px|Skyline of Pyongyang]]
[[Pyongyang]], the capital of [[North Korea]], has a downtown consisting of hundreds of [[High rise|high-rise]] apartments. North Korean citizens are provided housing by the government, and the quality of said housing is dependent on social status and household size.<ref name="Em 2018 26–45">{{Cite journal|last=Em|first=Pavel P.|date=2018|title=Urbanization in North Korea: An outline of Its Peculiarities and an Estimation of Its Real Rate|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/26632404|journal=North Korean Review|volume=14|issue=2|pages=26–45|jstor=26632404 |issn=1551-2789}}</ref> The city also has several extraordinarily expansive public spaces that are usually built around colossal monuments depicting Juche ideologies and/or monuments relating to [[Kim Jong-il]] and [[Kim Il Sung]].

Car ownership rates in Pyongyang are low, and thus public transportation is vital to the city. A two-line [[Pyongyang Metro|subway system]] serves the city, with a network of elaborate stations, many with high ceilings and murals on their walls. Additionally, an expansive [[Pyongyang Tram|tram network]] covers the city. There are no suburbs in Pyongyang as the government's city planning policies substitute lower density suburban expansion for high rise residential development in central areas.
{{clear}}

==People's Republic of China==
[[File:Around Cuiwei Rd, Haidian District, Beijing.jpg|thumb|1950–1980s flats in a residential area in Haidian, Beijing]]
{{also|Urban planning in China|Urban planning in Shanghai}}

The development of urban planning in the People's Republic of China (PRC) demonstrates a unique approach with Chinese characteristics. It started after communist takeover in the early 1950s. Through implementing new national urban policies, communist planners first introduced urban planning by applying centralised economic planning and industrialisation, especially in heavy industry.<ref name="ReferenceA">Tang, Wing-Shing; Chinese Urban Planning at Fifty: An Assessment of the Planning Theory Literature Journal of Planning Literature 2000 14: 347-66</ref><ref name="Xie 1993, Pages 103-114">Xie, Yichun and Costa F.J.: in: Cities, Volume 10, Issue 2, May 1993, Pages 103-114</ref>

===Phase 1 (1949–1960)===
Source:<ref>Kirkby clarifies China's urbanisation by using different phases, author modified the third phase based on Kirkby. Kirkby, R J. R. Urbanization in China: Town and Country in a Developing Economy, 1949–2000. New York: Columbia University Press, 1985. Print</ref>

In September 1952, there were two significant policies promulgated at an urban development conference: "construction of key cities in co-ordination with the national economic development programme" and "establishment of urban planning structure to strengthen city development".<ref>Xie, Yichun and Costa F.J.: in: Cities, Volume 10, Issue 2, May 1993, Pages 103</ref> These policies influenced China's urban planning significantly and at the same time were clearly defined by the main direction of the state – centralised economic and industrial development. During the First Five-year Plan (1953–58), the nation determined to develop 156 national key projects and 8 key industrial based cities.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> In this period, vast physical development projects such as industrial bases, community facilities and housing for workers were established to achieve national needs and goals. All of these projects were carried out with the aid of the experts from the Soviet Union, particularly in terms of urban economic development and physical urban design. Urban planning at that time was mainly based on Soviet planning principles and the model of the post-war Soviet planning practice. Soviet-style communist planning concentrated on "formalistic street patterns and grand design for public buildings and monuments, huge public squares, and the predominance of master plans".<ref>Tang, Wing-Shing; Chinese Urban Planning at Fifty: An Assessment of the Planning Theory Literature Journal of Planning Literature 2000 14: 350</ref> The role of communist planners during this period was to focus on location selection of factories and industrial plants, arrangement of service facilities, design of the layout of industrial towns, functional division of urban land use zones and development of residential districts.<ref name="ReferenceA"/><ref name="Xie 1993, Pages 103-114"/> Historic preservation was not a priority during this period of development. For example, Mao Zedong allowed Beijing's city walls to be demolished despite their historical significance in order to make room for other uses.<ref name="Campanella, T. J. 2011">Campanella, T. J. (2011). The concrete dragon: China's urban revolution and what it means for the world. Princeton Architectural.</ref> The bricks from the walls were used in new development projects ranging from homes to a subway system. By the end of 1959, there were 180 cities, 1400 towns and more than 2,000 suburban residential settlements that had been project plans prepared under communist planning.<ref name="Xie 1993, Pages 103-114"/>

===Phase 2 (1961–1976)===

From 1960 to 1976, due to the political climate changing, the development of urban planning in communist China had suffered severe catastrophes: planning institutions had to cease, planners were assigned to support development in rural areas and planning documents were destroyed or discarded.<ref name="Xie 1993, Pages 103-114"/>  During the [[Great Leap Forward]] in the early 1960s, the utopian socialist planning development which particularly overemphasized large-scale urban development was seen as superior to Western-style planning.<ref name="ReferenceA"/> However, due to the severe limitations of fiscal and labor resources, the first priority of urban planning was given to utopian socialist principles and then the second place to people's livelihood. Thus, giving little attention to the establishment of residential amenities and facilities, there were significant social and physical imbalances resulting in urban development.<ref name="Xie 1993, Pages 103-114"/> For instance, in the historic hutong neighborhoods in Beijing, courtyards were routinely replaced with new residential structures in order to accommodate more residents. By the end of this phase, about 30% of these courtyards had residential structures placed on them.<ref name="Campanella, T. J. 2011"/> Additionally, some anti-urban movements, a typical example being the People's Commune Movement, took place in communist China during this period. The purpose of setting up a commune, seen as a sub-community within cities, was to spread industrial values from urban to rural areas so that eventually the urban-rural gap would be eliminated.<ref name="ReferenceA"/><ref name="Xie 1993, Pages 103-114"/>

===Phase 3 (1977–1984)===
[[File:Shanghai Urban Planning Museum (1393107088).jpg|thumb|Shanghai Urban Planning Museum]]
In December 1978, a new era of economic and political reform had begun and accelerated. The major concern of urban planning in communist China shifted to the recognition of the function of cities. Consequently, a nationwide effective force to restore urban master plans was started. By the end of 1984, 241 cities and 1,071 counties throughout the nation as a whole completed their master plans.<ref name="Xie 1993, Pages 103-114"/> Although these master plans might not technically fulfill the needs of urban development, they at least acted as guidelines to lead to planned and organised urban construction. In addition, some concepts of mega-metropolitan areas were established during this period.

===Phase 4 (1985–present)===
[[File:Tall buildings in Panzhou, Guizhou, China, 21 June 2019t.jpg|thumb|Tall buildings in [[Panzhou]], [[Guizhou]], China, 21 June 2019.]]
Contemporary urban planning in China is undergoing rapid, unprecedented urbanization and industrialization. In fact, China's urbanization rate was almost 50% by the year 2010, a stark contrast from previous decades.<ref>Yu, L. (2015). City and citizens in modern China: Towards a scientific approach to urban development. Reading, United Kingdom.</ref> Based upon the current Chinese Urban and Rural Planning Act, two tiers – master plan and detailed plan – make up the Chinese urban planning system.<ref>Chen, Xiaoyan: Monitoring and Evaluation in China's Urban Planning System: A Case Study of Xuzhou, 2009, Available from http://www.unhabitat.org/grhs/2009{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> Reviewing the history of urban planning in China, the contemporary planning norm is neither simply following Soviet-style planning nor prohibiting advanced Western viewpoints of urban development. Urban renewal and redevelopment are common themes in contemporary Chinese planning. Large swathes of major cities are sometimes torn down at once to allow for new uses. In some cases, residents simply refuse to move out and developers have to adjust their plans accordingly.<ref name="Campanella, T. J. 2011"/> These residents have been dubbed "nail houses" or "dingzi hu", and there have been many famous cases of these [[Holdout (real estate)|holdouts]] in Chinese media.
{{clear}}

==Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia==

Post-WWII [[Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia|SFR Yugoslavia]] followed in line with the earlier urbanist experiments of the [[Soviet Union]], and often delved in urban planning projects.
The best known example would be the [[Novi Zagreb]] (''eng. "New Zagreb"'') urban development scheme of the [[Zagreb]] city – the capital of the Socialist republic of Croatia.
The district is mostly residential, consisting of blocks of [[Apartment|flats]] and [[tower block]]s that were built during the [[Socialist]] era (1945–1990). Although it is not as prestigious as downtown Zagreb, it has been praised for its good road network, public transportation connections and abundance of parks.

The project was started by the mayor of Zagreb, [[Većeslav Holjevac]], as there was a large expanse of empty and undeveloped land south of the [[Sava]] river. The land was seized from the Captol church administration following the victory of the communist partisans in World War II. The mayor, seeing the opportunity to set in motion the building of a completely new and modern city under the socialist administration, promptly organized a team of urbanist designers and city planners.

The first complete solution for habitation with public and commercial contents was made for the neighborhood [[Trnsko]] by urbanists [[Zdenko Kolacio]], [[Mirko Maretić]] and [[Josip Uhlik]] with horticulturist [[Mira Wenzler-Halambek]] in 1959–1960. It was followed by plans for neighborhood [[Zapruđe]] in 1962–1963, also made by Josip Uhlik.<ref name=Leksikon>''Zagrebački leksikon'' (knjiga druga). "LZMK", Zagreb 2006. godina, 129.-130. str.</ref>

The project was lauded as a great success, the district being known for its large amounts of foliage and recreational areas, including parks, museums and sports fields. A lot of care also went into building a modernized and efficient system of transportation and mass transit, such as tram and bus lines which were built by 1979. Lauding a typical Eastern bloc architectural style, it was designed to house a large capacity of residents, as the construction of the area was in part driven by the need for workforce to fuel the Zagreb industrialization projects recently put in motion. It also has examples of [[Brutalism|brutalist architecture]], rare for the late period the area was constructed in.

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Urban planning of Sydney
======================================================================

{{short description|none}}
{{use Australian English |date=October 2026}}
{{use dmy dates|date=October 2026}}
The '''urban planning of Sydney''', Australia has been done formally and informally since at least the city's establishment in 1788. The city has been characterised as an 'accidental city',<ref>{{Cite book|author=Ashton, Paul|url=https://worldcat.org/oclc/38377912|title=The accidental city : planning Sydney since 1788|date=1995|publisher=Hale & Iremonger|oclc=38377912}}</ref> with planning advocate JD Fitzgerald claiming that it was "a city without a plan, save whatever planning was due to the errant goat".<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Falconer|first=Delia|date=2018-04-10|title=The radical plan to split Sydney into three|url=http://www.theguardian.com/cities/2018/apr/10/the-radical-plan-to-split-sydney-into-three|access-date=2021-03-30|website=[[Guardian Australia|The Guardian]]|language=en}}</ref>

Planned and organic [[urban renewal in Sydney]] frequently occurs, with the redevelopment of housing and neighbourhoods.

== History ==
{{Missing information|section|each decade of urban planning and development|date=October 2026}}

=== Early colonial planning ===
[[File:Sydney Streets, 1832 (4930537203).jpg|thumb|Sydney streets in 1832.]]
The founder of [[Sydney]], [[Arthur Phillip|Governor Arthur Phillip]], planned from the beginning for the [[penal colony]] to eventually become a town, writing that the settlement (which he wanted to name 'Albion') should have uniform building style, streets that were 200 feet wide, as well as building allotments of 60 by 150 feet.<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|title=William Dawes|url=http://www.visitsydneyaustralia.com.au/william-dawes.html|access-date=2021-05-05|website=www.visitsydneyaustralia.com.au}}</ref> However, no architects, town planners, or surveyors came with the [[First Fleet]], with engineers [[Augustus Alt]] and [[William Dawes (British Marines officer)|William Dawes]] left to the task of following Phillip's intentions, and consequently drew up a plan for a grid pattern with a town centre on the western hills above where the [[Tank Stream]] ran into the [[Sydney Cove]].<ref name=":4" /> The contemporary Lang Street was meant to be the [[High Street]], and was meant to be a grand avenue with views across to [[Bennelong Point]].<ref name=":4" /> However, most of the plan never came to fruition.<ref name=":4" /> Instead, the early road network was at least in part based on [[Indigenous Australians|Indigenous]] walking paths, which themselves followed natural contours such as ridgelines or the Tank Stream.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2018-05-16|title=Were Sydney's roads built on tracks created by Aboriginal people?|url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2018-05-17/curious-sydney-aboriginal-pathways/9676076|access-date=2021-03-30|website=www.abc.net.au|language=en-AU}}</ref> However, their plan for [[Parramatta]] was realised, following a grid and with a 62 metre wide high street (now known as George Street).<ref name=":4" />

Governor [[Lachlan Macquarie]] and the [[New South Wales Government Architect]], [[Francis Greenway]], made major contributions to the planning and design of early colonial Sydney.<ref>{{Cite web|last=State Library of New South Wales|first=Sydney|date=2015-11-30|title=Francis Greenway: convict architect|url=https://www.sl.nsw.gov.au/stories/francis-greenway-convict-architect|access-date=2021-03-30|website=State Library of NSW}}</ref> This included 265 public works, such as [[Parramatta Road]] and [[Old South Head Road]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Macquarie, Lachlan|url=https://dictionaryofsydney.org/entry/macquarie_lachlan|access-date=2021-03-30|website=dictionaryofsydney.org}}</ref>  Greenway had also proposed making a complete plan for the town, with a grand square, major public buildings, as well as a bridge across the harbour at [[Dawes Point]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Johnson|first=Chris|date=2016-01-06|title=On the eve of bicentenary, letters reveal architect Francis Greenway's visions for Sydney|url=https://www.smh.com.au/national/nsw/on-the-eve-of-bicentenary-letters-reveal-architect-francis-greenways-visions-for-sydney-20160106-gm0bsy.html|access-date=2021-05-06|website=The Sydney Morning Herald|language=en}}</ref> Despite such early planning, many of the houses in the convict settlement were built erratically, with an 1832 ''Report on the Limits of Sydney''  by [[Surveyor General of New South Wales|Surveyor General]] [[Thomas Mitchell (explorer)|Thomas Mitchell]] noting that peripheral land of the settlement had "been alienated and that roads and boundary lines were oblique and irregular", which he tried in vain to regularize.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Planning|url=https://dictionaryofsydney.org/entry/planning|access-date=2021-03-30|website=dictionaryofsydney.org}}</ref> The first limits on building development were however passed with the Police Act of 1833, as well as the Street Alignments Act of 1834 and the Building Act of 1837, based on the [[London Building Act 1774]] ([[14 Geo. 3]]. c. 78 (Imp)).<ref name=":1" /> The incorporation of the [[City of Sydney]] in 1842 created local government ostensibly able to manage growth.<ref name=":1" /> However, its ability to govern was hampered by powerful local interests, and the city had severe problems by the 1870s.<ref name=":1" />

=== Late 1800s ===
[[File:John Sulman's proposal for Circular Quay.jpg|thumb|John Sulman's proposal for Circular Quay made for the 1909 Royal Commission.]]
In the 19th century, the [[sanitary movement]] agitated for urban improvement for better [[public health]]. Following the outbreaks of disease and accumulation of unsanitary buildings, the City of Sydney Improvement Act was passed in 1879.<ref name=":1" /> This was followed by the Land for Public Purposes Acquisition Act in 1880, allowing the creation of parklands.<ref name=":1" /> Parks from this era include [[Redfern Park]] and [[Belmore Park]]. A minimum width for streets of 20.1 metres was set in 1881.<ref name=":1" />

By the 1890s the ideas of [[laissez-faire]] liberalism were dominant.<ref name=":1" />

=== 1900s ===
In 1900, an outbreak of [[bubonic plague]] took place in the city.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Bubonic plague epidemic 1900|url=https://dictionaryofsydney.org/event/bubonic_plague_epidemic_1900|access-date=2021-04-21|website=dictionaryofsydney.org}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Inspired by British [[royal commission]]s into improving urban conditions, such as the [[Poor Law Commission]], the 1909 Royal Commission for the Improvement of the City of Sydney and Its Suburbs was established for a similar purpose.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Freestone|first=Robert|date=2006-07-01|title=Royal Commissions, planning reform and Sydney improvement 1908–1909|url=https://doi.org/10.1080/02665430600731096|journal=Planning Perspectives|volume=21|issue=3|pages=213–231|doi=10.1080/02665430600731096|s2cid=144569747|issn=0266-5433|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The commission recommended building underground railways in the city centre and electrifying the suburban lines.<ref name=":2" /> A new Building Act to regulate urban design was also suggested, as well as the demolishing of [[Darlinghurst Gaol]] for a park or a monumental building.<ref name=":2" />

A key figure in the beginning of formal planning in Sydney was [[John Sulman]]. His 1890 lecture 'The laying out of towns' (later published in the Brisbane Courier<ref>{{cite news
|url=https://trove.nla.gov.au/newspaper/article/3509301
|title=Laying out of towns
|author=John Sulman
|publisher=The Brisbane Courier
|date=1890-01-24
|page=7
}}</ref>) marked the beginning of town planning in Australia. He advocated for [[Garden city movement|garden suburbs]] and open space for the next 40 years.<ref name="CoSParks2016">{{cite web
|url=https://landscapeaustralia.com/articles/city-of-sydney-parks/
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161102050424/http://landscapeaustralia.com/articles/city-of-sydney-parks/
|url-status=live
|archive-date=2016-11-02
|access-date=2026-04-12
|author=Anne-Maree Whitaker
|publisher=Landscape Australia
|title=City of Sydney parks
|date=2016-10-06
}}</ref> He had begun advocating for planning in ''[[Daily Telegraph (Sydney)|The Daily Telegraph]]'' in 1907, and gave testimony to the 1909 Royal Commission.<ref name=":3">{{Citation|last1=Apperly|first1=Richard E.|title=Sulman, Sir John (1849–1934)|url=https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/sulman-sir-john-8714|work=Australian Dictionary of Biography|place=Canberra|publisher=National Centre of Biography, Australian National University|access-date=2021-04-23|last2=Reynolds|first2=Peter}}</ref> Instead of a [[grid plan]] (such as the [[Hoddle Grid]] in [[Melbourne]]), he advocated for a 'spider's web' network of roads.<ref name=":3" /> Sulman published ''Plan no 2'', which depicted new streets at diagonals through [[Chippendale, New South Wales|Chippendale]], [[Surry Hills]] and other suburbs.<ref>{{cite web
|url=https://archives.cityofsydney.nsw.gov.au/nodes/view/1967270
|title=Map - Royal Commission on Sydney Improvement - No 2 - J Sulman, circa 1908-1909
|year=1909
|website=City of Sydney Archives
|author=John Sulman
}}</ref> Other ideas of his included the extension of [[Martin Place]] and the widening of various streets.<ref name=":3" /> He also taught urban planning at the [[University of Sydney]].<ref name=":3" />

A vast number of maps were published in the ''Report of the Royal Commission for the improvement of the City of Sydney & its suburbs''.<ref>{{cite report
|title=Report of the Royal Commission for the improvement of the City of Sydney & its suburbs
|url=https://archives.cityofsydney.nsw.gov.au/nodes/view/1754742
|year=1909
|publisher=W A Gullick Government Printer
|website=City of Sydney Archives
}} {{cite report
|url=https://archives.cityofsydney.nsw.gov.au/assets/downloadwiz/3062243

|year=1909
|publisher=W A Gullick Government Printer
|website=City of Sydney Archives
|title=Report of the Royal Commission for the improvement of the City of Sydney & its suburbs
}}
</ref>

=== 1910s ===

[[File:Bradfield plan.png|thumb|Bradfield's proposed railways in Sydney.]]The [[City Beautiful movement]] became buzz words in Sydney planning circles in the early 20th century.<ref name=":1" /> Another influence was the [[garden city movement]], of which [[Daceyville]] (built 1912) was a model suburb.<ref name=":1" /> The husband-wife team of [[Walter Burley Griffin|Walter Burley]] and [[Marion Mahony Griffin]], who had planned [[Canberra]] with influence from both movements,<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hall|first=Peter|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0J1kAwAAQBAJ|title=Cities of Tomorrow: An Intellectual History of Urban Planning and Design Since 1880|date=2014-04-17|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-118-45651-4|pages=227|language=en}}</ref> also designed the suburb of [[Castlecrag]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Goad|first=Philip|title=The Encyclopedia of Australian Architecture|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2012|isbn=9780521888578|location=New York|pages=298}}</ref> At the time, Castlecrag was noted as an experiment in communal and community planning and living.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Poiner|first1=Gretchen|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Rh1LDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA165|title=Gardens of History and Imagination: Growing New South Wales|last2=Jack|first2=Sybil|date=3 June 2016|publisher=Sydney University Press|isbn=978-1-74332-456-1|page=165|language=en}}</ref>

=== 1920s ===
In the 1920s, government engineer [[John Bradfield (engineer)|John Bradfield]] proposed a railway scheme to improve transportation in the city, which included an underground rail loop under the CBD (later constructed as the [[City Circle]]) and a harbour crossing (which he built as the [[Sydney Harbour Bridge]]).<ref>{{Cite web|last=Alex|date=2018-09-16|title=Bradfield, 75 years on – part 3: Rapid Transit comes full circle|url=https://thestrategicweek.com/2018/09/17/bradfield-75-years-on-part-3-rapid-transit-comes-full-circle/|access-date=2021-04-22|website=StrategicMatters|language=en}}</ref>

Unrealised parts of the vision included three new inner-city rail lines, with a loop through the [[Eastern Suburbs (Sydney)|Eastern Suburbs]] (later built in a truncated form as the [[Eastern Suburbs railway line]]), a line to the west from [[Petersham, New South Wales|Petersham]] through [[Annandale, New South Wales|Annandale]], [[Leichhardt, New South Wales|Leichhardt]], [[Rozelle]] and [[Balmain, New South Wales|Balmain]] to the CBD, as well as a line over the bridge to the [[Northern Beaches]] (for which extra tracks were built on the bridge, used by trams until 1958 before conversion to traffic lanes).<ref>{{Cite web|last=Alex|date=2018-09-23|title=Bradfield, 75 years on – part 4: Unfinished business – Sydney's "missing metro"|url=https://thestrategicweek.com/2018/09/23/bradfield-75-years-on-part-4-unfinished-business-sydneys-missing-metro/|access-date=2021-04-22|website=StrategicMatters|language=en}}</ref>

=== 1940s - 1960s ===
{{See also|Cumberland County Council (New South Wales)#County of Cumberland Planning Scheme (1951)}}
In 1948, the [[County of Cumberland planning scheme]] was published.<ref name=":1" /> Drawing partial inspiration from the 1944 [[Greater London Plan]], it introduced [[zoning]], [[employment zone]]s, open space acquisitions, and a [[green belt]].<ref name=":1" /> The green belt was contentious, and in many ways the plan did not succeed.<ref name=":1" />

When the scheme was made, the accepted view was that much of[[Inner Sydney]] was [[Slum|slums]] and should be rebuilt. The Landlord and Tenant Act influenced many owners of large numbers of poor-condition homes to sell them to their tenants, making large-scale acquisition politically and financially difficult.<ref name="villageToMetropolis1984" details="p.15" />

In the 1957 the 45.7 metre height limit was lifted. In the 1950s, planning branches in local councils were rare.<ref name="villageToMetropolis1984" details="p.13">{{cite report
<!-- Source requests this is cited -->
|url=https://nswdpe.intersearch.com.au/nswdpejspui/handle/1/5926
|url-status=live
|access-date=2026-10-24
|title=Sydney: Village to Metropolis - A brief review of planning in the Sydney Region
|publisher=Department of Environment and Planning
|author=N.AW. ASHTON
|year=1984
|isbn=0724082859
}} {{webarchive
|url=http://web.archive.org/web/20250504061947/https://nswdpe.intersearch.com.au/nswdpejspui/bitstream/1/5926/1/Sydney%20Village%20to%20Metropolis%20a%20Brief%20Review%20of%20Planning%20in%20the%20Sydney%20Region%201984.pdf
|date=2025-05-04}}
</ref>

Construction of Sydney's first skyscraper, the [[AMP Building, Sydney|AMP Building]], was completed in 1962.<ref name=":1" />

=== 1970s ===
{{See also|Green ban}}
In the 1970s, local planning and environmental issues were receiving increased attention in local governments and within the community.<ref name="villageToMetropolis1984" />{{Reference page|page=13}}

The [[Sydney Cove Redevelopment Authority]] was set up in 1970 to oversee [[urban renewal]] in the inner-city. Its plans for a redevelopment of the historic [[The Rocks, New South Wales|Rocks]] precinct into high-rise towers was however blocked by the so-called [[green ban]]s, which enforced strikes on various controversial redevelopment projects throughout Sydney.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Green Bans movement
|url=https://dictionaryofsydney.org/entry/green_bans_movement
|author1=Meredith Burgmann
|author2=Verity Burgmann
|year=2011
|access-date=2026-10-24 |website=dictionaryofsydney.org}}</ref>

This led to changes in the New South Wales planning system, with the introduction of environmental and heritage conservation legislation.

In 1974, the NSW Government published ''Towards a New Planning System for New South Wales''.{{r|proposalsForANewPlanningSystem1975|at=Foreward}} In 1975 the Minister for Planning and Environment published the ''Proposals for a New Environmental Planning System for New South Wales''.<ref name="proposalsForANewPlanningSystem1975">{{cite report
<!-- The source requests to use this url -->
|url=https://nswdpe.intersearch.com.au/nswdpejspui/handle/1/1235
|date=June 1975
|title=Proposals for a New Environmental Planning System for New South Wales
|publisher=NSW Planning and Environment Commission
}} {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261024133631/https://nswdpe.intersearch.com.au/nswdpejspui/bitstream/1/1235/1/Proposals%20for%20a%20New%20Environmental%20Planning%20System%20for%20New%20South%20Wales%20June%201975.pdf
|date=2026-10-24}}</ref>

The [[Environmental Planning and Assessment Act 1979]] was the resultant legislation, along with the formation of the [[Land and Environment Court of New South Wales]].

=== 1980s and 1990s ===
As the city faced a scarcity of land in the 1980s following [[urban sprawl]], urban consolidation became the new target of planning.<ref name=":1" /> The new regional plan, [[Sydney Into Its Third Century]], aimed to increase urban density.<ref name="plan">{{cite book|author=Department of Environment, Planning|title=Sydney into Its Third Century: Metropolitan Strategy for the Sydney Region|year=1988|location=Sydney|author-link=Department of Planning and Environment (New South Wales)}}</ref><ref name="dos">{{cite web|author=Paul Ashton and Robert Freestone|year=2008|title=Planning|url=http://dictionaryofsydney.org/entry/planning|work=Dictionary of Sydney|publisher=Dictionary of Sydney Trust}}</ref>

In 1998, the NSW state government launched ''Action for Transport 2010''.<ref>{{cite press release
|archive-url=https://webarchive.nla.gov.au/awa/20050517032609/http://pandora.nla.gov.au/pan/49629/20050503-0000/www.transport.nsw.gov.au/news/media/1998/transport-2010.html
