======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Zoning in the United States
======================================================================

{{Short description|Provision in urban planning in the United States}}
{{more citations needed|date=June 2022}}
[[File:Broadway-1885-APL.jpeg|thumb|Unsightly wires were among the targets of late nineteenth century agitation for zoning.]]
Zoning is a system of laws that divides a jurisdiction's land into [[district]]s, or zones, and limits how land in each district can be used.<ref>{{Cite web |title=zoning |url=https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/zoning |access-date=2023-12-29 |website=LII / Legal Information Institute |language=en}}</ref><ref name="Hirt 2014">{{cite book |last1=Hirt |first1=Sonia A. |title=Zoned in the USA: The Origins and Implications of American Land-Use Regulation |date=2014 |publisher=Cornell University Press |isbn=978-0-8014-5305-2 |page=65 |oclc=879527609 |author-link=Sonia Hirt}}</ref> In the United States, [[zoning]] includes various [[land use]] laws enforced through the [[Police power (United States constitutional law)|police power]] rights of [[state government]]s (often delegated to their [[local government]]s) to exercise authority over privately owned [[real property]].<ref name=":62">{{Cite book |title=Zoning: a guide for 21st-century planning |date=2020 |editor1=Elliott Sclar |editor2=Bernadette Baird-Zars |editor3=Lauren Ames Fischer |editor4=Valerie E. Stahl |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-429-48922-8 |location=New York, NY |oclc=1124778006}}</ref>

[[Zoning]] laws in major cities originated with the [[New York City]] [[1916 Zoning Resolution]].<ref name="dunlap2">{{cite news |last=Dunlop |first=David W. |date=25 July 2016 |title=Zoning Arrived 100 Years Ago. It Changed New York City Forever. |work=New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/26/nyregion/new-yorks-first-zoning-resolution-which-brought-order-to-a-chaotic-building-boom-turns-100.html?_r=1 |url-status=live |access-date=19 November 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201053327/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/26/nyregion/new-yorks-first-zoning-resolution-which-brought-order-to-a-chaotic-building-boom-turns-100.html?_r=1 |archive-date=1 December 2017}}</ref> Before zoning, some cities had local ordinances like those in [[Los Angeles]] in 1904 limiting laundries (commonly referred to as "wash houses") from operating in a residential area.<ref name=":5">{{Cite book |last=Kolnick |first=Kathy A. |title=Order before zoning: land use regulation in Los Angeles, 1880-1915 |date=2008 |oclc=309352342}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> These early city ordinances were in some cases motivated by [[racism]] and [[classism]].

After the [[Supreme court|Supreme Court]] declared racial ordinances unconstitutional in 1917, many localities discovered zoning and began setting down citywide restrictions. In suburban localities, zoning often mandates single-family housing.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Lens |first=Michael C. |date=2022 |title=Zoning, Land Use, and the Reproduction of Urban Inequality |journal=Annual Review of Sociology |volume=48 |issue=1 |pages=421–439 |language=en |doi=10.1146/annurev-soc-030420-122027|pmid=38045490 |pmc=10691857 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Flores |first=Luis |date=2024 |title=Zoning as a labor market regulation |journal=Theory and Society |volume=53 |issue=2 |pages=357–394 |language=en |doi=10.1007/s11186-023-09539-y |issn=1573-7853}}</ref> Though not always explicitly [[Discrimination|discriminatory]], zoning ordinances were often applied in ways that prevented African Americans from moving into predominantly white neighborhoods, under the belief that their presence would lower property values.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shertzer |first1=Allison |last2=Twinam |first2=Tate |last3=Walsh |first3=Randall |date=2022 |title=Zoning and Segregation in Urban Economic History |journal=Regional Science and Urban Economics |volume=94 |article-number=103652 |doi=10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2021.103652 |s2cid=241887690}} [https://www.allisonshertzer.com/static/ShertzerAllison_RSUE.pdf Alt URL]</ref> The constitutionality of zoning ordinances was upheld by the [[Supreme Court of the United States]] in ''[[Village of Euclid, Ohio v. Ambler Realty Co.]]'' in 1926.

According to the ''New York Times'', "[[single-family zoning]] is practically gospel in America", as a vast number of cities zone land extensively for detached single-family homes.<ref name=":12">{{Cite news |last1=Badger |first1=Emily |last2=Bui |first2=Quoctrung |date=2019-06-18 |title=Cities Start to Question an American Ideal: A House With a Yard on Every Lot |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/06/18/upshot/cities-across-america-question-single-family-zoning.html |url-status=live |access-date=2020-08-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200803174003/https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/06/18/upshot/cities-across-america-question-single-family-zoning.html |archive-date=2020-08-03 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref> Low-density residential zoning is far more predominant in U.S. cities than in other countries.<ref name=":3" /> The housing shortage in many metropolitan areas, coupled with [[Residential segregation in the United States|racial residential segregation]], has growing public attention and political debate on zoning laws.<ref>{{cite book |last=Dougherty |first=Conor |title=Golden gates: fighting for housing in America |isbn=978-0-593-16532-4 |oclc=1161988433}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Einstein |first=Katherine Levine |title=Neighborhood defenders: participatory politics and America's housing crisis |year=2019 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-76949-5 |oclc=1135562802}}</ref> Studies indicate that strict zoning regulations constrain the supply of housing and inflate housing prices, increase homelessness, and contribute to inequality, a weaker economy, and racial [[housing segregation in the United States]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Trounstine |first=Jessica |chapter=The Production of Local Inequality: Race, Class, and Land Use in American Cities |date=2021 |chapter-url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/american-political-economy/production-of-local-inequality-race-class-and-land-use-in-american-cities/04D175F91ACC397ED2883D56F3D9F336 |title=The American Political Economy: Politics, Markets, and Power |pages=158–180 |editor-last=Hertel-Fernandez |editor-first=Alexander |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-316-51636-2 |editor2-last=Hacker |editor2-first=Jacob S. |editor3-last=Thelen |editor3-first=Kathleen |editor4-last=Pierson |editor4-first=Paul}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Brouwer |first1=N. R. |last2=Trounstine |first2=Jessica |date=2024 |title=NIMBYs, YIMBYs, and the Politics of Land Use in American Cities |journal=Annual Review of Political Science |language=en |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=165–184 |doi=10.1146/annurev-polisci-041322-041133 |issn=1094-2939|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Glaeser |first1=Edward |last2=Gyourko |first2=Joseph |date=2018 |title=The Economic Implications of Housing Supply |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |language=en |volume=32 |issue=1 |pages=3–30 |doi=10.1257/jep.32.1.3 |issn=0895-3309 |doi-access=free |s2cid=158965378}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Glaeser |first1=Edward L. |last2=Gyourko |first2=Joseph |last3=Saks |first3=Raven |date=2005 |title=Why Is Manhattan So Expensive? Regulation and the Rise in Housing Prices |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/429979 |url-status=live |journal=The Journal of Law and Economics |volume=48 |issue=2 |pages=331–369 |doi=10.1086/429979 |issn=0022-2186 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210129152432/https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/429979 |archive-date=2021-01-29 |access-date=2021-02-28 |s2cid=222330705|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Baum-Snow |first=Nathaniel |date=2023 |title=Constraints on City and Neighborhood Growth: The Central Role of Housing Supply |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives |language=en |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=53–74 |doi=10.1257/jep.37.2.53 |issn=0895-3309|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hsieh |first1=Chang-Tai |last2=Moretti |first2=Enrico |date=2019 |title=Housing Constraints and Spatial Misallocation |url=https://pubs.aeaweb.org/doi/10.1257/mac.20170388 |journal=American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics |language=en |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=1–39 |doi=10.1257/mac.20170388 |issn=1945-7707}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Parkhomenko |first=Andrii |date=2023 |title=Local causes and aggregate implications of land use regulation |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S009411902300075X |journal=Journal of Urban Economics |volume=138 |article-number=103605 |doi=10.1016/j.jue.2023.103605 |issn=0094-1190|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Dougherty |first=Conor |date=2016-07-04 |title=How Anti-Growth Sentiment, Reflected in Zoning Laws, Thwarts Equality |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/04/business/how-anti-growth-sentiment-reflected-in-zoning-laws-thwarts-equality.html |url-status=live |access-date=2021-06-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210607185844/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/04/business/how-anti-growth-sentiment-reflected-in-zoning-laws-thwarts-equality.html |archive-date=2021-06-07 |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dawkins |first=Casey J. |date=2023 |title=Homelessness and housing supply |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/07352166.2023.2168553 |journal=Journal of Urban Affairs |pages=1–19 |language=en |doi=10.1080/07352166.2023.2168553 |s2cid=256890658 |issn=0735-2166|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":02">{{Cite journal |last=Trounstine |first=Jessica |date=2020 |title=The Geography of Inequality: How Land Use Regulation Produces Segregation |journal=American Political Science Review |language=en |volume=114 |issue=2 |pages=443–455 |doi=10.1017/S0003055419000844 |issn=0003-0554 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Trounstine |first=Jessica |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/segregation-by-design/9CEF629688C0C684EDC387407F5878F2 |title=Segregation by Design: Local Politics and Inequality in American Cities |date=2018 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-55572-2 |language=en |doi=10.1017/9781108555722 |access-date=2020-06-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200831165644/https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/segregation-by-design/9CEF629688C0C684EDC387407F5878F2 |archive-date=2020-08-31 |url-status=live |s2cid=158682691}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shertzer |first1=Allison |last2=Twinam |first2=Tate |last3=Walsh |first3=Randall P. |date=2021 |title=Zoning and segregation in urban economic history |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166046221000120 |journal=Regional Science and Urban Economics |volume=94 |article-number=103652 |language=en |doi=10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2021.103652 |s2cid=234156620 |issn=0166-0462|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lyons |first=Ronan C |last2=Shertzer |first2=Allison |last3=Gray |first3=Rowena |last4=Agorastos |first4=David |date=2025 |title=The Price of Housing in the United States, 1890–2006 |url=https://academic.oup.com/qje/advance-article/doi/10.1093/qje/qjaf047/8280394 |journal=The Quarterly Journal of Economics |language=en |doi=10.1093/qje/qjaf047 |issn=0033-5533|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kulka |first=Amrita |last2=Sood |first2=Aradhya |last3=Chiumenti |first3=Nicholas |date=2026 |title=Under the (Neighbor)Hood: Understanding Interactions Among Zoning Regulations |url=https://doi.org/10.1162/rest.a.1736 |journal=Review of Economics and Statistics |doi=10.1162/rest.a.1736 |issn=0034-6535|url-access=subscription }}</ref>{{excessive citations inline|date=October 2024}}

Zoning laws that prioritize single-family housing have raised concerns regarding housing availability, housing affordability and environmental harms.<ref name=":12" /><ref>{{Cite news |date=2022-09-25 |title=Whatever Happened to the Starter Home? |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/09/25/upshot/starter-home-prices.html |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Manville |first1=Michael |last2=Monkkonen |first2=Paavo |last3=Lens |first3=Michael |date=2020 |title=It's Time to End Single-Family Zoning |journal=Journal of the American Planning Association |volume=86 |issue=1 |pages=106–112 |doi=10.1080/01944363.2019.1651216 |issn=0194-4363 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In the U.S., support for local zoning against multifamily housing is concentrated among white, affluent homeowners.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Manville |first1=Michael |last2=Monkkonen |first2=Paavo |date=2021 |title=Unwanted Housing: Localism and Politics of Housing Development |url=http://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0739456X21997903 |journal=Journal of Planning Education and Research |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=685–700 |language=en |doi=10.1177/0739456X21997903 |issn=0739-456X|url-access=subscription |pmc=12345617 }}</ref> There are no substantial differences between liberal and conservative homeowners in their opposition to the construction of dense housing in their neighborhoods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Nall |first1=Clayton |last2=Marble |first2=William |date=2021 |title=Where Self-Interest Trumps Ideology: Liberal Homeowners and Local Opposition to Housing Development |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/711717 |url-status=live |journal=The Journal of Politics |volume=83 |issue=4 |page=000 |doi=10.1086/711717 |issn=0022-3816 |s2cid=225013704 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210321232518/https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.1086/711717 |archive-date=2021-03-21 |access-date=2020-10-04|url-access=subscription }}</ref> However, among the mass public and elected officials, Democratic constituencies are more likely to support dense, multi-family housing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=de Benedictis-Kessner |first1=Justin |last2=Jones |first2=Daniel |last3=Warshaw |first3=Christopher |date=2024 |title=How partisanship in cities influences housing policy |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/ajps.12856 |journal=American Journal of Political Science |language=en |doi=10.1111/ajps.12856 |issn=0092-5853|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Some estimates suggest that restrictive zoning in the United States may result in hundreds of billions to over a trillion dollars per year in lost economic output.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hsieh |first1=Chang-Tai |last2=Moretti |first2=Enrico |date=2019 |title=Housing Constraints and Spatial Misallocation |journal=American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics |language=en |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=1–39 |doi=10.1257/mac.20170388 |issn=1945-7707 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Babalievsky |first1=Fil |title=The Impact of Commercial Real Estate Regulations on U.S. Output |date=November 2023 |type=Working Paper |url=https://www.nber.org/papers/w31895 |access-date=2024-03-15 |series=Working Paper Series |doi=10.3386/w31895 |last2=Herkenhoff |first2=Kyle F. |last3=Ohanian |first3=Lee E. |last4=Prescott |first4=Edward C.|publisher=National Bureau of Economic Research |location=Cambridge, MA |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Origins and history==
Some scholars trace that German urban planner [[Reinhard Baumeister]] was the first to develop a system of land use separation that influenced later zoning practices.<ref name="Hirt 2014" /> [[Frankfurt]]'s nineteenth century zoning plans served as models for urban planning in the United States and other countries in [[Western Europe]].[[File:Edward Murray Bassett.jpg|thumb|Edward Murray Bassett, "the father of American zoning"<ref>Schäfer, Axel R. (2000). ''American Progressives and German Social Reform, 1875-1920: Social Ethics, Moral Control, and the Regulatory State in a Transatlantic Context''. Stuttgart: Franz Steiner Verlag. p. 137. {{ISBN|978-3-515-07461-2}}.</ref>]]

The perceived need for formal zoning in America arose at the turn of the twentieth century, as rapidly growing cities like New York faced challenges, experiencing rapid [[Urbanization in the United States|urbanization]] and growth in industry, felt a growing need to reduce [[Traffic congestion|congestion]], stabilize property values, combat poor [[urban design]],<ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Bassett |first=Edward M. |title=The board of appeals in zoning. |date=1922 |publisher=Zoning Committee of New York |oclc=793218411}}</ref> and protect residents from issues such as crowded living conditions, outbreaks of disease, and [[Pollution|industrial pollution]],<ref name=":62" /> through legal means.<ref name="WSJ2025Appelbaum"/> [[Edward Bassett|Edward M. Bassett]], author of the first comprehensive zoning ordinance in the United States, wrote in 1922:<blockquote>Skyscrapers would be built to unnecessary height, their cornices projecting into the street and shutting out light and air. The lower floors needed artificial light in the daytime. Business centers instead of being rationally spread out were intensively congested. Transit and street facilities were overwhelmed...<ref name=":7" /></blockquote>Additionally, many of the earliest zoning laws in the United States were influenced by efforts to enforce class-,<ref name="Hirt 2014"/> ethnic-, and race-based segregation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shertzer |first1=Allison |last2=Twinam |first2=Tate |last3=Walsh |first3=Randall P. |date=2021 |title=Zoning and segregation in urban economic history |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166046221000120 |journal=Regional Science and Urban Economics |volume=94 |language=en |article-number=103652 |doi=10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2021.103652 |issn=0166-0462 |access-date=2021-02-24 |s2cid=234156620|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":22">{{Cite news |title=Facing Housing Crunch, California Cities Rethink Single-Family Neighborhoods |language=en |website=NPR.org |url=https://www.npr.org/2021/03/13/973770308/facing-housing-crunch-california-cities-rethink-single-family-neighborhoods |url-status=live |access-date=2021-03-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210313191955/https://www.npr.org/2021/03/13/973770308/facing-housing-crunch-california-cities-rethink-single-family-neighborhoods |archive-date=2021-03-13}}</ref> Early zoning ordinances in the United States were narrower in scope and later became more comprehensive.<ref name="Hirt 2014"/> [[Modesto, California]]'s 1885 ordinance banning wash houses from certain areas of the city is often cited to be America's first true zoning ordinance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A History of Zoning in Three Acts - Part I |url=https://www.strongtowns.org/journal/2017/6/28/a-history-of-zoning-in-three-acts-part-i |access-date=2021-12-06 |website=Strong Towns |date=28 June 2017 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="Appelbaum_Page_87">{{cite book |last1=Appelbaum |first1=Yoni |author1-link=Yoni Appelbaum |title=Stuck: How the Privileged and the Propertied Broke the Engine of American Opportunity |date=2025 |publisher=Random House |location=New York |pages=87–101 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RZ0REQAAQBAJ&pg=PA87}}</ref> [[Richmond, Virginia|Richmond's]] 1908 zoning ordinance regulating the height and arrangement of buildings was upheld by the [[Supreme Court of Virginia|Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals]] in 1910, a decision used as precedent in the implementation of New York City's [[1916 Zoning Resolution]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Silver |first=Christopher |title=Zoning in 20th-Century American Cities |date=2016-05-09 |encyclopedia=Oxford Research Encyclopedia of American History |publisher=Oxford University Press |doi=10.1093/acrefore/9780199329175.013.209 |isbn=978-0-19-932917-5 }}</ref>

=== 1904{{endash}}1930 ===

====Los Angeles, 1904-1909====
[[File:NIE 1905 Petroleum - oil wells at Los Angeles.jpg|thumb|Oil drilling operations in Los Angeles, 1905]]
Zoning in Los Angeles is commonly believed to have been first enacted in 1908, although [[Los Angeles City Council]] passed the first municipal zoning ordinance in the United States, Ordinance 9774, on July 25, 1904.<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Whittemore |first=Andrew |title=Planning Los Angeles |date=2012 |publisher=American Planning Association |others=David Charles Sloane |isbn=978-1-61190-004-0 |location=Chicago |page=108 |oclc=759173286}}</ref> Though the ordinance did not assign all parts of the city to a zoning map, as with later American ordinances, it did establish three residential districts in which laundries and wash houses were prohibited. The prohibition against laundries had a racial component since many were owned by Chinese residents and citizens.<ref name=":32">{{Cite book |last1=Manning Thomas |first1=June Manning |last2=Ritzdorf |first2=Marsha |title=Urban planning and the African American community: in the shadows |date=1997 |publisher=Sage Publications |isbn=0-8039-7233-4 |oclc=35084237}}</ref> This ordinance would later be replaced in 1908 with other ordinances that expanded the scope of the residential districts and greatly expanded the scope of prohibited industries.<ref name=":52">{{Cite book |last=Kolnick |first=Kathy A. |title=Order before zoning: land use regulation in Los Angeles, 1880-1915 |date=2008 |oclc=309352342}}</ref> Existing nuisance laws had already prohibited some industrial land uses in [[Los Angeles]]. Dangerous businesses (such as warehousing explosives) were illegal before 1908, as were odorous land uses, such as [[slaughterhouse]]s and [[Tanner (occupation)|tanneries]]. The [[California Supreme Court]] had already upheld such rules in [[Yick Wo v. Hopkins|''Yick Wo'']] (1886). Many later [[California]] court cases supported the 1908 ordinances, even in one case of ''ex post facto'' relocation of an existing brickyard.<ref name="weiss802">{{cite book |last=Weiss |first=Marc A. |title=The Rise of the Community Builders: The American Real Estate Industry and Urban Land Planning |publisher=Columbia University Press |year=1987 |isbn=0-231-06505-1 |location=New York |pages=80{{endash}}86}}</ref>

Ordinance 16170, adopted on September 16, 1908, established six industrial districts.<ref name=":52" /> These were drawn mainly in areas which had already hosted significant industrial development such as corridors along the freight railroads and the [[Los Angeles River]]. A new ordinance adopted on August 3, 1909, established that all land within Los Angeles that was not part of an industrial district would become a residence district.<ref name=":52" /> However, between 1909 and 1915, Los Angeles City Council responded to some requests by business interests to create exceptions to industrial bans within the three residential districts. They did this through the legal device of districts within districts. While some might have been benign, such as motion picture districts, some others were polluting, such as poultry slaughterhouse districts. Despite the expanding list of exceptions, new ordinances in other cities (i.e., 1914 Oakland ordinance) followed the 1908 Los Angeles model through about 1917.<ref name="weiss802" /> By 1913, twenty-two cities had zoning ordinances.<ref name="ccf2">{{cite book |author=Cheryl Caldwell Ferguson |title=Highland Park and River Oaks: The Origins of Garden Suburban Community Planning in Texas |publisher=University of Texas University Press |year=2014 |isbn=978-0-292-74836-1 |location=Austin |pages=10{{endash}}13}}</ref>

====Race-based zoning ordinances, 1910{{endash}}1917====
Many American cities passed residential segregation laws based on race between 1910 and 1917. [[Baltimore City Council]] passed such a law in December 1910.<ref name="erickson2">{{cite web |last=Erickson |first=Amanda |date=24 August 2012 |title=A Brief History of the Birth of Urban Planning |url=http://www.theatlanticcities.com/jobs-and-economy/2012/08/brief-history-birth-urban-planning/2365/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120825104747/http://www.theatlanticcities.com/jobs-and-economy/2012/08/brief-history-birth-urban-planning/2365/ |archive-date=25 August 2012 |access-date=20 November 2017 |work=The Atlantic Cities |publisher=[[Atlantic Media Company]]}}</ref><ref name="rice2">{{cite journal |last=Rice |first=Roger L. |year=1968 |title=Residential Segregation by Law, 1910{{endash}}1917 |journal=Journal of Southern History |volume=34 |issue=2 |pages=179{{endash}}199 |doi=10.2307/2204656 |jstor=2204656}}</ref> Unlike the Los Angeles Residential District which created well-defined areas for residential land use, the [[Baltimore]] scheme was implemented on a block-by-block basis. [[Druid Hill Park|Druid Hill]] had already existed as a ''de facto'' all-black neighborhood, but some whites in nearby neighborhoods protested for formal segregation. Just a few months later, [[Richmond, Virginia]] passed its race-based zoning law, which was upheld by the Supreme Court of Virginia in the 1915 case ''Hopkins v. City of Richmond''.<ref name=":32"/> Over the next few years, several southern cities established race-based residential zoning ordinances, including four other cities in [[Virginia]], one in [[North Carolina]], and another in [[South Carolina]]. [[Atlanta]] passed a law similar to 1910 Baltimore ordinance. Before 1918, race-based zoning ordinances were adopted in [[New Orleans]], [[Louisville, Kentucky|Louisville]], [[St. Louis]], and [[Oklahoma City]].<ref name="rice2" />

In the end, the United States Supreme Court struck down the Louisville ordinance, ruling in ''[[Buchanan v. Warley]]'' that race-based zoning was a violation of the Fourteenth Amendment;<ref name="erickson2" /><ref name="rice2" /> more specifically, the Court held that the law violated the "right to contract" and the right to alienate property.<ref name="rothstein2">{{cite book |author=Rothstein, Richard |title=The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America |publisher=Liveright Publishing Company |year=2017 |isbn=978-1-63149-285-3 |location=New York |pages=44{{endash}}48}}</ref> Despite the ''Buchanan'' ruling, the city of Atlanta devised a new race-based zoning ordinance, arguing that the Supreme Court had merely applied to specific defects of the Louisville ordinance. Even after the Georgia Supreme Court struck down the Atlanta ordinance, the city continued to use their racially based residential zoning maps. Other municipalities tested the limits of ''Buchanan''; [[Florida]], [[Apopka, Florida|Apopka]] and [[West Palm Beach, Florida|West Palm Beach]] drafted race-based residential zoning ordinances. [[Birmingham, Alabama|Birmingham]], [[Indianapolis]], and [[New Orleans]] all passed race-based zoning laws, while Atlanta, [[Austin, Texas|Austin]], [[Kansas City, Missouri]], and [[Norfolk, Virginia|Norfolk]] considered race in their "spot zoning" decisions. In some cases, these practices continued for decades after ''Buchanan''.<ref name="rothstein2" />

While not explicitly race-based, it is believed that [[Berkeley, California]] is where single-family zoning first originated, as an effort to keep minorities out of white neighborhoods.<ref name="SJMN_2021-03-012">{{cite news |last=Hansen |first=Louis |date=2021-03-01 |title=Is this the end of single-family zoning in the Bay Area? San Jose, Berkeley, other cities consider sweeping changes |newspaper=[[San Jose Mercury News]] |url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2021/03/01/is-this-the-end-of-single-family-zoning-in-the-bay-area/ |url-status=live |access-date=2021-03-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304070329/https://www.mercurynews.com/2021/03/01/is-this-the-end-of-single-family-zoning-in-the-bay-area/ |archive-date=2021-03-04 |quote=Single-family zoning, a form of exclusionary zoning, traces its roots in the U.S. to Berkeley in 1916, when city leaders sought to segregate white homeowners from apartment complexes rented by minority residents. It's become the default policy in cities and suburbs across the country.}}</ref><ref name="SJMN_2021-02-242">{{cite news |last=Ruggiero |first=Angela |date=2021-02-24 |title=Berkeley to end single-family residential zoning, citing racist ties |newspaper=[[San Jose Mercury News]] |url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2021/02/24/berkeley-to-end-single-family-residential-zoning-citing-racist-ties/ |url-status=live |access-date=2021-03-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210303035139/https://www.mercurynews.com/2021/02/24/berkeley-to-end-single-family-residential-zoning-citing-racist-ties/ |archive-date=2021-03-03 |quote=Berkeley is thought to be the birthplace of single-family residential zoning; it began in the Elmwood neighborhood in 1916, where it forbade the construction of anything other than one home per lot. That has historically made it difficult for people of color or those with lower incomes to purchase or lease property in sought-after neighborhoods, city officials said. ... Even after racial discrimination such as redlining — refusing home loans to those in low-income neighborhoods — was outlawed, it continued in the form of single-family zoning, he said.}}</ref>

====1916 New York Zoning Resolution====
{{Main|1916 Zoning Resolution}}
[[File:NYC_Equitable_Building_Before_1919_postcard.jpg|thumb|Early postcard picturing the Equitable Building]]
{{NYC_1916_setback_principle.svg}}
In 1916, [[New York City]] adopted the [[1916 Zoning Resolution|first zoning regulations]] to apply citywide as a reaction to construction of the [[Equitable Building (Manhattan)|Equitable Building]] (which still stands at 120 Broadway). The building towered over the neighboring residences, completely covering all available land area within the property boundary, blocking windows of neighboring buildings and diminishing the availability of sunshine for the people in the affected area.<ref name="nyc">{{cite web |publisher=NYC Department of City Planning |title=City Planning History |access-date=November 19, 2017 |url=https://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/about/city-planning-history.page |archive-date=November 11, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171111094653/http://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/about/city-planning-history.page |url-status=live}}</ref>

Bassett's zoning map established height restrictions for the entire city, expressed as ratios between maximum building height and the width of adjacent streets. Residential zones were the most restrictive, limiting building height to no higher than the width of adjoining streets. The law also regulated land use, preventing factories and warehousing from encroaching on retail districts.<ref name="dunlap">{{cite news |work=New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/26/nyregion/new-yorks-first-zoning-resolution-which-brought-order-to-a-chaotic-building-boom-turns-100.html?_r=1 |date=25 July 2016 |access-date=19 November 2017 |first=David W. |last=Dunlop |title=Zoning Arrived 100 Years Ago. It Changed New York City Forever. |archive-date=1 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201053327/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/07/26/nyregion/new-yorks-first-zoning-resolution-which-brought-order-to-a-chaotic-building-boom-turns-100.html?_r=1 |url-status=live}}</ref>

[[1916 Zoning Resolution|These laws]], written by a [[Government agency|commission]] headed by [[Edward Bassett]] and signed by [[Mayor]] [[John Purroy Mitchel]], became the [[blueprint]] for zoning in the rest of the country, partly because Bassett headed the group of planning lawyers who wrote [[The Standard State Zoning Enabling Act]] that was issued by the U.S. Department of Commerce in 1924 and accepted almost without change by most states. The effect of these zoning regulations on the shape of skyscrapers was illustrated famously by architect and illustrator [[Hugh Ferriss]].<ref>{{cite book |first=Hugh |last=Ferriss |title=The Metropolis of Tomorrow |location=New York |publisher=Princeton Architectural Press |year=1986 |version=Reprint of 1929 edition |isbn=0-910413-11-8 |title-link=The Metropolis of Tomorrow}} With essay by Carol Willis.</ref>

====Standard State Zoning Enabling Act====
{{Main|Standard State Zoning Enabling Act}}

The Standard State Zoning Enabling Act (SZEA) is a federal planning document first drafted and published through the [[United States Commerce Department]] in 1922,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Reed |first=Thomas H. |date=1923 |title=City Planning |journal=The American Political Science Review |volume=17 |issue=3 |page=431 |doi=10.2307/1944054 |jstor=1944054 |s2cid=241518778 |issn=0003-0554}}</ref> which gave states a model under which they could enact their own zoning enabling laws. The genesis for this act is the initiative of [[Herbert Hoover]] while he was Secretary of Commerce. Deriving from a general policy to increase home ownership in the United States, Secretary Hoover established the Advisory Committee on Zoning, which was assigned the task of drafting model zoning statutes. This committee was later known as the Advisory Committee on City Planning and Zoning. Among the members of this committee were Edward Bassett, [[Alfred Bettman]], [[Morris Knowles]], [[Nelson Lewis]], [[Frederick Law Olmsted Jr.]], and [[Lawrence Veiller]].<ref name="knack2">{{cite journal |author=Ruth Knack |author2=Stuart Meck |author3=Israel Stollman |date=February 1996 |title=The Real Story Behind the Standard Planning and Zoning Acts of the 1920 s |url=https://planning-org-uploaded-media.s3.amazonaws.com/legacy_resources/growingsmart/pdf/LULZDFeb96.pdf |url-status=live |journal=Land Use Law & Zoning Digest |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210116033035/https://planning-org-uploaded-media.s3.amazonaws.com/legacy_resources/growingsmart/pdf/LULZDFeb96.pdf |archive-date=January 16, 2021 |access-date=November 19, 2017}}Republished by the American Planning Association.</ref>

The Advisory Committee on Zoning appointed a subcommittee under the title of "Laws and Ordinances." This committee{{emdash}}which included Bassett, Knowles, Lewis, and Veiller{{emdash}}composed a series of drafts for SZEA, with one dated as early as December 15, 1921. A second draft came forth from the subcommittee in January 1922. Several drafts culminated in the first published document in 1924, which was revised and republished in 1926.<ref name="knack2" />

==== Initial reception ====
During their inception, zoning laws were harshly criticized as an overreach of government power.<ref name="Hirt 2014"/> Some believed that they were an unjust restriction of private action, while others believed that the power of zoning would be corrupted in the hands of bureaucrats. General P. Lincoln Mitchell went as far as to call zoning laws "an advanced form of communism."<ref name="Hirt 2014"/> Others supported zoning laws for their uniform and consistent application, and believed that they would be a force of social equality. The constitutionality of zoning laws was highly debated until the ruling of ''Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty''.<ref>{{Cite court|litigants=Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.|vol=272|reporter=U.S.|opinion=365|court=SC|date=November 22, 1926}}</ref>

====''Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.''====
{{Main|Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co.}}

The constitutionality of zoning ordinances was upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in ''[[Village of Euclid, Ohio v. Ambler Realty Co.]]'' in 1926. The zoning ordinance of [[Euclid, Ohio]] was challenged in court by a local land owner on the basis that restricting use of property violated the [[Fourteenth Amendment to the United States Constitution]]. Ambler Realty Company filed suit on November 13, 1922, against the Village of Euclid, Ohio, alleging that the local zoning ordinances effectively diminished its property values. The village had zoned an area of land held by Ambler Realty as a residential neighborhood. Ambler argued that it would lose money because if the land could be leased to industrial users it would have netted a great deal more money than as a residential area.  Ambler Realty claimed these breaches implied an unconstitutional [[Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution#Takings Clause|taking]] of property and denied equal protection under the law.<ref name="briefs">{{cite web |url=https://www.casebriefs.com/blog/law/property/property-law-keyed-to-cribbet/introduction-to-the-traditional-land-use-controls/village-of-euclid-v-ambler-realty-co/ |series=Case Briefs |publisher=Case Briefs LLC |access-date=19 November 2017 |title=Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty Co |archive-date=1 December 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201030854/https://www.casebriefs.com/blog/law/property/property-law-keyed-to-cribbet/introduction-to-the-traditional-land-use-controls/village-of-euclid-v-ambler-realty-co/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

The trial court originally ruled in Ambler's favor, holding zoning unconstitutional. Among other reasons, the trial court found that zoning was an illegitimate device to facilitate social and economic segregation. Nonetheless, the U.S. Supreme Court reversed that decision, holding that zoning was a nuisance-preventing device, and as such a proper exercise of the state regulatory police power.

====Houston, 1924{{endash}}1929====
[[File:Texas housing prices.webp|thumb|300px|Texas housing prices compared to Seattle
{{legend-line|#00A2FF solid 3px|[[Seattle, Washington]]}}

{{legend-line|#F8BA00 solid 3px|[[San Antonio, Texas]]}}
{{legend-line|#FF2600 solid 3px|[[Houston, Texas]]}}
]]
[[File:Harris County rent prices.webp|thumb|300px|[[Harris County, Texas|Harris County]] rent prices ([[Greater Houston|Houston Metro Area]])
{{legend-line|#00A2FF solid 3px|4 bedroom}}
{{legend-line|#61D836 solid 3px|3 bedroom}}

{{legend-line|#F8BA00 solid 3px|1 bedroom}}
{{legend-line|#FF2600 solid 3px|[[Studio apartment|Studio]]}}
