[[Houston]] remains an exception within the United States because it never adopted a zoning ordinance.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Houston doesn't have zoning, but there are workarounds |url=https://kinder.rice.edu/urbanedge/2020/01/09/no-zoning-in-Houston-there-are-workarounds |access-date=2021-12-03 |website=The Kinder Institute for Urban Research |language=en}}</ref> However, strong support existed for zoning in Houston among elements within municipal government and among the city's elites during the 1920s. In 1924, [[Oscar Holcombe|Mayor Oscar Holcombe]], appointed the first funded City Planning Commission. City Council voted in favor of hiring S. Herbert Hare of [[Hare and Hare]] as a planning consultant. Following the passage of a state zoning enabling statute in 1927, Holcombe appointed [[Will Hogg]] to chair a new City Planning Commission.<ref name="ccf2"/> Will Hogg was a co-founder of the [[River Oaks, Houston|River Oaks]] development, the son of a former Texas Governor and an heir to family oil wealth.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia |title=Hogg, William Clifford |encyclopedia=Handbook of Texas |publisher=Texas State Historical Association |url=https://www.tshaonline.org/handbook/entries/hogg-william-clifford |access-date=2023-01-23 |last=Lefevre Jr. |first=Arthur |date=2021-02-21}}</ref> By 1929, both Hare and Hogg abandoned efforts to push the zoning ordinance to a referendum. In their estimation, there was not enough support for it. Hogg resigned as chair of the City Planning Commission that year.<ref name="ccf2"/>

=== 1931{{endash}}2000 ===

==== Houston, 1948{{endash}}1993 ====
Houston is the largest city in the country with ''no'' zoning [[local ordinance|ordinances]]. Houston voters have rejected efforts to implement zoning in 1948, 1962, and 1993.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2007/11/18/lack-of-zoning-laws-a-challenge-in-houston/ |title=Lack of zoning laws a challenge in Houston |newspaper=Wall Street Journal |author=Hudson, Kris |date=November 18, 2007 |access-date=April 25, 2018 |archive-date=January 24, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120124113350/http://articles.chicagotribune.com/2007-11-18/business/0711150779_1_zoning-laws-land-use-houston-mayor-bill-white |url-status=live}} Republished by chicagotribune.com.</ref> Houston is similar, however, to other large cities throughout the [[Sun Belt]], who all experienced the bulk of their population growth during the [[automobile|Age of the Automobile]]. The largest of these cities, such as [[Los Angeles]], [[Atlanta]], [[Miami]], [[Tampa]], [[Dallas]], [[Phoenix, Arizona|Phoenix]], and [[Kansas City, Missouri|Kansas City]], have all expanded their metropolitan footprints along with Houston while having land use zoning.<ref name=autogenerated3>{{cite web |url=http://www.planetizen.com/node/109 |title=Zoning Without Zoning |access-date=2007-11-22 |archive-date=2008-10-16 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081016050640/http://www.planetizen.com/node/109 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=autogenerated4>"Land Use Regulation and Residential Segregation: Does Zoning Matter?" Christopher Berry, American Law and Economics Review V3 N2 2001 (251-274)</ref><ref>"Home From Nowhere" James Howard Kunstler, The Atlantic Monthly; September 1996</ref>

While Houston has no official zoning ordinances, many private properties have legal [[Covenant (law)|covenants]] or "deed restrictions" that limit the future uses of land, with effects similar to those of zoning systems.<ref name=autogenerated4 /><ref name=Houston_with_out_zoning>{{ cite news | last=Coy | first=Peter | title=How Houston gets along without zoning | url=http://www.businessweek.com/the_thread/hotproperty/archives/2007/10/how_houston_get.html | date=October 1, 2007 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081004210420/http://www.businessweek.com/the_thread/hotproperty/archives/2007/10/how_houston_get.html | archive-date=2008-10-04 }}</ref>

Also, the city has enacted development regulations that specify how lots are subdivided, standard setbacks, and parking requirements.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.houstontx.gov/planning/DevelopRegs/dev_regs_links.html |title=Houston Development and Regulations |access-date=2013-09-30 |archive-date=2013-10-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131002160416/http://www.houstontx.gov/planning/DevelopRegs/dev_regs_links.html |url-status=live}}</ref> The regulations have contributed to the city's [[automobile]]-dependent sprawl, by requiring the existence of large minimum residential lot sizes and large commercial parking lots.<ref name=lewyn>{{cite journal |author=Lewyn, Michael |journal=Wayne Law Journal |volume=50 |year=2005 |title=How Overregulation Creates Sprawl (Even in a City Without Zoning) |issue=1171 |pages=1172{{endash}}1214 |ssrn=837244}}</ref>

==== Mid 20th Century ====
During the mid-twentieth century, use-based zoning became flatter, and hierarchical provisions that allowed residential uses in industrial areas became less common.<ref name="Hirt 2014" /> Zoning districts also became larger, increasing the distance between properties zoned for different uses.<ref name="Hirt 2014" />

=== 21st century ===
In the early 21st century, several local and state governments across the United States have been relaxing or abolishing specific zoning classes (e.g. [[single-family zoning]]) to address various issues that have arisen as a result of zoning, such as housing affordability crises and racial and socio-economic segregation.<ref name="Kahlenberg">{{Cite web |url=https://tcf.org/content/report/minneapolis-ended-single-family-zoning/ |title=How Minneapolis Ended Single-Family Zoning |author=Richard D. Kahlenberg |work=The Century Foundation |publisher= |date=October 24, 2019 |access-date=June 8, 2022}}</ref><ref name="Kendall">{{Cite web |url=https://www.mercurynews.com/2021/09/16/gov-newsom-abolishes-single-family-zoning-in-california/ |title=Gov. Newsom abolishes most single-family zoning in California |author=Marisa Kendall |work=The Mercury News |date=September 16, 2021 |access-date=June 8, 2022}}</ref> In addition, federal legislation to reform [[exclusionary zoning]] has been proposed by national politicians from both the Republican and Democratic parties since at least the 2010s.<ref name="Kahlenberg"/>

==== California ====
In September 2021, the state of California adopted Senate Bill 9 allowing the development of up to four residential units on single-family lots, following a growing push from local governments such as [[Berkeley, California|Berkeley]] (set to phase out single-family zoning by December 2022), [[San Jose, California|San Jose]] and other cities across the state.<ref name="Kendall"/>

==== Massachusetts ====
In 2000, Republican governor [[Paul Cellucci]] of [[Massachusetts]] passed the Community Preservation Act for housing affordability.<ref name="Voorhis">{{Cite web |url=https://commonwealthmagazine.org/housing/bakers-housing-efforts-meet-resistance/ |title=Baker's housing efforts meet resistance |author=Scott Van Voorhis |work=CommonWealth Magazine |date=May 15, 2022 |access-date=June 8, 2022 |archive-date=June 2, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220602173932/https://commonwealthmagazine.org/housing/bakers-housing-efforts-meet-resistance/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> In 2004, Republican governor [[Mitt Romney]]  adopted the 40R law which provided financial incentives to cities, suburbs, and towns to adopt zoning legislation for new rental and condo units around rail stations.<ref name="Voorhis"/> In 2012, Democratic governor [[Deval Patrick]] expanded 40R with Compact Neighborhoods, incentivizing zoning for denser, multifamily housing near rail and transit hubs across the Commonwealth.<ref name="Voorhis"/> In November 2017, Republican governor [[Charlie Baker]] introduced the Housing Choice reform (adopted in January 2021), including relaxing the requirement of a two-thirds majority to a simple majority at the local level to pass zoning amendments for new housing, a requirement for 175 cities and towns in the [[Greater Boston]] area to rezone land for denser, multi-family housing near [[Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority|MBTA]] stations, and financial means of compliance to new zoning regulations on top of existing incentives.<ref name="Voorhis"/> Unlike California, where the state legislature has taken a more leading role in local zoning reform, the focus in Massachusetts is on local government control of zoning policy changes; both approaches have their advantages and disadvantages.<ref name="Voorhis"/> In February 2024, residents in the Town of Milton, a Boston suburb, voted to not comply with the law. Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Joy Campbell has filed suit to force compliance.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Fortin |first1=Matt |last2=Prichard |first2=Matt |last3=Rosenfield |first3=Michael |last4=Fortier|first4=Marc |date=2024-02-27 |title=Milton sued by Mass. after voting to not comply with MBTA housing law |url=https://www.nbcboston.com/news/local/milton-sued-by-ags-office-over-lack-of-compliance-to-mbta-housing-law/3291135/ |access-date=2024-03-04 |website=NBC Boston |language=en-US}}</ref> The ''Boston Globe'' has characterized efforts to update zoning codes as a "political minefield" for Boston Mayor Michelle Wu.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Platoff |first1=Emma |last2=Carlock |first2=Catherine |date=February 20, 2024|title=Mayor Wu wants to overhaul Boston's rules for what can be built where. She's stepping into a political minefield. |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2024/02/20/metro/wu-rezoning-politics-boston-real-estate/ |access-date=2024-03-04 |website=The Boston Globe|language=en-US}}</ref>

==== Minneapolis ====
On December 7, 2018, [[Minneapolis]] in [[Minnesota]] became the first U.S. city to decide to completely phase out exclusionary single-family zoning policies (then covering 70% of its residential land) in three stages.<ref name="Kahlenberg"/> It also planned to allow construction of new three-to-six story buildings near transit stops, abolish off-street minimum parking requirements (the fourth U.S. city to do so), require new apartment developments to set aside 10% of units for moderate-income households, and to increase funding for affordable housing to combat homelessness and support low-income renters.<ref name="Kahlenberg"/> Aside from increasing housing affordability and reducing racial and economic segregation, reducing commutes and making housing more environmentally friendly was an additional stated purpose.<ref name="Kahlenberg"/>

==== Oregon ====
The House Bill 2001, adopted by the Oregon Senate in a 17–9 vote on June 30, 2019, effectively eliminated single-family zoning in large Oregonian cities.<ref name="Njus">{{Cite web |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/politics/2019/06/bill-to-eliminate-single-family-zoning-in-oregon-neighborhoods-passes-final-legislative-hurdle.html |title=Bill to eliminate single-family zoning in Oregon neighborhoods passes final legislative hurdle |author=Elliot Njus |work=[[The Oregonian]] |date=June 30, 2019 |access-date=June 8, 2022}}</ref> Towns with at least 10,000 residents were required to allow the development of duplexes in single-family zones, while cities with over 25,000 residents and a few smaller places in the [[Portland metropolitan area, Oregon|Portland metropolitan area]] also had to permit triplexes, fourplexes, and "cottage clusters" (several small homes around a common yard) in addition to duplexes on land that had until then been reserved for single-family homes.<ref name="Njus"/>

==Scope==
[[File:Suburbia JC walk parking jeh.jpg|thumb|Parking provision is sometimes specified.]]
Theoretically, the primary purpose of zoning is to segregate uses that are thought to be incompatible and provide stability to property values.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bassett |first=Edward Murray |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CbErAAAAYAAJ&pg=PA311 |title=Zoning |date=1922 |publisher=National Municipal League |language=en}}</ref> In practice, zoning is also used as a permitting system to prevent new development from harming existing [[Residency (domicile)|residents]] or [[business]]es. Zoning is commonly exercised by local governments such as [[County (United States)|counties]] or [[municipalities]], although the state determines the nature of the zoning scheme with a zoning enabling law. [[Federal lands]] are not subject to state planning controls.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Land-use Planning Systems in the OECD: Country Fact Sheets |url=https://www.oecd-ilibrary.org/urban-rural-and-regional-development/land-use-planning-systems-in-the-oecd_9789264268579-en |access-date=2021-12-05 |series=OECD Regional Development Studies |year=2017 |language=en |doi=10.1787/9789264268579-en |isbn=978-92-64-26856-2}}</ref>

Zoning may include regulation of the kinds of activities that will be acceptable on particular [[Land lot|lots]] (such as open space, residential, [[agricultural]], [[Commerce|commercial]], or industrial), the densities at which those activities may be performed (from low-density [[House|housing]] such as single family homes to high-density such as [[Tower block|high-rise apartment buildings]]), the height of buildings, the amount of space structures may occupy, the location of a building on the lot ([[Building setback|setbacks]]), the proportions of the types of space on a lot (for example, how much [[landscape]]d space and how much [[Pavement (roads)|paved]] space), and how much [[Parking minimums and maximums|parking must be provided]]).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Manville |first=Michael |date=2013-01-02 |title=Parking Requirements and Housing Development |journal=Journal of the American Planning Association |volume=79 |issue=1 |pages=49–66 |doi=10.1080/01944363.2013.785346 |s2cid=153455938 |issn=0194-4363}}</ref> Some commercial zones specify what types of products may be sold by particular stores.<ref>''Hernandez v. City of Hanford'', [http://online.ceb.com/CalCases/C4/41C4t279.htm 41 Cal. 4th 279] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160122031833/http://online.ceb.com/CalCases/C4/41C4t279.htm|date=2016-01-22}} (2007) (upholding constitutionality of zoning ordinance regulating which types of stores in which zones may sell furniture in the city of [[Hanford, California|Hanford]], [[California]]).</ref>

== Implementation ==
Most zoning systems have a procedure for granting [[Variance (land use)|variances]]<ref>Cohen, Jonathan E. "A Constitutional Safety Valve: The Variance in Zoning and Land-Use Based Environmental Controls." ''BC Envtl. Aff. L. Rev.'' 22 (1994): 307.</ref> (exceptions to the zoning rules), usually because of some perceived hardship due to the particular nature of the [[property]] in question. If the variance is not warranted, then it may cause an allegation of [[spot zoning]] to arise. Most state zoning-enabling laws prohibit local zoning authorities from engaging in any spot zoning because it would undermine the purpose of a zoning scheme.<ref name="autogenerated12">{{cite court|litigants=Eves v. Zoning Board. of Adjustment of Lower Gwynedd Township|vol=401|reporter=Pa.|opinion=211|pinpoint=|court=Supreme Court of Pennsylvania, Eastern District|date=1960|quote=|postscript=|url=https://law.justia.com/cases/pennsylvania/supreme-court/1960/401-pa-211-0.html}}</ref>

Zoning laws in different jurisdictions can each specify their rules using their own systems. Although there are some general patterns, such as abbreviations starting with R for residential, C for commercial, and I for industrial, zoning laws do not follow any single consistent system.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What Are Zoning Codes? {{!}} Planopedia |url=https://www.planetizen.com/definition/zoning-codes |access-date=2024-01-31 |website=www.planetizen.com |language=en}}</ref> As one example, residential zones in one city might be coded as R1 for [[single-family home]]s and R5 for [[Apartment building|multiple-family homes]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=2019-08-06 |title=How to Understand Municipal Zoning Codes |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2019-08-06/how-to-understand-municipal-zoning-codes |access-date=2024-01-31 |work=Bloomberg.com |language=en}}</ref> In other places, the code R5 could refer to 5 residential housing units per acre or to homes on lots of at least 5,000 square feet.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Owens |first=David W. |title=Introduction to Zoning and Development Regulation, Fourth Edition |date=January 15, 2014 |publisher=UNC School of Government |isbn=978-1-56011-744-5 |edition=4th |location=Chapel Hill, NC, USA |page=35 |language=en}}</ref>

==Legal challenges==
There are several limitations to the ability of local governments in asserting police powers to control land use. First, constitutional constraints include freedom of speech (First Amendment), unjust takings of property through the use of zoning that denies land owners the ability to put their land to reasonable, income producing uses (Fifth Amendment), and equal protection (Fourteenth Amendment). There are also federal statutes that sometimes constrain local zoning. These include the Federal Housing Amendments Act of 1988, the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, and the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000.<ref name="tancredi">{{cite web |first=Dawn M. |last=Tancredi |url=https://www.law360.com/articles/565323/strike-you-re-out-how-zoning-codes-are-being-invalidated |title=Strike, You're Out! How Zoning Codes Are Being Invalidated |date=August 15, 2014 |access-date=November 20, 2017 |publisher=Law 360 |archive-date=December 1, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201042723/https://www.law360.com/articles/565323/strike-you-re-out-how-zoning-codes-are-being-invalidated |url-status=live}}</ref>

=== Freedom of speech ===
{{See also|Lawn sign}}
Local governments regulate signage on private property through zoning ordinances. Sometimes courts invalidate laws which regulate the content of speech rather than the manners and modes of speech. One court invalidated a local ordinance that prohibited "for sale" and "sold" signs on private property. Another court struck down a law which prohibited signs for adult cabarets.<ref name="tancredi"/>

=== Takings after 1987 ===

Beginning in 1987, several United States Supreme Court cases ruled against land use regulations as being a [[regulatory|taking]] requiring just [[Compensation (nationalization)|compensation]] pursuant to the [[United States Constitution/Amendment Five|Fifth Amendment to the Constitution]]. ''[[First English Evangelical Lutheran Church v. Los Angeles County]]'' ruled that even a temporary regulatory taking may require compensation.  ''[[Nollan v. California Coastal Commission]]'' ruled that [[construction permit]] conditions that fail to substantially advance the agency's authorized purposes, require compensation. ''[[Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council]]'' ruled that numerous environmental concerns were not sufficient to deny all development without compensation. ''[[Dolan v. City of Tigard]]'' ruled that conditions of a permit must be roughly proportional to the adverse impacts of the proposed new development. ''[[Palazzolo v. Rhode Island]]'' ruled property rights are not diminished by unconstitutional laws that exist without challenge at the time the complaining property owner acquired title.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022|reason=}}

=== Equal protection ===
Specific zoning laws have been overturned in some other U.S. cases where the laws were not applied evenly (violating [[equal protection]]) or were considered to violate [[free speech]]. In the [[Atlanta]] suburb of [[Roswell, Georgia|Roswell]], [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]], an [[local ordinance|ordinance]] banning [[billboard (advertising)|billboard]]s was overturned in court the grounds that it unconstitutionally violated the right to freedom of speech.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Weizel |first=Richard |date=2001-03-25 |title=In Georgia, a Plea to Advertisers |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2001/03/25/nyregion/in-georgia-a-plea-to-advertisers.html |access-date=2024-01-31 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref><ref>{{cite court|litigants=SMD L.L.P. v City of Roswell|vol=252|reporter=Ga. App.|opinion=438|pinpoint=|court=Court of Appeals of Georgia|date=OCTOBER 24, 2001|quote="the City defendants' unconstitutional conduct"|postscript=[https://web.archive.org/web/20240131040508/https://casetext.com/case/smd-llp-v-city-of-roswell]|url=}}</ref> Cities are now advised not to regulate [[signage|signs]] based on their content.<ref name=":8">University of Georgia Land Use Clinic, School of Law, and

College of Environment & Design, Sign Control on Rural Corridors: Model Provisions and Guidance, June 26, 2003, p. 6 https://rivercenter.uga.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Sign-Control-on-Rural-Corridors.pdf</ref> Roswell has amended its sign ordinance to regulate signs based strictly on dimensional and aesthetic features rather than the sign content.<ref name=":8" />

=== Religious exercise ===

On other occasions, religious institutions sought to circumvent zoning laws, citing the [[Religious Freedom Restoration Act]] of 1993 (RFRA). The Supreme Court eventually overturned RFRA in just such a case, ''[[City of Boerne v. Flores]]'' [[Case citation|521 U.S. 507]] (1997). Congress enacted the [[Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act]] (RLUIPA) in 2000, however, in an effort to correct the constitutionally objectionable problems of the RFRA.<ref name="aclu">{{cite web |url=https://www.aclu.org/files/assets/rluipa_outline_6-11.pdf |publisher=ACLU National Prison Project |access-date=20 November 2017 |title=The Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000 |archive-date=8 June 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130608185503/http://www.aclu.org/files/assets/rluipa_outline_6-11.pdf |url-status=live}}</ref> RLUIPA has been found to be constitutional as applied to institutionalized persons in three [[United States Supreme Court]] cases ([[Cutter v. Wilkinson]], Sossamon v. Texas, and [[Holt v. Hobbs]]), but as of 2020 no case had decided RLUIPA's constitutionality as it relates to religious land uses.<ref>Eric S. Dreiband, September 22, 2020, Report on the Twentieth Anniversary of the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act, U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division, https://www.justice.gov/media/1096176/dl?inline, pp. 7-8.</ref>

=== Wildlife sanctuaries ===
In early 2022, the town of [[Woodside, California]] drew widespread derision for declaring itself a "[[cougar|mountain lion]] habitat" to avoid [[California housing shortage|state affordable housing]] requirements.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dillon |first1=Liam |title=Wealthy town has an answer against building affordable housing: Mountain lions |url=https://www.latimes.com/homeless-housing/story/2022-02-04/well-heeled-town-affordable-housing-mountain-lions |access-date=6 February 2022 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=4 February 2022}}</ref> It backed down on that attempt after [[Attorney General of California|California Attorney General]] [[Rob Bonta]] denied this claim.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Woodside Reverses Housing Decision After AG Denies Mountain Lion Sanctuary Claim |url=https://www.nbcbayarea.com/news/local/making-it-in-the-bay/woodside-reverses-housing-decision-after-ag-denies-mountain-lion-sanctuary-status/2803141/ |date=February 7, 2022 |access-date=February 7, 2022 |website=NBC Bay Area |language=en-US}}</ref> Bonta wrote: "There is no valid basis to claim that the entire town of Woodside is a habitat for mountain lions. Land that is already developed — with, for example a single-family home — is not, by definition, habitat. (...) Our message to local governments is simple: act in good faith, follow the law, and do your part to increase the housing supply."<ref name="Cramer">{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/07/us/woodside-mountain-lion-housing.html |title=California Town Says Mountain Lions Don't Stop Housing After All |author=Maria Cramer and Alan Yuhas |work=The New York Times |date=February 7, 2022 |access-date=June 8, 2022}}</ref> According to housing advocate Sonja Trauss, this was just one of about 40 cases in which Californian towns attempted to limit, block or discourage housing development to maintain exclusionary single-family zones in violation of Senate Bill 9 (SB9) adopted in September 2021.<ref name="Cramer"/>

==Types==
{{Main|Zoning#Types|l1 = Zoning§Types}}

Zoning codes have evolved over the years as urban planning theory has changed, legal constraints have fluctuated, and political priorities have shifted.<ref>Holm, Ivar (2006). ''Ideas and Beliefs in Architecture and Industrial design: How attitudes, orientations, and underlying assumptions shape the built environment''. Oslo School of Architecture and Design. {{ISBN|82-547-0174-1}}.</ref> The various approaches to zoning may be divided into four categories: Use-based (known as Euclidean in the US), performance, incentive, and [[Form-based code|form-based]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-12-02 |title=Types of Land Use Zoning {{!}} The Geography of Transport Systems |url=https://transportgeography.org/contents/chapter8/urban-land-use-transportation/land-use-zoning/ |access-date=2024-04-30 |language=en-US}}</ref> Euclidean zoning codes with strict use separation are by far the most prevalent type in the United States.<ref name="Hirt 2014" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Gray |first=M. Nolan |title=Arbitrary lines: how zoning broke the American city and how to fix it |date=2022 |publisher=Island Press |isbn=978-1-64283-254-9 |location=Washington Covelo [Calif.]}}</ref>{{rp||page=38}} While the use of innovations such as form-based, performance, planned-unit development, and mixed-use zoning are common in the US, they tend to liberate relatively little land area from strict single-use zoning.<ref name="Hirt 2014" />{{rp||page=|pages=85–92}} Based on a survey of 25 cities, less than 5% of land allows mixed residential and commercial uses.<ref name="Hirt 2014" />{{rp||page=90}}

==Amendments to zoning regulations==

Amendments to zoning regulations may be subject to judicial review, should such amendments be challenged as [[ultra vires]] or unconstitutional.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022|reason=}}

The standard applied to the amendment to determine whether it may survive judicial scrutiny is the same as the review of a zoning ordinance: whether the restriction is arbitrary or whether it bears a reasonable relationship to the exercise of the police power of the state.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022|reason=}}

If the residents in the targeted neighborhood complain about the amendment, their argument in court does not allow them any vested right to keep the zoned district the same.<ref name=autogenerated2>Duggan</ref> However, they do not have to prove the difficult standard that the amendment amounts to a taking.<ref name=autogenerated2 /> If the gain to the public for the rezoning is small compared to the hardships that would affect the residents, then the amendment may be granted if it provides relief to the residents.<ref name=autogenerated2 />

If the local zoning authority passes the zoning amendment, then [[spot zoning]] allegations may arise should the rezoning be preferential in nature and not reasonably justified.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022|reason=}}

==Limitations and criticisms==

Land-use zoning is a tool in the treatment of certain social ills and part of the larger concept of [[Social engineering (political science)|social engineering]].<ref>{{Citation |last1=Wilson |first1=Bobby M. |chapter=Zoning as a Form of Social Engineering |date=2010-12-30 |title=Engineering Earth |pages=2053–2065 |place=Dordrecht |publisher=Springer Netherlands |last2=Appiah-Opoku |first2=Seth |doi=10.1007/978-90-481-9920-4_113 |isbn=978-90-481-9919-8}}</ref> There is criticism of zoning particularly amongst proponents of [[limited government]] or [[Laissez-faire]] political perspectives. The inherent danger of zoning, as a coercive force used against property owners seeking to build integrated housing, has been described in detail in [[Richard Rothstein]]'s book ''[[The Color of Law]]'' (2017).<ref name="rothstein2" />{{rp|159-160|page=|pages=85–92}} Government zoning was used significantly as an instrument to advance racism through enforced segregation in all regions of the U.S., not only in the South, from the early part of the 20th century up until recent decades.<ref name="rothstein2" />{{rp||page=7|pages=}}

===Circumventions===

Generally, existing development in a community is not affected by the new zoning laws because it is "[[Grandfather clause|grandfathered]]" or ''legally non-conforming'' as a [[nonconforming use]], meaning the prior development is exempt from compliance.<ref>Fischel, William A. "Zoning and land use regulation." ''Encyclopedia of law and economics'' 2 (2000): 403-423.</ref> Consequently, zoning may only affect new development in a growing community. In addition, if undeveloped land is zoned to allow development, that land becomes relatively expensive, causing developers to seek land that is not zoned for development with the intention to seek rezoning of that land. Communities generally react by not zoning undeveloped land to allow development until a developer requests rezoning and presents a suitable plan. Development under this practice appears to be piecemeal and uncoordinated. Communities try to influence the timing of development by government expenditures for new streets, sewers, and utilities usually desired for modern developments. Contrary to federal recommendations discouraging it, the development of interstate [[freeway]]s for purposes unrelated to planned community growth, creates an inexorable rush to develop the relatively cheap land near interchanges. [[Property tax]] suppression measures such as [[California Proposition 13 (1978)|California Proposition 13]] led many communities desperate to capture [[sales tax]] revenue to disregard their comprehensive plans and rezone undeveloped land for retail establishments.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Gabriel |first1=Stuart |last2=Katz |first2=Lawrence |last3=Wolch |first3=Jennifer |date=1980 |title=Local Land-Use Regulation and Proposition 13: Some Findings from a Recent Survey |url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/12r370cj |language=en |website=Fisher Center for Real Estate and Urban Economics |publisher=UC Berkeley}}</ref>

In Colorado, local governments are free to choose not to enforce their own zoning and other land regulation laws. This is called selective enforcement. Steamboat Springs, Colorado is an example of a location with illegal buildings and lax enforcement.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.steamboatpilot.com/news/2000/jul/27/case_against_council/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120913060740/http://www.steamboatpilot.com/news/2000/jul/27/case_against_council/ |archive-date=2012-09-13 |title=Steamboat Today: Case against council president dismissed}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Steamboat Today: Fire death questions linger |url=http://www.steamboatpilot.com/news/2008/jun/17/fire_death_questions_linger/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100223014137/http://www.steamboatpilot.com/news/2008/jun/17/fire_death_questions_linger/ |archive-date=2010-02-23 |access-date=2009-11-30}}</ref>

===Housing affordability===

Zoning also has been implicated as a primary driving factor in the rapidly accelerating lack of affordable housing in urban areas.<ref>Glaeser, Edward L. and Gyourko, Joseph, [http://post.economics.harvard.edu/hier/2002papers/HIER1948.pdf The Impact of Zoning on Housing Affordability], 2002 {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070926031356/http://post.economics.harvard.edu/hier/2002papers/HIER1948.pdf |date=September 26, 2007 }}</ref> One mechanism for this is zoning by many suburban and [[exurban]] communities for very large minimum residential lot and building sizes in order to preserve home values by limiting the total supply of housing, which thereby excludes poorer people. This shifts the market toward more expensive homes than ordinarily might be built. According to the Manhattan Institute, as much as half of the price paid for housing in some jurisdictions is directly attributable to the hidden costs of restrictive zoning regulation.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022|reason=}}

For example, the entire town of [[Los Altos Hills, California|Los Altos Hills]], [[California]] (with the exception of the local community college and a religious convent), is zoned for residential use with a minimum lot size of one acre (4,000 m<sup>2</sup>) and a limit to only one primary dwelling per lot. All these restrictions were upheld as constitutional by federal and state courts in the early 1970s.<ref>''Ybarra v. Town of Los Altos Hills'', 503 F.2d 250, 254 (9th Cir. 1974).</ref><ref>''Town of Los Altos Hills v. Adobe Creek Properties, Inc.'', [http://online.ceb.com/calcases/CA3/32CA3d488.htm 32 Cal.App.3d 488] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070929095503/http://online.ceb.com/calcases/CA3/32CA3d488.htm |date=2007-09-29 }} (1973).</ref> The town traditionally attempted to comply with state affordable housing requirements by counting secondary dwellings (that is, apartments over garages and guest houses) as affordable housing, and since 1989 also has allowed residents to build so-called "granny units".<ref>Town of Los Altos Hills, ''2002 General Plan, Housing Element'', 6.</ref>

In 1969 [[Massachusetts]] enacted the [[Massachusetts Comprehensive Permit Act: Chapter 40B]], originally referred to as the anti-snob zoning law. Under this statute, in municipalities with less than 10% affordable housing, a developer of affordable housing may seek waiver of local zoning and other requirements from the local zoning board of appeals, with review available from the state Housing Appeals Committee<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mass.gov/hed/economic/eohed/dhcd/hac.html |title=Housing Appeals Committee (HAC) |website=Mass.gov |access-date=2012-01-02 |archive-date=2011-12-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111231044250/http://www.mass.gov/hed/economic/eohed/dhcd/hac.html |url-status=live}}</ref> if the waiver is denied. Similar laws are in place in other parts of the United States (e.g., Rhode Island, Connecticut, and Illinois), although their effectiveness is disputed.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022|reason=}}

Critics of zoning note that zoning laws are a disincentive to provide housing which results in an increase in housing costs and a decrease in productive economic output.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.pbs.org/wnet/chasing-the-dream/2021/02/how-zoning-can-restrict-affordable-housing/ |title=How zoning can restrict, or even prevent, affordable housing |publisher=PBS |date=1 February 2021}}</ref> For example, A 2017 study showed that if all states deregulated their zoning laws only halfway to the level of Texas, a state known for low zoning regulations, their GDP would increase by 12 percent due to more productive workers and opportunity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Herkenhoff |first1=Kyle F. |last2=Ohanian |first2=Lee E. |last3=Prescott |first3=Edward C. |date=2018-01-01 |title=Tarnishing the golden and empire states: Land-use restrictions and the U.S. economic slowdown |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0304393217301265 |journal=Journal of Monetary Economics |series=Carnegie-Rochester-NYU Conference on Public Policy held at the Stern School of Business at New York University |volume=93 |pages=89–109 |doi=10.1016/j.jmoneco.2017.11.001 |issn=0304-3932|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Furthermore, critics note that it impedes the ability of those that wish to provide charitable housing from doing so. For example, in 2022, Gloversville's Free Methodist Church in New York wished to provide 40 beds for the homeless population in -4 degree weather and were inhibited from doing so.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://reason.com/2022/01/14/while-temperatures-drop-below-zero-degrees-zoning-officials-wont-let-this-cold-weather-homeless-shelter-open/ |title=Zoning Officials Stop Church From Opening 40-Bed Shelter in Sub-Zero Temperatures |publisher=Reason |date=14 January 2022}}</ref>

====Zoning tax====
According to a 2021 study, in San Francisco, the "zoning tax" -which refers to the artificially inflated land prices brought on by tight residential zoning rules-  is predicted to be more than $400,000 per home. The study found that the zoning tax in Seattle, New York City, and Los Angeles may reach $200,000. In Chicago, Philadelphia, Portland, and Washington, D.C., it reached $80,000.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Meyersohn |first1=Nathaniel |title=The invisible laws that led to America's housing crisis |url=https://edition.cnn.com/2023/08/05/business/single-family-zoning-laws/index.html |agency=CNN |date=2023}}</ref>

===Social===

In more recent times, zoning has been criticized by urban planners and scholars (most notably [[Jane Jacobs]]) as a source of new social ills, including [[urban sprawl]], the separation of homes from employment, and the rise of "[[Car dependency|car culture]]".{{r|Hirt 2014}} Some communities have begun to encourage development of denser, homogenized, mixed-use neighborhoods that promote walking and cycling to jobs and shopping. Nonetheless, a single-family home and car are major parts of the "[[American Dream]]" for [[Nuclear family|nuclear families]], and zoning laws often reflect this: in some cities, houses that do not have an attached [[Garage (house)|garage]] have been deemed "[[Blight (urban)|blighted]]" and are subject to [[redevelopment]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Claeys |first=Eric R. |date=2005 |title=Don't Waste a Teaching Moment: Kelo, Urban Renewal, and Blight |journal=Journal of Affordable Housing & Community Development Law |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=14–19 |jstor=25782771 |issn=1084-2268}}</ref> Movements that disapprove of Euclidean zoning, such as [[New urbanism|New Urbanism]] and [[Smart Growth]], generally try to reconcile these competing demands. New Urbanists in particular favor creative urban design solutions that hark back to 1920s and 1930s practices of hierarchical zoning,<ref>{{Cite web |title=A Town Well Planned: Hierarchical Zoning |url=https://www.strongtowns.org/journal/2017/8/29/a-town-well-planned-hierarchical-zoning |access-date=2021-12-05 |website=Strong Towns |date=30 August 2017 |language=en-US}}</ref> or form-based code.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Steuteville |first=Robert |date=2017-05-10 |title=Great idea: Form-based codes |url=https://www.cnu.org/publicsquare/2017/05/10/great-idea-form-based-codes |access-date=2021-12-05 |website=CNU |language=en}}</ref>

===Exclusionary===

Zoning has long been criticized as a tool of racial and socio-economic exclusion and segregation, primarily through minimum lot-size requirements and land-use segregation.<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |title=Zoning: a guide for 21st-century planning |date=2020 |editor1=Elliott Sclar |editor2=Bernadette Baird-Zars |editor3=Lauren Ames Fischer |editor4=Valerie E. Stahl |publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-0-429-48922-8 |location=New York, NY |oclc=1124778006}}</ref> Early zoning codes often were explicitly racist,<ref>{{cite web |author=June Manning Thomas |date=December 15, 1997 |title=RACE, RACISM, AND RACE RELATIONS: LINKAGE WITH URBAN AND REGIONAL PLANNING LITERATURE |url=http://gis.sarup.uwm.edu/acsp/Documents/Race_LitReview.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070809194948/http://gis.sarup.uwm.edu/acsp/Documents/Race_LitReview.pdf |archive-date=August 9, 2007}}</ref> or designed to separate social classes.{{r|Hirt 2014}}

Exclusionary practices remain common among suburbs wishing to keep out those deemed socioeconomically or ethnically undesirable: for example, representatives of the city of [[Barrington Hills, Illinois|Barrington Hills]], [[Illinois]] once told editors of the Real Estate section of the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' that the city's {{convert|5|acre|m2|adj=on}} minimum lot size helped to "keep out the riff-raff."{{Citation needed|date=December 2021}}

Occupancy restrictions, such as those restricting the number of unrelated occupants that can occupy a single-family dwelling, have been criticized for their rigidity to traditional ideas of the [[nuclear family]]. Supreme Court Justice [[William O. Douglas]] argued in the case ''[[Village of Belle Terre v. Boraas]]'' that argued it was the objective of the state to preserve traditional [[family values]],<ref>{{Citation |last=Ritzdorf |first=Marsha |chapter=A Feminist Analysis of Gender and Residential Zoning in the United States |date=1994 |title=Women and the Environment |pages=255–279 |place=Boston, MA |publisher=Springer US |doi=10.1007/978-1-4899-1504-7_10 |isbn=978-1-4899-1506-1 }}</ref> something critics have used as a pejorative against single-family zoning.{{Citation needed|date=June 2022|reason=}}

====Racially-segregated zoning====

Since 1910 in Baltimore,<ref>{{cite web |last=Erickson |first=Amanda |date=August 24, 2012 |title=A Brief History of the Birth of Urban Planning |url=http://www.theatlanticcities.com/jobs-and-economy/2012/08/brief-history-birth-urban-planning/2365/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120825104747/http://www.theatlanticcities.com/jobs-and-economy/2012/08/brief-history-birth-urban-planning/2365/ |archive-date=August 25, 2012 |access-date=August 24, 2012 |work=The Atlantic Cities |publisher=[[Atlantic Media Company]]}}</ref> numerous U.S. States created racial zoning laws; however such laws were ruled out in 1917 when the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that such laws interfered with the property rights of owners (''[[Buchanan v. Warley]]'').<ref>{{cite web |title=Stetson Kennedy Books |url=http://www.stetsonkennedy.com/jim_crow_guide/chapter6_1.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070928051526/http://www.stetsonkennedy.com/jim_crow_guide/chapter6_1.htm |archive-date=September 28, 2007 |access-date=October 19, 2007}}</ref> There were repeated attempts by various states, municipalities, and individuals since then to create zoning and housing laws based on race, however, such laws eventually were overturned by the courts. The legality of all discrimination in housing, by public or private entities, was ended by the [[Civil Rights Act of 1968|Fair Housing Act]] (Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968).<ref>[http://www.hum.wa.gov/FairHousing/History.htm Washington State Human Rights Commission<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070416234458/http://www.hum.wa.gov/FairHousing/History.htm|date=April 16, 2007}}</ref>  Despite such rulings, there is widespread evidence that zoning laws are still used for the purpose of racial segregation.<ref>{{cite web |title=Zoning promotes racism and sprawl |url=https://www.epi.org/publication/the-color-of-law-a-forgotten-history-of-how-our-government-segregated-america/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170125151826/https://www.epi.org/publication/the-color-of-law-a-forgotten-history-of-how-our-government-segregated-america/ |archive-date=2017-01-25}}</ref>  In the wake of the Fair Housing Act, localities increasingly used purportedly non-racial zoning laws to keep non-whites out of white neighborhoods.<ref name=":22"/> Localities prohibited duplexes, small homes, and multi-family buildings, which were more likely to be occupied by racial minorities, recent immigrants, and poor households.<ref name=":22"/> The outcome of segregating different areas of cities and regions by uses or characteristics of uses has resulted in increased racial and economic segregation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shertzer |first1=Allison |last2=Twinam |first2=Tate |last3=Walsh |first3=Randall P. |date=2022-05-01 |title=Zoning and segregation in urban economic history |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0166046221000120 |journal=Regional Science and Urban Economics |series=Urban Economics and History |volume=94 |article-number=103652 |doi=10.1016/j.regsciurbeco.2021.103652 |issn=0166-0462|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== Health and environmental concerns ===

A study of [[greenhouse gas emissions]] found that strict zoning laws "seem to be pushing new development towards places with higher emissions."<ref name="JUE_2010-052">{{cite journal |last1=Glaeser |first1=Edward |author-link1=Edward Glaeser |last2=Kahn |first2=Matthew |author-link2=Matthew Kahn |date=2010-05-01 |title=The greenness of cities: Carbon dioxide emissions and urban development |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0094119009001028 |journal=Journal of Urban Economics |volume=67 |issue=3 |pages=404–418 |doi=10.1016/j.jue.2009.11.006 |access-date=2020-04-23 |quote=We find that the lowest emissions areas are generally in California and that the highest emissions areas are in Texas and Oklahoma. There is a strong negative association between emissions and land use regulations. By restricting new development, the cleanest areas of the country would seem to be pushing new development towards places with higher emissions.|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Public officials have argued that, while zoning laws have historically had a negative impact on the environment through their promotion of low-density sprawl and car-centric development, zoning can be used to preserve [[Open space reserve|open space]] and as a tool to promote the usage of [[renewable energy]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Watson |first=Siobhan |chapter=Zoning to Adapt |date=2019-11-06 |title=Zoning |pages=128–147 |publisher=Routledge |doi=10.4324/9780429489228-7 |isbn=978-0-429-48922-8 |s2cid=210261274 }}</ref> These forms of development, by fostering [[car dependency]], may also contribute to a rise in [[sedentary lifestyle]]s and [[obesity]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Morabia |first1=Alfredo |last2=Mirer |first2=Franklin E. |last3=Amstislavski |first3=Tashia M. |last4=Eisl |first4=Holger M. |last5=Werbe-Fuentes |first5=Jordan |last6=Gorczynski |first6=John |last7=Goranson |first7=Chris |last8=Wolff |first8=Mary S. |last9=Markowitz |first9=Steven B. |date=December 2010 |title=Potential Health Impact of Switching From Car to Public Transportation When Commuting to Work |journal=American Journal of Public Health |volume=100 |issue=12 |pages=2388–2391 |doi=10.2105/ajph.2009.190132 |pmid=20966368 |pmc=2978174 |issn=0090-0036}}</ref>
